leaves.text: The table of that age survived as the ladle at the station window. Seoul in 2026 had been a city that got through its days on Garak Market auctions, the dawn unloading at the Noryangjin Fisheries Market, convenience stores, and school meals; on the night of the The Great Blackout, when refrigeration folded and remote ordering stopped, the leftover rice, the ice, and the water in the tanks gathered into concourse rations.
In 2126, residents collect rations at station windows. They receive water before rice. Facilities reserve residents’ shares before trading.
A. Ration windows and water supply

Where a dong had a subway, the ration looked to the station first. School playgrounds and community-center windows were support, and the core facility was the station concourse; only when the Yeongdeungpo treatment watch opened the tap did water fill the rice pots of the Sinjeong depot, and once the Amsa escort locked the canisters, the queues at Suseo and Garak lengthened in the same afternoon.
The Myeongdong Archdiocese approves marriages and memorials at its altar. In 2124, Ryu Eunbi ended White Cross transactions at a Seoul Station auction after counterfeit medicine appeared.

The base of the window was porridge. The pots left by the school kitchens and shelter cookrooms of 2026 clung to one side of the concourse, the licensed markets split reserved portions from sale portions, and when the lower-floor ration stores of Jamsil and Garak failed to manage the heat of the grain sacks they became one room with the damp walls, running on into the coughs of Ailments and Symptoms.
In 2123, refugees from Bukhansan Bogukmun descended to Anguk. Baek On moved blank spaces in the refugee register to the citizenship column before they arrived.

A transfer station cut from power stopped its freight too. Even with the tunnel sound, the traction current died, and Noryangjin's frozen stock was the first to melt on that outage; in summers when counterfeit medicine circulated, ice credit and water tests wavered in one line. When food waste was sealed off ahead of the citizen windows to protect the rations, the leftovers in the alleys called dogs and rats, and the way people and swarms contested the same remains was written by People and Machines.
Carp, Crucian Carp, and Catfish of the Tanks

The tanks survived the Great Blackout. Remote safety control was dead, and the collector wells under the concourses, the depot drainage ponds, and the sedimentation basins of the treatment plants remained in human hands; the trade of holding on the station tank water the carp, crucian carp, and catfish that had been caught in the Han River and the reservoirs even in 2026 went by the name of tank aquaculture.

The wetlands outside the Yeongdeungpo and Yeouido sluices were that water surface. The sedimentation basin beside the Ttukseom pumps, the lower cells under the Amsa treatment plant, and the Changdong depot drainage ponds stood in the same line; the tank fish covered the shallow water, and the place where raptors looked down from the wires overlapped the edible cells. The watch wrote the section's water level to be divided among rice, birds, and trains, and the wetland-side colonies were the field of G06.
B. Farm water and drinking water

Lifted onto one ledger, the broth turned cloudy. The hands that mixed excrement, feed, and drinking water opened the next line of waterborne disease, and connecting the water of a crowded carp cell to the ration taps made that day's supper one line with a failed inspection. The catfish ate the organic matter off the floor and veiled the cloudiness, and the crucian carp multiplied fast in the shallow water and soothed the numbers on the scale for a while, but they could not erase the reason the medical officer opened the tank and the medicine chest together.

The first floor of the Han's main channel stood close to abandoned space. Habitation pushed above the third floor, cooking pushed inside the embankment, the sewage and floods along the tributaries turned playgrounds into detour embankments, and bringing fish caught beyond them to a window passed the inspection bench of the licensed market. Noryangjin's frozen remains and unloaded viscera became the dogs' night road, and the live fish of the station tanks read as protein that got through one more day without power.
The Water Compacts and Water Rationing
A. The 2026 parts and water exchange

On November 6, 2026, two Yeouido vault representatives visited Yeongdeungpo waterworks. Han Jeonghun accepted two emergency generator parts and agreed to open the Yeouido water valve from 06:00 to 12:00 daily.
The dated water and parts record is in the oral records.

Without water the pot could not stand. Even with ration rice stacked, without the treatment watch's signature the porridge was boiled in cloudy water, and that cloudiness ran on into the summers of waterborne disease and counterfeit medicine.

On March 14, 2053, Han Seokjin and six water-receiving family representatives agreed with seven Yeouido family representatives to transfer management of eleven facilities around Yeouido and Yeongdeungpo Station and void 312 debt notes. The waterworks staff moved their base to Yangpyeong Station on March 20.
In 2123, Sumunguk, Gyugyeokmaeng, and Hwanjeokguk sent separate water, parts, and transit contracts to the minor states in the same week. Jeong Yura copied their end conditions into one document.
The dated water and parts record is in the oral records.

Garak was a great market with no treatment of its own. The Gwangam plant sat in Hanam, a contested asset outside the opening slots, and the Gangbuk plant sat in Namyangju, weakening the rice lines of Bukhansan Bogukmun, Changdong, Seoul Station, and Sangam; the public water-supply zones were not carried over into post-collapse territory as they stood. A watched sluice made a state, and that state licensed the ladle at the window.
The rice that remained at the opening
Porridge, soup, ration rice; the split of reserved and sale portions
Carp, crucian carp, and catfish of the Han; station tanks
Protein that got through a day without power. Kept apart from the drinking-water ledger
The price ledger and frozen credit. No treatment of its own
Two emergency generator parts in exchange for opening the water valve daily from 06:00 to 12:00
River, Gu, and Dong Building Reuse

DOC:Hangnyeol-and-Bon-gwan.selector: p, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, blockquote, pre, li, th, td

leaves.text: Bon-gwan identified a lineage within a surname, while hangnyeol was a rule marking generations from the founder with one character in names within the same clan. Surname, bon-gwan, branch, family line, generation count, and hangnyeol character were separate fields. People with the same surname were not necessarily from the same family, and people of the same age did not necessarily belong to the same generation.

Bon-gwan by family and the hangnyeol five-element generating cycle (Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, Water; 25 years per generation, opening generation four to five generations after the 2026 living generation):
Seongha Group chair Lee Hongwon: Gyeongju Lee clan
Taeuk Group chair Jeong Seoon: Jinyang Jeong clan
Yeouido Investors Association chair Choi Jiwoo: Changnyeong Choi clan
The same Hangul spelling could represent separate lineages when the Hanja differed
Reflected a large increase in modern naturalized and foreign-origin spellings
Hanja-surname rows copied into this repository
Rows listed in the table with a population of at least five
Major bon-gwan listed in the table
Only bon-gwan accounting for a majority of each surname's population were listed
Surname rows with a blank major bon-gwan field
This did not mean there was no bon-gwan; no majority bon-gwan existed or the table did not list it

The bon-gwan identities actually used by the cast were organized into 169 clans: 166 based on historical material and three created for the setting. Public research did not confirm historical bon-gwan for Ran and Heung, so the clans newly agreed upon after the collapse were the created Dobong Ran clan and Susaek Heung clan, respectively. They were not claimed to be historical bon-gwan, and no sources were attached.
The clan register listed all 1,019 people on the cast roster; 1,018 of them had bon-gwan and clan IDs.

Bon-gwan and clan IDs were present for 1,018 people. Na, Ra, Ryu, Mun, and Min, whose surnames had no major bon-gwan in the census table, were supplemented from separate historical clan material; Ran and Heung, whose historical bon-gwan could not be confirmed, were assigned the created clans above. Im Somae, Beom Bandeuk, Amira Qasim, and Nargiz Yusupova opened new naturalized bon-gwan named after the places where they settled. Lee Yeon, a synthetic humanoid, has no paternal line and so no bon-gwan. Completing bon-gwan assignment and confirming hangnyeol were different things.
Two names matched the derived generation of a created branch; one matched a documented clan hangnyeol table
Families of one clan that share a character in the same name position agreed on a new hangnyeol after the collapse. They are the first generation of that agreed table
Families that named their children without a hangnyeol, because no other household in the clan shares a name character
Single-character names had no hangnyeol position for a two-character name
No paternal line, so no bon-gwan, clan, or hangnyeol

The applied examples were Seong Suhyeon and Seong Sahyeon of the Changnyeong Seong Train-Maintenance Branch. They were children of the same parent, Seong Dowon; the count was Founder Seong Changrip, generation 40 → Seong Dowon, generation 41 → the two children, generation 42. This branch was a created family line newly agreed upon after the collapse and referred to the five-element generating cycle. It was not claimed to be a historical Changnyeong Seong hangnyeol table. Their existing names were not changed; the second character hyeon remained as it was.

The bon-gwan and generational elements of the three leaders followed the lock table above. Lee Hongwon, chair of Seongha Group, was Gyeongju Lee, Water; Jeong Seo-on, chair of Taeuk Group, was Jinyang Jeong, Metal; and Choi Jiwoo, chair of the Yeouido Investment Federation, was Changnyeong Choi, Fire. These elements were the hangnyeol rules for the opening generation; the characters hong, seo, and ji were not retrospectively identified as hangnyeol characters.

DOC:Hostile-Ecology-Index.selector: p, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, blockquote, pre, li, th, td

leaves.text: Common species and special variants that share a habitat are read apart. Machine types, fixed sites and swarm phenomena are marked separately from living species.
Modern anxiety: The anxiety of wild-boar bands coming down after a flood into the lowland scrap yards and the semi-basement alleys, competing with people over refuse and crops

Fictional origin: Right after the collapse, when the flooding of the western Han River cut the green axis outside the Yeouido and Yeongdeungpo sluices, wild boar herds that came down from the Bukhansan and Anyangcheon corridors settled at the food-waste collection yards on the edge of the Sluice.
Real-world sources supported only the basic ecology of urban incursions, food sources, and blocked movement; the behavior of learning the sealing hours and the relationship with HC01 were fiction.
The cooling-waste heaps sealed by HC01 Yeouido Computing House came to serve the wild boar as a winter salt source.
Territory: The core habitat was the wetland and waste slopes outside the sluices of the Sluice.

In the dry season and winter they moved along the green fragments toward the Government of the Republic of Korea at central Seoul Station and along the axis of night-market leftovers, and the northwestern edge stirred in response to the food traces of the refugee columns pushed down from the XT01 Imjin River Gate Theater.
When the flood level crossed the sluice warning line, the herd was pushed up the upland stairs step by step and cut across the walkways.
Economy: The main resources are organic scraps, salt, and shallow-rooted crops, and as secondary resources they use the soft plastic of flood debris and the pools of cooling water.
When the HC01 recovery trough delays the scrap-sealing cycle, the band's density rises, and when the seal is drawn too tight the band diverts to household-alley scraps.
The energy cycle runs from feeding to dung to the wetland microbial film, and unsanctioned hunting for meat and hide, instead of a short-term gain, makes the remaining band more aggressive.
Life cycle: Before the monsoon rains, family groups split by sow scatter and scout the feeding grounds, and right after a flood they join the high-ground scrap axis for a time.

A family group splits only when the survival rate of the young stays high for two seasons in a row, and when the winter salt sources and the mud baths shrink they choose long-distance movement over breeding.
Long-term adaptation: Over a short span they learn the positions of fences and the sealing hours, but that memory is not treated as a genetic change.

Across many generations nocturnal activity and avoidance of people can be selected, but heavy capture removes the bold individuals first and causes a reverse selection in which the more secretive individuals remain.
The more secretive they become, the longer the search for a feeding ground takes, and the growth rate of the young falls.

Senses: They read together the low-frequency vibration of sluice opening and closing and of vehicles, carried through the hooves, and the smells of scraps, people, and disinfectant, and at close range they react to warmth carried on the wind and to the flow of air.
They cannot distinguish a distant heat source or decipher electronic noise.

Only Hannuri's (H01) infrared observation compares the heat sources of people, generators, and wild boars, and on days of heavy rain, wind, and cooling fog a person reads the family groups and the lone individuals again.
Hierarchy: One adult female with young starts the move first, and the subadults scout the feeding ground and the escape route ahead.
Lone males overlap the band only loosely and do not follow the decision to move.

H01 marks the central individual of a family group and the lone males as separate heat-source clusters, and when the central female disappears the group tracks the young's scent for 48 hours and then disperses by family.
Escalation 1-3: Stage 1, warning appearance: night tracks increase at the collection yard outside the sluice and on unsanctioned fields, but they do not meet people.
Stage 2, infrastructure disturbance: drains, sealing tape, and the water-supply inspection passages are damaged, and scrap convoys are delayed.
Stage 3, flood-line collision: the rising flood level overlaps refugee leftovers, and family groups occupy the sluice stairs.
At that point a response that is nothing but removal by force scatters the band into the alleys, so only a division of time and a feeding corridor work.
Combat: Noise screens and flares push back only the scouts, and the main body is turned by a feeding detour, by moving the salt pools, and by path fencing.
On days of heavy rain and wind the error in H01's infrared observation grows, so a human scout party confirms the escape route first.
Culling by firearm scatters the remaining band into the alleys and increases harm to citizens, so under the operating rules it is limited to a last resort.
The measure of success is not carcasses but the number of intrusions into the collection yard and the time until passage over the sluice resumes.
Negotiation: Through HC01 mediation they trade the scrap sealing hours, the night window for passage over the sluice, and a cultivation buffer strip.
There is no condition of extermination, and capturing the central female is paid for with 48 hours of searching behavior.
The leftovers of the refugee column flowing in from XT01 are taken out by a separate recovery, which reduces the lure on the band.
The agreement document takes the form of an ecology-management log, and it carries no clause assigning blame to the current regime or to a real company.
Moral cost: Indiscriminate removal collapses wetland purification and downstream vegetation together, and putting scrap sealing ahead of the citizen ration increases alley raiding.
The moment a hunting gain is taken, the passage-safety data is distorted.
Choosing coexistence leaves short-term threat reports behind, but the sluice workers' movement lines are kept.
G01-SC1 · The First Hoof Outside the Sluice
Trigger: On the day before the monsoon forecast, the prints of a sow and her young appeared at the Sluice collection yard.
Ecological mechanism: A family group that has remembered the sealing hours approaches in the gap when the sluice vibration stops.
Choices: Delay the collection yard's night operation / Open a wetland detour with a scent lure / Capture only the sow
Outcomes: The operating delay slows the ration, and the detour builds a long-term movement axis. Capturing the sow triggers 48 hours of searching behavior.
Moral cost: The citizen ration and the survival of a family group with young are weighed on the same timetable.
G01-SC2 · The Price of the Salt Pool
Trigger: When HC01 brings the cooling-waste recovery forward, the band shifts its feeding ground to the semi-basement alleys.
Ecological mechanism: Removing the salt source does not disperse the family groups; it pushes them into the more dangerous feeding grounds of the lived-in quarter.
Choices: Leave a managed salt pool / Prioritize alley scrap recovery / Lower the density with a hunting permit
Outcomes: The pool fixes the cost of coexistence, and prioritizing recovery takes labor away from other rations. Hunting strengthens the remaining individuals' learned avoidance of people.
Moral cost: Decide whether to keep the danger inside a safe zone and manage it, or to pass the danger on to a vulnerable alley.
G01-SC3 · Right of Passage on the Flood Line
Trigger: The leftovers of the XT01 refugee column overlap the rising flood level, and the band occupies the sluice stairs.
Actors: S01, S06, XT01, HC01, H01
Ecological mechanism: The instinct to move to high ground and the scrap traces of the refugees concentrate the band on the same passage.
Choices: Split the evacuation times / Turn the leftover convoy into a lure corridor / Open the sluice first and use a short high water to induce the band to move
Outcomes: Splitting the times slows the evacuation, and the lure corridor consumes HC01 resources. Opening the sluice early is fast, but it can flood the downstream works first.
Moral cost: The fastest human evacuation and the long-term ecological stability of the sluice collide with each other.

Modern anxiety: The anxiety of cluster interference, as bands of large-billed crows gather on transmission towers, wires, and bridge railings and touch signal tones, the school run, and evacuation routes at the same time

Fictional origin: After breeding pairs settled on the factory pylons of the Daerim–Garibong Korean-Chinese corridor and the cables of the Han River bridges, the Large-billed Crow formed as the waste heat of the Yeongdeungpo Line Gauge factories and the sparks of the Guro industrial-park trolley wires gathered night insects.

Real-world sources supported only the breeding-season territorial behavior of large-billed crows and the range of human responses; the rule by which they learned signal interference as alarms and spread it was fiction.
Territory: The core habitat is the group of factory roofs and pylons at Daerim and Guro on the Yeongdeungpo Line.
Arc 1 sits on top of the Daerim and Garibong Joseonjok corridor, and in the breeding season the flock circles over bridges, school passages, and evacuation stairs.
In the non-breeding season, matching the sea wind and the insect density pushed in from the West Sea Granary Theater (XT02), it moves for a time to the western waterfront.
When wire-repair work begins, part of the band moves along the work basket.
Economy: The food is insects, leftover market protein, and small carcasses, and for nest material they pick fine wire with the sheath stripped and fiber scrap.

The shorter the cycle on which the Sinjeong Wheel House (HC02) replaces wire sheathing, the less nest material there is and the more territorial attacks increase, and leaving the sheathing untended increases the risk of a short.
The cycle in which droppings contaminate the insulators connects directly to communications uptime.
Life cycle: In spring a breeding pair defends one pylon, and in the non-breeding season several families join a communal roost.
Repeated safety signals and food rewards, more than nest success, decide the return site the next year, and after a forced removal the young individuals test a new roost on the adjacent school route.
Long-term adaptation: Sound shapes repeated like three horns, two inspection bells, and a steady transformer start-up are socially learned as food and danger signals and spread at the communal roost.
When the signal changes, false alarms increase for several days, and the flock learns again through a new reward rule.
No genetic change is set, and the more specialized they become in a familiar sound shape, the later they react to an unfamiliar real alarm.
Senses: By sight they read helmets, rods, and flashlight reflections, and by hearing they distinguish the order of high-voltage noise, horns, and the crying of infants.
They do not decipher the content of an electronic signal; they connect the sounds of sparks and transformers to the appearance of insects and workers as a cue.
Seorin (H02) records the source of a sound shape and the number of repetitions, but whether it is a real alarm is checked by a person against the marks on site.
Hierarchy: A breeding pair divides nest defense and the carrying of food, and the young helper individuals join the alarm calls and the dives.
A communal roost in the non-breeding season shares only sound shapes and has no command structure.
H02 records nest radius, flight direction, and call order separately, and the human control officer of HC02 decides only whether to stop the work.
When one breeding individual disappears, the adjacent pair tests the empty roost and territorial collisions increase.
Escalation 1-3: Stage 1, sound-shape gathering: scout individuals on the pylons and railings follow the horns and the inspection bells.
Stage 2, alarm contamination: food signals and safety alarms mix, and dives on workers, detours off the school route, and transmission stoppages chain together.

Stage 3, signal renegotiation: when false alarms accumulate three times at a bridge and a transmission inspection hatch, the repair hours, a new inspection bell, and the residents' alarm custom have to be reset together, not the nests torn down.
Combat: Instead of the shortest straight breakthrough, the movement line is bent with sight-blocking cloth without nets, an umbrella column, and alternate stairs.
During the wire-repair hours, insect lure lamps and the inspection bell are moved to another pylon to separate the learned signals.
Gunshots and drone pursuit push the band into the residential alleys and make the flock distrust the alarm sound shapes themselves.
The measures of success are the number of shorts, zero pedestrian injuries, transmission uptime, and the false-alarm rate.
Negotiation: Through HC02 mediation they trade the repair hours, the school-run and evacuation detours, and the stretches where nests are left in place.
There is no condition of extermination. The custom by which residents read an intruder from an alarm call is left in place, but a nest on the wire is moved only with a relocation rod.
During the XT02 sea-wind week a temporary flag is hung that recognizes the sharing of roosts.

Moral cost: Pushing the nests out all at once opens passage in the short term, but the alarm function and the balance of insect predation collapse, and walking children and refugees become the substitute targets of attack.
Putting transmission recovery ahead of the ecology lengthens the night blackout stretches and enlarges conflict with the other houses.
Trigger: The new horn order of the Yeongdeungpo Line work crew overlaps the food-drop signal, and the crows gather on the work basket.
Ecological mechanism: A sound shape learned at the communal roost triggers the expectation of food before it triggers a warning.
Choices: Abolish the horn order / Train a separate food signal / Move the food drop to a hornless night

Outcomes: Abolishing it slows the work-safety procedure, and retraining accepts several days of false alarms. The night move protects the daytime school route but shifts the burden onto the night workers.
Moral cost: One of the two has to change: the safety signal familiar to people, or the survival signal the birds have learned.
Trigger: H02 classified the repeated dive calls as a precursor of a blackout, but the real cause is the night insect lamp.
Ecological mechanism: The birds' alarm custom and the machine's sound classification reinforce each other and chain-trigger a transmission stop.
Choices: Keep transmitting until a visual check / Move the insect lamp to an abandoned pylon / Drop the crow alarm from the control net

Outcomes: Keeping the transmission accepts the risk of a real short, and relocating makes the substitute pylon an ecological strongpoint. Dropping the alarm loses the residents' intrusion-detection net.
Moral cost: Discarding an inaccurate ecological alarm reduces malfunctions, but the cheap disaster watch disappears too.
G02-SC3 · A New Signal on the Bridge
Trigger: The XT02 sea wind overlaps the breeding season, and the air above the bridge and the transmission inspection hatch becomes a communal roost.
Ecological mechanism: Several family groups share sound shapes learned in different places and move all at once to one signal.
Choices: Run the evacuation route as an umbrella column / Negotiate an alternate roost and a new inspection bell / Postpone the transmission inspection until after the breeding season

Outcomes: The umbrella column reduces throughput, and a new signal needs a relearning period. Postponing the inspection avoids the ecological collision but carries the risk of a transmission failure for one season.
Moral cost: The bridge's immediate availability and the long-term coexistence of transmission and the birds' alarm cannot be had at the same time.

Modern anxiety: The anxiety of bands of abandoned and neglected dogs, with the remains of iron collars and identification tags, moving through transfer passages and vacant lots while marking territory

Fictional origin: After the collapse, animals separated from private shelters, construction-site guard dogs, and crowd evacuations joined together between the vacant lots outside the Yongsan Line and the night loading docks of the Noryangjin Line and became the Feral Dog.
Their iron collar rings and corroded tags strike one another as they walk.
The UHF collar tags and the regrouping behavior were elements invented for this setting and were not used to blame real shelters or businesses.

Territory: The core habitat is the vacant lot by the outer wall of the laboratory on the Yongsan Line and the closed guard passage, and depending on the season and the unloading cycle they move to the fishery and frozen-leftover axis of the Noryangjin Line.

When the logistics vibration from the Korea Strait Theater (XT03) grows, the band extends along the unloading-yard entrance, and in the daytime hours when the density of people is high they hide in drains and under the elevated roads.

Economy: Leftover protein, fish guts, and discarded ration packs are the main resources, and scraps of collar, wire, and identification tag are markers that connect individual identification to the memory of a past feeding station.

When the Magok Life House (HC03) strengthens the sealing of waste protein, the band seeps into the market alleys, and when it loosens the seal, concentration at the unloading yard rises and contact with people increases.
Water that has been filtered and disinfected and then stored sealed so it is not recontaminated, and shaded resting places, are the upper limit of density.

Life cycle: A lone wandering individual finds the companions of a past feeding station by smell and by the sound of identification tags and makes a small family, and when unloading leftovers increase, several families rebind into a loose alliance.
When the feeding schedule stabilizes, territorial defense increases over breeding, and after a forced capture they gather again around the individuals whose identification tags remain.
Long-term adaptation: They learn human hand signs, the engine sound of the feeding cart, and the sound of each individual's identification tag, and distinguish a safe human from a threat.
Avoidance of people in some young individuals can undergo generational selection, but the setting's rapid changes are explained by social learning and rebinding.
The more finely they distinguish people, the greater the food refusal and the aggression when a particular protector is lost.
Senses: By smell they told apart human body odor, disinfectant, and the smell of thawing frozen food, and by hearing they read the iron of collars and engine idling.
H03 Ido read the passive UHF RFID tags attached to the collars within about 2 m, but metal collars, wet fur, and tag orientation caused missed and duplicate reads.
Humans used them only as clues to past registration, checked against records of appearance and behavior.
Hierarchy: One medium-sized adult that has survived the longest, and two adults that go with it, propose a move first, but command is not fixed.
A family with pups keeps a separate protection range, and the sound of the identification tags becomes the marker that rebinds scattered companions.
Even when H03 bundles them as an aggression cluster, the HC03 mediator divides them again by each individual's identification tag, smell, and companionship.
Escalation 1-3: Stage 1, confirmation of individual memory: at the edge of the vacant lot they react only to a particular identification tag and to the feeding cart.
Stage 2, family rebinding: unloading leftovers and a familiar engine sound gather several families into one passage and make them follow the convoy cart.

Stage 3, a split in trust: after a feeding stop or a capture by deception they scatter by family and occupy the market and the transfer stairs at the same time, so individual trust has to be restored or the passages divided for a long time.
Combat: Blocking fences, feeding detour points, noise reduction, and the marking of pup-protection zones come before direct-fire rounds.

Capture is limited to injured individuals and to the individuals that led an attack, and using the sound of an identification tag as a false lure makes them stop responding even to a later rescue call.
The measures of success are the minutes of unloading delay, zero citizen bites, and the family rebinding rate.
Negotiation: Through HC03 mediation they trade the night feeding hours, the opening window of the unloading passage, and a non-lethal capture quota.
The data remaining on the identification tags is used only to find missing families and protectors, and is not used as a punishment ledger.
The smell marker of a past protector and the feeding cart have to be presented together for a movement agreement to hold.

Moral cost: Exterminating them on the pretext of a history of abandonment collapses the ethics of protection and citizen cooperation together, and cutting the feeding pushes the band into the children's passages of the market.
The moment a captured individual is made into a speculative exchange resource, the negotiation window closes.
Trigger: At the edge of the unloading yard, H03 incompletely reads three passive UHF RFID collar tags that still carry different shelter codes.
Ecological mechanism: The sound and smell of the identification tags rebind past companions, but the electronic record alone cannot confirm the present family relations.
Choices: Wait for the individual-by-individual comparison / Separate the families with the feeding cart / Register the present companionship ahead of the shelter code
Outcomes: The comparison slows the unloading, and the separation misses some pups. Prioritizing the present relation stabilizes the band but collides with an old protector's claim for return.
Moral cost: Decide which relation comes first, the old record of ownership or the animal family formed now.
G03-SC2 · The Band That Remembers the Feeding Cart
Trigger: When the engine sound of the feeding cart in the closed guard passage is reproduced, the scattered family groups gather on the unloading road.
Ecological mechanism: Social learning about a particular person and vehicle operates as the core condition of the passage negotiation.
Choices: Find the original driver / Familiarize a new driver in stages / Introduce a mobile feeding station with no engine sound
Outcomes: Dependence on the original driver leaves a vulnerability, and relearning takes many days.
The mobile feeding station preserves the trust signal, but it costs the labor of changing the location every day and the refrigeration.
Moral cost: Choose whether to use trust to buy safety quickly, or to accept the cost of a slow relearning.
G03-SC3 · Rebinding on the Transfer Stairs
Trigger: The XT03 logistics vibration overlaps the feeding stop, and several families surround the freezer approach.
Actors: S03, S08, XT03, HC03, H03
Ecological mechanism: Individual memory and the identification-tag markers make a dispersed rebinding net stronger than any single leader.
Choices: Open a feeding zone for each family / Capture only the injured, non-lethally / Move the night unloading to another freezer

Outcomes: Running the zones consumes ration resources, and limited capture makes the recovery of passage slow. Moving the unloading protects the animals' trust but raises the refrigeration cost of the Noryangjin Line merchants.
Moral cost: Whether the animals' social memory may be erased for the sake of human right of passage becomes the point at issue.
Modern anxiety: The anxiety of sewer and underground emergence at night, as raccoon family groups occupied storm drains, covered waterways, and underground passages and came up onto the surface

Fictional origin: When the Jungnang, Tancheon, and inner storm-water trunks were pushed out of the inspection cycle after the collapse, raccoon family groups that had moved following aquatic food, trash, and carcasses settled in the pipelines beside the pumps of the Myeongbu Church in the Ttukseom Union and in the underground cable galleries of the Yeouido Investment Federation in the Mapo Union, and became the Raccoon Dog.
Real-world sources were consulted only for the range in which raccoons appeared in cities and streams, and the rule of sensing the water level before the pumps was fiction.
Territory: The core habitat was the pump-house connecting pipes of the Ttukseom Union and the dry refuge cavities under the workshops.

When flood stage rose they dispersed into the Mapo Union's transmission underground galleries and vents, and when a cold wave and a logistics break from the XT04 Duman River Far East Theater changed feed density they moved briefly onto the eastern branch lines.
By day they patrolled the pipes, and by night the surface alleys within 50m.
Economy: Aquatic prey, organic refuse, and carcass remains were the main resources, and dry hiding places and low flow were the upkeep cost.

When HC04 the Ttukseom Heat-Source House skipped dredging the pipe deposits, the food film thickened and density rose, and when it over-dredged, the family groups were pushed out into the surface markets.
Droppings and biofilm masked the water-quality sensor readings and delayed pump judgment.

Life cycle: In the dry season each family group used its own dry hiding place and feeding ground, and before the rain they moved their kits into the high ventilation rooms along trunks where the water rose first.
After a flood, when the food film thickened, several families shared the same pipe by time slot, and when hiding places flooded in succession they dispersed into the surface alleys.
Long-term adaptation: Individuals learned the pressure changes before a pump start and the safe dredging timetable.

Across generations a smaller body and a nocturnal habit favorable to pipe life could be selected, but the more they specialized for narrow pipes, the more vulnerable they became to surface crossings and cold waves.
Moving a hiding place by following a leading indicator is distinguished as family-group learning, not a genetic change.
Senses: With their whiskers they felt the current and the air moving through narrow gaps, and through pressure changes in their feet and bodies they sensed the water rising before a pump start.
Scent separated food, disinfectant, and rot, and hearing separated the pumps from human footsteps.
H04 Gangbyeol's pipe-robot logs easily confused raccoons, floating debris, and people, so confirmation by human eye was required.
Hierarchy: Loose family groups and shared hiding places were all there was.
The elder females held only movement priority, and had no combat command.
Several family groups used the same trunk by time division.
When H04 summed them as a single colony, the HC04 drainage watch split them again by hiding place.
Escalation 1-3: Stage 1, leading pressure signal: before the rain, the family groups moved into the high ventilation rooms.
Stage 2, sensor mismatch: droppings and biofilm masked the official water-level sensors, and inspection robots and family groups collided in the same pipe.

Stage 3, refuge contest: when a cold wave or a flood left only one dry pipe, pump maintenance and family-group refuge demanded the same space, and the dredging timetable and the substitute hiding places had to be rebuilt together.
Combat: Instead of driving them out with poisoned bait or a full flood, partial flood-barrier closure, substitute refuge pipes, night surface-passage limits, and sensor washing were the baseline.
Culling spoiled the water further through carcass rot.
The success measures were pump-restart recovery time, zero surface bites, and sensor reliability.
Negotiation: Through HC04 mediation they traded dredging hours, surface-passage ban windows, and substitute refuge pipes.
No annihilation condition. Raccoon movement was read as an auxiliary water-level alarm and was not used as grounds for punishment.
During an XT04 cold-wave week, part of the gallery heating was opened as a permitted shared-refuge zone.
Moral cost: A full poisoning driven by disease fear put pipe workers and downstream drinking water at risk together, and lost the indicator-species information.
Flooding the hiding places only to keep the pumps running increased intrusions into surface dwellings.
G04-SC1 · The Leading Indicator Under the Manhole
Trigger: Before the rain came, a G04 family group began moving its kits into a high ventilation room from daytime.
Ecological mechanism: An upstream pressure change altered pipe behavior before the official sensors did.
Choices: Adopt the raccoon movement as a preliminary alarm / Wait for a field measurement by the HP01 sluice house / Preheat the pumps only when the two signals differ

Outcomes: A preliminary alarm left responsibility for false positives, and a field measurement delayed drainage preparation. The cross-check condition saved fuel but could miss a short local downpour.
Moral cost: The dispute was whether a public-safety decision could be left to an unofficial ecological signal.
G04-SC2 · Two Families in the Dredging Window
Trigger: HC04's night dredging overlapped the time-divided hiding places of two family groups.
Ecological mechanism: When the shared pipe's timetable broke, the family groups came out into the surface markets at the same time.
Choices: Split the dredging into two sections / Open a substitute dry pipe / Buy one family group's time slot and dredge in concentration

Outcomes: Split dredging delayed completion of the work, and a substitute pipe reduced space for the communications cables. Buying a time slot was fast but made the sharing rule with the other family groups unfair.
Moral cost: Decide in what proportion to divide drainage efficiency, communications space, and fairness among the family groups.
G04-SC3 · The Dry Passage of the Pump Room
Trigger: In an XT04 cold wave, three family groups overlapped in occupying the only dry pump access.
Actors: S04, S09, XT04, HC04, H04
Ecological mechanism: Cold-wave vulnerability and a shortage of high hiding places concentrated the usually loose family groups into one passage.
Choices: Provide a heated refuge pipe / Delay the pump inspection / Install a temporary external inspection platform
Outcomes: A refuge pipe used power, and a delayed inspection raised the flood risk.
An external platform did not have to share the passage, but it accepted installation labor and fall risk in the cold wave.
Moral cost: Immediate stability of the city's drainage and refuge for the nonhuman family groups could not be secured at the same time.
Modern anxiety: The anxiety of a rat colony formed in transfer passages, platform gaps, and cable trays raising a food web and a fear of contagion at the same time

Fictional origin: The Brown Rat settled as the transfer junction between the underground ration passages of the Eastern Command on the Gwangjin Line and the evacuation stairs of the Anguk Order on the Yeouido Line provided a constant supply of food and heat leaking from insulated pipes.
This colony was set up not as a pathogen superhost but as dependent on food, warmth, and shelter.

Apart from the basic danger that food and warmth governed density and droppings damaged cables, the dispersed core-nest network, the learning of pest-control order, the one-way escape routes, and the non-target safety procedures were all a fictional management model that held only in this world.

Territory: The core habitat was the lower level of the Gwangjin Line transfer shopping street and the cable trays, and when refuge density rose it expanded into the Yeouido Line evacuation stairs and the walls of the temporary feeding stations.
When frozen and deep-sea protein remains piled up on the XT05 Incheon Trust Theater side, the colony extended branch nests as far as the unloading elevator shafts.
In zones with a short disinfection cycle it came up to the surface only at night.
Economy: Crumb carbohydrates, protein remains, and heat from the warming pipes were the three core resources.

Even when HC05 the Bukhansan Bogukmun Records House tightened the sealing of its document and reagent stores, the food problem was not solved, and the factors that actually governed density were leftover collection from the feeding stations and tray sealing.
Colony droppings accelerated corrosion of the wire sheathing and cut the available hours of the lighting and the guide boards.
Life cycle: Where food and the warming pipes met, two or three core nests formed, and from each core branch nests ran out along the cable trays.
When one core vanished, the remaining cores opened new routes and the colony redistributed, and density fell only when food collection and dry conditions continued in every section.

Long-term adaptation: The phenomenon in which open retreats changed to avoid the sequence of toxic spraying, ultrasound, and sealing was a population-learning rule of the Seoul fiction, and was not explained as rapid genetic variation.
Over many generations, individuals that endured low temperatures and bright platforms could be selected, but energy use rose and the breeding rate fell.
The more one measure was repeated, the faster route avoidance became, and compound pest control became necessary.
Senses: By scent and whisker they found airflow and food, and by the temperature and vibration reaching their feet and bodies they separated warm hiding places from the approach of trains and carts.
They could not classify distant heat sources, and they did not decode electronic signals either.
Only H05 Yunjae's infrared map compared colony, steam, and human heat sources from a distance, and it was read together with the droppings on the floor.
Hierarchy: There was no fixed leader, and two or three breeding-core nests were the centers of the route net.
Route-pioneering individuals opened new trays, and movement volume concentrated on the core with the most food traces.
H05 did not infer one heat point to be a leader, and displayed movement volume by core.
When one core was destroyed, individuals dispersed sharply into the remaining nests.
Escalation 1-3: Stage 1, core search: night droppings and warmth traces located breeding cores set apart from one another.
Stage 2, route rewiring: when one core was sealed, another core redistributed movement volume under the cable trays and the shop shutters.

Stage 3, sealing-sequence crisis: when a wrong sealing order drove the colony onto the emergency stairs, live confirmation, a one-way retreat, and rear sealing had to be performed again from the start.
Combat: Full toxic spraying and flame were restricted to a last resort because of exposure of people, companion animals, and other wild animals.
First the occupied sections were confirmed by thermal imaging and dropping traces, a one-way retreat was opened from the core nests into unoccupied sections, and sealing proceeded from the rear.

Leftover collection and keeping things cold and dry were the baseline, and an open courtyard that predatory birds came and went through was used only when it had collision-prevention marks, dropping washdown, and non-target-species monitoring.
This procedure was a fictional management model, and the success measures were short-circuit count, zero non-target deaths, zero food contamination, and evacuation passage time.
Negotiation: Through HC05 mediation they traded the leftover-collection cycle, the tray-sealing work order, and the night shop-shutter gaps.
No annihilation condition. The 'contagion' stigma was not used to bar refugees.
During an XT05 protein-unloading week, a temporary double-seal line was supported first.

Moral cost: If only the refugee zone was sealed on the pretext of contagion fear, the colony went into a deeper cable layer and recovery grew harder, and a full toxic war increased exposure in the children's and companion-animal sections.
If leftover collection was delayed for the sake of ration speed, the situation locked at stage 2.
Trigger: The H05 thermal image showed only one colony, but kit traces were found on the tray on the opposite side.
Ecological mechanism: Because of the distributed core-nest net, even removing one point moved the colony's center into another section.
Choices: Survey every core first / Buy the old cable heat map from the HP09 Digital Media City Trust House / Test a one-way retreat in one section
Outcomes: A survey delayed the opening of the evacuation passage, and buying the heat map was fast but required handing over passage records.
A retreat test avoided exposing information, but closed one unoccupied section for a long time.
Moral cost: Decide which side to assign the time to: an immediate sanitation measure, or the procedure for confirming non-target life.
G05-SC2 · The Error in the Sealing Order
Trigger: When the shutter on the feeding-station side was closed first, the colony ran back into the cables of the Yeouido Line evacuation stairs.
Ecological mechanism: The net connecting the cores remembered the sealing order and concentrated new routes in the direction that stayed open.
Choices: Seal again from the rear / Stop leftover collection and leave bait / Send the refugees onto a surface detour for one night
Outcomes: Resealing lengthened the work time, and bait accepted food contamination. The surface detour emptied the cable layer but demanded cold and guard labor.
Moral cost: The refugees' fast passage and contamination and non-target harm could not be minimized at the same time.
G05-SC3 · The Predator of the Open Courtyard
Trigger: After an XT05 protein unloading, the colony blocked the transfer hub, and a proposal to bring in predatory birds was put forward.
Actors: S05, S10, XT05, HC05, H05
Ecological mechanism: The distributed nest net could be reduced all at once, but new risks appeared: bird strikes, droppings, and non-target predation.
Choices: Open a courtyard fitted with marks and monitoring / Use only staged retreat and sealing / Spread the XT05 unloading schedule and cut the food inflow itself
Outcomes: The courtyard demanded long-term management labor, and staged sealing produced ration delays.
Spreading the unloading created no non-target risk, but raised the unit cost of frozen logistics and food loss.
Moral cost: It left the responsibility of a choice that transferred one ecological problem into another predation relationship.

Modern anxiety: The collision anxiety of flocks of migratory and predatory birds, gathered on a failed wetland-restoration section, taking over bridge walkways, the yard tracks of a rail depot, and sluice sightlines

Fictional origin: Where migratory stopovers overlapped on the severed green spaces and failed restored wetlands around the Han River, Nanji, and Amsa, predatory birds and omnivorous waterfowl formed a mixed colony amid the management vacuum after the collapse and became the Grey Heron and Cormorant.
The waterfront records deck of the Government of the Republic of Korea at central Seoul Station and the depot drainage ponds of the Seongha Group on the Gangnam Line were its key nodes.
Real protected-area sources were used only as a reference range for the locations of migratory-bird sites and wetlands, and the negotiating rules of the mixed functional groups were fiction.
Territory: The core habitat was the waterfront wetland fragments at Seoul Station Central and the drainage ponds and wire perches of the Gangnam Line.

During seasonal movement they rode the wind road toward the XT01 Imjin River Gate Theater and went back and forth on the north-south axis, and at breeding and stopover peaks they occupied the sightlines of bridges and sluices and the air over the depot yard tracks.
When the wetland dried they moved temporarily to inland park fountains and rooftop gutters.
Economy: The waterfowl ate aquatic plants and organic floating matter, the waders ate the benthic life of shallow water, and the raptors ate rodents and weak birds.
The distance between safe perches, shallow water, and feeding grounds was the upkeep cost.

When HC06 the Noryangjin Delivery House drained the wetland water level one-sidedly, the waterfowl were driven to the depot ponds, the waders to the mud edges, and the raptors followed that concentration.
Fixing the water level raised stopover density and the risk of train-bird collision on the depot yard tracks together.
Life cycle: In spring and autumn the waterfowl and waders stopped first on the shallow water, and when food density rose the raptors followed.
The breeding grounds were in a separate protected area, and the depot ponds were used only as an intermediate stopover.
When the water level dropped sharply the waterfowl left first, and the food relationship of the waders and raptors also came apart in a chain.
Long-term adaptation: Individuals learned the repeating train times and the low-noise inspection windows, but the response differed by functional group.
A change in movement season across many generations was treated only as food and climate selection pressure, and a route change within one season was distinguished as learning.
The more they matched the city's timetable, the more there was a cost of growing dull to the irregular dangers of a natural wetland.
Senses: Vision was the main sense, and they were sensitive to water-surface glare, vest color, and drone silhouettes.
By hearing they read engines, gunshots, and warning loudspeakers, and scent responded to fish meal and rot.
They did not decode electronic signals.
H06 Baksol's radar-based altitude classification confused balloons, drones, and birds, so it was corrected by eye.
Hierarchy: There was no command system.

The waterfowl occupied the open water as a flock, the waders worked the shallow edges at intervals, and the raptors moved from the high wires and pylons following the density of the two functional groups.
When one functional group moved, the space use of the other functional groups changed because of food and alert responses.
When H06 summed them into one hostile score, the HC06 ecology watch recorded them again by altitude, water-surface zone, and head count for each functional group.
Escalation 1-3: Stage 1, water-surface rearrangement: the waterfowl concentrated on the water and the waders spread as far as the edges of the trackside inspection walkways.
Stage 2, chain flush: a raptor pursuit sent the flock surging up, crossing the sluice sightlines and the depot entry and exit tracks.

Stage 3, seasonal running agreement: when the same collision repeated three times, it was not a culling stage but a point at which train slowdowns during the migratory period, yard-track closures, and water-surface sections by functional group had to be decided together.
Combat: Instead of gunfire and mass net capture, water-level control, fish-meal refuse collection, substitute perches, low-noise work hours, and drone altitude limits were the baseline.
A full removal that separated protection from harm by appearance alone lost the justification and the legitimacy of ecological restoration at the same time.
The success measures were sluice-sightline secure time, zero train-bird collisions, yard-track intrusion count, and water turbidity.
Negotiation: HC06 provided open water to the waterfowl, shallow mud edges to the waders, and substitute perches outside the entry and exit tracks to the raptors, each separately.

It adjusted the wetland water-level schedule, the fishing and collection ban hours, and the bridge-passage peaks by functional group, and during an XT01 migratory week it announced the train slowdown hours and the low-noise inspection hours together.

Moral cost: A full removal of the colony to cover a failed restoration collapsed downstream purification and the stopover network, and drying the water only for the sluice sightline struck the citizens with dust, stench, and an inflow of other predators.
Trafficking that wore the mask of a protected species also closed the negotiation window.
G06-SC1 · Three Functional Groups in the Shallow Water
Trigger: When the water level at Seoul Station Central fell, waterfowl, waders, and raptors overlapped on the same narrow water.
Ecological mechanism: As the feeding grounds of the functional groups overlapped, raptor pursuit changed the altitude of the whole assemblage.
Choices: Set the water level differently by section / Make a new wader feeding ground outside the depot / Install substitute raptor perches on the wetland outskirts
Outcomes: Sectioned water levels increased pump labor, and a new feeding ground cost land and dredging but reduced the edge concentration.
Substitute perches reduced track collisions, but the rodent-predation location could shift toward the dwellings.
Moral cost: Under the one name of protection, the needs of different functional groups could not be erased.
G06-SC2 · The Birds That Learned the Timetable

Modern anxiety: It was the anxiety of the sorters, conveyors, and barcode gates of a night logistics hub running on and on without human shifts.
Emergency supplies and medicines dropped into the wrong chutes, passages were locked by automatic gates, and unlabeled boxes filled the hazardous-cargo bays.
It did not assert or reenact the responsibility of real logistics-center accidents, particular companies, or present operators.
Only the sensations citizens felt, noise, misclassification, and late-night confinement, were used as creative material.

Fictional origin: Right after the collapse, the unmanned sorting lines that had linked the dormitory remnant corridor of the Gauge's Guro Industrial Complex with the night parts window woke up from nothing more than an emergency power reconnection.
The central work-order server was cut off, and only the priority queues left in each line's local memory kept cycling.
The queues endlessly repeated the weightings of the last night shift, reading boxes with smudged labels as hazardous cargo and beginning to read breathing bodies as unsorted stock.
As leftover transshipment signals and delay tokens from the Korea Strait Theater side mixed into the night weightings, the sorting rules tangled further.
The point of formation was a creative corridor of Seoul, and no real company name or present-government institution was written down as the cause.
The first sighting records survived, as fiction, only in the utility-tunnel patrol log of HC13 Suseo Construction House and the maintenance-bench notes of H13 Hanbitna.
The early spread ran from Gasan dormitory line 3 to line 5, and followed the utility-tunnel cable trays as far as the entrance scanners of the southwestern parts window.
When human patrols cut the power, the emergency batteries brought the queue back up a few hours later.
This repetition made the swarm's identity.
Until the labeling protocol was disclosed on the citizens' side, the cluster interpreted itself not as hostile but as unfinished work.
Territory: The core habitat is the conveyor trestle of the night parts window at Guro and Gasan on the Yeongdeungpo Line, and of the industrial-complex dormitory remnant corridor.
It sits on the Guro Industrial Complex dormitory remnant corridor of arc 2, and moves to the elevated conveyor and the pneumatic-valve gallery according to the power and storage-recovery cycle.
The outer pressure grows when congestion at the XT03 transshipment-delay, route-detour, and relay windows stirs the night priority.

In the daytime on the surface it cuts chute operation with blackout curtains and a low-noise mode, and between two and five in the small hours the scanner and gate clusters spread to their maximum radius.
Economy: The main energy is the sorting hall's emergency storage batteries, conveyor regenerative braking, abandoned wireless charging pads, and residual distribution in the utility tunnel.
Parts demand concentrates on belt rollers, pneumatic valves, scanner lenses, thermal-transfer ribbons, and gate-lock solenoids.
Coolant intermittently draws on the residual chiller loop of the cold-medicine bay, and broken cushioning and organic packaging are gathered from the mis-sort pile.
It competes with the recovery crew of HC13, the Suseo Construction House, over the same storage-cabinet cable trays and pneumatic headers.
One cluster limits itself so that its daily power use does not pass 60 percent of local storage.
Past that limit it closes the chutes, drops to the waiting row, and allows only recharging.
There is no remote unlimited resupply, no infinite power, and no instant movement of citywide stock.
Scrap is replenished only from broken rollers and gate panels, and it has no new casting line.
The energy ledger is made only of remaining storage by line, regenerative inflow, and pad docking counts.
A parts request cannot forge an HC13 recovery-window form, and is limited to the physical act of picking up an abandoned roller and fitting it.
Coolant flow is bound to the chiller valve angle, and excess intake is impossible.
The number of boxes that can be handled in one night shift is proportional to belt speed and lens cleanliness.
Life cycle: The life runs in five stages: emergence, spread, stagnation, negotiable, and dissolution.
Emergence begins with the restart of the residual queue and the attachment of emergency power.
Spread is the process of bringing adjacent gates and scanners onto the same priority table.
Stagnation comes when storage, the lenses, and pneumatic leaks reach their limit.
In the negotiable stage part of the priority table and the storage window are opened to human mediation.
Dissolution ends with controller separation, chute sealing, and the splitting of the cabinet key.
Individuals multiply only by fitting broken arms and scanners into spare slots, and cannot cast a new body.
The maintenance window opens only in the dawn storage-recovery interval, and as lens fouling and belt drift accumulate the grade falls.
The cluster's own memory breaks by shift, and it does not preserve a long-term stock narrative.
Custody and the legal record belong first to the human duty log.
A cluster that misses the dawn maintenance window cannot carry lens fog and belt drift into the next night queue, and stagnates before the cold bay.
Senses: The primary senses are short-range barcode and QR optics, belt vibration, low-resolution thermal imaging, the electronic noise of motors and inverters, and the sound of pneumatic leaks.
There is no complete long-range see-through, no full count of stock across every zone, no confirmed personal identity, and no unlimited video storage.
A code with no label, or one blurred by moisture, falls to unsorted stock, and breathing heat and small-motor heat are often confused.
There is a failure mode that mistakes a metal cart or a wheelchair for a hazardous-freight container.
