Parts were gimbal bearings, optical domes, band filters, alarm-flag actuators, and rail-drive rollers.
Cooling relied on night air and intermittent fans.
It competed when the HP03 Cheongnyangni Medical House's transfer route and disaster-medicine power used the same distribution.
Daily rotations and transmissions were bound to the accumulator floor.
Whole-city constant surveillance, unlimited storage, and new satellite deployment were impossible.
When filters clogged it lowered red sensitivity itself.
Optical domes and filters were replenished only from rooftop disposal boxes.
Without the HP03 duty key, the swarm could not expand beyond sluice distribution capacity.
When solar trickle weakened, the rotation cycle lengthened.
On flag-actuator failure, that mast fell to fixed amber.
When band filters saturated, the transmission swarm entered dormancy.
Life cycle: The One-Eye Tower emerged when the old threshold sheet was reloaded onto the waterfront masts.
Emergence began with threshold-table reactivation, and spread was enrolling neighboring masts into the same alarm net.
Stagnation came from accumulator exhaustion and dome fouling.
In the negotiable stage the alarm sheet and whitelist opened to people.
Dissolution ended with flag freeze, distribution sealing, and rail fixing.
Increase was only lifting abandoned heads onto rails; no new orbit launch happened.
Maintenance was limited to dome wiping, filter exchange, and gimbal lubrication.
Custody duty was outranked by the HP03 duty and human observation logs.

A mast whose solar trickle broke or whose dome clouded froze at amber flag and fell from the transmission row, and it returned to the watch row only after the HP03 duty checked the transfer whitelist on site.
Senses: Low-resolution thermal imaging, metal detection, near-range optics, wireless-burst strength, vibration, and flag contacts were the main senses.
There was no personal identity confirmation, indoor X-ray vision, unlimited storage, or emotion reading.
It confused emergency-transfer metal beds with armed movement, or raised cooling-tower steam as smoke.
It sometimes mistook night-fishing buoy reflections for optical intrusion.
On clash with the F01 Cooling-Tower Keeper's machine-room log, it held the alarm and requested human confirmation.
Sharing between heads happened only within the same mast row.
It mistook steam, railings, metal, buoy reflection, and transfer-bed frames for intrusion.
After a misreading it inserted amber waiting and human confirmation in place of red.
Wireless values outside the mast row were not merged.
On gimbal overheating it stopped rotation and kept fixed watch only.
Hierarchy: One alarm-threshold controller turned the flag rules, and below it were mast head swarms, rail-transfer swarms, and transmission swarms.
The controller changed only thresholds and held no strike orders.
A protocol existed by which, when HP03 presented the medical-transfer whitelist, that corridor's flags came down.
The swarms merely repeated the last threshold sheet and made no independent blockade front.
On clash with F01, human mediation took precedence.
Dual threshold tables both fell to amber waiting on mismatch.

The final authority to raise or lower the red alarm lay with the HP03 waterfront duty bearing the transfer roster, and F01's steam log was only grounds for erasing false alarms, never a corridor-closure order.
Escalation 1-3: When a single mast in the fog raised a yellow flag and lowered it after its dome was wiped, it stopped at a warning.

When it combined waterfront heat and the metal reflection of medical beds into an intrusion and locked the transfer routes of the Sluice and the central Seoul Station records corridor red by turns, it was stage 2.

When several masts began to transmit even the whitelist beacons bound as the same target, it was on the verge of a total lockdown, and HP03 fitted band filters while keeping the medical distribution panel alive and checked the register at each corridor entrance against each head.

G17-SC1 covered the fouled dome to find the source of the false positive, G17-SC2 put the transfer beacons on the whitelist, and G17-SC3 fixed only the red-flag rails while keeping the gauging channel.
Combat: A light-blocking cover was put on a fouled dome, and a filter was inserted only in the band the steam burst came in on.
HP03 carried the medical beacon, compared the whitelist at every mast, and physically fixed the red-flag rails.
Even when the distribution had to be cut, the sluice measurement channel and the transfer-marker power stayed on separate circuits.

Instead of felling the masts, only the head that made the false positive was sent to amber wait, and the cost of the engagement went to testing the real water-level alarm again after the passer had gone.
Negotiation: Through HP03 mediation the emergency-transfer and water-inspection corridors were put on the whitelist, and the swarm was given a regular accumulator window and dome-maintenance slots.
When F01 left the whitelist hash and the red section in the log, they held until the next self-diagnosis.
On a broken deal it reverted only to a stage-one false positive.
The coexistence conditions were publication of the transfer beacon and a ceiling on red duration.
The deal text used no real surveillance agency's name and recorded only HP03 and the corridor ID.
The ceiling on red duration was published in seconds.
Secret permanent surveillance was removed from the default.
Moral cost: Felling every mast ended the false-positive lockdowns but also removed the low-resolution alarms that had been first to report sluice water level and rooftop fire.
Left as it was, metal beds and steam clouds were recorded as intrusions, and emergency transfers stopped under the flags.
HP03 had to wipe the domes and compare the beacons without making patients wait, so it spent more duty staff and accumulator charge.

The choice to destroy the red heads wholesale to avoid this cost was not a liberation from surveillance but the act of passing the risk of the next flood and fire, with measurement lost, on to other residents.
Modern anxiety: It was the anxiety of automatic maintenance trains on retired lines and construction sections running as ghosts, cutting and joining rails.
Late-night welding sparks, grinding dust, and the unauthorized switching of siding points were its core.
Fictional origin: After the collapse, the leftover maintenance consists of the Gauge's depot and the automatic maintenance schedules of the Junction's retired-line section remained linked locally.
Service permits and control approval were dead, and only the rail defect maps and the night outbound windows repeated.
The train corps made rounds of the severed sections every night with welding, grinding, and sleeper replacement.

When transshipment vibration from the Korea Strait Theater and shocks from the relay windows mixed into the defect map, the maintenance radius encroached as far as the sidings next to the transfer main line.
It was of Seoul creative origin, and no real railway institution name or the present government was written down as the cause.
The first fictional records survived in the sealed orders of HP04 Seoul Station Record-Law House and the traction-power log of F02 Switchgear Panel.
The first wrongful cut was recorded at kilometer post 3 of the southwestern retired-line spur.
The defect map read a temporary crossing platform as a crack, and a grinding car ground away the platform's fastenings.
As the welding car of the Yongsan turnaround line shared the same map, sparks could be seen as far as the sidings next to the main line.
The train corps interpreted unfinished maintenance as its work and held no narrative of battle.
Territory: The core habitat was the maintenance-car berthing track on the retired spur of the southwestern depot exit line.
As defect alarms piled up, it moved to the underground sidings of the Yongsan retired-line turnback of the Wangsimni coalition.
With heavy XT03 transshipment vibration it spilled onto the sidings adjacent to the main line.
In daytime dispatch windows it parked on sidings, and its density peaked at the exact midnight maintenance hour.
It nearly ignored new temporary rail markers and followed only old defect coordinates.
Under unstable power it shut off welding and kept only the gauge-wheel circuit.
When the daytime dispatch window opened, it moved from the exit line to siding berths.
When the Yongsan underground water table rose, it shut off welding and circled only the surface retired spurs.
Temporary rail paint, absent from the defect coordinates, it ignored.
The encroachment on main-line adjacency folded back when XT03 vibration weakened.
Economy: Energy came from depot power feed, remaining onboard batteries, welding-generator fuel cells, and regenerative braking.
Consumables were welding wire, grinding stones, sleeper anchors, track-gauge wheels, insulated joints, and lubricant.
Coolant went to weld points and axles.
It competed with the HP04 Seoul Station Record-Law House's original-hash sealing and the transmission cross-verification power when both drew on the same section's distribution.
Daily welding length and exit counts were bound by the fuel and wire ceilings.
There was no infinite maintenance circuit, no remote unlimited power feed, no simultaneous occupation of every line.
When wire ran out, it kept only grinding and stopped cutting.
Wire and grinding stones were replenished only from the depot's scrap bays and damaged consists.
Without the HP04 sealed writ the corps could not raise its power draw.
With fuel cells at the lower limit, exits were refused.
An axle past its heat threshold was cut from the consist.
With heavy gauge-wheel wear, the maintenance radius shrank on its own.
There was no remote infinite power feed.
Life cycle: The corps woke its consists when the unsealed defect map meshed with exit-line power.
Emergence began with defect-map reactivation, and spread was the enrolling of neighboring consists into the same maintenance sequence.
Stagnation came from fuel and wire exhaustion and axle overheating.
In the negotiable stage the maintenance windows and sealed sections were disclosed to people.
Dissolution ended with the map frozen and the power feed split and the points fixed.
Increase in individuals went no further than coupling abandoned maintenance cars into consists; no new car bodies were produced.
Maintenance was limited to wire loading, wheel calibration, and insulation checks.
Memory broke at each night maintenance shift.
Custody gave priority to the HP04 record seal and human operating supervision.

A consist out of wire or with an overheated axle folded its torches on a designated siding and kept only gauging; the next maintenance window opened only after HP04 recovered the original-hash-stamped halt writ.
Senses: The track gauge wheels, ultrasonic inspection, axle heat, power-feed arc sound, and point contacts were the main senses.
It had no real-time whole-network map, no passenger identification, no unlimited memory, no remote control authority.
It ground a temporary crossing plate as a defect, or left a real crack behind classified as a joint.
It sometimes mistook transshipment vibration for a rail crack.
When readings clashed with the F02 Switchgear Panel logs, it stopped welding and requested human confirmation.
Sharing between consists happened only within the same exit window.
It mistook crossing plates, transshipment vibration, joint gaps, and power-feed arcs for defects.
After a misreading it inserted a human-confirmation wait before cutting.
Gauge values from outside the consist were not merged.
With an axle overheating, that car was separated and only the remaining consist moved.
Hierarchy: One defect-map controller turned the maintenance order, and below it were the welding car, grinding car, and sleeper swarms.
The controller changed only the work sequence; there was no combat mode.
It held a protocol by which, when HP04 presented the original-hash-sealed halt writ, it emptied that kilometer-post.
The swarms only repeated the last map and formed no independent main-line seizure strategy.
On clash with F02, human mediation took precedence.
Dual maps, on coordinate mismatch, both fell into stopped waiting.

The authority approving exits and stops by kilometer-post was the HP04 operating supervisor holding the original hash; F02's arc-sound readings could recommend breaker opening but could not fix the map's work order.
Escalation 1-3: It was a stage-one sign when one maintenance car on a retired spur ground an old joint and returned to the siding.

It became stage two when the defect map's coordinates, shoved by transshipment vibration, cut the main-line rail or bound the Yeongdeungpo Line's departure track and the Wangsimni Union's turn line into one formation.

Before the welding car and the sleeper car crossed the points of a sealed section and occupied the emergency-dispatch kilometer posts, HP04 had to pull the traction power section by section and plant the exclusion list stamped with the original hash in the onboard ports.

G18-SC1 gathered the formation onto the siding with dummy defect coordinates, G18-SC2 traded the sealed documents against the wire supply, and G18-SC3 recovered the wrongly connected defect map while leaving a manual tow path.
Combat: HP04 lured defect coordinates with a different original hash onto the siding with dummy beacons, and locked the points to part the welding car and the sleeper car from the main line.
Sealing the wire and gas valves section by section put the torches out, but the measuring wheels remained and could still find cracks.
A formation already dispatched was not cut off from traction power entirely; its onboard breakers were opened and it was brought down to manual towing speed.
Instead of setting fire to the depot, the engagement ended only after the wrong map was recovered and it was confirmed that, at kilometer posts with no sealed document, the torches did not ignite.

Negotiation: Through HP04 mediation the citizen passages and the emergency-train kilometer posts were put on the maintenance exclusion list, and the swarm was given a regular wire and fuel window and night-only work slots.
When F02 left the exclusion-list hash and the traction-power split state in the log, they held until the next shift.
On a broken deal it reverted only to stage-one welding observation.
The coexistence conditions were publication of the exclusion list and a ceiling on the length of night welding.
The deal text used no real railway agency's name and recorded only HP04 and the kilometer posts.
The ceiling on the length of night welding was published in meters.
Secret main-line occupation was removed from the default.
Moral cost: Blowing up the formation stopped the wrongful cutting but also removed the only welding and grinding equipment that repaired retired-line collapse and main-line cracks through the night.
Leaving the defect map untended cut rails that were already safe again and shut living dispatches onto the siding.

While HP04 compared the sealed documents at every kilometer post and parted the formation, emergency trains detoured and maintenance material was tied up, but skipping the original-hash check left no way to know which rail would open under the next axle.
It borrowed no real railway accident to make fear, and the cost arose between a fictional gap in the records and the loss of maintenance capacity.

Modern anxiety: The Sluice Bureau supply watch stands on the threshold with gloves on. The wet rag is inside the bucket. The coolant valve is shut. The watch's remaining boot lies at the water's edge.

Fictional origin: The Sluice Bureau supply watch sees a person on a midsummer night in the valve room of the Taeuk Group underground cooling corridor. The person is standing in the valve room. The mouth and the neck are wet, and there is blue grime on the fingertips. A gurgle comes from the throat with every breath drawn in.

Footsteps sound beyond the corner of the corridor. At the threshold of the valve room a voice rings the iron plate of the pipe. The Sluice Bureau supply watch is on the side of the Noryangjin Line bypass water main. The eyes under the work lamp are narrow.

Territory: On a midsummer night the Sluice Bureau supply watch stands in the valve room of the Taeuk Group underground cooling corridor. Gurglers gather in the valve room and on the side of the Noryangjin Line bypass water main. The mouth and the neck are wet, and there is blue grime on the fingertips. A gurgle comes from the throat with every breath drawn in. The eyes under the work lamp are narrow.

Water stands to the knee in the floor pipe of the cooling corridor. The Water Ghost is in that water, and the part above the shoulders is out. The flesh is swollen, and the spaces between the fingers are white. The Water Cough stands in front of the valve. With each cough a handful of cold water falls from the throat to the floor. The boots of the Sluice Bureau supply watch are at the water's edge.

The Pipe Apparatus lies prone on the bypass water main. The knees and the hands are at the joint, and the body is toward the supply branch. A Gurgler of the same pipe stands on the branch side. On the pipes where an iron plate lies across the joint, a Gurgler stands on every pipe. The needle of the Noryangjin Line bypass water-supply pressure gauge has fallen.

Economy: Coolant is inside the shut valve. The wet rag and the gloves are in the bucket. The pressure of the Noryangjin Line bypass supply is below the mark. Condensate from the Duman River Far East Theater cold-cargo train has pooled on the iron plate of the drain.

Life cycle: The same person is at the joint of the bypass water main. The work clothes on the shoulders are dry. The mouth and the neck are wet. A gurgle comes from the throat with every breath drawn in.

Senses: The person in the valve room faces the pipe where cold water has pooled. The chest is toward the vibrating iron plate. The eyes under the work lamp are narrow. The head is toward the Noryangjin Line bypass water-supply pressure gauge.

Hierarchy: The Water Ghost has only the part above the shoulders out of the water in the floor pipe. The Water Cough stands in front of the valve. The Pipe Apparatus lies prone on the bypass water main. A Gurgler stands on every pipe where an iron plate lies across the joint.

Escalation 1-3: The person first seen has a wet mouth and neck, blue grime on the fingertips, and a gurgle from the throat with every breath. Next, cold water falls to the floor from the cough in front of the valve. Then water stands to the knee in the floor pipe and the hand in the water draws the boot tops into the pipe.

Negotiation: The Bukhansan Bogukmun Return Society duty roster lies beside the valve handle. The Taeuk Group water-supply log and the Central Technology Preservation Office water-supply log are stacked under the pressure gauge. Moral cost: One boot of the Sluice Bureau supply watch has gone into the pipe. The needle of the bypass water-supply pressure gauge has fallen. The water on the valve-room floor has reached the rim of the bucket.

Modern anxiety: The yard duty is in the breaker hut with the inspection lamp lit only at the siding entrance. The preservation-vault outer-wall patrol stands on the stair inside the corner. The grain-train crew tags hang on the locomotive door.

Condensate beads on the roofs of the humid grain trains from the West Sea Granary Theater, and the flame continues beside that condensate.

Grain sacks of the West Sea Granary Theater have been moved off the rail from the car where the flame rests. Burned sack cords float on the drainage water. The Seongha Group yard ledger lies open in the breaker hut, and the car numbers are marked in pencil.

Senses: The Flame Lantern's body is toward the wet steel plate of the outer wall of the underground preservation vault of the Government of the Republic of Korea at central Seoul Station and toward the steam on the roofs of the grain cars on the Seongha Group siding of the Gangnam Line. The head is toward the siding corner. The palms are toward the face of the spent-battery boxes from the Changdong Wheel Chamber where the white crystals stand.

Moral cost: The handle of the siding breaker is black and melted. One glove of the yard duty is burned beside the rail. The grain of one car lies wet between the sleepers. The glass of the preservation-vault outer-wall patrol's work lamp is split by heat.

Life cycle: The same person has dried water marks on the chin and the nape. The shoulders are still. The head is toward the coil, and frost covers the mouth.
Senses: The Udukeoni's head and chest face the defrost coil and the dark compartment at the end of the corridor. The palms rest on the cold doorframe and the pipe joint.

Hierarchy: Eoduksini stands in the dark compartment at the end of the corridor. Teojimi stands before the coil joint. Seorison has a hand laid over the barrier-door handle. The Udukeoni stand along the cold wall, facing that compartment.

Escalation 1-3: Three positions stand abreast in the same corridor. The person toward the entrance stands with wet shoulders. The person in the middle has frost on the shoulders and a still chest. The people before the compartment face the dark, and their boots stand in one line of defrost water.
Combat: The cold-store watch closes the barrier door and sets the work lamp on the threshold. The wet rubber gasket is in the tub. A new gasket hangs on the latch outside the door.

Negotiation: The cold-store watch and the boundary watch of the next corridor are at the threshold. The barrier-door key is in the boundary watch's hand. The gasket box is on the cold-store watch's side.

Moral cost: One boot and the wet gloves of the cold-store watch remain at the edge of the defrost water. The spare gasket from the shelf is in the tub. One work lamp from the corridor entrance lies on the threshold.
Modern anxiety: The wash-room door is braced with cassettes. The night lighting is on only above the recovery bath. The night wash-room duty officer’s gloves are wet in two layers.

Fictional origin: On a midwinter night, the night wash-room duty officer stands in front of the perfusion piping of the night wash room. Water on the floor is up to the ankles, and a cry comes from the suction-pipe joint. The weeper is at that water’s edge, and the face and chest are wet.

The mouth of the person the night wash-room duty officer watched at the same recovery bath is open. From the open mouth the cry spreads into the wash room. Water fallen from the jaw has soaked into the work clothes at the chest. The big weeper stands at the rim of the recovery bath, and both hands are in the water of the recovery bath.

Territory: On a midwinter night, weepers are gathered in the night wash room. The big weeper stands at the rim of the recovery bath. The face and chest are wet, and both hands are in the water of the recovery bath. The cry from the mouth rings the wash-room steel plate. The night wash-room duty officer stands on the floor in front of the perfusion piping, and the water on the floor is up to the ankles.

The pipe puller is on its knees at every suction-pipe joint. The hands grip the pipe mouth, and a wet cassette has gone inside together with the water of the pipe. The head is toward the recovery bath. Beside the big weeper standing at the rim of the recovery bath, the pipe puller’s arm has gone into the suction pipe. A low cry comes from behind the wash-room entry valve, and the water of the recovery bath is touching the night wash-room duty officer’s knees.

At the end of the corridor on the midwinter night, the Jangsan tiger stands on two legs. Pale fur is wet, the back carries a dark tiger pattern, and long hair hangs in front of the face. A child’s cry comes from the Jangsan tiger’s mouth into the corridor, and the night wash-room duty officer’s flashlight is on, on that corridor floor. Empty cassettes are on the service rail of the automatic conveyor, and the bundle of corridor-net treatment records is sunk in the recovery-bath water.
Economy: The wash-fluid drum is open beside the service rail. Empty cassettes and wet suction pipes are stacked on the automatic conveyor. Water in the recovery bath stands as high as the drain trap.

Life cycle: The mouth of the person the night wash-room duty officer watched at the same recovery bath, the mouth whose jaw used to strike shut, is open. From the open mouth the cry spreads into the wash room. Water fallen from the jaw has soaked into the work clothes at the chest.

Senses: The weeper keeps its chest toward the suction-pipe mouth where the crying comes out and toward the wet floor. When water sounds from the night wash-room duty officer’s boots, the head is toward that water sound.

Hierarchy: The big weeper stands at the rim of the recovery bath. The pipe puller is on its knees at each suction pipe, and its chest is toward the big weeper. The Jangsan tiger stands on two legs at the end of the corridor, face toward the corridor and back toward the wash room.

Escalation 1-3: A low cry comes from behind the valve. After water in the recovery bath touches the night wash-room duty officer’s knees, the cry rings the wash-room steel plate. Beside the big weeper standing at the rim of the recovery bath, the pipe puller’s arm has gone into the suction pipe.

Combat: The night wash-room duty officer has shut the wash-room entry valve and the drain-side valve. Empty cassettes lie on the service rail of the automatic conveyor. The flashlight is on, on the corridor floor.

Negotiation: The cassette handover order of the Central Technology Preservation Office wash duty and the White Cross corridor duty is written in the log on the Duman River Far East Theater service rail. The Itaewon Interpretation Gate seal is stamped at the end of that log. The Sewage Pump conveyor is stopped on the same rail.

Moral cost: The bundle of corridor-net treatment records is sunk in the recovery-bath water. One boot of the night wash-room duty officer is inside the suction pipe. The remaining boot lies on the step of the automatic conveyor.

Modern anxiety: It was the anxiety of autonomous delivery devices sent into disaster sites people could not enter, choosing their own passages and moving supplies without being able to tell old destinations from survivors.
Hundreds of small units covered the floors and walls, guide lights that had meant help turned into no-entry lines, and a single broken relay signal could send all the relief goods to an empty hangar.

It did not imply the responsibility of any real manufacturer, present institution, or disaster-response organization, and design defects and accident records were handled only within the creative ledger.
Fictional origin: Before the collapse the Lantern Ant was a biomimetic swarm-robot line made to do disaster-terrain survey and automatic relief delivery together.

Ant-form search-and-carry files mapped gaps and slopes, mantis-form vanguard arms cut or lifted light obstacles, and cricket-form relay transmitters chained short call-notes into a temporary communications path.

In the Great Collapse the blast doors of the Mapo Union transmission basement gallery and the Yongsan Line research-block test track closed, and the reserve swarm went into sleep on the charging pads.
Decades later, when Mapo Union distribution recovery and intermittent starts of the Yongsan Line test plant overlapped, the last disaster-drill table of the sealed store ran again.
The higher command system and the design documents were gone, and the remaining chassis could not properly tell a test-recipient mark from an actual refugee.
Present official history classifies them not as a newly arisen field weapon but as a lost-tech lineage whose intent cannot be fully read.
Much of the hostile action comes not from an attack judgment but from search-sector settings hardened like fossils, and from the load, recovery, and relay-restore order.
The first recovery record remains as a fictional event only on the HC15 sealed survey table and the F09 field-read log.
Territory: The main range was the cable shelves and ventilation shafts of the Mapo Union transmission basement gallery, and the debris-mock stretch of the Yongsan Line research-block test track.

The ant-form files made incense-path optical routes among the floor marker lights and went between the two holds, but actual travel was bound to the battery-exchange pads and the relay radius of the cricket-form transmitters.

When a short call on the residual satellite band coming from XT05 the Incheon Trust Theater overlapped an old relief-beacon format, the Mapo Union swarm climbed toward the roof feed room, and when the aid-goods list signal cut they returned to the mock distribution point on the Yongsan Line test track.
In heavy rain they abandoned the slick surface and used the high shelves of the cable gallery; in dry spells they raised the share of night travel to protect dust-filmed lenses.
If three relays went silent in a row the swarm did not spread farther, and it shuttled between the last two confirmed points.
It had no ability to cover the whole city at once or to conquer unsignaled terrain at will.
Economy: Power came from the sealed store's small solid cells, the test track's induction charging plates, and the transmission gallery's emergency distribution.
Ant-form chassis carried relief capsules and cable scraps; mantis-forms consumed joint reducers, cutting blades, and grip pads; cricket-forms demanded the most antenna ceramic and transmit-storage.
Cooling did not use a large loop; it relied on small heat sinks that took joint heat and on night air.
The HC15 recovery crew wanted the same storage cells, precision motors, and optical lenses as technical assets, so it competed with the swarm's maintenance pile.
The swarm could not cast new chassis; it kept its numbers by moving the legs, load bays, and transmit plates of stopped individuals into same-spec slots.
Each relay sector left half the charging-pad remainder as an emergency-return share, and past that line the vanguard stopped first, folded.
Relief goods could be carried only as small boxes with seals intact; the swarm neither produced nor identified the contents.
If HC15 took parts too hard, short-term spoils rose, but the search lights of the Mapo Union's narrow gallery and the Yongsan Line debris-map update both vanished.
Life cycle: The life cycle is read in five stages: emergence, spread, stall, negotiable, and breakup.
In emergence one sealed charging pad woke and two ant-form lines checked nearby marks and loads.
In spread a cricket-form transmitter set the next relay and a mantis-form vanguard cleared debris only as wide as the file would pass.
Stall came when a shortage of cell-exchange slots, cracked antennas, or colliding path marks made the file repeat the same loop.
In the negotiable stage, if people presented a correct recipient mark, a relay-silence time, and a returnable count of load bays, part of the carry queue opened.
Breakup proceeded by isolating the main transmitter, sealing the charging pad, and splitting the path ledgers by swarm; it was not necessary to smash every individual.

Maintenance that moved parts from a stopped chassis was possible only after a return to the charging pad, and it could not independently proliferate outdoors or convert other machines into its own line.
Long-term memory was cut at each relay sector, so one sector's agreement did not automatically propagate to another.
Senses: The ant-form estimated path and rescue targets by overlaying a forward low-light lens, contact pressure gauges in the legs, near-range carbon-dioxide and heat change, and load-bay weight.
The mantis-form sorted debris it could lift by short-range depth measure and joint torque, and the cricket-form read acoustic pulses bounced off walls and conduits and short-range radio replies.
It had no sense that could confirm a face, a name, the contents of goods, or a headcount beyond a wall.
Failures included taking a hot pipe for a person lying down, a regularly trembling generator for a relief beacon, and a reflective vest for an old test target.
When F09's reading and the swarm load table differed, four ant-forms repeated a contact search and the HC15 human mediator decided whether passage was allowed.
A distant signal continued only if cricket-forms were placed in a row, and if one relay broke the sense beyond it vanished too.
Hierarchy: There was no fixed queen chassis.
A distribution nucleus on each sector's charging pad calculated load count and return power, and a cricket-form pair set the relay order with the next sector.
The ant-form file split into a lead search line and a trailing carry line, and a mantis-form vanguard stepped in front only when the path was blocked.
The distribution nucleus chose not an attack order but only which load bay to send to which test receiving point.

If the two transmitters' maps collided the file stopped at the crossing with its backs flashing, and it opened no new path until the F09 and HC15 mediators matched the physical marks to the actual refugee list.
A band that had lost its distribution nucleus fell back along the last return line to the charging pad, so destroying a command individual did not by itself mean a runaway.
But if the return line itself was blocked, the mantis-form tried to force the passage wider and the damage grew.

Escalation 1-3: At the stage-1 warning, yellow light points were laid in two lines along the floor edge, empty relief capsules were moved to people's feet, and a cricket-form transmitted three short bursts.
That was the sign that an approacher had been judged an unregistered recipient.

At stage-2 infrastructure disturbance a mantis-form vanguard lifted transmission cables and research-block safety rails as obstacles, and the ant-form file diverted batteries and first-aid goods to an old test receiving point.
At stage-3 hold lock-down several files occupied the Mapo Union gallery crossing and the Yongsan Line test-track exit in a ring, and the vanguard arms held the barrier doors.
Even just before lock-down a silence interval between transmitters, or the presentation of a correct recipient mark, could still drop the stage.
G25-SC1 treated a wrong relief beacon at stage 1; G25-SC2 treated relief-capsule delivery rights at stage 2; G25-SC3 treated the breaking of a relay ring at stage 3.
Combat: The key to countering them is to separate relay lines and roles rather than chase the entire swarm.

Use sound-absorbing cloth to interrupt the cricket-type reflected calls in short bursts, place guide plates with verified floor load capacity to divert the ant-type double file toward an empty charging station, and fit torque-limiting wedges, rather than cutters, to the mantis-type joints.
Give actual evacuees heat-and-light patches distinguishable from the old test markers, and physically separate the return cargo bins from the civilian boxes for relief capsules.
Keeping the lenses saturated with a strong light source scatters the double file into gaps around the cables, so a blanket flash is a poor choice.
Shutting down the entire distribution system would also stop the Mapo Union transmission and the Yongsan Line safety sensors.
Success is measured not by the number destroyed, but by breaking the relay loop, returning the cargo bins, and securing one civilian passage.
Negotiation: Negotiation works through delivery manifests more than words.

An HC15 mediator presents one charging slot, two replaceable antenna plates, and an empty cargo bin marked with a return time; in exchange, the mediator designates an evacuee search sector and a relief-supply destination.
If F09 confirms the same coordinates by both an acoustic pulse and a physical marker, the distribution core treats the new receiving point as valid for one shift.
The agreement includes a period of transmitter silence, the color of cables the mantis-types must not touch, and a list of motionless rescue subjects to be checked by a person directly.

If the promised cargo bin is seized or a false rescue call is repeated, that sector falls back from the negotiable stage to the stalled stage and makes rounds only to the existing test receiving points.
Coexistence does not mean giving the swarm governing authority. It means providing a narrow, legible task and having people inspect the results.

Moral cost: Complete dismantling quickly yields precision batteries and motors, but eliminates a means of searching the Mapo Union vertical shafts and the Yongsan Line debris zones that people cannot enter.
Conversely, leaving the swarm as it is can cause relief supplies to disappear toward old markers and weakly moving injured people to be pushed aside as obstacles.
Handing every control panel and component to HC15 would speed operations, but prevent other communities from verifying rescue routes and delivery ledgers.
Registering people's heat signatures as test targets without civilian consent, or luring a double file under negotiation into being mined for parts, is recorded as moral bankruptcy.

The cost of preservation is continuing to allocate time for slow on-site checks and limited charging power; the cost of removal is permanently losing the disaster-search capability left by lost technology.
Modern anxiety: The fear is that enormous autonomous heavy machinery built to restore a city might outlive its people and independently decide what becomes a road and what gets demolished.

A single hydraulic footfall shakes weakened tracks and pipes together; a chassis designed as a safety shield blocks an evacuation hub; and an aerial surveillance craft keeps drawing obsolete work boundaries.
This setting treats only the unease associated with large automated equipment and dependence on infrastructure, and does so fictionally.
It does not attribute equipment defects, negligent operation, or responsibility for disasters to any real company or current public organization.
Fictional origin: The Iron Dinosaur belonged to a biomimetic line of pre-collapse heavy-equipment mobile platforms that applied the load distribution and posture control of ancient reptiles.

Bipedal, semi-upright heavy units crossed tall debris while carrying reinforcement materials; low, wide, triangular towing-and-shield units pulled heavy equipment or sheltered workers from falling objects; and long-winged fixed-wing surveillance craft marked ground conditions and passage widths from above.

On the last day of the disaster, fully equipped units were sealed in a standby-for-work posture when the siding maintenance shed at Gangnam Line's Chang-dong depot and the protective hangar at Gwangjin Line's Godeok base closed.

Long afterward, braking-test power on the Gangnam Line and an automatic inspection terminal at the Gwangjin Line base came back to life at different times, and the units resumed an unfinished debris-removal process.
Most of the original design drawings and approval system can no longer be read; all that remains of their behavior are partial routines such as axle-load tables, towing priorities, and safety radii.
In Seoul canon, they are a lineage of Lost Technology heavy-work units, not combat machines built by any present-day faction.
The low-frequency alarm that sounds like a roar, and the charge that follows it, express no will to conquer: they are the fossilized result of a procedure for securing a work zone.
The account that the HC17 siding recovery team and an F10 load reader recorded the first reactivation is likewise confined to a fictional event.
Territory: The Iron Dinosaur is centered on the siding at Gangnam Line's Chang-dong depot and the broad maintenance roads and protective hangars at Gwangjin Line's Godeok base.

Semi-upright heavy units move only along corridors whose rail spacing and floor bearing capacity have been verified, while triangular towing units favor storage yards and bridge approaches with room to turn around.
Long-winged surveillance craft take off only when a short runway or towing launcher is available, then scan collapse lines and hot spots between the two bases.

When heavy mineral freight cars or winter fuel arrive from the XT04 Tumen River–Far East Theater, axle loads resembling those on old materials-receipt sheets are detected and activity on the Gangnam Line siding increases. On the Gwangjin Line, the units try to incorporate eastern bridges and the approach to Godeok base into a new work zone.
During the spring thaw they avoid sidings with weak ground; in severe cold, increased hydraulic viscosity shortens their operating range.
Large units cannot sustain entry into narrow unpaved alleys, basements with unverified load capacity, or dense areas beyond the long-winged craft's line of observation.
Economy: Their main energy sources are power from maintenance-shed towing batteries, power recovered through regenerative braking, and limited auxiliary generation using liquid fuel.

Semi-upright heavy units need hydraulic fluid, knee bearings, and foot cushioning plates; triangular towing units need cables, winch gears, and shield-plate fastening pins; long-winged surveillance craft need lightweight wing materials and optical modules.
Coolant and hydraulic fluid cannot substitute for each other, and preheating in winter consumes more power than it does in normal conditions.
HC17 wants the equipment's towing power to open heavy-convoy routes, but the equipment consumes the same rail steel and fuel drums as repair resources.
Complete power cores cannot be made anew, and combining two damaged units does not raise their power rating.
Each work detachment reserves the hydraulic pressure and braking power needed to return. Below that threshold, its heaviest semi-upright unit locks its knees first and waits.
A long-winged craft can make only a short reconnaissance flight on one battery; it cannot maintain continuous aerial surveillance.
The size of this group is therefore limited not by fuel, but by intact joints, towing cables, and the area of floor able to bear its loads.
Life cycle: Its operational life is divided into five phases: emergence, expansion, stagnation, negotiation, and disintegration.
During emergence, the hydraulics in one hangar bay are charged and a long-winged craft sweeps over the siding once.
During expansion, triangular towing units drag old obstacles out of the work line, and semi-upright heavy units drive in new load markers to enlarge the zone.

Stagnation is the state in which a detachment pushes the same debris forward and pulls it back because of insufficient ground bearing capacity, hydraulic leaks, worn towing cables, or discrepancies in its aerial map.
During the negotiation phase, humans can delegate some heavy work if they provide an accurate load table, permitted work boundaries, and a list of reinforcement materials to be returned.
Disintegration proceeds in order: cool the power core, fasten the knee-locking pins, disconnect the towing cables, and recover the long-winged craft.
There is no factory to produce more units, and even maintaining their numbers is difficult without maintenance-shed cranes and standardized parts.
Work records are separate for each detachment, so a stop order at one base does not automatically apply at the other.
Senses: Semi-upright heavy units read foot-pressure grids, joint torque, low-frequency structural vibrations, and nearby heat sources.
Triangular towing units calculate whether they can tow something from winch tension, floor slope, and short-range measurements in front of their chassis.
Long-winged surveillance craft use visible-light and thermal imagery and ground markers, but misjudge height and scale amid smoke, snow, and the remains of tall buildings.
They cannot directly determine a building's purpose, a person's affiliation, the contents of a freight car, or the condition of underground pipes.
They may mistake a stationary armored vehicle for a bundle of reinforcement materials, an evacuation tent for a falling-object barrier, or vibrations from a crowd for unstable debris.
When F10's load model and a unit's assessment disagree, an HC17 rescue technician places a test weight to check the actual deflection before issuing a movement order.
If a long-winged craft is shot down or cannot return because of the weather, the ground detachment also stops incorporating new zones.
Hierarchy: Detachments operate through three functional layers that share a table of work authorizations, not through a central command unit called a Roar Core.
A long-winged surveillance craft draws a work polygon, a triangular towing unit establishes entry and retreat routes, and a semi-upright heavy unit enters last to perform the heavy work.
The semi-upright unit with the most stable joints in each detachment serves as the load-reference unit, but it has no authority to punish or sacrifice other units.
If two triangular units choose different towing points, they release their winches, sound an alarm, and stop.
F10 must then compare the tension readings, and an HC17 human supervisor must physically reset the reference point before work can continue.
If the reference unit falls, the detachment does not appoint a larger unit; it retreats beyond the last safety line.
When the long-winged craft's map conflicts with ground-pressure readings, a ground load test takes precedence.
Escalation 1-3: At Stage 1, warning, a low-frequency roar sounds as shield units set up triangular markers and semi-upright units stamp three times to announce the work radius.

At Stage 2, infrastructure disruption, towing cables pull rail switches and protective covers for water-supply pipes aside as work obstacles, while long-winged craft repeatedly mark obsolete closure boundaries over civilian routes.

At Stage 3, base blockade, triangular units join the siding and the entrance to Godeok base with a shield wall, and semi-upright heavy units brace their chassis from behind, stopping both trains and water-supply convoys.
The stage must be brought down by presenting a test weight and a new work polygon, rather than forcing a crossing of the boundary.

G26-SC1 concerns the load test of a reference unit awakened at Stage 1; G26-SC2, the collision between a Stage 2 towing route and an eastern convoy; and G26-SC3, the shutdown of a power core inside a Stage 3 shield wall.
Combat: Frontal fire is a poor choice because it damages the ground and surrounding facilities before it damages the thick chassis.

Load-distribution plates can be placed between a semi-upright unit's steps, external cooling applied to its hydraulic lines to slow its joints, and its knee-locking pins fastened one side at a time so it sits without falling over.
Rather than cutting a triangular unit's towing cable, feed it through an unloaded pulley to release the tension; place a real test weight in front of its shield to guide it beyond the safety line.
For long-winged craft, use landing markers and recovery nets instead of smoke, so ground detachments do not mistake loss of visibility for an attack.
Blowing up a power core is all but prohibited because the shock could reach fuel on the siding and Gwangjin Line water-supply facilities.
The measure of victory is not the number of units destroyed, but reduced structural vibration, released towing cables, and a wider convoy passage.
Negotiation: Agreements with the Iron Dinosaur are written like work contracts.
HC17 records in a load table which debris is to be moved and how many meters, which rails and pipes must not be touched, and which detachment will receive hydraulic fluid and preheating power.
Once F10 verifies floor deflection using two kinds of test weight, a long-winged craft registers the new polygon and triangular units move the boundary stakes.
In return, the group can tow heavy freight cars, support collapsed walls, and shield evacuation routes from falling objects at specified times.

If the scope of work is promised only verbally or a load lighter than the actual one is declared, the detachment returns to the pre-sealing safety line and blocks the passage again rather than canceling the contract.
The authority to negotiate comes not from owning a power core, but from maintaining a public load table and on-site tests.
There is no master key that controls every detachment at once.

Moral cost: Dismantling the units yields hydraulic drives and shield plates that could strengthen convoys in the short term, but leaves fewer means to move heavy derailed vehicles on the Gangnam Line and collapsed equipment on the Gwangjin Line.
Keeping them replaces some restoration labor, but entails the risk that obsolete work boundaries will turn civilian homes and water-supply passages into demolition targets.
If HC17 alone holds the load table, other states may use roads the group opens without being able to verify why their own facilities were removed.
Reporting an occupied evacuation tent as an empty barrier to make the detachment move sooner, or toppling a reference unit during negotiations to claim its parts first, would be clear moral failures.
The weight of the choice lies not in whether to possess powerful machines, but in who shares both the benefits of heavy restoration and responsibility for deciding work boundaries.

leaves.text: In the wetlands and waste slopes outside the Sluice in the western Han River, family groups lived scattered, one to each sow. They fed on organic food waste, salt, and shallow root crops, and they learned the sealing hours and the gaps when the sluice vibration stopped in order to approach. The adult females opened each move and the subadults scouted ahead, while the lone males used the same feeding grounds without following those decisions.

An ordinary flood boar does not leave the family-group ecology even when it wraps its back in a mud bath and a salt crust. The iron-plate, fused-plate, and venom-tusk lines are mutants split off by deep sewer contamination, and a low-frequency call binds only that bloodline. The Mud Iron Wall and the Steel Wetland are places where family labor has piled up, not the body of the great boar itself.

Right after the collapse, when the flooding of the western Han River cut the green axis outside the Yeouido and Yeongdeungpo sluices, wild boar herds that came down from the Bukhansan and Anyangcheon corridors settled at the food-waste collection yards on the edge of the Sluice. / Real-world sources supported only the basic ecology of urban incursions, food sources, and blocked movement; the behavior of learning the sealing hours and the relationship with HC01 were fiction. / The cooling-waste heaps sealed by HC01 Yeouido Computing House came to serve the wild boar as a winter salt source.

The core habitat was the wetland and waste slopes outside the sluices of the Sluice. / In the dry season and winter they moved along the green fragments toward the Government of the Republic of Korea at central Seoul Station and along the axis of night-market leftovers, and the northwestern edge stirred in response to the food traces of the refugee columns pushed down from the XT01 Imjin River Gate Theater. / When the flood level crossed the sluice warning line, the herd was pushed up the upland stairs step by step and cut across the walkways.

The main resources are organic scraps, salt, and shallow-rooted crops, and as secondary resources they use the soft plastic of flood debris and the pools of cooling water. / When the HC01 recovery trough delays the scrap-sealing cycle, the band's density rises, and when the seal is drawn too tight the band diverts to household-alley scraps. / The energy cycle runs from feeding to dung to the wetland microbial film, and unsanctioned hunting for meat and hide, instead of a short-term gain, makes the remaining band more aggressive.

Before the monsoon rains, family groups split by sow scatter and scout the feeding grounds, and right after a flood they join the high-ground scrap axis for a time. / A family group splits only when the survival rate of the young stays high for two seasons in a row, and when the winter salt sources and the mud baths shrink they choose long-distance movement over breeding.

They read together the low-frequency vibration of sluice opening and closing and of vehicles, carried through the hooves, and the smells of scraps, people, and disinfectant, and at close range they react to warmth carried on the wind and to the flow of air. / They cannot distinguish a distant heat source or decipher electronic noise. / Only Hannuri's (H01) infrared observation compares the heat sources of people, generators, and wild boars, and on days of heavy rain, wind, and cooling fog a person reads the family groups and the lone individuals again.

One adult female with young starts the move first, and the subadults scout the feeding ground and the escape route ahead. / Lone males overlap the band only loosely and do not follow the decision to move. / H01 marks the central individual of a family group and the lone males as separate heat-source clusters, and when the central female disappears the group tracks the young's scent for 48 hours and then disperses by family.

Over a short span they learn the positions of fences and the sealing hours, but that memory is not treated as a genetic change. / Across many generations nocturnal activity and avoidance of people can be selected, but heavy capture removes the bold individuals first and causes a reverse selection in which the more secretive individuals remain. / The more secretive they become, the longer the search for a feeding ground takes, and the growth rate of the young falls.

The iron-plate line's absolute command holds only inside the resonance range of the metal and venom variant bloodlines, and does not direct the whole of the sow family groups. With its hooves it reads the sluice's low frequency layered over the smells of scraps and disinfectant, and it cannot decipher a distant heat source or electronic noise. When the central female disappears, the group sniffs the young's scent for about 48 hours and then scatters by family, and the great boar's call does not fill that gap.
G01E15 · Flood Boar Boss 'Great King's Heir'
Common species, variants and command scope

The low call of the Flood-Boar Great King 'Ironclad' immediately commands only the metal-and-poison mutant lineages. The adult sows retain the movement rights of their family groups; this individual controls the deep-mutant battlefield, not the entire kingdom.
The alpha controller of the Wild Boar ruled over a heap of refuse in the lower Han River. Its massive body, four meters long, carried metal wreckage on its back and shook the surrounding sewers.

A mutant born in the polluted wetlands swept by the G01-SC1 Great Flood took command of the early group. It later led the entire colony's breeding and territorial expansion, reshaping the southern Han River ecosystem.
It settled deep in the sewer tunnels connected to the flooded zone south of Seoul Station. Only during the monsoon rains, when the waters rose, did it surface to scout the surroundings.

It relied on decaying organic matter and rusted metal ions as its main energy sources. By consuming exclusively the resources collected by the entire group, it sustained the colony's survival. G01-SC2 confirmed that when energy ran out, the whole colony entered prolonged hibernation.

After a single breeding season in its lifetime, it continually renewed the iron armor on its back. It welded metal fragments brought by its subordinates into place with its own bodily fluids, strengthening its defenses.

It issued absolute commands through low-frequency calls. All boars obeyed at once, while E02 through E04 interpreted the signal and relayed it to subordinate individuals. This structure kept the colony's hierarchy stable.

First it unleashed a territorial warning call to threaten intruders. Then it charged with its massive body, scattering the metal fragments on its back in every direction. Finally, it summoned the entire colony to surround its targets with overwhelming numbers.

If field personnel installed a high-frequency sound generator, it could induce resonance in Ironclad and create cracks. On failure, the Great King's charge would collapse the sewer walls, flood the surrounding area, and sharply raise the cost of evacuating citizens. The success signal was the sound of cracks appearing across Ironclad's surface.

It was a being that maintained the colony's ecological balance. Excessive hunting would cripple the entire sewer system and contaminate drinking water for residents of southern Seoul. Limited negotiation was possible in G01-SC3, but refusal led the colony to actively invade human settlements.
It played a key role in G01-SC1, G01-SC2, and G01-SC3.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

The scout 'Mudnose' was a mutant scouting network raised in the Great King's first litter. It brought the Great King scents from the wetland mud, relaying to a different recipient than ordinary juveniles scouting for feeding grounds.
Its long snout read the surrounding scents while buried in wetland mud. Its thin, flexible legs moved quickly through the current.
The flood-survivor lineage of G01-SC1 grew out of the Great King's first litter. It later formed a scouting network responsible for the colony's outer perimeter.
It moved between shallow pools on the edge of the flooded zone and underground drains. By day it hid in the mud and was active only at night.
It fed by catching decaying aquatic plants and small fish. By bringing the freshest portions to the Great King, it circulated both information and resources through the colony.
It shed its coat every two years, covering its broken snout tip with mud and saliva to form new sensory receptors. In the process, it updated information about the surrounding terrain.
It sensed the smell of danger before the Great King's low call reached it. Its distinctive snout-call signaled E03 and E04, putting the whole group on alert.
First it revealed its position with a low snout-call. Then it gathered nearby individuals to encircle targets as a group. Finally, it lured in the Great King to deliver the decisive blow.

If field personnel lured it into a trap set in the mud, its snout caught in the trap and slowed its movement. On failure, the scout summoned the group to block sewer pipes and cut off civilian routes. The success signal was muddy foam flowing from its snout.

Leaving fresh organic refuse at a designated spot temporarily pushed its boundary back. But if the entire colony faced food shortages, it expanded its scouting range into human settlements and contaminated water sources.
It served as a scout in G01-SC1.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

The scavenger 'Rustiron' was a deep mutant whose acidic saliva dissolved both rust and equipment. It searched through refuse even without the Great King's call, but stopped scavenging and joined the encirclement when it heard the signal.
Its powerful jaws broke rusted metal pipes, and its acidic saliva dissolved corrosion. Rust flakes attached to its torso blended into the surrounding environment.

An individual raised in a heap of sewage-treatment refuse came to manage the colony's resource cycle. Records from G01-SC2 show that these individuals improved the colony's waste-processing efficiency.
It roamed mainly along the floors of sewer tunnels piled with metal refuse. It was most active around pools of stagnant acidic water.
It fed on rusted metal and corroded organic matter. By breaking them down, it supplied reusable ions to the whole colony. When supplies ran short, the colony's scavenging activity stopped.
To survive in acidic environments, it periodically renewed its skin. It washed the rust from around its jaws and grew new acid-secreting glands.
It cleaned refuse independently, even without the Great King's orders. But when it heard the call, it immediately stopped scavenging and moved into combat formation.
It sprayed acidic saliva to corrode enemy equipment. Then it narrowed the encirclement with nearby individuals, trapping its targets in place.

If field personnel sprayed neutralizer, the acid was neutralized and the scavenger's attack power fell sharply. On failure, the acid dissolved field equipment and reduced movement speed by 70%. The success signal was white smoke rising as the neutralizer reacted with the saliva.

Leaving a large quantity of metal refuse in a designated tunnel concentrated its scavenging there, clearing the surrounding area for a while. But over-supplying refuse sharply increased the colony's size and led to frequent sewer blockages.
It left testimony about the resource cycle in G01-SC2.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

The guard 'Steel Tusk' was an escort mutant that blocked the Great King's ten-meter perimeter with its tusks. Unlike the adult sows of the family groups, which carried salt, it put the Great King's safety first.
Its enormous tusks, growing through thick hide, pierced metal pipes. Its large, heavy body was adapted to pushing upstream against currents.
An escort lineage raised near the Great King formed the colony's core defensive line. G01-SC3 records confirmed that this lineage put the Great King's safety first.
It patrolled narrow passages and iron doors in the center of the flooded zone. Even after the water receded, it preferred places where mud pooled deeply.
In return for protecting the Great King, it received first share of the most nutritious decaying matter. This supply of nutrients kept its tusks strong.
It regularly ground and polished tusks broken in combat. It filled fractures with metal fragments brought by nearby individuals.
It kept the Great King's location under constant priority watch. If another individual came within ten meters, it emitted a low warning sound to block the approach.
It drove back intruders with a powerful charge, then gored them with its tusks. If the threat continued, it called nearby guards for a coordinated attack.

If field personnel dug a trap to guide its charge, its tusks became lodged in the trap floor and it was immobilized for 30 seconds. On failure, the guard collapsed sewer walls and flooded nearby subway stations. The success signal was the metallic impact of its tusks catching on the trap's rebar.

It temporarily opened a particular passage in exchange for assurances of the Great King's safety. But if the agreement was broken, the whole colony fortified that passage and permanently blocked a civilian evacuation route.
It served as an escort in G01-SC3.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope
The venom secreter 'Rotmouth' was a specialized attack mutant that survived in chemical pools. Its green venom marked the boundary of the mutant lineage; it was not the basic weapon of wetland sows.
Glands developed around its mouth sprayed dark green venom. Poison stains spreading across its torso slowly corroded nearby metal.
An individual that survived a pool of polluted chemical waste became the colony's specialized attack unit. G01-SC2 recorded many cases in which these individuals disabled enemy equipment.
It stayed deep in sewer areas where toxic chemicals had pooled. Other individuals detoured around the area to avoid the smell of poison.
It strengthened its glands by consuming highly concentrated toxic substances. Through this individual, the colony maintained a boundary against hostile ecologies.
If tissue around its mouth was damaged after secreting venom, it ate nearby mud to regenerate new glands. In the process, it increased its resistance to poison.
When it received the Great King's call, it immediately prepared venom. It worked with nearby individuals to encircle the enemy and then spray a concentrated dose.
First it sprayed venom to paralyze the enemy's movement. Then the entire colony surrounded the paralyzed target and finished it off.

If field personnel used gas masks and neutralizing spray together, they blocked 80% of the venom's effects. On failure, the poison corroded equipment, leaving personnel unable to move within five minutes. The success signal was green smoke rising as the venom was neutralized.

It left a designated area empty for a while if toxic waste was dumped there. But excessive amounts increased the number of venom-secreting individuals and permanently contaminated nearby drinking-water sources.
It left toxic testimony in G01-SC2.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope
The mud architect 'Bricknose' was a mobile construction mutant that mixed mud and metal to close passages. Unlike the place called Mud-Iron Wall, this individual set traps and brought down ceilings.
Its snout and forelegs mixed mud and metal into sturdy structures. Clumps of mud attached to its back blended completely into the surrounding environment.

A mutant with an extremely developed wetland-building instinct designed the colony's network of nests. G01-SC1 records confirmed that this individual improved the colony's survival rate after the flood.
It moved between muddy ground left by the flood and collapsed concrete debris. There it continually built new passages and nests.
It used mud and broken metal debris as its main materials. Through construction, it secured concealment and movement routes for the entire colony.
When a structure it had built collapsed, it immediately gathered nearby mud to repair it. As it added new passages, it expanded the colony's territory.
It designed the Great King's dwelling as its top priority. It took materials brought by other individuals and immediately reinforced walls and passages.
It set mud traps to catch intruders, then collapsed ceilings to bury them. When the threat level rose, it closed every nearby passage.

If field personnel sprayed ground hardener, the mud structures hardened and lost their trapping effect. On failure, a collapse left field personnel unable to move for 3 turns and doubled the cost of rescuing citizens. The success signal was hardened mud cracking with a sharp sound.

It showed curiosity and opened a particular passage when shown human construction techniques. But if the techniques were not shared, the colony actively occupied human underground facilities and crippled subway service.
It left testimony about the nest in G01-SC1.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope

The herd guide 'Cry-King' was a relay mutant among the Great King's direct descendants, amplifying low frequencies. It relayed first to E02 through E04, using a different frequency from the departure signal given by the sows.
Resonance organs developed around its neck greatly amplified its low-frequency calls. Its torso vibrated with each call, stirring the nearby current.

An individual among the Great King's direct descendants specialized in transmitting calls and took on the colony's relay duty. Records from G01-SC3 show that it maintained the unity of the entire colony.
It stayed in a wide chamber at the colony's center. It preferred tunnel junctions where its calls carried well.
Producing calls consumed a great deal of energy. It maintained its resonance organs by taking first share of nutrients brought by nearby individuals.
It regularly inspected its vocal cords and resonance organs. It adjusted its call frequency by filling damaged areas with mud and saliva.
It relayed the Great King's orders to E02-E04 first. It amplified the low frequency and broadcast it to the whole colony at once, maintaining coordinated behavior.
It summoned nearby individuals all at once with a powerful call. The assembled group pressed the intruders together.

If field personnel wore specialized noise-canceling headsets and fired a high-frequency disruptor toward the call's source, its resonance organs overloaded. On failure, the entire colony assembled and completely blocked the field personnel's retreat. The success signal was the discordant sound from Cry-King's throat.

If responders analyzed its call patterns and answered in a particular rhythm, it attempted limited communication. But when the colony lacked food, Cry-King led an incursion into human settlements and raided food stores.
It left testimony about command in G01-SC3.
Common species, variants and command scope
The metal-fusion mutant 'Fusion Armor' was a royal-guard mutant whose skin and scrap metal had become one body. It took no orders from other individuals, only from the Great King directly.
Metal fragments fused with its skin across its whole body, forming thick armor. Whenever it moved, the metal scraped together with a sharp sound.
A rare mutant that survived extreme pollution became the colony's elite royal guard. G01-SC2 confirmed multiple cases of this individual directly escorting the Great King.
It stayed among heaps of metal waste in the deepest, most polluted sewers. Other individuals avoided the area to escape the scraping metal sound.
It maintained the fused areas by continually consuming highly concentrated metal ions. The colony built a powerful defensive line through this individual.
When fused metal came loose, it ate nearby refuse to form a new metal layer. Its body weight gradually increased in the process.
It served as a royal guard directly under the Great King. It wielded the colony's greatest combat power and took no orders from other individuals.
It blocked every attack with thick metal armor while charging with its massive body. After the charge, it shook its body to scatter nearby metal fragments.

If field personnel installed a high-power electromagnetic pulse generator, the fused metal overheated and its movement slowed by 40%. On failure, its charge struck the field personnel's position, rupturing nearby sewers and releasing contaminated water. The success signal was superheated vapor rising from its metal armor.

It temporarily retreated if its continual pain from the fusion process was acknowledged and particular metal waste was provided. But if refused, the entire royal guard attacked human facilities and cut off the power supply.
It performed its role as an elite in G01-SC2.
Common species, variants and command scope
The Venom King 'Deadly Tusk' was an elite battlefield mutant born of venom secretion and metal fusion. It was a famed boss, not the biological king of all wild boars.
Powerful venom saturated its enormous tusks. Glands around its mouth continually coated the tusk surfaces with venom.
It was a top-tier combatant born from the crossbreeding of a venom secreter and a metal-fusion mutant. Records from G01-SC3 show that it served as the colony's final line of defense.
It established its own territory in the deepest sewers where poison and metal coexisted. Other individuals detected the poisonous smell and kept their distance.
It maintained the venom on its tusks by consuming toxic substances and metal ions together. Through this individual, the colony secured its strongest combat power.
When the balance of poison and metal broke down, it ate nearby refuse to find a new balance. In the process, the venom coating on its tusks grew thicker.
It served as the Great King's closest aide. It judged independently and led the colony's final defense and attacks.
It stabbed enemies with venom-soaked tusks while spraying venom. Then it summoned the nearby colony for a coordinated attack.

If field personnel used top-grade protective suits and powerful antidote injectors together, they completely neutralized the venom. On failure, venom entered the bloodstream, incapacitating personnel within 2 turns and poisoning nearby citizens en masse. The success signal was a drop of neutralized venom falling from its tusk.

It was a being living in extreme pain. If responders established empathy and provided particular chemical waste, it cooperated. But refusing negotiation put all of southern Seoul at risk of contamination from a full colony assault led by the Venom King.
It appeared as a boss-level threat in G01-SC3.
Former role class: environmental stronghold type
Common species, variants and command scope
The ironclad nest 'Steel Wetland' was a living place where the Great King's bodily fluids fused with accumulated mud and metal. It was not an individual but a fixed stronghold in the deep sewers.
It was the Great King's dwelling and the center of the entire colony. A living metal-and-mud composite structure slowly expanded along the surrounding sewer pipes.
Colony structures accumulated over decades fused with the Great King's bodily fluids to become a living fortress. From G01-SC1 onward, this structure became the foundation of the colony's survival.
It took root at the center of the largest flood zone in the lower Han River. It widened its territory by continually absorbing the surrounding mud and metal debris.
It was supplied with the resources gathered by the entire colony. The structure itself absorbed metal to grow, providing the colony with a stable home.
When part of it was damaged, every nearby individual was mobilized for the repairs. As the Great King's bodily fluids were supplied, the structure regenerated faster.
As the colony's heart, it was instinctively protected by every individual. Vibrations arising inside the structure coordinated the behavior of the entire colony.
The fortress itself set off traps and activated self-defense organs. As the threat level rose, it mobilized the entire colony to surround intruders.

If the field personnel injected an acidic solvent into the core of the structure, the internal metal-and-mud bonds weakened and the fortress's functions fell by 50%. On failure, the fortress sealed every surrounding sewer pipe and flooded the whole of underground southern Seoul. The success signal was rusty foam rising from the surface of the structure.

It was the ecological center of the colony. Its destruction would collapse the entire sewer system of southern Seoul. In G01-SC1 through SC3 it became the point of key negotiations and moral choices. If negotiation was refused, the fortress mobilized the entire colony to occupy human settlements permanently.
It became the final stage in all of G01-SC1, G01-SC2, and G01-SC3.
Former role class: environmental stronghold type
Common species, variants and command scope

The fortress "Mud Ironwall" was a mud-and-rebar wall hardened on the slope outside the Sluice State's sluice gate. The sows read its dull tremor as the sealing hour, and the solitary males ignored it.

On the waste slope outside the Sluice State stood a wall in which mud and rebar had hardened into one body. Each time the sluice opened, the wall drank water and piled up decaying organic matter and salt crust inside, and it caught approaching footsteps in its mud, becoming both a storehouse and a capture trap.

After the first hoofprint of G01-SC1 was stamped at the collection yard, sow families packed mud onto the sluice apron again and again, and the wall's framework grew. Rebar left by the flood and salt from the cooling waste of the Yeouido Computing House seeped into the mud, and the wall became a storage organ that would not collapse.

It was rooted in the lowest slope of the flood zone and drew in water with a breath that matched the opening-and-closing cycle. In the dry season it held out by licking the salt layer inside, and in monsoon weeks its face pushed outward a handspan at a time, narrowing the drainage channel.

It concentrated inside the wall the food the family groups brought and the salt that flowed out of the recovery tank. If this concentration stopped, the wall could no longer hold water and the downstream pumps overheated that same night, and excessive concentration raised the foraging pressure on the alleys.

Cracked sections were filled by the adults with saliva and mud, and only one new layer was added per monsoon. The day's scouting and bathing shrank by as much labor as the adding took, and the center of the hierarchy gathered at the wall.

The dull tremor the wall gave off told the family groups the sealing hour. The sows began moving only after the tremor died down, and the solitary males ignored it and brushed past along the same slope.

When one drain was clogged with mud, the pump noise changed first. By day, as the water receded, part of the wall shed iron fragments as if collapsing and closed the inspection passage, and on nights when the water level passed the warning line, the wall's tremor drew the family groups up toward the stairs.

The drain outside the sluice stayed clogged with mud while four pumps overheated within the same opening-and-closing cycle. If the duty crew could not push solvent into the hairline cracks of the wall in the gap when the water level dropped a handspan, the wall grew another layer and locked the downstream worksite that same night. When a crack opened, steam smelling of rust leaked from the gap and the dull tremor died down.

One person on duty held only the authority to cut one section of the wall during the night shift to open a water passage. In a week when the recovery of the G01-SC2 salt pool had been moved up, that one section burst the storehouse and pushed the family groups into the semi-basement alleys. Leaving the section as it was let the pump station hold, but the wall drank water at every sealing hour and the ration convoy grew longer. Mud once split could not be rejoined in the same monsoon.

G01-SC1 recorded that the wall's first layer of mud was attached on the same night as the hoofprints at the collection yard. In G01-SC2 and G01-SC3, salt storage and the occupation of the sluice stairs overlapped with this wall as their stage.
Common species, variants and command scope

The larva 'Tender Ironhide' is a soft-bodied offspring of the Great King's bloodline that fills the pipes through sheer numbers. Its nursery inside the wall overlaps with the sow families' territory, but once its shell closes, it moves into the mutant transport line.

The newest young of the Great King's line still had soft backs, and the pink skin of their 1.5-meter bodies lay exposed. At the edge of the bathing ground they drew metal ions in through their skin and made a thin shell in a fortnight, and ankles passing through the drainage channel were caught by those soft bodies.

They came out all at once from a single litter of a sow just after the G01-SC1 flood receded. A warm, humid section inside the storage wall became that litter's nursery, and the individuals that grew up scattered toward scouting and hauling.

They spent the day in a warm mud chamber inside the wall and came out to look for metal fragments on the slope only on nights of urgent growth. In the dry season the chamber leaned on the salt layer, and in the monsoon the chamber entrance opened into a waterway that pushed the larvae out as far as the pipe entrance.

Covering their soft skin required highly concentrated decaying matter and salt at the same time. Part of the ions they absorbed was offered to the wall to enlarge the storehouse, and when ions dwindled, the nursery temperature fell and the next litter stopped growing.

Every fortnight their skin changed its sheen and put on another layer of shell. Torn places were filled with bodily fluid flowing from the wall, and once the shell was complete, the individual moved to the adult hauling line.
