The larvae followed only the sows and the wall's tremor. Once their shells closed they rose to the subadult post in charge of the forward feeding ground, and until then they only filled the slope with their numbers.

At first the young bodies gathered on the pipe floor and soaked the steps of passersby. After their shells opened thinly, they tried short charges with iron fragments stuck to their bodies, and when they returned to the nursery, empty cells in the wall were filled by as many as their number and the detour disappeared.

When the metallic sheen of the larvae's skin halted for a second day, that cluster could not widen the pipe. A short burst of high frequency run along the edge of the bathing ground disturbed only their growth rhythm. If the rhythm stayed as it was, the same drainage channel filled with young a fortnight later and the alley detour grew longer.

When the hoofprints at the G01-SC1 collection yard became visible, the recovery tank and a sow faced each other over the same scent bait. Pulling the bait back toward the wetland kept the larvae inside the wall for another fortnight, but the night ration came one meal late. Taking the sow on the spot sent the scent of her young around the alleys for 48 hours, and that window opened and closed within a day.

G01-SC1 opened the moment when larval hoofprints were stamped among those at the collection yard. The salt exhaustion of G01-SC2 slowed the forming of shells, and the crowding on the stairs in G01-SC3 led to scenes of young bodies caught between people's feet.
Common species, variants and command scope

The adult 'Rusty Ironplate' is the transport workhorse of an ordinary family group, clad in rusty iron plates across its 3-meter body. Despite the aging label, it is a working adult and enters the same tunnel only after the sow sets out.

Rusted iron plates encircled its fully grown 3-meter trunk, and those plates scraped the walls of the sewer tunnels as it hauled salt crust and organic matter. In the middle of the hauling line, its tusks pushed at the sidewalk rebar and briefly folded up the human path.

Adults that held out in the early wetlands of G01-SC1 piled metal on their backs and took this form. One body served for both labor and brief clashes, and it entered the same tunnel only after the sow's movement had begun.

It made its bed in the tunnels of the middle flood level, and in dry-season weeks it went back and forth almost only along the wall. On monsoon nights a hauling route opened between the salt pool and the slope, and that route overlapped with the alley drainage.

To keep up its iron plates it ate metal and decaying matter together and passed the surplus salt to the wall and the larvae. When the Cheongram recovery tank collected the pool early, the plates crumbled and a week's hauling volume fell by half.
Scraped plates were brought back to the wall and stuck on with bodily fluid. Because scouting went empty on the nights of this work, the family groups did not use that time as a movement window.

It took the sow's departure and the wall's tremor and told the subadults their order in the tunnel. The solitary males did not follow this order and crossed paths with the adult line at the same feeding ground.

When the sound of metal rang at the tunnel entrance, the day's hauling had begun. When the sound rose to the sidewalk, iron fragments flew up and blocked the water-supply inspection covers, and when several adults gathered at the same bend, the water pressure of the morning ration dropped.

At the hour when an adult came out of the tunnel carrying salt crust on its back, the electromagnetic pulse of a recovery-tank cart met it at the same bend. When the pulse grazed its body, flakes of rust fell away in a seagull pattern. If the cart was a beat late, its tusks pushed the sidewalk rebar and the water-supply hose was pulled out overnight.

The sluice government, the Cheongram recovery tank, and the alley delegates sat down together to divide up the adults' hauling nights. Leaving the salt pool in the wetland tied the watch crew to that spot for a season, and clearing only the alley food waste first made the adults open a path into another semi-basement. The price G01-SC2 left behind was not carcasses but to which door the watch labor moved.

The price of the G01-SC2 pool showed in the thickness of the adults' iron plates. The hoofprint record of G01-SC1 and the occupation of the stairs in G01-SC3 left the points where this hauling line overlapped with human routes.
Common species, variants and command scope

The coexisting form 'Peaceful Ironhide' occupies the edge of the family group. Its flexible ironhide selects only the scents from the waste shelf. If collections are missed for two weeks, its back hardens and it opens covers like a wild adult.

The individual that moved only on the outskirts of human zones had thin, pliant iron hide and could pick out the smells on the waste shelves. With the permission of the wall and the sow it went back and forth near the drainage-channel covers, and the sight of it choosing metal fragments from the shelves remained in the patrol records.

It was a form that appeared after the leftover-food convoys were diverted into a bait corridor in G01-SC3. Once it steadily received waste chosen by people, its body adapted to collection instead of attack.

It stayed at the drainage channels with shelves between the wetland and the alleys. It checked the shelves in time with the sealing hour, and on days when they were empty it withdrew deep toward the wall.

Sorted metal and a small amount of salt were this individual's staple food. While the supply continued, the colony's pressure on the alleys eased, and when it was cut off, the same body opened covers like a wild adult.

It lived by carving the shelf cycle into its body rather than by breeding. When the cycle was kept its iron hide stayed pliant, and when two weeks went empty its back hardened and was fitted for charging instead of camouflage.
It took only the sow's direct signals and did not share routes with the other adults. On nights when the shelf was stocked it remained in the peaceful tier and took the edge of resource distribution.

While the shelf was kept, even warning calls were rare. Three days after the collection rounds stopped, its back hardened and it took over the drainage channel, and at the next sealing hour the family groups stamped muddy footprints through that cover all the way to the alley kitchens.

Stocking the waste shelf to the same weight at the same hour every week kept the thin iron hide from hardening. Then a low rumble carried on without a break from the wetland side. When the shelf stood empty for two weeks its skin thickened, and the same body opened the cover and pushed muddy water as far as the drinking-water valve.

Placing sorted metal fragments on the shelf was a duty without a signature for the households on the outskirts. If that shelf was stocked before the evacuation leftovers of G01-SC3 piled up on the stairs, the symbiotic form withdrew toward the wall. If even one household skipped a collection round, the window for reversal shrank to the next sealing hour, and that household's water-supply hose took in mud first.

The passage-rights agreement of G01-SC3 was kept or broken by the weight of this shelf. G01-SC1 and G01-SC2 could be read as the history, left in this individual's pliant iron hide, of the feeding-ground movements before the shelf existed.
G01E15 · Flood Boar Boss 'Great King's Heir'
Common species, variants and command scope

The boss 'Great King's Heir' is a large female of the bloodline that will succeed to the armored king's place. She holds several family groups in one column. She is a distinct mustering individual on the battlefield; solitary males remain outside her column.

The heir who would take the place of the E01 Great King had a 5-meter back close to the thickness of the storage wall and held several family groups in a single column with a low call. On nights when the flood level rose, she came out of the deepest storage section and made the sluice stairs her stage.

The largest female line that survived the G01-SC2 salt crisis grew into the heir. She became the body that rearranged the order of movement in seasons short of energy, setting the time of the western Han River wetlands to her own call.

She stayed in the deepest salt section of the wall, and when a water-level warning came up she crossed the entire tunnel in one move. In ordinary times she barely moved, and even on Hannuri's heat-source display she was caught only as a single mass.

She ate a great deal of resources but shared the surplus salt and decaying matter back out to the family groups. When the sharing stopped, the heir's call rang hollow, the herd scattered into the alleys, and the area of harm on the citizens' side widened.

She rubbed the Great King's memory of movement into the grooves of her back and filled the grooves with her subordinates' iron fragments. When the filling went too far, the subadults' scouting went empty and the escape route in the next flood came late.

She gave the departure signal after the Great King fell asleep. The sows aligned their columns to that signal, and as it overlapped with the wall's tremor the gaps between families narrowed, leaving only the solitary males outside the column.

There were nights when her low call alone drove back the scouting crews. When the call meshed with the trap sections of the wall, iron fragments poured down all at once, and at hours when the water level and the evacuation leftovers coincided, the heir filled the southern stairs in a single column.

Even as the flood level began to swallow the sluice stairs, the heir's low call held the family groups in a single column. The scouting crew set up a frequency screen at the seam where the storage wall met her back armor. When the screen covered the seam, the mass of heat broke apart into family units, and when it missed, the evacuation column met the hooves on the same stairs.

Even after Hannuri had marked a single large heat source, the human scouting crew could push that marker aside and separate the family groups from the solitary males. On a night when the evacuation time of G01-SC3 overlapped, pushing the marker delayed the heir's muster and briefly emptied the stairs, and trusting the marker as it stood let the herd take its place first, following the smell of the leftovers. The postponed evacuation turn was borne by the last row of the column bound for Imjin.

The flood line of G01-SC3 used the same timetable as the heir's mustering call. The first hoofprints of G01-SC1 and the salt price of G01-SC2 were the first part of the departure rules this body inherited.
Common species, variants and command scope

The variant 'Bukhansan Ironplate' belongs to an upstream family with ridge moss growing on its back. It responds only faintly to the Great King's call, and its own sow initiates movement along the hiking trail.

The body adapted to the foot of Bukhansan and the Anyangcheon corridor had moss and grass stuck in the gaps of its armor, the same color as the slope. It went back and forth between the abandoned rail embankment and the wetland, rising from the grassy shade to cut off the trail.

During the G01-SC1 flood, some families were pushed upstream and planted plant fibers in their backs. They lived to a rhythm different from the downstream storage wall, and when drought came they went back down toward the sluice and thickened the main herd.

By day they clung to the ridge wetlands and the areas around abandoned railroad ties and held out through their daytime activity by photosynthesis. At the end of the dry season, moving along Anyangcheon in search of downstream salt became a necessity.
Besides decaying matter, the sugars the moss made became supplementary food. When the moss burned in a drought, the variant families' hauling stopped and the downstream storehouse thinned as well.
Symbiotic plants covered scraped armor and helped it regenerate. When polluted water rose onto the ridge, the moss died, their backs lay exposed, and the camouflage broke.
On the ridge their own sow opened each movement, and they answered the Great King's call only faintly. Only on nights when they went downstream did they mix information with the wall's tremor.

A body rising from the mossy shade blocked the trail in one move. Within the same week plant sap mixed into the valley water and changed the smell at the intake, and when the family joined the downstream herd, the night hoofprints on the sluice stairs were stamped with bits of ridge moss mixed in.

A back whose moss had burned away was already exposed like a lump of iron before it went downstream. A trail keeper soaked only the symbiotic seams with solvent. When the soaked strip reached beyond the ridge, the variant family came down along Anyangcheon and added a layer to the storage wall outside the sluice.

The quarantine strip written down once in spring carried over unchanged into the next year until one side broke it. Keeping the strip left the trail on the Bukhansan side empty by day, and pushing it aside to open the junction with the downstream herd added the variant's camouflaged charge to the flood line of G01-SC3. The cost fell separately on the weekend hikers of the ridge and the duty crew of the downstream pumps.

The upstream evacuation of G01-SC1 was the reason this variant settled on the ridge. The salt drought of G01-SC2 and the converging flood of G01-SC3 turned on whether the quarantine strip was kept or broken.
After the water of the western Han River split the embankments from the green axis, a night order unlike the one before took hold in the wetlands outside the Sluice.

The wild boar family groups that came down from the Bukhansan and Anyangcheon corridors crossed the severed green belts of Yeouido and Yeongdeungpo and settled at the food-waste collection yards and waste slopes, and from the cooling-waste heaps sealed by HC01 Yeouido Computing House they drew the salt to last the winter.
After floods the wild boar came down into the semi-basement alleys to root through trash bags and shallow root crops.

Urban incursions, shifts in food sources, and severed movement routes could be explained by real wildlife observation, but the behavior of remembering the sealing hours and the sluice operating cycle to time an approach, and the managed relationship with HC01, were a fictional order that arose only in this region after the collapse.
The territory of the Wild Boar was set less by lines drawn on a map than by a continuity of water level and smell.

The core habitat was the wetland and waste slopes outside the sluices of the Sluice, and in the dry season and winter they moved along the cut green belts toward the Government of the Republic of Korea at central Seoul Station and along the axis of night-market leftovers.
When refugee columns pushed down from the XT01 Imjin River Gate Theater, the food traces left on the northwestern roads became new corridors.
When the flood level crossed the warning line, the lowland family groups climbed all at once to the upland stairs and overlapped with human walkways.
This movement was not a march to attack the city but a choice to seek food and dry ground together, yet the semi-basement residents and sluice workers could not easily feel that difference.
The economy they relied on consisted of organic food waste, salt, and shallow root crops.

Soft plastics and coolant pools also served as secondary resources, and the droppings left after feeding nourished the wetland microbial mats and the downstream vegetation, making feeding grounds again.
When HC01 delayed sealing its collection tanks, family groups crowded onto a single spot, and when it tightened the seals too far, the herd turned toward the household alleys.
Unlicensed hunting for meat and hide left immediate food and trade goods, but it scattered the survivors and distorted even the passage-safety records.
Because a measure meant to protect civilian rations could increase food raids in vulnerable alleys, the cost of this ecology always moved to someone else's doorstep.
Before the monsoon, the family groups split up, one to each sow with young, to scout feeding grounds and escape routes.
Right after a flood they briefly joined the upland food axis, but they did not become one great herd.
When an adult female began to move, the subadults scouted ahead, and the lone males used the same feeding grounds without following that decision.
When the central female disappeared, the family group swept the same area over and over for about 48 hours, following the scent of the young and the sows, and then scattered.

Only when the survival rate of the young stayed high for two seasons in a row did a family group split, and when winter salt sources and mud wallows ran short, it chose long-range movement over breeding.
They could learn the fence positions and sealing hours of the moment, but that was not a long-term change in the body.
Nocturnal activity and the avoidance of people could persist over several generations, and heavy trapping backfired by removing the boldest animals first and leaving only the more secretive lines.
Yet the more secretive they became, the longer it took them to find food, and the slower their young grew.

Through their hooves and the ground, the Wild Boar read the opening and closing of the sluices and the low-frequency vibration of vehicle generators, and judged by layering the smell of food over the smell of human disinfectant.
At close range they also responded to warmth and air currents carried on the wind, but they could not precisely tell distant heat sources apart or work out the meaning of electronic noise.
H01 Hannuri only compared and marked the infrared masses that looked like people, generators, or family groups; it was not the final judge.

In heavy wind and rain or thick cooling fog, the thermal images blurred and a lone male and subadults looked like a single cluster, so a human scouting team had to confirm the escape routes and the traces of young first.
When a family group was mistaken for a single hostile group and its central female was removed, two days of unpredictable searching behavior filled the place of the vanished order.
The crisis grew in three stages.
At first only the night hoofprints multiplied at the collection yards and unauthorized plots outside the sluice, and contact with people was rare.
Next the drainage ditches, the sealing tape, and the water-inspection passages were damaged, and the food convoys and sluice maintenance fell behind.
At the last, flood levels and refugee leftovers coincided and the family groups took over the sluice stairs.
Noise barriers and flashes could briefly drive back the scouts in front, but for the main body food detours, relocated salt pools, and route fencing worked better.
Removal led by firearms scattered the family groups into every alley and increased the harm to civilians, so it remained only a last resort.
The success of a response was judged not by the number of carcasses but by the reduction in collection-yard intrusions, the time to reopen passage, and alley damage.
G01-SC1 ‘The First Hoof Outside the Sluice’ began when the prints of a sow and her young appeared at the Sluice collection yard on the day before the monsoon forecast.
The family group remembered the sealing hours and approached in the gaps when the sluice vibration stopped.
The Sluice and HC01 could avoid contact by delaying night operations, but civilian rations were delayed with them.
Opening a wetland detour with scent bait cost labor and resources at once but could create a long-term movement axis.
Trapping only the sow looked fastest, but H01 then recorded, for the next 48 hours, the heat sources of the young returning again and again in search of her.
The judgment in that moment meant putting people's mealtimes and the survival time of a family group with young on the same table.
In G01-SC2 ‘The Price of the Salt Pool,’ HC01 moved up its collection of cooling waste, and the herd then shifted its feeding grounds to the semi-basement alleys toward central Seoul Station.
It came to light that removing the salt source did not make the family groups disappear but pushed them into a more dangerous living sphere.
Leaving a managed pool in the wetland held the danger in one place but meant accepting the cost of continuous watch.
Putting alley food collection first reduced the harm to residents but left other rations and maintenance labor short.
Lowering density through hunting permits gave clear short-term results but strengthened the survivors' learned avoidance of people and their night intrusions.
Whichever choice was made, there was no escaping responsibility for whether to leave a controlled danger in a safe zone or to shift the burden onto a less visible vulnerable zone.
G01-SC3 ‘Passage Rights on the Flood Line’ broke out when the leftovers of the XT01 refugee column and the rising flood level drew people and family groups onto the same sluice stairs.
Splitting the evacuation times reduced direct clashes, but those whose turn came late had to endure the water and the dark longer.
Diverting the leftover convoys into a bait corridor could lead the herd toward the wetland, but it used up HC01's transport resources and sealed containers.
Opening the sluice first to create a brief high water had a chance of hastening the move, but it could flood the downstream workshops in advance.
So the agreement HC01 brokered bound together the food sealing hours, a night passage window, a cultivation buffer strip, and separate collection of the XT01 leftovers.
Extermination was not the goal, and choosing coexistence meant threat reports never fully disappeared.
In exchange, wetland purification, downstream vegetation, and the working routes of the sluice laborers could be kept.
Negotiating with the Wild Boar was less a promise to tame the wild than a contract limiting human desire and convenience so that the two sides' timetables did not overlap.
Long-term management depended on joint patrols in which S01, HC01, and the semi-basement residents redrew the boundaries of food and passage every season.

Before the monsoon they recorded each sow's prints and mud wallows without tagging, and after a flood they adjusted the night food-disposal hours and the positions of the managed salt pools so that the family groups did not lose their familiar escape routes.

The key indicators were alley intrusions per hundred nights, the time taken to clear the sluice stairs, the proportion of traces with young, the area of rooted-up ground, and the distance of human encounters by corridor, and carcass counts were kept only in the supplementary record.
Even if intrusions fell, a sharp drop in traces of young or shorter encounter distances were read not as stability but as trapping pressure and food shortage.

When a fence collapse or a mistaken capture scattered the family groups, pursuit and night collection stopped for 48 hours, water and salt were spread out in the directions where old droppings and prints remained, and the passage windows were then restored step by step.
Recovery was confirmed less by the return of the central female than by whether the young passed through the same corridor twice in a row and alley re-intrusions decreased.
When this procedure held for a long time, residents too came to put out food waste at set hours, which could reduce the rats' food sources and the damage to underground wiring.

Yet when hoof disturbance concentrated in predictable corridors, the reed belts thinned and the floating trash of the next flood reached the sluice intakes faster, a secondary cost, so even the safe coexistence zones had to be rested every few years and the detour wetlands opened in turn.
G01-SC1 · The First Hoof Outside the Sluice
Trigger: On the day before the monsoon forecast, the prints of a sow and her young appeared at the Sluice collection yard.
Ecological mechanism: A family group that has remembered the sealing hours approaches in the gap when the sluice vibration stops.
Choices: Delay the collection yard's night operation / Open a wetland detour with a scent lure / Capture only the sow
Outcomes: The operating delay slows the ration, and the detour builds a long-term movement axis. Capturing the sow triggers 48 hours of searching behavior.
Moral cost: The citizen ration and the survival of a family group with young are weighed on the same timetable.
G01-SC2 · The Price of the Salt Pool
Trigger: When HC01 brings the cooling-waste recovery forward, the band shifts its feeding ground to the semi-basement alleys.
Ecological mechanism: Removing the salt source does not disperse the family groups; it pushes them into the more dangerous feeding grounds of the lived-in quarter.
Choices: Leave a managed salt pool / Prioritize alley scrap recovery / Lower the density with a hunting permit
Outcomes: The pool fixes the cost of coexistence, and prioritizing recovery takes labor away from other rations. Hunting strengthens the remaining individuals' learned avoidance of people.
Moral cost: Decide whether to keep the danger inside a safe zone and manage it, or to pass the danger on to a vulnerable alley.
G01-SC3 · Right of Passage on the Flood Line
Trigger: The leftovers of the XT01 refugee column overlap the rising flood level, and the band occupies the sluice stairs.
Actors: S01, S06, XT01, HC01, H01
Ecological mechanism: The instinct to move to high ground and the scrap traces of the refugees concentrate the band on the same passage.
Choices: Split the evacuation times / Turn the leftover convoy into a lure corridor / Open the sluice first and use a short high water to induce the band to move
Outcomes: Splitting the times slows the evacuation, and the lure corridor consumes HC01 resources. Opening the sluice early is fast, but it can flood the downstream works first.
Moral cost: The fastest human evacuation and the long-term ecological stability of the sluice collide with each other.

G02.selector: p, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, blockquote, pre, li, th, td

leaves.text: At the factory pylons of Daerim and Garibong, the roofs of the Yeongdeungpo Line Gauge, and the overhead-wire junctions of the Wangsimni Union, breeding pairs of large-billed crows and non-breeding communal roosts overlapped. They fed on night insects and leftover market protein, and stripped fine wire and fibers went into their nests. They learned horns, inspection bells, and transformer start-up sounds as food or danger, but they did not read the content of the radio waves.

The base form of the Large-billed Crow is a wild bird that moves by the sound shapes it has learned. The Residual-Tower Cross-Iron Tone and the bridge inspection-hatch cylinder are not birds but place mechanisms made by repeated wind and lamps, and the Simultaneous Circle is a temporary phenomenon in which several families gather in one circle. The Shore-Feather Perch is a regional branch of the same species tuned to the sea wind and the breakwater bell, not a different being that deciphers transmissions.

After breeding pairs settled on the factory pylons of the Daerim–Garibong Korean-Chinese corridor and the cables of the Han River bridges, the Large-billed Crow formed as the waste heat of the Yeongdeungpo Line Gauge factories and the sparks of the Guro industrial-park trolley wires gathered night insects. / Real-world sources supported only the breeding-season territorial behavior of large-billed crows and the range of human responses; the rule by which they learned signal interference as alarms and spread it was fiction.

The core habitat is the group of factory roofs and pylons at Daerim and Guro on the Yeongdeungpo Line. / Arc 1 sits on top of the Daerim and Garibong Joseonjok corridor, and in the breeding season the flock circles over bridges, school passages, and evacuation stairs. / In the non-breeding season, matching the sea wind and the insect density pushed in from the West Sea Granary Theater (XT02), it moves for a time to the western waterfront. / When wire-repair work begins, part of the band moves along the work basket.

The food is insects, leftover market protein, and small carcasses, and for nest material they pick fine wire with the sheath stripped and fiber scrap. / The shorter the cycle on which the Sinjeong Wheel House (HC02) replaces wire sheathing, the less nest material there is and the more territorial attacks increase, and leaving the sheathing untended increases the risk of a short. / The cycle in which droppings contaminate the insulators connects directly to communications uptime.

In spring a breeding pair defends one pylon, and in the non-breeding season several families join a communal roost. / Repeated safety signals and food rewards, more than nest success, decide the return site the next year, and after a forced removal the young individuals test a new roost on the adjacent school route.

By sight they read helmets, rods, and flashlight reflections, and by hearing they distinguish the order of high-voltage noise, horns, and the crying of infants. / They do not decipher the content of an electronic signal; they connect the sounds of sparks and transformers to the appearance of insects and workers as a cue. / Seorin (H02) records the source of a sound shape and the number of repetitions, but whether it is a real alarm is checked by a person against the marks on site.

A breeding pair divides nest defense and the carrying of food, and the young helper individuals join the alarm calls and the dives. / A communal roost in the non-breeding season shares only sound shapes and has no command structure. / H02 records nest radius, flight direction, and call order separately, and the human control officer of HC02 decides only whether to stop the work. / When one breeding individual disappears, the adjacent pair tests the empty roost and territorial collisions increase.

Sound shapes repeated like three horns, two inspection bells, and a steady transformer start-up are socially learned as food and danger signals and spread at the communal roost. / When the signal changes, false alarms increase for several days, and the flock learns again through a new reward rule. / No genetic change is set, and the more specialized they become in a familiar sound shape, the later they react to an unfamiliar real alarm.

Only the spring breeding pairs divide and hold the upper and lower parts of one tower, and a non-breeding roost has no commander. They read helmet outlines, rod angles, and flashlight reflections with the eye, and they separate high-voltage noise and the order of horns by ear. The name sovereign is closer to a nickname for the breeding pair that gathers horn imitations, and when one side empties, the adjacent pair only tests the empty place.
G02E05 · Radio Crow Fine-Wire Weaver 'Sheathing Hand'
G02E06 · Radio Crow Spark Forager 'Insect Neck'
G02E07 · Radio Crow Insulator Fouler 'White Rim'
G02E08 · Radio Crow Breeding Defender 'Paired Radius'
G02E09 · Radio Crow Sound-Pattern Core 'Mixed Bells'
G02E10 · Radio Crow Remnant-Tower Organ 'Crossbeam Tone'
G02E11 · Radio Crow Bridge Cylinder 'Inspection Hollow'
G02E13 · Radio Crow Elder Vocal Type 'Startup Sound'
G02E14 · Radio Crow Coexistence Roost 'Flag Altitude'
G02E15 · Signal Crow Bridge Convergence 'Synchronized Circle'
G02E16 · Signal Crow Sea-Wind Variant 'Shore-Feather Perch'
Common species, variants and command scope

The broadcast crow lord 'Signal King' is the breeding pair at the Sangam transmission tower, not the king of the leaderless roost. Its imitation of three horn blasts merely serves as the communal roost's evening clock.

The breeding pair at the top of the Sangam tower gathered sparks in their metal feathers and held a horn imitation in their whole bodies. At dusk, when that imitation spread over the factory roofs, the dark bodies of the communal roost leaned in one direction and the flock swarmed over the work basket.

Even before G02-SC1, factory waste heat and catenary sparks drew insects, and a pair claimed the tower. After they memorized three horn blasts as the promise of food, the whole roost began to divide the evening sky over Seoul Station by that pattern.

They clung by day to the roofs of the Gauge on the Yeongdeungpo Line and the tops of disused railway towers, and flew far only at night. Outside the breeding season the roost shared only call patterns without a leader, so this pair's pattern became the temporary clock of the communal roost.

Insects, small carcasses, and the heat left by sparks were the pair's fare. When the pattern weakened, the flock could not cover the basket and daytime roof work became easier, but insects stayed in the inspection openings instead and drew the next sparks.
They changed their metal feathers every season and filled the gaps with fine wire their subordinates carried in. When the filling was clumsy, the imitation split and the roost divided into two beats.

In the breeding season the pair divided nest defense and food hauling between them, and young helpers joined the dives. The nonbreeding roost had no leader, so this pair's horn imitation alone became the center of repeated learning.

When the horn imitation mixed with the inspection bell, the workers' helmets were the first to lose direction. That same evening the flock came down on the basket and scattered the tools, and after the third horn blast the sky over the bridge was bound into a single call pattern, tangling the basket and the schoolchildren's umbrellas in the same wind.

Fitting a reverse-phase noise generator to the base of the tower threw the horn imitation gathered by the ruling pair one beat off. On that missed beat the flock tore into two branches in midair. If the generator came later than the third horn blast, the work basket was covered with claws all the same, and the day shift put off the roof work by a day.

Whether to publish the three-blast pattern in the work log or keep it as a call known only to the roof watch was borne by the day-shift foreman. A published pattern was memorized by the communal roost overnight and could not be taken back, and if it was hidden, a new shift worker called the expectation of food down onto the same basket. G02-SC1 also recorded the price of the human safety call going empty for several days while that pattern was retired.

The three horn blasts of G02-SC1 became, through this pair's bodies, the clock of the whole roost. The misclassification of G02-SC2 and the convergence at the bridge in G02-SC3 left behind the nights when that clock overlapped with human calls.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

The scout 'Shadowwing' is a stealthy observer that counts only helmet outlines and cannot read electronic content. It passes its report to the breeding pair by call, providing coordinates for the afternoon dive.

The metal feathers of its thin wings scattered the surrounding light, so that when it clung between two buildings its shape was hard to see. Flying low at school commuting hours it read the lines of people by eye, and only after sunset did it pass their positions to the breeding pair by call.

It was one of a litter the ruling pair sent out on their first reconnaissance early in G02-SC1. Its stealth flight gave the roost an advantage in information, but it had no ability to read electronic content.

It darted between buildings and over disused tracks, only counting the lines while concealed by day and climbing to the top only for the night report. It had to fly clear of high-voltage noise to keep its concealment.

It pecked at small insects and scraps of insulation and offered its gathered position calls to the pair to keep the whole roost's feeding clock running. When the reconnaissance broke off, the dive coordinates went astray and only the school walls grew more dangerous.

Its wings were often torn in flights through narrow gaps and were regenerated by the call pattern at the tower top. When regeneration fell behind, the morning flight path went empty and the calls on the school side spread a day late.

Following the pair's instructions, it gathered only positions and did not share its flight path with the attacking and relaying individuals. The order of the reports made the information hierarchy within the roost.

There were mornings when it counted only helmet outlines while concealed. When fellow scouts gathered, they imitated the inspection bell together to confuse those below the wall, and when that imitation rose to the tower top, the afternoon dive headed for the right school gate.

If the reconnaissance coordinates crossed to the breeding pair before the school commuting hours ended, the afternoon dive was redrawn around the school wall. Hanging a visual screening cloth across the flight path between two buildings made the scattering feathers lose their own outline and cut off the daytime reports. If one wing flashed back the light briefly each time the cloth fluttered, the number of people taking the detour below the wall did not grow that day.

The school-commute marshal set the limit first: the screening cloth would be tested for only three days and taken down on the fourth morning. If the dives left the wall within those three days, the scout's calls stayed only on the tower side, and if the limit was exceeded, young individuals tried out a new roost on the stair handrails. In the week when the communal bridge roost of G02-SC3 opened, even those three days overlapped with the numbers of the umbrella procession.

The umbrella procession of G02-SC3 used the same wall as this scout's flight path. The horn learning of G02-SC1 and the call misclassification of G02-SC2 made the route by which the reconnaissance coordinates remained in the logs on the human side.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope
The attacker 'Ironbeak' is built to descend and split concrete joints. It dives only when the pair’s command and reconnaissance coordinates coincide, and it keeps its route separate from the relay’s.

Its metal beak split concrete joints, and its short wings gathered speed while dropping from roof height. After spotting the target railing from the top, it came down in one stroke and split the open walkway.

Amid the sparks and transformer noise of G02-SC1, the individuals with hard beaks took on the attacking role. Afterward, the physical pressure of the roost was counted by the number of this body's dives.

It waited on high roofs, and when coordinates came down it struck the catenary and the ground-level railings by turns. Because the difference in height was the force of the dive, daytime walking and night repairs used the same vertical line.

It passed the insects and protein gained after a dive to the roost, and made up the wear on its beak through the call pattern at the top. When dives missed and empty-handed returns grew, the breeding pair's feeding clock wavered.
Its beak wore down with every dive, and without regular regeneration it could not split joints. The number of regenerations it had received changed the order of attack within the roost.

It threw its body only when the pair's dive order and the reconnaissance coordinates coincided. It did not share its flight path with the relaying individuals, so its line of descent was drawn separately.

Right after the horn imitation, the first dive struck the railing. The shock of the beak widened the cracks and exposed the cable sheathing, and when fellow attackers kept to the same vertical line, the umbrellas in the school passage folded all at once and the waiting line stretched to the bridge entrance.

The dive collapsed into a glide before the concrete joint, and the tip of the beak only grazed the railing. This was the result of the bridge repair team hanging acoustic screens across the dive path at different heights. If a screen hung lower than the catenary, the beak tore the sheathing, leaving walking injuries and a season of short-circuit inspections.

On the roof where the horns of G02-SC1 called up the expectation of food, the bridge team and the Haeryun Mobile Gate left only a single lane as a dive corridor. Fixing the corridor until spring breeding kept the walkway open but made the work basket avoid that lane, and removing the lane meant the nest radius was redrawn only in the next breeding season. The corridor disappeared only when the two parties took down the markers together.
G02-SC1 supplied the trigger call pattern for the dive. The false-alarm weeks of G02-SC2 and the sea-wind breeding of G02-SC3 made the calendar on which the corridor markers had to be redrawn.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

The relay 'Linkfeather' is an echo-bodied bird that carries the inspection bell’s overtones to the next tower. It stays out of scout and attack flight paths; only the clarity of its echo determines which tower takes priority.

The radiating organ in its throat and the arrangement of its wings carried the overtones of the inspection bell on to the next tower. Its body went back and forth at the middle height of the towers, and when it clung near communications equipment, the echo of the bell came a beat early.
In G02-SC1, the individuals the ruling pair chose to send their call patterns far divided this relaying role among themselves. The time stability of the roost depended on the quality of their echoes.

It moved ceaselessly between the overhead-wire crossings of the Wangsimni Union's Junction and the factory towers, keeping to the best height. In weeks when the sheathing was replaced, that height overlapped with the work basket.
The strength it used for radiating came from the calls of the pair at the top. The clearer the echo, the more the flock's movements crowded into a single hour, tangling the inspection crew's routes.

It often corrected the angle of its feathers to match the overtones, and when they were torn, it clung to a neighboring relay and borrowed its angle to recover. An individual whose angle had collapsed was pushed back in the radiating order within the roost.
It did only the work of carrying the pair's call pattern and did not join the scouting or attack flight paths. The clarity of the echo decided the priority tower of the day.

When the overtones slipped slightly, the times in the work log wavered first. As the slippage grew, the flock settled on the wrong tower and wore itself out waiting for tools, and the amplified false echo bound even the neighboring roosts to the same bell, so that a single inspection bell emptied three towers at once.

Only the single inspection-bell overtone mimicked by the relay's throat organ was killed first. If the overtone remained, the next tower took down the work order from a false echo. The insulation inspection crew climbed an empty tower, and the main line's sheathing stayed stripped that same week.

Before the false outage classification of G02-SC2 sounded, the Haeryun Mobile Gate, the track workers of the Railway Successor State, and the alley bellkeeper left only one keeper of the relay roost. In a week when the keeper changed, the echo route of the inspection bell was moved by human hands, and if the hands went empty, the call attached itself again as an outage warning. A single wrong work order led to an insulation gap at another tower, and the track workers' shift bore that debt.
The false outage of G02-SC2 tested the echo quality of this relay. The horn pattern of G02-SC1 and the communal roost of G02-SC3 borrowed the same tower height in the week the keeper changed.
G02E05 · Radio Crow Fine-Wire Weaver 'Sheathing Hand'
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope
Fine-Wire Weaver 'Sheathing Hand' is a weaving body that coils stripped wire into a cup. It gives no orders; when the cup grows light, it starts by pulling screws from the railing.

In the roof gutters of the Gauge factories on the Yeongdeungpo Line lived a weaving body that pulled stripped fine wire with its beak and wound it into a cup. Its claws were worn from holding fiber scraps in place, and when the winding stopped, the breeding pair tore replacement material from the railings of the school passage and the morning commute grew longer.

In the spring when the Sinjeong Wheel House stripped the wire sheathing all at once, the scraps piled up in the roof gutters, and one individual began winding, remembering only the feel of copper and the elasticity of fiber. Unable to read the content of the radio waves, it kept only the pairing of glitter and softness, and that habit hardened into a fictional weaving labor.

By day it hid the cup in the shade of the brackets and came down to the edge of the sheathing only in the evening, when the work noise had died down. In the breeding season the cup moved to the windward side facing the bridge, and in weeks when the sea wind of the XT02 West Sea Granary Theater shook the fine wire, the low arm of the Nanji remnant tower became a temporary winding place.

Keeping up the nest required a palmful of stripped fine wire and fiber every week. When Haeryun moved the collection up, the material ran short and railings and sign posts were torn apart, and when the sheathing was left alone, the cup grew thick but the chance of a short circuit grew and the transmission minutes were cut.

When the outer loops came loose in the rain they were rewound that evening, and the inner loops were given only one added layer a season. By as much evening as the winding labor took away, insect gathering shrank, and the breeding pair of the same tower leaned more on leftover protein from the market.

The weaving gesture gave no orders, and when the cup grew light it moved first toward the material. The breeding pair adjusted its defense radius by watching that movement alone, and the young helpers only carried fiber in their beaks and never learned the winding order.

At first only the scraps in the roof gutters disappeared. When material ran short the screws came out of the school-route railings, and in weeks when the cup went empty even the sign posts were stripped, the number of people on the detour grew, and access for the basket became rougher.

When the fine-wire loops of the nest cup reached three turns in a week, the beak no longer tore at the school railings. If the replacement crew skipped the window in which a handful of scraps was deliberately left beside the cup, the loops met the morning unwound. When the cup was empty, the same beak pulled the screws from the sign posts on the school route and the daytime detour numbers grew.

One member of the sheathing replacement crew chose, only during the replacement week, whether to leave the fine-wire scraps beside the cup or collect them all. Leaving them let the railings hold, but the expectation of food that overlapped with the horns of G02-SC1 attached to the cup, and access for the basket grew rougher for another day. Sweeping up all the scraps lightened the work basket of G02-SC1, but the railing screws went missing first.

G02-SC1 recorded whether the window for leaving fine-wire scraps opened in the same week as the horn pattern. The false outage of G02-SC2 overlapped with the insulator fouling on towers where the cup was thick, and the sky over the bridge in G02-SC3 opened as a communal roost only after the winding place had moved to the railings.
G02E06 · Radio Crow Spark Forager 'Insect Neck'
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope

Spark Forager 'Insect Neck' is a foraging body that chases insects drawn by trolley-wire sparks and mistakes the backs of gloved hands for insects, pecking them. Even when the breeding pair begins its dives, it does not leave the crossing until the insect cloud disperses.

The gathering body that chased the night insects drawn by sparks at the catenary crossings of the Wangsimni Union's Junction had neck feathers scorched by ions. Its beak could not tell the backs of the gloves at the edge of the work basket from insects and pecked them, and those wounds pushed the welding shift back an hour.

When factory waste heat and overhead-wire sparks made clouds of insects every night, one individual learned the path of following the basket and picking up only the exposed bugs. It was not drawn to the equipment itself; it linked the repeated work noise, the scraps of sheathing, and the glitter of the bugs into a single line, and that line became the gathering role.

After sundown it circled only within twenty meters beneath the catenary, and by day it rested clinging to the shade of the crossing's steel poles. When the repair basket went up it compared that height with the insect lamps, and in weeks when the sea wind pushed the bugs out to the western waterside, it moved briefly to the lower chord of the bridge.

To keep gathering, the density of night insects had to be kept away from the height of the basket. Setting the lamps level with the basket tore gloves and wire sheathing together, and turning the lamps off sent the gathering body down toward the market's leftover protein, disrupting the unloading alleys.

Its scorched neck feathers were scrubbed dry in a sand bath the day after rain, and a broken crop grew anew within three days. If it chose its bathing place not in the catenary gravel but in the school playground, the daytime class bell mixed with its gathering memory, and misdirected approaches grew the next night.

The gathering individual did not direct the basket but followed only the height of the insect lamps. Even when the breeding pair opened a dive, this body did not leave the crossing before the cloud of bugs scattered, and the young helpers only picked up fallen insects and carried them to the nest.

On the first day only the bugs around the lamps grew fewer. When the lamps and the basket stayed at the same height, holes opened in the gloves, and when those holes went on for three days, the welding schedule slipped and the gathering route leaked toward the daytime walls.

If the insect lamp under the catenary sparks stayed at the same height as the basket, the gathering individual pecked the backs of the gloves first.
