Common species, variants and command scope

Sea-Wind Variant 'Shore-Feather Perch' is a waterside branch that remembers the breakwater bell and lighthouse first. It does not imitate inland horn sequences, and its space does not overlap with the bridge circle even on the same evening.

It was a regional variant, a sea-wind type that wove scraps of fiber and net into the disused towers on the western waterside and the breakwater railings. The edges of its beak were worn by salt, so it chose wet fiber over fine wire, and its eyes read the bands of insects carried on the sea wind and the glint of the breakwater lighthouse. It remembered the waves and the breakwater bell before the inland horn pattern, and knew nothing of the content of the radio waves or the insulation of the distant bridges.

It split off as part of the nonbreeding flock moved temporarily to the western waterside following the sea wind and insect density pushing in from the XT02 side. After young individuals whose city towers had been demolished took a disused tower on the Nanji shore as a test roost, the breakwater bell became a food reward and changed where they returned the next year.

Only in the dry and sea-wind weeks did it leave the Yeongdeungpo Line factory roofs and stay at the disused towers and breakwater railings of the western waterside. In the breeding season it did not return to the bridge circle but kept its shore roost, so even on the same evening as the inland merged circle, their spaces did not overlap.

Its food was insects driven in by the sea wind and leftovers from the waterside markets, and its nest material was fragments of net and wet fiber. Cutting off the inland sheathing did not reduce this variant, and moving the insect lamps to a disused tower made that tower a new feeding ground and base.

When the sea wind died down it emptied the shore roost and went back to the factory roofs, but when the breakwater bell repeated for a season it put off its return. If its salty feathers were not rinsed in fresh water the imitation split, and after a forced demolition it tried out new seats on the awnings of the neighboring fish market.

The shore roost had no leader either and shared only call patterns. It did not follow the horn imitation of the inland breeding pairs, and even when H02 raised a dive call as an outage warning, if the marker on site was the breakwater lighthouse, people sorted it out again. HC02 control decided only on halting waterside work and did not count the bridge circle together with this variant.

In the first stage it memorized the breakwater bell and the lighthouse blinking as food signals. In the second stage it gathered at a disused tower following the insect lamps and covered the waterside inspection basket. In the third stage, without a sea-wind-week flag, its test roosts spread to the fish-market awnings, and it made coastal walkers without school umbrellas the targets of its dives.

Inland umbrella processions folded in the coastal wind and had no effect, and drone pursuit pushed the variant into the fish-market alleys. Switching off the insect lamps and changing the breakwater bell to a beat different from the inspection bell shook its learning for a few days, and screening only the basket with a visual cloth without nets was the safer course. The measures of success were waterside short circuits, coastal walking injuries, and the false-alarm rate.

Leaving the insect lamps on the disused shore tower to protect the inland school routes made the waterside labor and the fish market bear the cost of a new base. Moving the lighthouse back to the city towers made the school railings test roosts again. The choice of hanging the temporary sea-wind-week flag only on the breakwater and moving only the net nests with relocation poles delayed the restoration of transmission, but did not sell children's passage and coastal livelihoods on the same evening.

The insect-lamp relocation of G02-SC2 made this variant's base, the sea-wind weeks of G02-SC3 grew its shore roost, and the retirement of the horns in G02-SC1 left the breakwater bell as its new feeding clock.

At dusk, black flocks settled tier upon tier on the factory pylons of the Daerim–Garibong Korean-Chinese corridor, the cables of the Han River bridges, and the industrial-park trolley wires of the Yeongdeungpo Line Gauge.

When the waste heat of the Yeongdeungpo Line Gauge factory roofs and the sparks of the overhead wires drew in night insects, the breeding pairs began to use these structures as both nest and feeding ground, and people called them the Large-billed Crow.
That large-billed crows guarded territories in the breeding season and adapted to human behavior rested on real ecology.

But the rule by which they learned the sequences of horns, inspection bells, and transformer start-up sounds as signals of food and danger and spread them through the communal roosts belonged to the fictional history of this place.
They did not read the content of the radio waves.
They only remembered the relationships repeated among sparks, sounds, and the appearance of workers.
The core territory was the factory roofs and pylon clusters of the Yeongdeungpo Line and the rail overhead-wire junctions of the Wangsimni Union.
In the spring breeding season they circled in rings centered on their nests above the bridges, school passages, and evacuation stairs, and dived when a helmet or a long pole came within the radius.

In the non-breeding season several families joined the communal roosts, and moved briefly to the western waterfront following the sea wind from the XT02 West Sea Granary Theater and the density of insects.

When wire repairs began, some birds followed the work baskets, not because they were drawn to the equipment itself but because they chased the exposed insects, scraps of insulation, and the repeated sounds of work.
Because of this, the separate human routes of school commutes, evacuation, and transmission inspection could all be blocked at once beneath a single pylon.
They fed on insects, protein left at the markets, and small carcasses, and stripped fine wire and scraps of fiber went into their nests.

When HC02 Sinjeong Wheel House replaced wire insulation often, the risk of short circuits and the supply of nest material both fell, but the breeding pairs that lost their material could tear at the railings and signs of the nearby school routes and step up their territorial attacks.
Conversely, when damaged insulation was left alone, the nest supply stabilized but the chance of short circuits and fire grew.
When droppings built up on the insulators, transmission uptime fell, and when maintenance crews came in the dives increased, so a cycle formed in which work stoppages let the fouling pile up again.
Because the benefit to one zone that drove the crows out moved on as danger to other bridges and residential alleys, simple removal alone could not erase the cost.
In spring the breeding pairs divided a single pylon between them to guard.
While one bird defended the nest and chicks, the other carried food, and young helpers joined in the alarm calls and dives.
The non-breeding communal roosts had no leader and shared only one another's sound patterns and reactions.

When one breeding bird vanished, neighboring pairs tested the empty roost and territorial clashes rose, and after forced removal the young made new places on nearby school passages or evacuation stairs.
What decided where they returned the next year was not only nest success but the safety signals and food rewards repeated there.

A familiar sequence such as three horn blasts or two inspection bells could spread through a whole communal roost within days, but this was social learning, not a bodily change passed through generations.
A flock grown too used to a particular sound pattern paid the price of reacting late to an unfamiliar real alarm.

They read the outline of a helmet, the angle of a pole, and the glint of a flashlight by sight, and by hearing they separated the order in which high-voltage noise, horns, and an infant's cry followed one another.
They did not know the technical meaning of a signal; they linked it to the experience that insects, food, workers, or a threat to the nest had appeared after a particular sound.
H02 Seorin recorded the source and repetition count of a sound pattern, the nest radius, the flight direction, and the order of calls separately.

But whether a dive call was the forerunner of a real short circuit or a feeding response to an insect lamp could be judged only when people checked the markings on site against the state of the insulation.

When automatic classification combined with the residents' old alarm customs, wrong judgments reinforced one another, and a single small false alarm could spread into a transmission shutdown and the closure of evacuation routes.
The interference of the Large-billed Crow first appeared as the collecting of sound patterns.
Scout birds mimicked horns and inspection bells from the pylons and railings, and carried the sounds tied to food back to the communal roost.
In the next stage, food signals and safety alarms became tangled, and dives at workers, school-route detours, and transmission stops followed one after another.

When false alarms piled up three times at the same inspection hatch, the maintenance hours, the inspection bells, and the residents' alarm customs had to be reset together instead of tearing out the nests.
Bending the route with sight-blocking cloth, umbrella columns, and alternative stairs was safer than pushing straight through.
Moving the insect-lure lamps and inspection bells to a different pylon could also separate the learned signals.
Gunfire and aerial pursuit drove the flock into residential alleys and left distrust of every alarm sound.
Results were measured not by the number of birds removed but by fewer short circuits, pedestrian injuries prevented, transmission uptime, and the false-alarm rate.
G02-SC1 ‘Three Horn Blasts’ began when a new horn sequence introduced by a Yeongdeungpo Line work crew overlapped with the feeding signal.
The crows that learned it at the communal roost swarmed the work baskets instead of withdrawing from the warning.
Scrapping the horn sequence reduced the birds' approach, but work slowed while a safety procedure familiar to people was built again.
Teaching a separate feeding signal could separate the two sound patterns in the long run, but meant accepting more false alarms for several days.
Moving the feeding to horn-free nights protected the daytime school routes, but passed the danger and fatigue on to the night workers.
HC02 and H02 could not judge which signal was more legitimate; they could only choose whether to change human habit or the birds' survival learning first.
In G02-SC2 ‘The False Blackout Alarm,’ H02 classified repeated dive calls as the forerunner of a blackout, but the real cause turned out to be a night insect lamp.

Because residents had long used the crows' calls as a cheap disaster alarm, machine classification and human custom confirmed one another and set off a chain of transmission stops on the Yeongdeungpo Line and in the Wangsimni Union.
Keeping transmission running until visual confirmation reduced needless stoppages but left the risk of missing a real short circuit.
Moving the insect lamp to a disused pylon untangled the present confusion, but that pylon then had to be recognized as a new feeding ground and ecological base.
Dropping the crow alarm from the control network entirely reduced malfunctions, but the residents' watch network that had first noticed intruders and equipment faults disappeared with it.
The cost of keeping inaccurate alarms and the cost of losing cheap surveillance fell on different groups.

G02-SC3 ‘The New Signal over the Bridge’ reached its final stage when the XT02 sea wind and the breeding season coincided and the air above the bridges and transmission inspection hatches became a communal roost for many families.
Because sound patterns learned in different places had mixed, the whole flock moved at once at a single inspection bell.
Running the evacuation route as umbrella columns reduced direct attacks, but the flow of traffic fell and the refugees at the back waited long.
Providing alternative roosts together with a new inspection bell laid the base for long-term coexistence, but meant accepting the confusion and management cost of the relearning period.
Putting off transmission inspection until after the breeding season reduced clashes but meant carrying the risk of breakdown for a whole season.

The agreement HC02 brokered bound into one the maintenance hours, school and evacuation detours, the zones where nests were left in place, the use of relocation poles, and the recognition of temporary roosts in the weeks of the XT02 sea wind.
Pushing the nests out all at once opened the bridges briefly, but insect predation and the residents' alarms vanished together, and children and refugees became the new targets of attack.

The choice to divide the signals again rather than remove the birds entirely meant giving up immediate convenience, but it was the only bargain that let humans and birds share the same infrastructure without wrecking each other's alarm systems.
To protect the Large-billed Crow and the infrastructure together, the Yeongdeungpo Line and the Wangsimni Union had to keep a history of sounds for each pylon.
HC02 had to renew the rules of use before and after the breeding season.

Horns and inspection bells were not changed at will, the time of occurrence, food exposure, and dive direction were recorded together, and the insulation state and nest radius confirmed by the workers on site were always added to H02's judgments.

Management results were read separately as transmission uptime, dives per thousand work hours, the share of alarms cancelled after visual confirmation, the amount of insulator fouling, the number of fledged young per nest, and the reuse rate of alternative roosts.

When a short circuit or large-scale nest removal caused a failure, the old sound patterns were halted for three days and the work zone closed with visual markers alone, and then the insect lamps and food exposure resumed first at the alternative roosts.
After that, the new inspection bell was not spread all at once but played pylon by pylon at staggered times, and main-line work was restored once the mimicry at the communal roost had settled.

Recovery was judged not by whether the crows had gone but by whether they spread out to the designated roosts instead of swarming at alarm sounds, and whether residents could tell a real breakdown from a bird reaction.

When fixed silent hours and maintenance timetables held for a long time, market haulers and unauthorized scavengers too came to watch the crows' movements and guess the moments when the equipment stood empty.

So to stop the side effect of a predictable signal system lowering bird clashes while becoming a clock for human intrusion, the published safety signals had to be kept while the actual inspection order and material routes were run irregularly.
Trigger: The new horn order of the Yeongdeungpo Line work crew overlaps the food-drop signal, and the crows gather on the work basket.
Ecological mechanism: A sound shape learned at the communal roost triggers the expectation of food before it triggers a warning.
Choices: Abolish the horn order / Train a separate food signal / Move the food drop to a hornless night

Outcomes: Abolishing it slows the work-safety procedure, and retraining accepts several days of false alarms. The night move protects the daytime school route but shifts the burden onto the night workers.
Moral cost: One of the two has to change: the safety signal familiar to people, or the survival signal the birds have learned.
Trigger: H02 classified the repeated dive calls as a precursor of a blackout, but the real cause is the night insect lamp.
Ecological mechanism: The birds' alarm custom and the machine's sound classification reinforce each other and chain-trigger a transmission stop.
Choices: Keep transmitting until a visual check / Move the insect lamp to an abandoned pylon / Drop the crow alarm from the control net

Outcomes: Keeping the transmission accepts the risk of a real short, and relocating makes the substitute pylon an ecological strongpoint. Dropping the alarm loses the residents' intrusion-detection net.
Moral cost: Discarding an inaccurate ecological alarm reduces malfunctions, but the cheap disaster watch disappears too.
G02-SC3 · A New Signal on the Bridge
Trigger: The XT02 sea wind overlaps the breeding season, and the air above the bridge and the transmission inspection hatch becomes a communal roost.
Ecological mechanism: Several family groups share sound shapes learned in different places and move all at once to one signal.
Choices: Run the evacuation route as an umbrella column / Negotiate an alternate roost and a new inspection bell / Postpone the transmission inspection until after the breeding season

Outcomes: The umbrella column reduces throughput, and a new signal needs a relearning period. Postponing the inspection avoids the ecological collision but carries the risk of a transmission failure for one season.
Moral cost: The bridge's immediate availability and the long-term coexistence of transmission and the birds' alarm cannot be had at the same time.

G03.selector: p, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, blockquote, pre, li, th, td

leaves.text: They were small families of abandoned dogs going back and forth between the vacant lots outside the walls of the Taeuk Group on the Yongsan Line and the night loading docks of the Central Technology Preservation Office on the Noryangjin Line. Their name came from the clink of rusted collar rings striking identification tags, and protein leftovers, feeding packs, sealed water, and shade set their density. The longest-lived medium-sized adult proposed moves, but there was no permanent leader, and families with pups refused even those proposals.

From the empty-ring dogs to the cart-side dogs, these are ordinary dogs made by neglect and social learning. The Transfer Rebinding Core is not the dictatorship of one animal but a phase in which the sounds of several families overlap on the cold-storage approach, and the Strait Unloading Dog is a regional branch of the same species tuned to the salt wind. A torn tag and a slow lead dog are accident and aging, not a new biological stratum.

After the collapse, animals separated from private shelters, construction-site guard dogs, and crowd evacuations joined together between the vacant lots outside the Yongsan Line and the night loading docks of the Noryangjin Line and became the Feral Dog. / Their iron collar rings and corroded tags strike one another as they walk. / The UHF collar tags and the regrouping behavior were elements invented for this setting and were not used to blame real shelters or businesses.

The core habitat is the vacant lot by the outer wall of the laboratory on the Yongsan Line and the closed guard passage, and depending on the season and the unloading cycle they move to the fishery and frozen-leftover axis of the Noryangjin Line. / When the logistics vibration from the Korea Strait Theater (XT03) grows, the band extends along the unloading-yard entrance, and in the daytime hours when the density of people is high they hide in drains and under the elevated roads.

Leftover protein, fish guts, and discarded ration packs are the main resources, and scraps of collar, wire, and identification tag are markers that connect individual identification to the memory of a past feeding station. / When the Magok Life House (HC03) strengthens the sealing of waste protein, the band seeps into the market alleys, and when it loosens the seal, concentration at the unloading yard rises and contact with people increases. / Water that has been filtered and disinfected and then stored sealed so it is not recontaminated, and shaded resting places, are the upper limit of density.

A lone wandering individual finds the companions of a past feeding station by smell and by the sound of identification tags and makes a small family, and when unloading leftovers increase, several families rebind into a loose alliance. / When the feeding schedule stabilizes, territorial defense increases over breeding, and after a forced capture they gather again around the individuals whose identification tags remain.

By smell they told apart human body odor, disinfectant, and the smell of thawing frozen food, and by hearing they read the iron of collars and engine idling. / H03 Ido read the passive UHF RFID tags attached to the collars within about 2 m, but metal collars, wet fur, and tag orientation caused missed and duplicate reads. / Humans used them only as clues to past registration, checked against records of appearance and behavior.

One medium-sized adult that has survived the longest, and two adults that go with it, propose a move first, but command is not fixed. / A family with pups keeps a separate protection range, and the sound of the identification tags becomes the marker that rebinds scattered companions. / Even when H03 bundles them as an aggression cluster, the HC03 mediator divides them again by each individual's identification tag, smell, and companionship.

They learn human hand signs, the engine sound of the feeding cart, and the sound of each individual's identification tag, and distinguish a safe human from a threat. / Avoidance of people in some young individuals can undergo generational selection, but the setting's rapid changes are explained by social learning and rebinding. / The more finely they distinguish people, the greater the food refusal and the aggression when a particular protector is lost.

By smell they separate body scent, disinfectant, and the smell of thawing, and by hearing they read the iron tags and an engine idling. The passive tags of Ido (H03) are read only inside about 2 meters, and wet fur and metal rings make a reading drop out or get counted twice. The lead dog's silence means it is not waiting for a new order, and a capture by deception kills every rescue call after it.
G03E01 · Stray Dog Iron Company Leading Adult 'Ironstep'
G03E02 · Stray Dog Iron Company Wanderer 'Empty Ring'
G03E03 · Stray Dog Iron Company Unloading Feeder 'Offal Nose'
G03E04 · Stray Dog Iron Company Daytime Hider 'Drain Shade'
G03E05 · Stray Dog Iron Company Reunion Worker 'Metal-Shard Cry'
G03E06 · Feral Dog Feeding Memory 'Idling Ear'
G03E07 · Feral Dog Nursery Specialist 'Pup Shield'
G03E08 · Feral Dog First Elite 'Cart Tooth'
G03E01 · Stray Dog Iron Company Leading Adult 'Ironstep'
Common species, variants and command scope
The leading adult 'Ironstep' is the longest-lived medium-sized adult and merely proposes movement first. It has no authority to command; the two adults beside it accept or reject its proposal.

It was the controller, the longest-surviving medium-sized adult. The rusted ring on its collar clinked with iron at every step, and its nose told apart human scent, disinfectant, and the smell of thawing frozen goods. It held no right of command and only proposed movement first, and the passive tag on its collar could be read by H03 Ido only within about 2 meters and was often missed because of wet fur and the metal ring.

After the collapse, an individual that went back and forth between private shelters that had closed their doors and construction-site guard posts joined other wandering families in the vacant lot by the outer wall of the Taeuk Group on the Yongsan Line. As the clink of iron became a sign that gathered its companions, people came to call its gait the lead, but it had never been chosen as chief.

By day it rested in the closed guard passages of the Yongsan Line and under the overpasses, and when unloading leftovers increased, it went down to the edge of the night unloading yard of the Central Technology Preservation Office on the Noryangjin Line. On nights when the XT03 logistics vibration grew, its proposed routes stretched as far as the freezer ramps.

Protein leftovers, discarded meal packs, and water sealed after filtering set the density. When the HC03 Magok Life House sealed its discarded protein too tightly, this gait proposed a detour through the market alleys, and when it sealed it loosely, crowding built up at the unloading yard and contact with people grew.

When feeding was stable it proposed territorial defense before breeding, and when forced capture scattered the pack, it gathered again where the identification tags remained. When the ring broke, the clink of iron disappeared and regrouping came late, so winding a broken ring with wire was not decoration but survival maintenance.

The two adults beside it accepted or rejected its proposals, and the families with pups kept a separate protected area. Even when H03 reported them together as an aggressive cluster, the HC03 mediators separated them again by each individual's identification tag, scent, and companions. Even if the leading individual fell silent, the families only returned to their last sleeping places and did not wait for new orders.

In the first stage it responded only to particular identification tags and feeding trucks and kept to the edge of the vacant lot. In the second stage, a familiar engine sound and unloading leftovers gathered several families into one passage and made them follow the escort carts. In the third stage, after feeding stopped or after a deceptive capture, the families occupied the markets and the transfer stairs at the same time.

Direct fire and wholesale capture only pushed the families out of their living area. Barrier fences, detour feeding points, noise reduction, and flags for the pup zones came first, and capture was limited to injured individuals or individuals that had actually led attacks. Success was zero bites on citizens, fewer minutes of unloading delay, and the share of families regrouped.

Delaying the unloading until the shelter-code checks were finished reduced misjudgments but let the food thaw. Registering present companions and pup care first stabilized the pack, but clashed with belated return claims by former guardians. Removing only the leading individual on the pretext of its abandonment history left not 48 hours but days of scattered occupation and shut down the citizens' reporting network.

The incomplete reading of the rusted name tag in G03-SC1 overlapped with this gait's proposal, and the engine sound of G03-SC2 and the freezer encirclement of G03-SC3 took place after the proposal was rejected.
G03E02 · Stray Dog Iron Company Wanderer 'Empty Ring'
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

The wanderer 'Empty Ring' is a lone dog with an empty collar that has been unable to join any family. It does not follow the leader's proposals and is often omitted from the ledger because it has no tag reading.

It was an ordinary ecological type, a lone wanderer whose collar ring was empty and made almost no clink of iron. It sought the scent of old feeding stations by smell and gauged companions by hearing, borrowing the clatter of other dogs' identification tags. Its tag was missing or broken, so it often remained a blank in H03's short-range readings.

An individual separated from people during a crowd evacuation, which never attached itself to any family, went back and forth between the vacant lots and the drains. The empty ring was not decoration but the record of a failed regrouping.

It circled alone along the edge of the vacant lot by the Yongsan Line outer wall and the drain behind the market, and approached the Noryangjin Line entrance only on nights rich in unloading leftovers. When the daytime crowds were thick, it clung to the shade under the overpass and did not move.

A scrap of a small meal pack and a sip of sealed water got it through a day, and when the protein was sealed away it went down to the leftovers along the children's passages. In stretches where there was neither shade nor water, it stopped moving.
It did not breed before it had found a small family by smell and the clink of iron. When forced into a cage it refused food, and after its release it avoided the same feeding truck.

It did not follow the leading adult's proposals and only checked the scents from afar. It approached when it heard the sound of an identification tag, and withdrew at once when an engine sound coincided with an unfamiliar person's gesture. The blank in H03's log was a sign not to count this individual as nonexistent.

In the first stage it left only footprints at the edge of the vacant lot. In the second stage it followed the cart wheels at the unloading entrance and made passersby hesitate. In the third stage, after suffering a deceptive capture, it sat alone on the transfer stairs, not to threaten passage but because it was following the leftovers of the children's alley.

A capture net for it alone only pushed this individual into the market. When a detour feeding dish was set toward the vacant lot and people stood still, it broke off its approach on its own. Luring it by filling the empty ring with fake iron meant it would not come out even for a rescue call later.

Tying the empty individual to a feeding cart to fold it into an existing family filled the numbers in the ledger but created a false kinship and reduced the room for pups. Leaving it wandering increased intrusions into the market, but there was no return dispute if its former guardian appeared. The moment a tagless body was entered in the punishment ledger, the window for negotiation closed.
The unreadable fourth blank in G03-SC1 was this individual, and the engine sound of G03-SC2 drew the wanderer onto the unloading route and made it look like a family regrouping.
G03E03 · Stray Dog Iron Company Unloading Feeder 'Offal Nose'
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope
The unloading feeder 'Offal Nose' feeds at the entrance, its nose fixed on thawing drips and fish offal. It rejects the vacant-lot leader's proposal and guards only the unloading corridor.

It was an ordinary ecological type, an unloading-yard feeder whose nose was fixed on fish offal and the smell of thawing frozen goods. Its paw pads had adapted to floors wet with melted ice, so it preferred only slippery unloading yards, and its collar fragment was short, so its clink of iron was low. It followed the strength of the thawing smell before human gestures.

Once the stream of leftovers from the night unloading on the Noryangjin Line became steady, it split off from the vacant-lot family and made the unloading-yard entrance its sleeping place. The night waiting of its guard-dog line remained, but it had no duty of guarding people.

Its core was the Noryangjin Line stream of fishery and frozen leftovers and the shade of the unloading yard. By day it withdrew to the drains, and when the XT03 logistics vibration grew, it pushed its nose as far as the lip of the freezer ramp.

Its main resources were fish offal and thaw drip, and when the sealing was tightened, it seeped into the market alleys at once. Without sealed water it drank the thaw water as it was, and the density clung to one place.

The more regular the unloading cycle, the more territorial urine piled up at the entrance, and breeding did not increase. When the unloading moved to another freezer, its nose followed the new drip within three days and its sleeping place moved.

It refused the leading adult's vacant-lot proposals and kept only to the unloading stream. It fed loosely with only two or three others of the same offal smell and did not enter the zone of the families with pups. Even when H03 counted it into the unloading-yard cluster, the mediators split it off again by the route of the thawing smell.

In the first stage it went over the offal only after the unloading was finished. In the second stage it blocked the entrance before the carts stopped and lengthened the unloading minutes. In the third stage, on nights when the feeding was cut off, it circled the lip of the freezer and overlapped with the merchants' passage.

Turning the disinfection of the unloading yard into poison bait made carcasses ruin the water quality and sent the remaining noses into the alleys. Putting the leftovers in sealed drums, moving them to a detour feeding dish at the vacant lot, and lowering only the noise at the entrance restored the spacing of the carts. Success was the minutes of unloading delay and zero bites.

Sealing the discarded protein more tightly cleaned up the unloading yard, but the children's passages became the substitute feeding ground. Moving the night unloading to another freezer preserved this nose's memory but raised the transport and refrigeration costs of the Noryangjin Line merchants. Using the offal dish as bait for capture meant the nose no longer responded even to regular feeding afterward.

When the engine sound of G03-SC2 gathered families on the unloading route, this individual took the entrance first, and in the freezer encirclement of G03-SC3 the offal stream became the point of contention.
G03E04 · Stray Dog Iron Company Daytime Hider 'Drain Shade'
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope
The daytime hider 'Drain Shade' stays in drains and beneath overpasses to avoid daytime crowds. While daylight remains, it does not move even if the leader heads for the vacant lot.

It was an ordinary ecological type, a hiding individual that avoided the daytime crowds and pressed its body into the drains and under the overpasses. It read the temperature differences of the shade and the lingering smell of disinfectant more than it used its eyes, and went in and out of pipe openings on short legs. Its iron was wrapped in tape so it would not touch the pipe walls, so by day it made almost no sound.

When the crowded daytime market took away the vacant lot, individuals that were not part of the unloading families learned to use the shade of the drains and overpasses as sleeping places. The tape was not a trace of people wrapping it but leftover fiber the dogs rubbed on themselves so as not to be startled by the noise of the pipes.

The drains between the Yongsan Line vacant lot and the Noryangjin Line market and the shade under the overpasses were its daytime territory. It joined the unloading stream only at night, and when the shade was removed, it was pushed under the transfer stairs.
Shade and sealed water that had not been recontaminated set the ceiling on its density. When resting space ran shorter than food, it lay down across the daytime walkways.

When the tape came loose, it was startled by the pipe vibration, abandoned the shade, and came out onto the stairs. When forced searches emptied the drains, the hiding place formed again on the transfer stairs that same evening.

Even when the lead's proposal pointed toward the vacant lot, it did not move while the sun was still up. It shared the shade with the families with pups by dividing the time, but their feeding turns did not overlap. Even when H03's daytime log was empty, the heat sources in the shade had to be confirmed by people with flashlights.

In the first stage only footprints were left at the drain openings. In the second stage its line of sight crossed with daytime walkers under the overpasses. In the third stage, after the shade was removed, it occupied the transfer stairs even by day.

High-pressure hosing and toxic smoke pushed the dogs into the alleys and increased bites. Opening substitute shade screens and sealed water drums toward the vacant lot and only partly damming the drains restored daytime passage. Success was the daytime encounter distance and the time the stairs were occupied.

Emptying the underside of the overpasses with constant lighting to gain security moved the hiding to the transfer stairs. Leaving the shade to recognize the animals' daytime rest let theft gangs read their gathering times as gaps in the warehouses, so the location records had to be shared with a delay. Making the daytime hiding a target of extermination brought down protective ethics and reporting together.

When the reading at the edge of the unloading yard in G03-SC1 did not match the daytime blanks, this shade became a candidate cause, and in G03-SC3 the occupation of the stairs was the price of removing the shade.
G03E05 · Stray Dog Iron Company Reunion Worker 'Metal-Shard Cry'
Common species, variants and command scope

The reunion worker 'Metal-Shard Cry' performs the signaling work of wearing identification-tag fragments to call scattered companions. It gives no orders, and duplicate readings can easily leave one dog recorded under two codes.

It was a specialist type, an individual that hung collar rings and fragments of identification tags all over its body and used the clink of iron as a regrouping signal. Its hearing told the cycles of metal clashes apart more finely than engine sounds, and its sense of smell confirmed its companions' scent by overlapping it with sound. Because it had several tags, H03 easily read one body twice under two codes.

The habit of families scattered after a forced capture regrouping around an individual that still had its identification tag concentrated in this body. Adding more iron was not decoration but the marker labor of a dispersed regrouping network.

It went back and forth between the vacant lot and the unloading yard and chose spots under concrete walls that reflected sound well. On dirt floors and in flooded stretches the signal died, so it seldom stayed there.

More than food, dropped tag fragments and wire were the material for keeping up its specialty. When the markers were confiscated, family regrouping came late, and simultaneous appearances in the markets and on the stairs increased.

When its rings rusted and the sound dulled, it picked up new iron and hung it on again. When the double reading continued for three days, this individual remained in the ledger as "two dogs" until the mediators compared its appearance.
It moved later than the leading adult, but called scattered companions by sound and attached them to small families. There were no orders, only markers. In the pup zone it lowered its sound.

In the first stage it called only its companions at the vacant lot with short clinks of iron. In the second stage it amplified the reflected sound in the unloading passage and gathered several families into a single line. In the third stage, after its sound had been exploited by deceptive bait, it ignored every rhythm like that of a rescue call.

Recording the clink of iron to lure them made short-term capture easy, but every rescue signal afterward died. Reducing only the reflection with sound-absorbing cloth under the walls and detour feeding dishes brought the regrouping back to the vacant lot. Success was the share of families regrouped and fewer false calls.

Using the remaining tag data only for finding missing families put up with the confusion of double readings but did not create a punishment ledger. Cutting off all the iron to gain quiet brought down the regrouping network and increased the occupation of the stairs. The price of gathering them with false rescue signals was a silence that turned away from real injuries.
The three different shelter codes of G03-SC1 could be double readings of a single body, and the dispersed regrouping network of G03-SC3 stood on these iron markers.
G03E06 · Feral Dog Feeding Memory 'Idling Ear'
Common species, variants and command scope

Feeding Memory 'Idling Ear' remembers the engine sound of a particular feeding truck as a safety signal. On hearing it idle, it puts the vehicle ahead of the leader's proposal and draws its family to the loading route.

It was a specialist type, an individual that remembered the idling engine and wheel sounds of a particular feeding truck as a safe human signal. Its hearing told the idling cycle apart from unfamiliar engines, and its sense of smell let down its guard only when the original driver's scent overlapped. It did not approach at gestures alone.

Even after the feeding truck of the closed guard passage stopped coming, the learning by which scattered families gathered on the unloading route whenever the same idling was reproduced remained in its body. The social learning of G03-SC2 was the original form of this specialty.

It appeared between the entrance of the Yongsan Line guard passage and the Noryangjin Line unloading route only on nights when engine sounds could be heard. In front of a mobile feeding station without an engine, it stopped one lap away.
More than the meal packs, the familiar idling itself was the condition for its approach. When the vehicle changed, it refused food for several days and its dependence on unloading leftovers grew.

When the original driver disappeared, its aggression and food refusal rose together. Learning a new driver's scent by overlapping it with the feeding procedure took many days, and during that time the unloading volume had to be reduced.

It put the vehicle before the leading adult. When it heard the idling, it drew the families onto the unloading route and temporarily overrode the right of proposal. Even when H03 recorded it as a cluster movement, the mediators divided it up by vehicle.

In the first stage it pricked up its ears only in front of the old passage. In the second stage, when the idling was reproduced, it attached several families to the carts. In the third stage, after an engine sound was used in a deceptive capture, it was hostile to every vehicle's approach.

Putting it in a cage with the engine sound as bait opened passage for the moment but made trust a consumable. Setting a mobile feeding station without idling in a different place every day preserved the signal but took labor and refrigeration. Success was the speed of the unloading recovery, the number of days of relearning, and zero bites.

Relying on the one original driver emptied the passage at once, but that person's absence brought down the whole agreement. Letting it learn a new driver slowly meant people bore several days of ration losses. The choice of buying safety quickly by deceiving its trust turned even the rescue workers into enemies afterward.
The pack that remembered the feeding truck of G03-SC2 was the stage of this specialty, and when the halt in feeding of G03-SC3 overlapped, it became the encirclement of a night without idling.
G03E07 · Feral Dog Nursery Specialist 'Pup Shield'
Common species, variants and command scope

Nursery Specialist 'Pup Shield' holds a veto that blocks even the leader's proposal within the pups' area. It is a barrier outside the command structure; if a feeding cart crosses it, pups are left behind.

It was a specialist type, an adult that guarded the separate protected zone of families with pups. Though smaller than the leading individual, it blocked noses approaching within the shade screen first and remembered the smell of disinfectant and unfamiliar gestures as threats. Tag readings were missed more often on the pups' side.

As unloading leftovers increased and several families joined together, a pair with pups fixed one corner of the vacant lot as its sleeping place, and the nursery zone came into being. Even the lead's proposals were rejected in front of this screen.

It was the shade of the Yongsan Line vacant lot and dry ground one alley away from the unloading yard. It did not take the pups onto the freezer ramps, and when the vibration grew, it moved toward the drains.

Meal packs for the pups, shade, and sealed water came before the adults' share. When the rations gathered only at the unloading yard, the nursery screen emptied and the pups were exposed to the cart wheels.

Even when feeding was stable, breeding did not explode; only the defense of the screen grew stronger. When capture took out an adult, the screen stood again by the sound of the remaining tags, but the survival of the pups fell before then.

It was a veto outside the chain of command. Even when the leading adult and the iron specialist went to the unloading route, the screen remained. When an HC03 flag marked the pup zone, it held back from approaching only within it.

In the first stage there was only a screen in the corner of the vacant lot. In the second stage the feeding carts crossed the screen, and pups followed the carts and got lost. In the third stage, after the feeding stopped, the screen was moved under the transfer stairs.

Capturing the whole screen brought down trust and scattered the adults into the markets. Taking out only the injured adults by nonlethal means and leaving the screen in the shade slowed the recovery of passage but kept the pup zone. Success was regrouping with pups and zero bites.

Separating the families with feeding carts to check their tags sped up the unloading, but pups that could not follow the carts were left behind. Registering present companion relationships before codes clashed with old ownership claims. Erasing the nursery screen for the sake of human passage was a choice to delete the animals' present family.
The separation option of G03-SC1 tested this screen, and the family-by-family feeding zones of G03-SC3 were the path to recognizing the screen as an official cost.
G03E08 · Feral Dog First Elite 'Cart Tooth'
Common species, variants and command scope

First Elite 'Cart Tooth' is a real biter that learned escort-cart wheels and ankle height as biting range. It is an exception that prioritizes the cart over the leader and does not use its teeth in front of the pup barrier.

It was the first elite, a medium-sized adult that had learned the height of escort-cart wheels and human ankles as the height of its teeth. Its sense of smell told apart the thaw drip and the disinfectant on the carts, and its hearing separated the creaking of cart axles from engine sounds. It was an individual that could lead actual bites, and its tag reading was often only partly read because of its metal collar.

When several families gathered into one passage during the second-stage family regrouping, an individual that followed the carts and resisted remembered the distance of its teeth. The chase learning of its guard-dog history remained, but it had no owner, and after suffering one deceptive capture it stored the cart itself as a threat.

It was the short straight stretch where the Noryangjin Line unloading passage met the transfer stairs. At the vacant lot it stayed behind the leading adult, and it came out to the lip of the freezer only on nights when the XT03 vibration and a halt in feeding coincided.

The leftover protein on the carts was its main resource, so when the sealing was tightened it followed people's bags instead of the wheels. When water and shade ran short, the warning time before it used its teeth grew shorter.

When its teeth were damaged, it chewed on cart rubber to readjust their height. When few individuals were treated after nonlethal capture and rejoined their original companions, this elite remained a lone chaser.

It was the exception that put cart movement before the lead's proposals. It did not use its teeth in front of the pup screen, but when deceptive signals overlapped, it bit passersby while trying to guard the screen. The mediators recorded it separately, as an individual leading attacks.

In the first stage it walked beside the carts and sniffed only at the wheels. In the second stage it blocked the escort line and drove the unloading minutes up. In the third stage, after the halt in feeding and a deceptive capture, it attacked at ankle height first in the markets and on the stairs.

Removing this individual alone by direct fire scattered the remaining families into a wider living area. The principle was the ceiling of separating the cart track from the pup screen with barrier fences and capturing only this individual, which had led the bites, by nonlethal means. Using the clink of iron as bait killed not only the elite but every rescue call.

Moving the night unloading to another freezer to empty the reach of its teeth protected the animals' memory but raised the merchants' costs. Making captured individuals into resources for exchange closed the window for negotiation. Whether to erase the memory of the carts for the sake of passage rights was a question humans had to answer with additional cost.
The front row of the regrouping that followed the carts in G03-SC2 was this elite, and the option of limited capture of injured individuals in G03-SC3 set the ceiling on its teeth.

The Rust-Ring Escort is a body with overlapping rings that takes the left flank of the leading adult. It is not a leader and does not push the pack toward the loading area before the leader steps out.

In the vacant lot by the outer wall of the Magok research institute, the Rust-Ring Escort guarded the left flank of the longest-lived medium-sized adult, knocking the layers of rusted collar rings against its side.

Its shoulders were thick, and the scars on its muzzle were scrapes from helmet rims; the sound of its rings did not carry commands but was closer to a marker that drew scattered companions together by the smell of the same wind.
This individual was not the chief, and it did not push the pack toward the unloading yard before the leading adult took its first step.
An individual that had remained a construction-site guard dog and lost its people in an evacuation column was drawn by the clink of iron in the closed guard passage and joined the Feral Dog.

The shelter code on its identification tag survived only in H03 Ido's incomplete readings, and its present family was decided not by that code but by where they slept together and by the protected zone of the pups.

By day it pressed itself to the Yongsan Line outer wall and the shade under the overpasses, and went down to the edge of the Noryangjin Line night unloading yard only on nights when the smell of thawing grew strong.

On days when the XT03 logistics vibration grew, it did not cross the freezer ramp but only sniffed the wind at the passage entrance, and it did not appear on the transfer stairs in the crowded daytime.
Its energy came from fish offal and the protein of discarded meal packs, and without sealed water that had not been recontaminated, it could not keep up even its rest in the shade for long.
When the rust on its rings froze fast, the clink of iron broke off and regrouping came late, so on nights when rain or unloading water soaked the rings, it cut back its own movement.
When HC03 sealed the discarded protein too tightly, this individual was pushed into the market alleys without being able to step aside.
Every season it shed its coat and tore out with its teeth the salt and scales caught between the rings.

When a forced capture cut its rings, it wandered for days trying to find the leading adult by smell alone, and in the meantime the families with pups kept their separate zone and rejected its proposals.
When territorial defense grew more than breeding, only the radius of its escort narrowed; no right of command arose.
When the leading adult and its two companion adults proposed movement first, the Rust-Ring Escort took the left outer flank and told carts apart from human scent.

Families with pups might not follow this individual's clink of iron, and even when H03 recorded them together as an aggressive cluster, the HC03 mediators separated them again by identification tags, scent, and companion relationships.
In the first stage it shook its rings at the edge of the vacant lot only for particular identification tags and the engine sound of the feeding truck.
In the second stage, when a familiar idling gathered several families into one passage, it guarded the flank of the escort carts and followed along.

After the third-stage halt in feeding or a deceptive capture, it split from the leading adult and joined the dispersed regrouping that occupied the transfer stairs and the market entrance at the same time.
Barrier fences, noise reduction, and flags for the pup zones came before direct fire.

If the clink of iron was used as false bait, it would not shake its rings even for rescue calls afterward, and capture had to be limited to individuals that had actually led attacks and to the injured.
Success was measured not by the number removed but by zero bites on citizens, fewer minutes of unloading delay, and the share of families gathering again in the same shade.

When HC03 bargained over the night feeding times and the unloading windows, the choice split between using the Rust-Ring Escort's iron as a lure signal and waiting until the individual checks were finished.
Luring emptied the passage quickly but burned up the trust of rescue, and checking delayed the unloading.
The moment the old guard records were entered in the punishment ledger, this individual's flank remembered human scent only as a threat.
In G03-SC1 it settled the companion relationships of the multi-ring individual among the three incompletely read tags.

In G03-SC2 the escort's radius attached itself to the unloading route at the engine sound of the old feeding truck, and in G03-SC3 it took the outer edge of the dispersed regrouping that surrounded the freezer ramp.

The Loading-Shadow Keeper is a resting body that protects the shade area of the Noryangjin Line loading zone itself. It is an animal that slips to market eaves when the shade, rather than the place, is taken away.
On the floor where the shade of the Noryangjin Line night unloading yard overlapped with the draft from the frozen leftovers, the Loading-Shadow Keeper was short.
With its broad body and wet paw pads it fixed its resting place.

Unlike the moving escort dogs, this individual guarded the area of shade itself, and when people cleared the shade away, its place slid not to another sleeping place but under the eaves of the market alleys.
It had only one collar ring, but a corroded identification tag caught on its foot and gave off not an individual number but the warning sound of the shade.

After the feeding times of the private shelters that had closed their doors stopped, a small family that found both the smell of thawing and shade under the sunscreens of the unloading yard fixed this spot as its sleeping place.
The fictional UHF tag kept only a past cage number; the present base was the location of the shade and the sealed water drums.
Its core was the shade on the downwind side of the Noryangjin Line unloading, and when the daytime crowds were thick, it withdrew only as far as the drain openings.
It did not go back and forth to the Yongsan Line vacant lot every day, and when the XT03 vibration was strong, it gave up the shade and clung to the freezer wall, following only the temperature.
Water that had not been recontaminated and the area of shade, more than protein leftovers, set the ceiling on its density.

When HC03 left the discarded protein loosely sealed, families crowded into the shade and human contact grew, and when the sealing was tightened, this individual lost its shade and slid under the eaves of the children's passage.

When the shade disappeared three days in a row it moved its sleeping place, and when the water was contaminated it licked the puddles of thaw water and then abandoned the zone at the smell of disinfectant.
Breeding was attempted only in seasons when the shade was stable, and after a forced removal, they came back under the same pillar, centered on an individual that still had its identification tag.
Even when it received the leading adult's proposal, it did not follow if pups were in the shade.
When an unloading cart brushed the shade it gave only a low warning, and within an alliance without a right of command, this individual held only a veto over its place.
In the first stage it responded only to feeding trucks at the edge of the shade.

In the second stage, when the engine sound was reproduced, the families followed out of the shade onto the unloading route, and at the third-stage halt in feeding, they emptied the shade and took the transfer stairs and the freezer ramp at the same time.
Removing the shade wholesale only moved the base into the alleys.
Placing detour feeding points and pup flags beside the shade and turning the unloading routes was the safer course, and the measures of success were the time spent in the shade and zero bites.
Taking down the sunscreens for the sake of unloading speed briefly opened citizen passage, but families without shade were pushed into the markets.
Leaving the shade gathered the density in one place and left the risk of contact.
The moment this base was made into a place for speculative storage, the window for negotiation closed.
The tag check of G03-SC1 asked whether the relationship of sleeping together in the shade should be seen as the present family.
In G03-SC2 the engine sound drew the shade base out onto the unloading route, and in G03-SC3 the families who had given up the shade surrounded the freezer ramp.

The Underpass Sleeper marks its daytime sleeping place beneath the Yongsan Line viaduct with urine. Unlike the Loading-Shadow Keeper, it occupies a hiding place from daytime crowds, not a nighttime loading area.
On the dry ledge where the underside of the Yongsan Line overpass met a drain, the Underpass Sleeper marked its daytime sleeping place with its long body and mud-caked claws.

Unlike the Loading-Shadow Keeper, this base was not the night unloading but a hiding place for avoiding the daytime density of people, and even when its territorial urine was wiped away, it was left again at the foot of the same pillar.

A companion animal separated during a crowd evacuation came in under the overpass along the drain outside the institute wall, and made the cooling of the concrete and the humidity of the shade, rather than the clink of iron, the conditions of its sleeping place.
The old residence code on its tag was only a clue; the companions under the pillar were its present zone.
Its core was the underside of the Yongsan Line overpass, and even when unloading leftovers increased, it did not go down to S08 every day.
When rain filled the drain it moved its ledge up one step, and on days when the XT03 vibration shook the pillars, it left its sleeping place empty for a while.
Sealed water, a dry ledge, and little lingering disinfectant were its upkeep costs.
Protein was enough in the meal packs left at the vacant lot, but when the water was recontaminated, it abandoned its sleeping place and went up into the shade of the transfer stairs.
When the mud on the ledge hardened, it scraped out an air vent with its claws, and when a disinfection vehicle passed, it left its place empty for a day.
In weeks when it had pups, it rejected the leading adult's unloading proposals and guarded the foot of the pillar.
It had no right of command; this individual kept only the times of coming and going at the sleeping place.
Even when H03 counted the underside of the overpass as a single cluster, HC03 separated the families by the locations of urine and the number of pups.
In the first stage it came out only briefly for the feeding truck at the edge of the vacant lot.

When the second-stage engine sound rang in the guard passage, even the families under the overpass were drawn onto the unloading route, and in the third stage it emptied its sleeping place and occupied the transfer stairs.
Driving the underside of the overpass out with water moved the sleeping place to the transfer stairs.
Leaving the urine markers beside the detour arrows and dividing the passage reduced clashes, and wholesale disinfection fixed the smell of disinfectant as a memory of threat.
Erasing the markers for the sake of daytime passage made things easier for people, but the dogs lost their boundaries and met on the stairs.
Keeping the markers as a rule meant the citizens had to detour.
Using the sleeping place as a hive storage cut off the reporting network.
In G03-SC1 the point of contention was whether the companions under the overpass took priority over the shelter code.
The engine sound of G03-SC2 shook even this sleeping place, and the underside of the overpass emptied in G03-SC3 became the starting point of the regrouping on the transfer stairs.

The Torn Name Tag is an injured individual whose tag was torn on a cart. Its irregular metal-scrap sound gathers companions, but the machine ledger cannot confirm an owner.
One side of the Torn Name Tag's collar was broken.
It was a medium-sized dog at the damaged stage, whose passive UHF tag had flipped over in its wet fur, so that H03 counted the same individual twice within 2 meters or missed it.
With every step the broken iron gave off an irregular sound, so its companions gathered, but the machine ledger could not settle its owner.
On the night when different shelter codes were read at the edge of the unloading yard, its tag caught on a cart and tore.
That damage was not a mutation but an accident, and its regrouping afterward carried on only by sound and smell.

It went back and forth between the edge of the Noryangjin Line unloading and the Yongsan Line vacant lot, but because its tag was missed more often beside metal fences, it chose the shade on the drain side.
It avoided the transfer stairs in the daytime crowds.
It needed thawed protein and sealed water, but it approached only when the gesture of a person who would fix the direction of its tag overlapped with a familiar feeding cart.
The smell of unfamiliar gloves was a threat more than food was.
The broken ring did not regrow, and as its fur grew, it hid the tag further.
Readings were at their worst while it was wet after disinfection, and until it dried, one more phantom individual appeared in the ledger.
It followed the leading adult, but because of its irregular iron, the families with pups stopped first.
It could not form a hierarchy, and the sound of its damage itself became both a regrouping marker and a cause of misjudgment.
The first-stage incomplete reading brought up three codes at once.

When the sound of its damage mixed with the second-stage engine sound, several families attached themselves to one cart, and after the third-stage deceptive capture, the stairs and the market were occupied at the same time by this sound alone.
Forcibly removing the damaged tag made the individual refuse rescue calls permanently.
Waiting for the checks of appearance and companions and keeping a brief distance with a feeding cart was the safer course.
The point of contention for this individual was which to register: the old ownership in the electronic records, or the animal family it slept with now.

Waiting for the checks delayed the unloading, separating them with carts made the pups that could not follow the sound of its damage fall behind, and putting present relationships first clashed with belated return claims.

It stood at the very center of G03-SC1 "The Rusted Name Tag"; in G03-SC2 the sound of its damage overlapped with the engine sound and fed the misjudgment, and in G03-SC3 it became the dispersed marker that kept the ledger from summing them into a single register.

The Slow Leading Adult is an elderly leader with stiff joints, carrying forward through aging the place of the 'longest-lived medium-sized dog,' as does Iron-Step. It steps toward the loading wind only when two companions stay beside it.
The Slow Leading Adult was the longest-surviving medium-sized adult of the Feral Dog; it proposed movement first but had no permanent right of command.
Its hind legs were stiff and its rings were rusted so their sound was low, and it took steps toward the unloading wind only when its two companion adults kept to its side.

It was an individual that passed through a private shelter, a construction site, and an evacuation column and remained at the vacant lot by the Magok outer wall, and once the feeding schedule was stable, it increased territorial defense rather than breeding.
Its fictional tag history left several cage numbers, but its present standing was only its age and its companions.
It used the shade tunnel of the Yongsan Line vacant lot as its daytime sleeping place and went slowly down to the Noryangjin Line entrance only on nights when the unloading was late.
On days when the XT03 vibration was strong, it made no proposals and stayed in the tunnel.
Soft protein, sealed water, and short travel distances were the conditions for keeping it going.
Cutting off the feeding changed its proposals toward the market alleys, and a crowded unloading yard damaged its joints further.
With age it went back and forth along the unloading route fewer times, and when a companion adult disappeared, it went over the same scent line again and again for nearly 48 hours.
Forcing a reorganization by the remaining identification tags alone after a forced capture scattered the families with pups first.
It made proposals, but received the veto of the pup zone.
Even when H03 marked this individual as the controller, the HC03 mediators separated them again by companion relationships and wrote no order of slaughter.
In the first stage it slowly attached itself only to the familiar carts at the edge of the vacant lot.

At the second-stage engine sound it came out onto the unloading route with its two companions, and at the third-stage halt in feeding its proposals ended in a failure to divide the passages, and the stairs and the market were occupied at the same time.
Capturing the aged individual first did not disband the pack but dispersed it.
Detour carts, extended shade, and short opening windows came first, and success was measured by the share of families that followed after the lead came out of the tunnel.
The choice split between waiting for its slow proposals for the sake of the unloading and capturing the injured and aged by nonlethal means to open the passage quickly.
Waiting left delays in the food, and capture burned up trust and killed the rescue calls.
Concentrating this individual's trust on the one original driver also left a vulnerability.

In G03-SC1 it was the subject against which the old tags and the present lead position were checked, in G03-SC2 it was the center that remembered the engine sound, and in G03-SC3 whether to open zone feeding without slaughter even after its proposals had been rejected depended on this individual.

The Cart-Side Dog is a coexisting body with a shoulder shaped to the spokes of a feeding cart. If that person disappears, it refuses food or bites tires; it is a knot of trust, not a commander.
The Cart-Side Dog was a symbiotic form with a soft mouth, a low-wagging tail, and a shoulder scar used to the spokes of feeding carts.
It had learned human gestures and the idling of a particular engine as safety, but when that person disappeared, it refused food or bit the cart tires.

It was an individual that survived by following the feeding truck of the closed guard passage, and the fictional regrouping rule put vehicle sounds and the smell of carts on the same layer as companion markers.
It did not serve as grounds for blaming any real shelter.

It went back and forth with the carts between the entrance of the Yongsan Line guard passage and the Noryangjin Line unloading route, and in the daytime, when there were no carts, it hid under the overpasses.
It did not enter the children's passages on its own, but when the feeding was cut off, that line was broken.
It needed the wheel sound of a familiar cart, meal packs at fixed times, and a human scent fainter than disinfectant.
When the mobile feeding station changed its place every day it followed, but that shifted the cost of refrigeration labor onto people.
It learned a new driver's smell over several days, and during that time the unloading volume had to be reduced for the attacks to diminish.
Once it had suffered a deceptive capture, it would not approach even the same cart.
It looked to the cart before the leading adult and yielded the place beside the cart to the families with pups.
It was not a leader but a knot of trust, and when the knot was concentrated on one person, the whole alliance became vulnerable.
In the first stage it attached itself only to a particular cart.
At the second-stage reproduction of the engine sound, scattered families gathered on the unloading route, and at the third-stage halt in feeding they occupied the stairs where there were no carts.
Using the cart as a bait cage turned the symbiotic form into a hostile form at once.
There were three paths, finding the original driver, gradually teaching it a new driver, or using a mobile feeding station without engine sound, and the muzzle of a gun was not a solution.
Relying on the original driver emptied the passage at once, but the absence of one person brought down the agreement.
Relearning cost several days of unloading losses, and a silent feeding station preserved the trust signal but took daily labor and refrigeration.
If trust was treated as a consumable, every rescue afterward was powerless.

It was the core of G03-SC2 "The Pack That Remembered the Feeding Truck"; in the tag check of G03-SC1 its companions beside the cart became evidence, and in G03-SC3 it remained as the knot that opened the family-by-family feeding zones.

The Transfer Regrouping Core is not a single tyrant but a boss phase created when the sounds of several families overlap at the cold-storage approach. H03 logs it as one colony, but each family's right to refuse is stronger than the leading proposal.
The Transfer Regrouping Core was not a single tyrant but, when the identification-tag sounds and scents of several families overlapped at the freezer.
ramp, the central adult of the scenario boss phase that arose.
Its body was medium-sized, but its iron sounded all at once with the multi-ring, damaged, and low lead tones, so in H03's log it registered as a single colony.

On a night when the XT03 logistics vibration and a halt in feeding coincided, small families from the Magok vacant lot, the Noryangjin unloading, and under the overpasses surrounded the same ramp, and this phase arose.
It was a created regrouping network, not a legendary line of chiefs.
At the highest stage it held the Noryangjin Line freezer ramp and the landing of the transfer stairs at the same time, and in ordinary times it scattered back into the Yongsan Line shade tunnel.
In the daytime crowds the core could not be seen.
Without family-by-family feeding zones, sealed stores, and shade to care for injured individuals, the core did not disband but spread into a wider living area.
Even when protein was poured out in one place, if the zones were not divided, only the crowding grew.
This phase was not the lifespan of an individual but the length of time that trust had been broken.
Unless the engine sound and the carts were retired for a set period after a deceptive capture, the core gathered again at the same hour.

Even when the sensors summed them into one, the mediators had to split them by sleeping places, number of pups, and times of coming and going.
Even when it seemed to skip the first and second stages, it was in fact the end of accumulated memory checks and regrouping.

Family-by-family feeding zones, nonlethal capture of the injured only, and moving the night unloading to another freezer were the three axes of the response, and the results were the speed of recovering passage, zero bites, and the regrouping rate.
