It was the boss phase of G03-SC3 "Regrouping on the Transfer Stairs," and the tag misjudgment of G03-SC1 and the engine-sound learning of G03-SC2 overlapped to make this core.
The choice of writing no order of slaughter and only extending the shade tunnel was the lower limit of coexistence.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Strait-Loading Dog is a regional branch that sets its night routes by the Noryangjin Line's salt wind and XT03 vibrations, not Magok dust. It does not always follow the open-ground leader's proposal; small families along the loading axis set their own times.

The Strait-Loading Dog was a regional variant that lengthened its night routes to match the salt wind of the Noryangjin Line fishery unloading and the XT03 logistics vibration instead of the dry dust of the Magok vacant lot.
Its paw pads were always wet and its identification tag corroded quickly, and it responded to the smell of thawing frozen goods before the families on the institute-wall side did.

It was a small family that spread along the unloading-yard entrance as the vibration on the Strait Three Routes side grew; it used the same Iron Pack name but did not share sleeping places with the vacant-lot lead.
It was a created regional adaptation, not an explanation of any real port accident.
The night Noryangjin Line unloading stream and the freezer walls were its core, and by day it hid in the drains behind the market.
It went up briefly to the Yongsan Line vacant lot only when the leftovers dwindled after a storm.
Fish offal and frozen leftovers were its staple food, and when the sealing was tightened, it seeped into the market alleys at once.
Sealed water was easily recontaminated by the unloading hoses, so a separate drum in the shade was needed.
Salt rusted its rings quickly and raised the pitch of its iron, and that sound fell out of step with the vacant-lot families, so its regrouping came late.
When the unloading cycle was stable, defense of the entrance grew more than breeding, and when the vibration stopped, its routes grew shorter.
It did not always follow the proposals of the Magok leading adult; the small families of the unloading stream set their own times of movement.
When H03 summed them into a single pack, it missed their different directions of evacuation.

It grew from tag responses at the edge of the unloading in the first stage, to crowding at the entrance at the vibration and engine sound in the second stage, to the blockade of the freezer ramp at the halt in feeding in the third stage.
When it broke out at the same time as the vacant-lot side, the overlap reached even the transfer stairs.
Moving the vacant-lot fences to the unloading yard as they were only made them slip on the wet floor.
The unloading windows, the sealing of the alleys, and the sealing of the offal leftovers had to be bound in the unloading ledger, and gunshots pushed it into the market.
Recognizing this variant as a separate family increased the feeding zones and raised the merchants' costs.
Summing them into a single pack and driving them out all at once briefly opened the unloading, but the children's passages became substitute habitat.
Making the vibration timetable too public let theft gangs read the empty warehouses.

It was directly connected to the logistics-vibration axis of G03-SC3, left the unloading code among the different shelter codes of G03-SC1, and turned the engine-sound learning of G03-SC2 into a matter of unloading hoses.
The Feral Dog was a pack of dogs that lived around the laboratory walls, closed guard passages, and weed-covered vacant lots on the outskirts of the Yongsan Line.
At night some went down as far as the fish loading docks of the Noryangjin Line, and by day they hid in drains and under overpasses.
Rusted collar rings and corroded identification tags struck one another with every step and made a clink of iron.
This sound was heard in the transfer passages before footsteps, giving citizens the unease that old abandonment and neglect were coming back all at once.
But they were not a single attacking group.

It was an alliance of loose families joined by animals from private shelters that closed after the collapse, construction-site guard dogs, and pets that lost their people in the evacuating crowds, following food and familiar smells.
The UHF collar tags and the regrouping mediated by those tags were a fictional order that held only in this region, and gave no grounds for blaming any real shelter or business.
The core territory was the vacant lots outside the Yongsan Line walls, but there was no fixed boundary.

In seasons when fish guts and frozen leftovers increased, they moved to the night loading axis of the Noryangjin Line, and when the logistics vibration from the XT03 Korea Strait Theater grew, they extended their territory to the cold-storage approaches and loading-dock entrances, while conversely they withdrew to the drains behind the market or under the overpasses when the daytime crowds thickened.
Protein leftovers, discarded feeding packs, uncontaminated water, and shade decided the density of the pack.

When HC03 Magok Life House sealed its waste protein too tightly, hungry families scattered into market alleys and children's passages, and when it managed it too loosely, they crowded into a single loading dock and contact with people increased.
For water, filtration and disinfection were not enough; sealed storage was needed to prevent recontamination.
Removing food and creating safety were not the same thing.
Animals that had wandered alone found companions they had met at old feeding stations by scent and the clink of iron, and formed small families of two or three.
When loading-dock leftovers became plentiful, several families regrouped into an alliance that used the same paths while keeping different eating orders and resting places.
The longest-surviving medium-sized adult and the two adults beside it proposed moves first, but there was no permanent leader or chain of command.
Families with pups kept separate protected ranges and, depending on the situation, refused even the lead animal's proposals.
When feeding times stabilized, territorial defense grew stronger rather than breeding exploding, and when forced capture scattered the pack, it gathered again around the animals that still had tags.
So a report that the pack had been dispersed once did not mean a long-term solution.
Their rapid changes came from learning rather than bodily mutation.

They told apart human hand gestures, the wheel sounds of feeding carts, idling vehicles, disinfectant, and the smell of thawing frozen food, and remembered individually the people who had been safe and the people who had threatened them.

A tendency among the young to keep away from people might persist over many generations, but changing passages within days or following particular vehicles had to be seen as social learning within the family.
Smell read body odor and degrees of decay, and hearing separated familiar collar sounds from engine noise.
H03 Ido could read passive UHF RFID tags within about 2 meters, but because of wet fur, metal rings, and tag orientation it counted the same animal twice or missed it altogether.
The electronic record was only a clue to past registration, not proof of present family relations, and people had to check appearance, behavior, and companionship again.
The danger grew in three stages, depending less on numbers than on the way trust broke down.
At first they reacted only to particular tags and feeding vehicles and kept to the edges of the vacant lots.
Next, familiar engine sounds and loading-dock leftovers drew several families into a single passage and set them trailing the convoy carts.
Finally, when feeding stopped or a deceptive capture took place, they scattered by family and occupied the market entrances, transfer stairs, and freezer approaches all at once.
At that point gunfire or mass capture only pushed the scattered animals into a wider living sphere.

Barrier fences, feeding detour points, noise reduction, and visual markers for the pup-protection zones came first, and capture had to be limited to injured animals or those that had actually led attacks.
Success was judged not by the number removed but by 0 bites to citizens, reduced loading delays, and the rate at which families regrouped.
G03-SC1 ‘The Rusted Name Tag’ began when H03 made incomplete reads, at the edge of the loading dock, of three tags carrying different shelter codes.

The Yongsan Line and HC03 could delay the loading until the record check was finished, could split the families with feeding carts to confirm them, or could register first the relationships of those who now slept together and looked after the pups, rather than the old codes.
The first choice reduced misjudgment but delayed the food unloading.
The second was fast but could separate pups that failed to follow the cart from their families.
The third made the pack most stable but clashed with the return claims of former owners who appeared later.
What had to be decided here was not only the accuracy of the data.
The heart of it was which relationship to give greater right: the old ownership records, or the animal families formed on their own after the collapse.

In G03-SC2 ‘The Pack That Remembers the Feeding Truck,’ the engine sound of an old feeding truck rang through a closed guard passage, and the families scattered across the Yongsan Line and the Noryangjin Line gathered on the loading route.
Finding the original driver to clear the passage worked at once but left a weakness in which one person's absence could collapse the whole agreement.
Accustoming a new driver step by step to the smells and the feeding procedure meant cutting loading volume for several days, but it could spread dependence in the long run.
Introducing a mobile feeding station without engine noise did not damage the existing trust signals, but needed staff and refrigeration to change its position every day.

Animals that had lost a particular person could refuse food or grow more aggressive, so building a structure in which trust did not concentrate on one person mattered more than restoring passage at once.
G03-SC3 ‘Regrouping on the Transfer Stairs’ was a situation in which the logistics vibration of XT03 and a halt in feeding coincided and several families gathered at the cold storage.
Opening feeding zones for each family could divide the passage without harming the dispersed regrouping network, but used up ration staff and sealed stores for a long time.
Capturing only the injured animals by non-lethal means limited the damage to trust but slowed the restoration of passage.
Moving night unloading to a different freezer preserved the animals' social memory but increased the transport distance and freezing costs of the Noryangjin Line merchants.

The HC03 mediator could keep the agreement only by trading the feeding times, passage-opening windows, and capture limits as a bundle, and presenting the former owners' scent markers together with the familiar carts.
Tag data was to be used only to find missing families or owners, never turned into a punishment ledger or a speculative asset.
Coexistence with the Feral Dog lay not in believing they were gentle.
It lay in admitting the possibility of attack while never treating trust as a consumable.
Using the clink of iron as a false rescue signal made every later rescue call useless, and cutting off feeding made the danger vanish only by moving it to alleys walked by weaker citizens.
Extermination could clear the transfer routes in the short term but collapsed the ethics of care and the citizens' reporting network together.
Territorial markings could be kept alongside detour lines and used as mutual rules of passage rather than being erased without condition.

Whether the animals' present families and memories could be deleted for the sake of securing human passage, or whether the boundaries would be divided again at extra cost and inconvenience, was in the end a choice humans had to bear.

The responsibility for caring for the Feral Dog over the long term lay in binding the outer management of the Yongsan Line, the waste control of the Noryangjin Line, and the water and veterinary care of HC03 into one ledger, while keeping trust from concentrating on any single feeder.

Every season they had to record together each family's sleeping places and whether the pups survived, the rate of duplicate reads of the same animal, bacteria redetected in the sealed water tanks, time spent on the loading route (in minutes), citizen bites and chase reports, and the share of injured animals that rejoined their original companions after treatment.
A simple drop in numbers left out the families pushed into the alleys, so it could not serve as an indicator of stability.

When deceptive capture or a sudden halt in feeding collapsed the trust network, the engine sounds and carts that had been used were retired for a time, and keepers with different smells and walking habits were paired to accustom the pack again, starting with water at a distance.

Recovery was judged not at the moment they took food but by whether adults came out of the passage leaving the pups behind, and whether the family did not scatter in all directions when rescue staff approached.
After deaths or disappearances, regrouping was not forced by following the remaining tags alone; night companionship was observed for several days and the new family boundaries redrawn.

Meanwhile, if travel times and feeding locations were disclosed too precisely, theft gangs could read the dogs' gatherings as the work timetable of the cold storage and find empty warehouses and bypasses.
So location records were shared with delay and only to the extent needed for rescue and disease control, and market guards were not to consume the animals' regularity as a surveillance device.
Only then did the clink of iron remain a promise of safety and not become the signal of yet another exploitation.
Trigger: At the edge of the unloading yard, H03 incompletely reads three passive UHF RFID collar tags that still carry different shelter codes.
Ecological mechanism: The sound and smell of the identification tags rebind past companions, but the electronic record alone cannot confirm the present family relations.
Choices: Wait for the individual-by-individual comparison / Separate the families with the feeding cart / Register the present companionship ahead of the shelter code
Outcomes: The comparison slows the unloading, and the separation misses some pups. Prioritizing the present relation stabilizes the band but collides with an old protector's claim for return.
Moral cost: Decide which relation comes first, the old record of ownership or the animal family formed now.
G03-SC2 · The Band That Remembers the Feeding Cart
Trigger: When the engine sound of the feeding cart in the closed guard passage is reproduced, the scattered family groups gather on the unloading road.
Ecological mechanism: Social learning about a particular person and vehicle operates as the core condition of the passage negotiation.
Choices: Find the original driver / Familiarize a new driver in stages / Introduce a mobile feeding station with no engine sound
Outcomes: Dependence on the original driver leaves a vulnerability, and relearning takes many days.
The mobile feeding station preserves the trust signal, but it costs the labor of changing the location every day and the refrigeration.
Moral cost: Choose whether to use trust to buy safety quickly, or to accept the cost of a slow relearning.
G03-SC3 · Rebinding on the Transfer Stairs
Trigger: The XT03 logistics vibration overlaps the feeding stop, and several families surround the freezer approach.
Actors: S03, S08, XT03, HC03, H03
Ecological mechanism: Individual memory and the identification-tag markers make a dispersed rebinding net stronger than any single leader.
Choices: Open a feeding zone for each family / Capture only the injured, non-lethally / Move the night unloading to another freezer

Outcomes: Running the zones consumes ration resources, and limited capture makes the recovery of passage slow. Moving the unloading protects the animals' trust but raises the refrigeration cost of the Noryangjin Line merchants.
Moral cost: Whether the animals' social memory may be erased for the sake of human right of passage becomes the point at issue.

leaves.text: They were raccoon family groups going back and forth between the pipelines connected to the pumping station of the Myeongbu Church in the Ttukseom Union, the shelters beneath the workshops, and the cable galleries of the Yeouido Investment Federation in the Mapo Union. By day they stayed beneath manholes and by night they circled the alleys within about 50 meters of the exits, eating aquatic food, trash, carcasses, and microbial mats. The elder female held priority only in moving the young and at narrow passages, and there was no battle command.

From conduit patrol to conduit bones, these were ordinary raccoons adapted to the urban streams. Climbing to a high ventilation room before the pumps did was family learning shared from flood memory, not a supernatural power, and the dry refuge cavities and cable trays were hiding places animals had filled, not machine strongholds. This batch held no mutant individuals, and the missing E13 through E16 belonged to an excluded batch.

When the Jungnang, Tancheon, and inner storm-water trunks were pushed out of the inspection cycle after the collapse, raccoon family groups that had moved following aquatic food, trash, and carcasses settled in the pipelines beside the pumps of the Myeongbu Church in the Ttukseom Union and in the underground cable galleries of the Yeouido Investment Federation in the Mapo Union, and became the Raccoon Dog. / Real-world sources were consulted only for the range in which raccoons appeared in cities and streams, and the rule of sensing the water level before the pumps was fiction.

The core habitat was the pump-house connecting pipes of the Ttukseom Union and the dry refuge cavities under the workshops. / When flood stage rose they dispersed into the Mapo Union's transmission underground galleries and vents, and when a cold wave and a logistics break from the XT04 Duman River Far East Theater changed feed density they moved briefly onto the eastern branch lines. / By day they patrolled the pipes, and by night the surface alleys within 50m.

Aquatic prey, organic refuse, and carcass remains were the main resources, and dry hiding places and low flow were the upkeep cost. / When HC04 the Ttukseom Heat-Source House skipped dredging the pipe deposits, the food film thickened and density rose, and when it over-dredged, the family groups were pushed out into the surface markets. / Droppings and biofilm masked the water-quality sensor readings and delayed pump judgment.

In the dry season each family group used its own dry hiding place and feeding ground, and before the rain they moved their kits into the high ventilation rooms along trunks where the water rose first. / After a flood, when the food film thickened, several families shared the same pipe by time slot, and when hiding places flooded in succession they dispersed into the surface alleys.

With their whiskers they felt the current and the air moving through narrow gaps, and through pressure changes in their feet and bodies they sensed the water rising before a pump start. / Scent separated food, disinfectant, and rot, and hearing separated the pumps from human footsteps. / H04 Gangbyeol's pipe-robot logs easily confused raccoons, floating debris, and people, so confirmation by human eye was required.

Loose family groups and shared hiding places were all there was. / The elder females held only movement priority, and had no combat command. / Several family groups used the same trunk by time division. / When H04 summed them as a single colony, the HC04 drainage watch split them again by hiding place.

Individuals learned the pressure changes before a pump start and the safe dredging timetable. / Across generations a smaller body and a nocturnal habit favorable to pipe life could be selected, but the more they specialized for narrow pipes, the more vulnerable they became to surface crossings and cold waves. / Moving a hiding place by following a leading indicator is distinguished as family-group learning, not a genetic change.

They read the current and the air moving through gaps with their whiskers, and felt pre-start pressure changes through their feet and bodies. When a pipe filled or an air layer broke, the same senses went dead, and a move that ran ahead of the official sensors was not always right. Even when H04 Gangbyeol's robot summed the heat sources into one colony, the drainage watch split them again by sleeping place and entry time.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Dry-Cavern Elder Female is a named controller, but has priority only over moving the young and passing narrow ledges, not over combat command. It reads pressure with its body before the pump starts and climbs first to the high ventilation room.
The Dry-Cavern Elder Female was a named controller of the Raccoon Dog, but she held no combat command, only priority over the movement of the young and over narrow passing points.
Her whiskers were long and the rust of the pipes had soaked into her paw pads; she read the change in pressure before the pumps started with her body and climbed first to the high ventilation room.
She was the elder female of a family group that settled in the dry refuge chamber beside the Ttukseom Union pumps after the inspection of the Jungnang and Tancheon trunk lines broke off.
The rule that she knew the water level before the pumps did was fiction, and no accident was attributed to any real local government.
Her core was the dry burrows in the pipes connected to the Ttukseom Union pumping station and the refuge chamber under the workshop.
When the flood level rose she moved her young to the underground transmission gallery of the Mapo Union, and in the XT04 cold wave she shared the only dry approach with other families.
Aquatic food, organic garbage, and carcass leftovers were her energy, and low current speeds and dry shelters were her upkeep costs.
When HC04 skipped dredging, the food film thickened and the density rose, and when it overdredged, this female pushed her young into the surface markets.
In the dry season each family used its own shelter, and at the leading pressure before rain they moved to the ventilation room.
When the shelters were flooded again and again, they gave up the division of time and scattered into the alleys.
Her priority was not a hereditary line but the experience of having survived.
She gave no combat orders to the other families.
Even when the H04 robot summed the heat sources into a single colony, the HC04 drainage duty split them by sleeping places and times of coming and going, and the human eye had the final word.
In the first stage, her move to the ventilation room before rain became an unofficial alarm.

In the second stage, droppings and microbial film covered the water-level sensors and clashed with the inspection robots, and in the third stage, in a cold wave or flood, pump maintenance and evacuation competed in the one dry pipe.
Poison bait and full flooding harmed both the downstream and the workers through rotting carcasses.

Partial damming, substitute shelter pipes, washing the sensors, and restricting night passage on the surface were the basics, and success was the pump recovery time, the reliability of the sensors, and zero bites on the surface.

Adopting the raccoons' movement as a preliminary alarm bought preparation time but left the responsibility for false positives, and waiting for the measurements of the HP01 Sluice House could be too late for a sudden inflow.
Preheating the pumps only when the two signals differed saved fuel but missed short local downpours.
Whether to entrust public safety to an unofficial ecological signal was this controller's moral cost.

She made the central movement of G04-SC1 "The Leading Indicator Beneath the Manhole," in G04-SC2 she held one family's priority in the division of time that overlapped with the dredging window, and in the dry passage of the G04-SC3 cold wave she forced one of three choices: heated shelter pipes, delayed inspection, or outside footholds.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

The Pipe-巡回 Raccoon is an ordinary adult that circles pipes by day and alleys within 50 meters of an exit at night. It recognizes the elder female's priority only at chokepoints and follows its own schedule elsewhere.
The Pipe-Patrol Raccoon was an ordinary ecological type of the Raccoon Dog that hid in the pipes beneath the manholes by day and circled the alleys within about 50 meters of an exit at night.
It read the current and the airflow of the gaps with its whiskers and told pump vibration apart from the sound of boots by hearing, and its body was not combat claws but wet fur and narrow shoulders.
It was an ordinary adult of a family group that came into the stormwater trunk lines emptied by people, following aquatic food, garbage, and carcasses.
On the basis of records of appearances in urban streams, it observed the ecological order affecting pipe operations in 2126.
The low-current pipes of the Ttukseom Union were its base, and when the water level rose it dispersed briefly toward the Mapo Union vents.
When the density of food changed in a cold wave, it moved to the eastern branch lines, and after the thaw it came back to its familiar pipes.
Microbial film, organic garbage, and carcass leftovers were its food, and without a dry shelter its stays on the surface grew longer.
When dredging cleared away the food film all at once, this individual was the first to be pushed out into the market alleys.
In the dry season it circled only its own family's feeding grounds, and after a flood the families divided the hours and used the same trunk line.
A small build suited to narrow pipes could survive across generations, but it grew weaker at surface crossings and in cold waves.
Changing refuges within a few days was learning, not heredity.
It recognized the elder female's priority only at passing points, and otherwise followed its own timetable.
Because the robot logs confused floating debris with this individual, it was not counted in the colony numbers until people had confirmed it.

In the first stage it followed up to the high ventilation room before rain, in the second stage it met the inspection robots in pipes where the sensors were covered, and in the third stage, when only one dry pipe was left, it overlapped with the pump approach.
Driving it out of the alleys only shortened its 50-meter rounds to the doorsteps of homes.
Dividing the night passage windows, opening substitute shelter pipes, and washing the sensors were the response, and culling ruined the water quality further.
Dividing the 50-meter alley into no-passage windows inconvenienced people and kept the raccoons in the pipes.
Driving them out on the surface reduced complaints at once but increased intrusions into homes.
Poisoning out of fear of disease endangered both the pipe workers and the downstream drinking water, and lost a leading-indicator species.

In G04-SC1 it made the density of the alarm as an ordinary individual climbing to the ventilation room after the female, when the dredging window of G04-SC2 broke it became the first wave to come out into the surface markets, and in G04-SC3 it overlapped with the dry passage as one line among the three families.
Common species, variants and command scope

Current-Whiskers presses its belly to the low-flow floor beside a pump and reads the current with its whiskers. When a pipe fills, that same sense goes blind, setting its niche apart from surface patrols.

Role and Body: It was an ordinary ecological individual of the Raccoon Dog that pressed its belly to the floor of the low-current pipes beside the pumps and read the direction and strength of the current with its whiskers. Its build was smaller than a surface adult's, and its paw pads were broad to suit slippery concrete. It felt the change in pressure before the water rose with its feet and chest, but when the pipe filled or the air layer broke off, the same sense went dead.

Origin: After the collapse, once the inspection of the Jungnang and Tancheon trunk lines broke off, it followed aquatic food and stayed in the Ttukseom Union Myeongbu Church pump branch that people had emptied. The saying that it knew the water level before the pumps was fictional family learning, not an accident of any real institution.

Habitat: By day it clung to the floors of slow-current pipes and the ledges beneath the manholes, and even at night it hardly went out toward the exits. When the flood level rose it only moved to a high joint of the same pipe; the Mapo Union gallery was not within this individual's daily range.

Needs: Small aquatic food and the microbial film on the pipe walls were its staple food, and a gentle current had to be kept for it to save swimming energy. When disinfectant flowed thick, its whiskers were dulled for several days and it lost track of where the food was.

Life Cycle and Maintenance: In the dry season it went back and forth along only one branch line and rubbed its whiskers to remove foreign matter. When continuous rain lifted the floor, it moved its own body to the joints first, not its young, and after the thaw it came back to the familiar low-current stretch.

Behavior and Hierarchy: It gave no combat orders and stepped aside only when the elder female passed a narrow ledge. Even when the H04 Gangbyeol log marked this individual as floating debris, the HC04 drainage duty had to tell it apart again by its times of coming and going and its sleeping place.

Escalation: In the first stage it clung to the joints before rain and became an unofficial leading signal. In the second stage droppings piled up in the same pipe, the official water gauge read low, and it came nose to nose with the inspection robots. In the third stage the remaining low-current stretch overlapped with the footholds of the maintenance crews.

Engagement and Response: Poison bait and full flooding ruined the downstream along with it through rotting carcasses. If partial damming briefly lowered the current, the sensors were washed, and the detour pipes were opened, Current-Whiskers went back to its familiar floor and shortened the time for the pumps to resume.

Negotiation and Moral Choice: Adopting this individual's move to the joints as a preliminary alarm bought preparation time, but the fuel responsibility for false positives stayed with the Ttukseom Union and HC04. Waiting only for the on-site measurements of the HP01 Sluice House was too late for short inflows, and preheating the pumps only when the two signals disagreed saved everyday fuel but missed simultaneous delays. Reading the current could not be made grounds for punishment.
Scenario Links: In G04-SC1 "The Leading Indicator Beneath the Manhole," its daytime move to the joints appeared before the official sensors.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Fifty-Meter Nightwalker patrols above ground only at night, covering about 50 meters of alley from a manhole exit. It is poor at reading whiskers on deep pipe floors and retreats straight into the pipe if it crosses that boundary.

Role and body: An ordinary ecological member of the Raccoon Dog, it patrols above ground only at night, circling alleys about 50 meters from a manhole exit. Its hind claws suit wet asphalt, and at the entrance its ears distinguish pump vibrations from people's boots. It is poor at reading whiskers on deep pipe floors.

Origin: It came from a family that formed a surface circuit around exit refuse and market leftovers in a year when food inside the pipes dwindled. It became the face of fears that sewage would backflow into living areas, but is not a scout for an underground army.

Habitat: By day it hides in dry shade below an exit ledge; at night it circles only within 50 meters of the workshop alleys of the Ttukseom Union and the alleys toward the Mapo Union transmission site. If it crosses that line, exposure to dogs and vehicles drives it straight back into the pipe.

Needs: Nighttime refuse and carrion are its staples; it needs a dry ledge with an unblocked exit to maintain its circuit. If dredging lifts the exit all at once, the circuit extends deeper into the market.

Life and maintenance: If the pads on its feet crack, it stays off the surface for a while and waits for leftovers on the ledge. When alleys freeze in a cold wave, it folds its circuit and stays inside the entrance; on the first thawed night, it steps on the same corner again to check its route.

Behavior and hierarchy: It shares emergence times with the family that uses the same exit; who goes first is decided after the elder female passes. It forms no combat formation and breaks off its circuit midway when boot sounds approach.

Escalation: At stage 1, it leaves only footprints at an alley corner. At stage 2, the dredging window overlaps the access time and two families emerge into the market together. At stage 3, repeated flooding of the exit breaks the 50-meter rule and pushes it into passageways.

Engagement and response: Limiting nighttime surface passage to within 50 meters of the exit and opening an alternative dry ledge reduces market intrusion. Poison bait endangers alley dogs and sanitation workers alike; success is measured by zero surface bite injuries.

Negotiation and moral choice: Closing the night market early shortens its circuit but reduces merchants' selling hours. Keeping passage open reduces complaints but increases responsibility for simultaneous emergence during the next dredging. Fixing the Fifty-Meter Nightwalker's circuit as a prohibited line and recognizing its feeding hours are not the same cost.
Scenario link: In G04-SC2, 'Two Families in the Dredging Window,' a broken timetable extends this individual's 50-meter circuit into market complaints.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Dredging-Time Keeper has memorized the intervals of HC04's nighttime dredging vibrations through its ears and paws. Without combat orders, when it vacates a branch first, families in the same window read that absence.

Role and body: A specialized member of the Raccoon Dog, it remembers the intervals of nighttime dredging vibrations from HC04, the Ttukseom Heat-Source House, through its ears and paw pads. Sediment dust on its shoulders visibly shows the date of the last dredging; if the equipment's entry rhythm is off, it immediately changes its hiding direction.

Origin: This is the result of a family that survived repeated dredging noise learning a safe timetable. It did not inherit a clock; it remembers how an individual that saw a missed window become a death site taught the others the vibration rhythm.

Habitat: It moves between the Ttukseom Union main branch visited by dredging equipment and the vacant branch entrance beside it. By day, when there is no construction, it sleeps at that entrance; when vibrations begin, it briefly moves toward the Mapo Union.
Needs: Organic sediment and aquatic leftovers accumulated between dredgings make its feeding calendar. If the schedule is unexpectedly advanced, food and hiding places disappear together.

Life and maintenance: After memorizing one season's vibration cycle, it tests the first equipment of the next season by avoiding it. After three exposures to an incorrect rhythm, it abandons that main; returning requires a quiet night after the thaw.

Behavior and hierarchy: It gives no combat orders to other families. But if it vacates a branch first, families using the same time window read that absence. Even if H04 counts several movement points as one colony, the Dredging-Time Keeper's access times must be logged separately.

Escalation: At stage 1, it appears only as a branch emptying before equipment enters. At stage 2, nighttime dredging overlaps with rotational hiding, pushing two families above ground. At stage 3, equipment is concentrated into one window regardless of the timetable, breaking the shared rules.

Engagement and response: Dividing dredging into two sections and keeping vibration warnings on the same rhythm lets this individual retreat to a branch. Concentrated dredging is faster but increases simultaneous appearances during later rain.

Negotiation and moral choice: Matching dredging times to raccoon memory delays completion and increases night labor. Buying off one family's time slot with food and clearing it is fastest, but unfairly breaks the rotation another family kept. Whether to put the Time Keeper's memory on the work calendar is a matter of fairness in HC04's ledger.
Scenario link: The nighttime window of G04-SC2, 'Two Families in the Dredging Window,' is triggered when it overlaps the vibration intervals this individual memorized.
Common species, variants and command scope
The Biofilm Forager eats microbial film off pipe walls, leaving residue that obscures the official water-level gauge. It is not a weapon attacking sensors but a forager seeking thick film.

Role and body: A specialist member of the sewer raccoon clan, it uses its nose and forepaws to scrape biofilm and piles of waste from pipe walls and eat them. This food film can obscure official water-quality and water-level sensors, but the animal itself is a forager seeking thick film, not a weapon that attacks sensors.

Origin: When the film thickened in a section where HC04 had postponed sediment dredging, a foraging habit favoring film over aquatic food took hold within the family. This was not sabotage intended to cultivate the film.

Habitat: It stays beneath sensor housings and in sediment pockets with almost no current. If the film washes away, it moves to another housing in the same pipe; if excessive dredging exposes the bottom, it is driven toward surface garbage.

Needs: Thick organic film and microbes on carcasses provide all its energy. When disinfectant concentrations rise, its nasal lining cannot distinguish food quality for several days. Without a dry shelter, it loses body heat while eating film with wet fur.

Life cycle and upkeep: It strips film from the edges of housings with its incisors. Once its teeth wear down, it eats only the softer film downstream. After clearing a housing, it rests for several days while the film regrows; that gap is a brief window in which sensor reliability recovers.

Behavior and hierarchy: It does not command other families, only claims spots where the film is thick. It climbs down from a housing when an elder female passes. A point that an H04 robot marks as debris must be viewed three times by a person with a flashlight to distinguish a forager from floating debris.

Escalation: At stage 1, sensor readings come back consistently low. At stage 2, the cleaning crew and a forager meet at the same housing, halting inspection. At stage 3, scraping away the film all at once sends the family spilling into the market.

Engagement and response: Clean the sensors and partially block the water first, leaving film in one section to create an alternative feeding route. Flooding the entire area and using poisoned bait make the film of decomposing carcasses thicker. The measures of success are sensor reliability and the delay in pump decisions.

Negotiation and moral choice: Frequent housing cleaning restores pump decision-making but removes both the film forager's staple food and its shelter. Delaying cleaning reduces conflict over food, but makes official water-level readings false, putting the early warning signs in G04-SC1 at odds with instrument readings. Whether to recognize the film as a resource is a matter of putting drainage safety and foraging ecology on the same ledger, not a matter of disgust.
Scenario connection: In G04-SC1, an obscured water-level gauge forces a wait for on-site measurement. In G04-SC2, dredging removes the film all at once and pushes the foragers to the surface.
Common species, variants and command scope

The litter-carrier mother is a caregiving animal that responds to pre-rain pressure changes by carrying her young to a ventilation room in her mouth. She uses her right of way only for this task and does not take feeding grounds from other families.

Role and body: A specialist member of the sewer raccoon clan, she senses pressure changes before rain and carries her young by mouth, gripping them by the scruff, to a higher ventilation room. She uses an elder female's right of way only for this task and does not give combat orders to other family members. Folds like a chest pouch hold her young's body heat against her wet fur.

Origin: Mothers that lost young left in low-lying pipes during floods established a place within the family for moving them to ventilation rooms as soon as they sensed pressure changes before the pumps started. This is a learned sequence of movements that aided survival, not a genetic change that occurred in days.

Habitat: She relies chiefly on the floor of the ventilation room beside the Ttukseom Union pumps and the dry ladder leading up to it. If the ventilation room floods, she leads her line of young onto high cable supports in the Mapo Union gallery.

Needs: She needs a high space where her young can dry off and nearby scraps to make up for the brief interruption in feeding while she moves them. Closing a vent because of the smell diverts her carrying route into the alleys.

Life cycle and upkeep: The strength of her neck determines how many young she can move from one litter. When exhausted, she leaves one on an intermediate ledge and makes a return trip. If the ventilation room freezes during a cold snap, she stops moving and endures by covering them with the folds of her body.

Behavior and hierarchy: She asserts right of way only at narrow passage points and does not take other families' feeding grounds. If people are in the ventilation room, she routes her line of young around them. Even if H04 displays people, young, and debris as a single heat spot, no team should be sent out before visual confirmation.

Escalation: At stage 1, young climb to the ventilation room during the day, before any rain. At stage 2, closing the ventilation room puts their route across a work platform. At stage 3, the only dry space left is the pump access route, bringing maintenance and caregiving into conflict.

Engagement and response: An alternative shelter pipe and limited opening of the ventilation room come first. Flooding the entire area kills the line of young at once and worsens water quality as their bodies decay. Success means zero surface bites and surviving young, not the number captured.

Negotiation and moral choice: Using the mother's daytime movement as an advance warning partially entrusts public safety to informal caregiving behavior. Closing the ventilation room and waiting only for HP01 measurements provides clear evidence, but brings the young into the alleys. A compromise of preheating the pumps only when the two signals differ saves fuel, but leaves a gap in which people act only after the mother has already moved them.
Scenario connection: G04-SC1, ‘The Leading Indicator Beneath the Manhole,’ begins with this animal carrying her young to the ventilation room during the day.
Common species, variants and command scope

The shift-change burrow keeper maintains the time-sharing arrangement between two families using the same main pipe by blocking the way with its body. It has no combat command authority; outside its family's allotted window, it lies across the entrance only to slow passage.

Role and body: The sewer raccoon clan's first elite, it maintains the time-sharing arrangement between two families using the same main pipe through scent marks and by blocking the way with its body. It has no combat command authority; outside its family's allotted window, it lies across the entrance only to slow passage. The scent from its neck glands fades after a few hours, so it does not create permanent territory.

Origin: After a flood thickened the food film and multiple families began using one pipe, the habit of the first arrivals guarding their allotted window grew strong in this animal. It is not a crowned ruler, but a keeper of the shift rule in its body.

Habitat: It stays below the branch manhole where the Ttukseom Union main pipe splits toward the Mapo Union route, retreating to a dry refuge chamber when its window ends. If dredging begins in violation of the windows, it is pushed toward the surface market along with both families.

Needs: It needs enough body scent to maintain its marks, and film and scraps to eat between windows. If one window is bought out, leaving only one family, it loses its role and disperses into the alleys.

Life cycle and upkeep: It renews the scent line two or three times a day. If rain washes it away, it abandons the shift arrangement for that night. If an injury prevents it from lying across the entrance, another adult guards it temporarily, but the rule soon loosens.

Behavior and hierarchy: It always makes way for an elder female moving her young. Otherwise, it asserts only its family's allotted window. If H04 merges two heat sources into one point, HC04 must separate them again using their entry and exit times.

Escalation: At stage 1, only the shifts at the branch entrance are visible. At stage 2, nighttime dredging disrupts both windows at once, prompting complaints from both sides of the market. At stage 3, after one window is bought out, the remaining family abandons the rule.

Engagement and response: If dredging is divided into two sections, the shift-change burrow keeper renews its marks. Opening an alternative dry pipe reduces competition for the entrance but reduces spare cable space for the Mapo Union. Flooding the entrance drives entire families into the alleys; it does not merely end the rule.

Negotiation and moral choice: Buying one family's time slot with food and a safe passage makes construction fastest, but turns the fair window the burrow keeper guarded into a transaction. Split dredging delays completion, while the alternative pipe trades away communications capacity. Pursuing efficiency alone increases simultaneous surface appearances during the next rain.
Scenario connection: In G04-SC2, ‘Two Families in the Dredging Window,’ both families surface at once when this animal's branch mark is broken.
Common species, variants and command scope

During an XT04 cold snap, the thaw-path guide uses its paw pads and whiskers to find an unfrozen passage first. It cannot summon other families, but several follow it onto the dry ledge where it stops.

Role and body: The sewer raccoon clan's second elite, it uses its paw pads and whiskers to distinguish ice from residual warmth on pipe walls and find an unfrozen passage first during an XT04 cold snap. It cannot summon other families, but several follow it onto the dry ledge where it stops. Its surface crossings are brief and clumsy.

Origin: During a winter when cold from the Tumen River–Far East theater and a logistics disruption changed the distribution of feed, an animal that survived when only an unfrozen pump access route remained passed its memory of warmth on through family learning. It has no history of claiming to be a commander.

Habitat: During cold-snap weeks, it moves between the residual heating in the Mapo Union Yeouido Investment Federation's underground gallery and the dry access route to the Ttukseom Union pump room. When thawing begins, it returns along the eastern branch line as though guiding others back to a familiar pipe.

Needs: Unfrozen ground and a little residual heat are central to its survival; it chooses dry space before food. Cutting the gallery's heat brings three families together on a single pump access route.

Life cycle and upkeep: When cracks in its paw pads deepen, it becomes slower to detect ice and spends a season on the branch line alone. The first warm water after the thaw offers a chance to wash its wounds, but if it arrives too quickly, it floods the access route again.

Behavior and hierarchy: What looks like leading is a search for warmth, not an order. It yields its route when an elder female moves her young. Even if H04 merges them into one heat spot, HC04 records the number of families and their entry and exit times separately.

Escalation: At stage 1, tracks appear first toward the gallery. At stage 2, diminished residual heat causes their use of the access route to overlap. At stage 3, three families block the only dry passage to the pumps, stopping maintenance.

Engagement and response: Temporarily opening a heated shelter pipe and restricting nighttime surface travel disperses their routes. Poisoned bait and flooding add bodies that have frozen to death. A temporary external inspection platform permits maintenance without clearing the passage, but the work crew bears the risk of falling in the cold snap.

Negotiation and moral choice: Opening part of the gallery's heating as shared shelter requires other Mapo Union facilities to give up power. Postponing pump inspection avoids a clash but increases flood risk during a thaw or sudden rain. Whether to use the guide's memory of warmth as an official detour hinges on the inability to secure both city drainage and nonhuman refuge at once.
Scenario connection: In G04-SC3, ‘The Dry Passage to the Pump Room,’ three families converge on the access route where this animal first stops.
Common species, variants and command scope

The dry refuge keeper braces its shoulders inside the dry refuge chamber beneath the Ttukseom Union pump station, filling the space so other families cannot enter all at once. It is not a fixed command post but an animal guarding dry storage space with a low current.

Role and body: An environmental-stronghold form of the Raccoon Dog, this burrow keeper has settled into the dry refuge chamber beneath the pump station of the Ttukseom Union's Myeongbu Church, where its body fits closely. Its shoulders catch against a ceiling joint, physically filling the chamber so other families cannot enter all at once. It senses airflow with its flanks more than with its whiskers.

Origin: A family that used a refuge chamber vacated by people as a dry-season sleeping place refused to give up the dry space even after sending its young to the high ventilation room during a flood, producing this stronghold animal. The chamber is not a fixed command post but dry, low-current storage space.

Habitat: Its entire range is the dry shelf inside the refuge chamber and the ledge at its entrance. When the water rises above the entrance, it gives up the chamber and moves to the ventilation room. During a cold snap, the chamber adjoins the only unfrozen pump access route, putting it in the same space as maintenance workers.

Needs: Staying dry itself saves energy, and it survives on the small amount of scraps washed into the chamber. Converting the chamber into a human-only inspection route shifts the cost of losing its stronghold onto the surface alleys.

Life cycle and upkeep: It times its entries and exits by how long its fur takes to dry, and scrapes away floor dirt if dampness persists for more than two days. If the entrance floods repeatedly, it abandons the stronghold and folds the sharing arrangement.

Behavior and hierarchy: Inside the chamber, the first arrival holds its place but does not drive others out by fighting. It yields the shelf when an elder female arrives with a line of young, and a ‘debris’ point in the H04 log is corrected to burrow keeper only after visual confirmation by flashlight.

Escalation: At stage 1, only fur and tracks appear at the refuge chamber entrance. At stage 2, an inspection robot and the burrow keeper meet at the entrance. At stage 3, a cold snap makes this dry chamber the only space available for both pump access and refuge.

Engagement and response: Partial water blocking delays flooding at the entrance, while opening an alternative shelter pipe spreads out the pressure on the stronghold. Flooding the entire chamber opens access to the pumps immediately but increases incursions into surface homes. The measures of success are restored pump operation and zero surface bites.

Negotiation and moral choice: Leaving the dry refuge chamber as an ecological buffer lengthens the maintenance route. Sealing it as a human-only shaft speeds drainage, but during a cold snap three families block the remaining access route. A temporary external platform avoids sharing the chamber, but someone must decide who bears the fall risk of the installation work.
Scenario connection: The competition for space in G04-SC3, ‘The Dry Passage to the Pump Room,’ intensifies when this stronghold remains unfrozen.
Common species, variants and command scope

The cable-gap dweller has made a home in empty Mapo Union trays and gaps by the vents, forming a second dry shelter. It is not a group trying to seize the communications network, but a home for a family that dispersed when the water rose.

Role and body: An environmental-stronghold type of the sewer raccoon clan, it has made a home in spare trays and gaps by the vents of the Mapo Union Yeouido Investment Federation's underground cable gallery. It moves with its belly raised to avoid getting oil on the cable sheathing. It does not respond to audible transmission frequencies, distinguishing only human boots from low-frequency pump sounds.

Origin: A family dispersing from the Ttukseom Union pipes as the water rose discovered the gallery's dry warmth and empty trays and settled there. It is not a group trying to seize the communications network, but a second dry-shelter stronghold.

Habitat: It lives among the empty cable tiers in the middle of the gallery and at the base of the vents, moving to tiers that retain residual heating during XT04 cold-snap weeks. If communications expansion fills the spare space, the stronghold is pushed back toward the pump access route.

Needs: Dry warmth and organic scraps mixed into the dust beneath the trays sustain it. Opening this space as an alternative shelter pipe reduces surface appearances but reduces spare transmission cores.

Life cycle and upkeep: It shakes cable dust from its fur in the vent breeze and vacates a tier for several days if it leaves scuff marks on the sheathing. If power rationing removes the residual heat, it abandons the stronghold and returns to the Ttukseom Union route.

Behavior and hierarchy: Even in the gallery, it moves only with its own family and does not command other families. When an inspector shines a flashlight, it slips behind a tray. If H04 marks one heat source as a colony, the duty officer separates the sightings again by tier number.

Escalation: At stage 1, only fur accumulates in the empty trays. At stage 2, a proposal for an alternative dry pipe trades this home against communications expansion. At stage 3, failure to share heating sends three families down to the pump passage.

Engagement and response: Tape restricting nighttime surface travel and limited opening of designated tiers are effective. Clearing the gallery with toxic disinfectant damages both the cable sheathing and downstream water quality. Success is measured by transmission availability and surface bites, not removals.

Negotiation and moral choice: Providing empty, dry trays as alternative shelter reduces market appearances in G04-SC2, but costs the Mapo Union communications headroom. Sharing heating only during cold-snap weeks makes other facilities endure the cold. Treating the cable-gap dweller solely as an illegal occupant sends the costs back to the pump room during the next dredging operation or cold snap.
Scenario connection: The alternative dry pipe in G04-SC2 and the heated shelter pipe in G04-SC3 refer to this stronghold's trays and residual heat.
Common species, variants and command scope

The pipe-bound youngling is a growth stage whose small size suits narrow pipes. It can scarcely complete the 50-meter surface circuit or cross during a cold snap, so it stays close to adult strongholds and further constricts maintenance space.

Role and body: A growth-stage member of the sewer raccoon clan, it has a small body suited to narrow pipes and whiskers that are still short. It slips between adults to eat scraps but can scarcely complete the 50-meter surface circuit or cross during a cold snap. It is strongly nocturnal but poor at judging what it finds, mistaking floating debris for food.

Origin: The name was given to small-bodied young that survived in families living in pipes for many generations. The speed with which they move shelter in response to leading indicators is learned by following their mothers, not inherited.

Habitat: Its main spaces are narrow joints in the Ttukseom Union branch lines and the area beneath ventilation ladders. When adults disperse to the gallery, it often cannot follow and remains beneath a refuge-chamber shelf. Restoring the designed flow rate eliminates this habitat altogether.
Needs: It needs only film scraps left by adults, small aquatic prey, and a low current that lets it dry. Loss of body heat threatens its life before lack of food does.

Life cycle and upkeep: If it cannot join the group carried to the ventilation room before its first flood, it grows exhausted on an intermediate ledge. After a season, its whiskers lengthen and it begins to read the current, but raising the flow rate before then cuts its growth short.

Behavior and hierarchy: It is at the bottom of the hierarchy and waits its turn to be carried by an elder female. If it goes to an exit alone, it confuses the sound of boots with the sound of pumps. H04 misses this small heat spot as debris more often than it misses adults.

Escalation: At stage 1, young that could not join the group moving to the ventilation room remain at pipe joints even during the day. At stage 2, they meet a robot head-on in a narrow pipe. At stage 3, unable to cross the dry passage during a cold snap on their own, they cling to an adult stronghold and further constrict maintenance space.

Engagement and response: Immediately raising the flow to its design rate or flooding the entire area wipes out a growing generation at once. Partial water blocking, alternative shelter, and sensor cleaning take priority; capture numbers cannot serve as a measure of success.

Negotiation and moral choice: Allowing a low flow rate for one more season lets the pipe-bound younglings grow and learn to read the current, but delays the recovery of pump capacity. Raising the flow immediately stabilizes drainage but also reduces the next generation's ability to adapt to the pipes and the information available from this indicator species. Moving these animals to the gallery's heating during a cold snap draws power from the Mapo Union; leaving them in the refuge chamber lets them occupy the maintenance platform.
Scenario connection: This is the growth stage left out of the group carried in G04-SC1 and the one that clings to the dry passage in G04-SC3, narrowing the space further.

The Raccoon Dog were raccoon family groups going back and forth between the pipelines connected to the pumping station of the Myeongbu Church in the Ttukseom Union, the dry shelters beneath the workshops, and the underground cable galleries of the Yeouido Investment Federation in the Mapo Union.

After the collapse, when the inspection cycles of the Jungnang, Tancheon, and inner storm-water trunks were cut off, animals that had moved following aquatic food, trash, and carcass remains settled in the pipelines people had abandoned.
By day they hid beneath manholes and by night they patrolled the alleys within about 50 meters of the exits.
The sight of wet fur rising from storm drains and covered channels stirred the fear that sewage was flowing back into living spaces, but seeing them as a single underground army was wrong.
The part that touched reality went no further than the fact that wildlife could appear around urban streams and facilities.
The order of sensing the water level before the pumps and influencing pipeline operations was a fiction set in this region, and did not explain accidents at any real institution or business.
The core habitat was the low-velocity pipelines and dry shelters beside the Ttukseom Union pumps.
When rain continued and the water rose, the families moved their young to the high ventilation rooms and then dispersed into the transmission galleries and ventilation shafts of the Mapo Union.

When cold snaps and logistics breakdowns struck from the direction of the XT04 Duman River Far East Theater and changed the distribution of feed and waste, they moved briefly to the eastern branch lines and returned to their familiar pipes after the thaw.
Aquatic food, organic trash, carcasses, and microbial mats became their food, and dry shelters and gentle currents lowered the cost of survival.

When HC04 Ttukseom Heat-Source House put off sediment dredging too long, the food film thickened and density rose, and when it scraped everything out at once, the family groups were pushed out into the surface markets.
Droppings and microbial mats covered the water-quality sensors and slowed even the pumps' judgments, so it could not be reduced to a problem of too much food.
The Raccoon Dog had no fixed leader.
In the dry season each family used its own feeding ground and dry shelter, and when several families used the same trunk they divided the hours.
The elder female only held priority in moving the young and at narrow passing points, and gave no battle orders to other families.

When the food film thickened after a flood, different families took turns using one pipeline, and when their shelters flooded repeatedly, they gave up the sharing rules and scattered into the surface alleys.

Even when the pipeline robots of H04 Gangbyeol added up several heat sources and movements into a single colony, the HC04 drainage watch had to divide them again by sleeping places, numbers of young, and times of coming and going.
Treating the family groups as a single swarm did not make their movement routes easier to predict; it meant missing their different escape directions all at once.
With their whiskers they read currents and the airflow in narrow gaps, and through pressure changes felt in their feet and bodies they sensed the water rising before the pumps started.
By smell they told food from disinfectant and rotting carcasses, and by hearing they separated pump vibration from the sound of human boots.
There were times they moved to high ground before the official sensors did, but they were not always right.
For it could be the result of families sharing past flood experience and learning the safe dredging timetable.
Over many generations a small build suited to narrow pipes and strong nocturnality might remain, but such adaptations lowered their ability to cross the surface and their resistance to cold.
Changing shelters within a few days had to be distinguished as family learning, not genetic change.
H04's logs confused raccoons with floating debris and crouching people, so the final judgment required human visual confirmation.
Conflict began with pressure precursor signals and grew through sensor disagreement and competition for shelter.
In the first stage, before rain, the family groups moved to the high ventilation rooms and served as an unofficial alarm.
In the second stage, droppings and microbial mats made the official water gauges read low, and the inspection robots met the family groups face to face in narrow pipes.
In the last stage, floods or cold snaps left only one dry pipe, and the pump maintenance crews and several families demanded the same space.
Poison bait and total flooding looked like quick solutions, but the decay of carcasses worsened water quality and endangered both the downstream and the workers.

Partial water-blocking, sensor cleaning, alternative shelter pipes, and limited night surface passage came first, and results were measured not by the number removed but by pump recovery time, sensor reliability, and 0 bites on the surface.
G04-SC1 ‘The Leading Indicator Beneath the Manhole’ began when, though rain had not yet come, the family groups moved their young to the high ventilation rooms from daytime on.

The Ttukseom Union and HC04 could adopt this movement at once as a preliminary alarm, could wait until the field measurements of HP01 Sluice House were finished, or could preheat the pumps only when the ecological signal and the measured values disagreed.
The first choice bought preparation time, but left the question of responsibility when a false alarm wasted fuel and labor.
The second was clear in its grounds but could be late for a short, sudden inflow.
The third saved fuel in ordinary times but risked missing a local downpour in which both signals came late together.
The raccoons' behavior could be useful supplementary data, but must never become grounds for punishment or culling.
Whether to entrust part of public safety to an unofficial ecological signal was the burden of this choice.
In G04-SC2 ‘Two Families at the Dredging Window,’ the night dredging time HC04 had set overlapped with the alternating shelter times of two families.

Putting in the equipment as planned brought both families out into the surface markets of the Ttukseom Union and the Mapo Union at once, and complaints arose on both the cable passage and the drainage side.
Dividing the dredging into two sections kept each family's escape route but delayed the completion of the work.
Opening an empty dry pipe as an alternative shelter could reduce surface appearances but meant giving up the Mapo Union's spare space for communication cables.
Buying out one family's hours of use with food and a safe passage and dredging intensively was fastest, but unfairly changed the time-sharing rules the other family had kept.
Judged by efficiency alone the last choice could be advantageous, but sharing rules once broken came back as larger simultaneous appearances in later rains.
G04-SC3 ‘The Dry Passage of the Pump Room’ was the stage at which, in the XT04 cold snap, three families occupied the only unfrozen pump approach together.
Providing heated alternative shelter pipes could clear the inspection route and disperse the families, but power rations fell and the Mapo Union's other facilities had to endure the cold.
Putting off pump inspection avoided the immediate clash but increased the risk of flooding at thaw or in a sudden rain.
Installing temporary external inspection platforms allowed maintenance without clearing the pipes, but the work crew had to bear the labor of installation in the cold and the risk of falls.
HC04 adjusted the dredging times, surface curfew times, and heating of the alternative pipes in one ledger.

At the last sluice inspection just before the flood, the Ttukseom Union slowed the upstream inflow and, instead of clearing the sediment from the side ditches, accepted a plan to preserve the continuity of the dry passages and feeding grounds the Raccoon Dog had used.

The Mapo Union closed the temporary outfalls that had hidden sources of pollution and disclosed its water-quality records in the joint ledger, and XT04 linked the alarm network with bypass channels so that the evacuation routes would not be submerged even when the water rose sharply.

HC04 took on the treatment of injured animals and the moving of the young while stopping indiscriminate capture, and H04 brought night patrols and residents' representatives together to reduce dumping and food conflicts around the passages.
With this, the central sump became not a barrier dividing human zones from habitat zones but a buffer zone sharing the times for water, waste, and movement.

Each group agreed not merely to stay out of the other's territory but to take turns with inspection, cleaning, and rescue at set hours, and when damage occurred, to investigate its cause jointly first and then divide the burden according to contribution to inflow and capacity for recovery.
When the passages held and the backflow stopped even after the first rain, the old expulsion order was withdrawn.
The Raccoon Dog was recognized as lawful residents of the underground, and the five parties accepted one another as neighbors in the same watershed rather than as objects of surveillance.
So that this agreement would not remain a one-time truce, later management hardened not into a seasonal joint stewardship but into a system of joint care.

The Ttukseom Union and XT04 measured water level, flow velocity, dissolved oxygen, turbidity, and ammoniacal nitrogen every week, the Mapo Union recorded monthly traces of illegal discharge and the weight of floating waste, and HC04 and H04 disclosed together every quarter the number of animals, survival of the young, rates of skin and respiratory abnormalities, passage use, the number of resident reports, and response times.

The standards were set at no more than 1 rainy-season backflow a month, at least 95 percent operation of the main passages, a decrease in the share of injured animals from the previous year, and initial response to emergency reports within 30 minutes.

When the standards were missed twice in a row, the alarm network automatically moved up a stage, and after temporary embankments, cutting off pollution sources, moving vulnerable animals, and independent sample retests were carried out in order, only the section at fault was closed on a limited basis.

If data were lost or a responsible party withdrew, the records were restored through paper ledgers and dispersed observers, and part of the next season's management authority was entrusted to the joint committee to restore trust.

As the stench and trash lessened, the distribution of night insects changed, the bats and birds that pursued them increased and widened the food web around the drains, and on the now safer walking paths late-hour activity by residents increased.

As a result ecological recovery could come back as new pressure from noise and light, so they included light-level limits, low-noise hours, and seasonal detour sections among the indicators and kept revising the scope of coexistence.
G04-SC1 · The Leading Indicator Under the Manhole
Trigger: Before the rain came, a G04 family group began moving its kits into a high ventilation room from daytime.
Ecological mechanism: An upstream pressure change altered pipe behavior before the official sensors did.
Choices: Adopt the raccoon movement as a preliminary alarm / Wait for a field measurement by the HP01 sluice house / Preheat the pumps only when the two signals differ

Outcomes: A preliminary alarm left responsibility for false positives, and a field measurement delayed drainage preparation. The cross-check condition saved fuel but could miss a short local downpour.
Moral cost: The dispute was whether a public-safety decision could be left to an unofficial ecological signal.
G04-SC2 · Two Families in the Dredging Window
Trigger: HC04's night dredging overlapped the time-divided hiding places of two family groups.
Ecological mechanism: When the shared pipe's timetable broke, the family groups came out into the surface markets at the same time.
Choices: Split the dredging into two sections / Open a substitute dry pipe / Buy one family group's time slot and dredge in concentration

Outcomes: Split dredging delayed completion of the work, and a substitute pipe reduced space for the communications cables. Buying a time slot was fast but made the sharing rule with the other family groups unfair.
Moral cost: Decide in what proportion to divide drainage efficiency, communications space, and fairness among the family groups.
G04-SC3 · The Dry Passage of the Pump Room
Trigger: In an XT04 cold wave, three family groups overlapped in occupying the only dry pump access.
Actors: S04, S09, XT04, HC04, H04
Ecological mechanism: Cold-wave vulnerability and a shortage of high hiding places concentrated the usually loose family groups into one passage.
Choices: Provide a heated refuge pipe / Delay the pump inspection / Install a temporary external inspection platform
Outcomes: A refuge pipe used power, and a delayed inspection raised the flood risk.
An external platform did not have to share the passage, but it accepted installation labor and fall risk in the cold wave.
Moral cost: Immediate stability of the city's drainage and refuge for the nonhuman family groups could not be secured at the same time.

leaves.text: It was an ordinary rat colony formed between the underside of the Eastern Command's transfer arcade and cable trays on the Gwangjin Line and the evacuation stairs of the Anguk Order on the Yeouido Line. Crumbs of carbohydrate, protein leftovers, and the heat of insulated piping made its density, and it spread no special pathogens. It had no fixed leader, and when food traces shifted, even the core that seemed to be the center moved.

Gap-whisker, warm core, and counter-core were path and breeding concentrations of the same species, not a king and a guard. The tray-warmer and the closed-shop shade were facility sections the rats occupied, and the unloading film was a phenomenon in which, after a protein unloading, several kinds gathered on the hub floor. The cold-gap was a local branch timed to elevator drip, and E01 through E06 remained in an excluded batch.
