G05, the Brown Rat, was an urban animal community formed at the transfer junction where the underground ration passages of the Eastern Command on the Gwangjin Line met the evacuation stairs of the Anguk Order on the Yeouido Line.
Food crumbs fell beneath the floor of the transfer arcade, and heat lingered between the cable trays and insulated pipes even in winter.

Each time a tail vanished into a gap in the platform or a guide display suddenly went dark, people thought first of contagion and contamination, but this colony was not something that spread special pathogens.
It was close to an ordinary animal community whose density rose where food, warmth, and shelter overlapped.

But the dispersed core-nest network, the pattern of learning the order of pest control, and the management procedure using one-way escape routes were not real disease-control guidelines but fictional ecological rules that held only in this world.
So explanations that blamed the colony's appearance on the uncleanliness of a particular group or on refugees neither fit the facts nor helped the response.
The core habitat was the underside of the Gwangjin Line transfer arcade and the cable trays, but the colony's boundaries shifted with human movement and the state of rations.

When evacuation density on the Yeouido Line rose, branch nests reached into the walls of the temporary feeding stations and the cables of the evacuation stairs, and in the weeks when large volumes of frozen and deep-sea protein leftovers came in from the XT05 Incheon Trust Theater, movement traces ran as far as the unloading elevator passages.
Into the bright surface zones where disinfection was frequent they came up only at night, and they used the backs of shutters where traffic had stopped as temporary stores.
Three resources sustained the colony's economy: crumbs of carbohydrate, protein leftovers, and the heat of insulated piping.
However tightly HC05 Bukhansan Bogukmun Records House sealed its archives and reagent stores, the overall density did not fall as long as meal leftovers remained and the trays were open.
When droppings and moisture hastened damage to wire insulation, the uptime of lighting and guide displays decreased, which in turn increased the congestion and anxiety of the evacuation passages.
In sectors where food and heat met, two or three breeding cores usually formed.
Each core was linked to branch nests reaching along the cable trays, and even if one core disappeared, the colony as a whole did not collapse at once.
Animals crowded into the remaining cores, and shutter gaps and pipe supports that had been little used became new movement routes.
To lower density over the long term, leftover collection and dry conditions had to be kept in every sector, and removing one conspicuous nest was only a temporary relocation.
When the sequence of poison, ultrasound, and sealing work repeated, the population found open escape routes ever faster.
This was not a sudden bodily change but learning by which the surviving animals and the route-pioneering animals avoided the dangerous sequence.
A tendency to endure cold or bright platforms might persist over several generations, but at the price of higher energy use and a lower breeding rate.
The Brown Rat had no fixed leader.
A core with heavy traffic only looked like the center for a while, and when the food traces shifted, the center moved too.

The route-pioneering animals probed airflow and gaps with whiskers and smell, and told trains, ration carts, and approaching people apart by the temperature and vibration felt through their feet and bodies.
They could not precisely classify distant heat sources or read electronic signals.
The infrared maps of H05 Yunjae made up for these limits, but a single hot spot on the screen must not be taken for a leader or a nest.
For steam, people, and heat leaking from pipes could all appear as similar masses.

H05 had to mark night dropping traces, the footprints of the young, and the traffic of each core together, and just after one spot disappeared, it tracked first the flow spreading to the remaining nests.
The situation worsened through three stages: core search, route rewiring, and a crisis of sealing order.
At first, the key was confirming the separate breeding cores.
If only one was sealed off, animals crowded under the shop shutters and into other trays, and the second stage began.
If the feeding-station side was closed first in the wrong order and the colony entered the emergency stairs, the earlier work had in effect failed.
The occupied sectors had to be confirmed again, a one-way escape route opened from the cores to sectors people did not use, and the sectors sealed one after another from the back.
Full-scale poison spraying and fire were kept only as a last resort because of the exposure of children, pets, and other wildlife.

Leftover collection and keeping things cold and dry were the basic response, and success was judged not by numbers captured but by the number of electrical shorts, 0 cases of food contamination, 0 non-target deaths, and evacuation transit time.
There could be no direct dialogue with the colony, but among the surrounding human groups there was ample room for negotiation.

HC05 Bukhansan Bogukmun Records House mediated between the Gwangjin Line and the Yeouido Line over the leftover collection cycle, the order of tray-sealing work, and the intervals of the night shop shutters.
During the weeks of XT05 protein unloading, temporary double-sealing lines were supported first, and keeping the ration speed meant bearing the cost of dividing the unloading times.
Coexistence was possible at the level of reducing access to food and keeping movement routes apart from the evacuation passages.
Conversely, if fear of contagion was used to seal off only the refugee zones, the colony went into deeper cable layers and the cost of recovery grew.
If leftover collection was put off for the sake of fast rations, the rewired routes became fixed.
Whose passage and labor to slow in order to gain safety was the real moral cost of this ecological problem.
G05-SC1 ‘The Second Core Nest’ began when only one large colony appeared on H05's thermal images, but traces of young were found in the tray on the opposite side.
The Gwangjin Line and HC05 could survey every core first to confirm non-target creatures and the evacuation passages.
This choice was the safest but delayed the opening of the passage.
Buying an old cable heat map from HP09 Digital Media City Trust House could shorten the survey time, but past passage records had to be handed over as payment.
To avoid exposing private lives, a one-way escape route could be tested in a single sector, but a space people did not use had to be closed for a long time in case of failure.
Whichever was chosen, conflict arose between those who wanted immediate sanitation measures and those trying to prevent mistaken captures.
Ignoring the unseen second core and removing only the first nest moved the center of the colony to the opposite side and raised the cost of the next stage.
In G05-SC2 ‘The Sealing-Order Error,’ after the feeding-station shutters were closed first, the colony ran backward into the cables of the Yeouido Line evacuation stairs.
S05, the Yeouido Line, HC05, and H05 could stop the work and seal again from the back.
In that case contamination fell, but the evacuation-passage work and ration delays grew longer.
Pausing leftover collection and leaving bait to lure the colony back to its original sector could clear the walkway quickly, but meant deliberately accepting food contamination.
Sending the refugees along a surface detour for the night made the cable-layer work safe, but required heating and guards to protect people vulnerable to the cold.
No path could make evacuation speed, food safety, and non-target harm all as good as possible.
Above all, pushing the danger onto the refugees and declaring the work a success collapsed the basis for later negotiation.
G05-SC3 ‘The Predators of the Open Courtyard’ was raised when the colony blocked the transfer hub after the XT05 protein unloading.

The Gwangjin Line and the Yeouido Line could draw predatory birds in on a limited basis into an open courtyard equipped with collision-prevention markers, dropping washing, and non-target species monitoring.
This could shrink the colony quickly, but needed standing staff to manage bird collisions and the new dropping problem.
Holding only to stepwise escape routes and sealing without bringing in a predator relationship had few ecological side effects, but delayed rations and evacuation for a long time.
If XT05 spread out its unloading schedule to reduce the inflow of food itself, it created no non-target risk, but the unit cost of cold logistics and food losses rose.
Whatever the choice, HC05 and H05 had to disclose shorts, contamination, transit time, and non-target deaths together.

The moment one ecological problem was shifted onto another animal's predation, responsibility did not shift with it, and coexistence with the Brown Rat was in the end a matter of deciding who would bear the invisible labor of cleaning and slowed rations.

Long-term management had to harden not into one-time capture but into the work of S05, the Yeouido Line, and HC05 accumulating in a joint ledger the changes in food, heat, and shelter in each transfer sector.

The Gwangjin Line measured the weight of leftovers and collection delays after closing every day, the Yeouido Line recorded night crossing traces per 100 meters of evacuation stairs and the 95th percentile of transit time, and HC05 compared cable insulation damage rates, insulation resistance, humidity, and sightings of non-target animals monthly.

H05's hot spots were judged active cores only when they matched the number of fresh droppings, footprints of young, and bait loss by tray, and even without shorts or food contamination, a preemptive inspection began when movement traces increased two weeks in a row.

When a sealing failure spread the colony into the evacuation passages, further sealing stopped, one earlier escape route was reopened to lower the pressure, and then the food storage lines were temporarily doubled and human detour routes secured first.

Recovery was complete not by the amount captured but when there had been no traces of backward running for three days, no signs of a new core for seven nights, and insulation resistance and evacuation transit time had returned to baseline.

The same workers took charge of the sectors each season so that they remembered even small changes, while the unloading, ration, and facility divisions shared the rotating costs so that responsibility did not settle on the cleaning staff alone.

If the colony was reduced sharply at such a time, the fine leftovers it had been consuming could ferment in the drain grooves and raise insect density, which increased chemical use and drainpipe washing and in fact enlarged the management burden of the food zones.
So watching the decay of leftovers and the insect catch together even after the numbers fell was part of long-term stability.
Trigger: The H05 thermal image showed only one colony, but kit traces were found on the tray on the opposite side.
Ecological mechanism: Because of the distributed core-nest net, even removing one point moved the colony's center into another section.
Choices: Survey every core first / Buy the old cable heat map from the HP09 Digital Media City Trust House / Test a one-way retreat in one section
Outcomes: A survey delayed the opening of the evacuation passage, and buying the heat map was fast but required handing over passage records.
A retreat test avoided exposing information, but closed one unoccupied section for a long time.
Moral cost: Decide which side to assign the time to: an immediate sanitation measure, or the procedure for confirming non-target life.
G05-SC2 · The Error in the Sealing Order
Trigger: When the shutter on the feeding-station side was closed first, the colony ran back into the cables of the Yeouido Line evacuation stairs.
Ecological mechanism: The net connecting the cores remembered the sealing order and concentrated new routes in the direction that stayed open.
Choices: Seal again from the rear / Stop leftover collection and leave bait / Send the refugees onto a surface detour for one night
Outcomes: Resealing lengthened the work time, and bait accepted food contamination. The surface detour emptied the cable layer but demanded cold and guard labor.
Moral cost: The refugees' fast passage and contamination and non-target harm could not be minimized at the same time.
G05-SC3 · The Predator of the Open Courtyard
Trigger: After an XT05 protein unloading, the colony blocked the transfer hub, and a proposal to bring in predatory birds was put forward.
Actors: S05, S10, XT05, HC05, H05
Ecological mechanism: The distributed nest net could be reduced all at once, but new risks appeared: bird strikes, droppings, and non-target predation.
Choices: Open a courtyard fitted with marks and monitoring / Use only staged retreat and sealing / Spread the XT05 unloading schedule and cut the food inflow itself
Outcomes: The courtyard demanded long-term management labor, and staged sealing produced ration delays.
Spreading the unloading created no non-target risk, but raised the unit cost of frozen logistics and food loss.
Moral cost: It left the responsibility of a choice that transferred one ecological problem into another predation relationship.

G06.selector: p, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, blockquote, pre, li, th, td

leaves.text: It was a mixed stopover in which waterfowl, waders, and raptors overlapped at the waterfront records deck of the Government of the Republic of Korea at central Seoul Station and the drainage ponds of the Seongha Group on the Gangnam Line. Waterfowl ate aquatic plants and floating matter, waders benthic creatures, and raptors rodents and exhausted small birds. There was no unified command and no aim of attacking the city.

From the broad-feather perch to the pursuit wing, these were wild birds of different functional groups. The pond mirror and the open mirror were the water surface of an intermediate stopover itself, and the three-layer flight was a knot in the air where three heights overlapped on one bridge cross-section. The rooftop gutter was a branch of the same waterfowl, using inland fountains and rooftop gutters in the dry season when the wetland dried.

Where migratory stopovers overlapped on the severed green spaces and failed restored wetlands around the Han River, Nanji, and Amsa, predatory birds and omnivorous waterfowl formed a mixed colony amid the management vacuum after the collapse and became the Grey Heron and Cormorant. / The waterfront records deck of the Government of the Republic of Korea at central Seoul Station and the depot drainage ponds of the Seongha Group on the Gangnam Line were its key nodes. / Real protected-area sources were used only as a reference range for the locations of migratory-bird sites and wetlands, and the negotiating rules of the mixed functional groups were fiction.

The core habitat was the waterfront wetland fragments at Seoul Station Central and the drainage ponds and wire perches of the Gangnam Line. / During seasonal movement they rode the wind road toward the XT01 Imjin River Gate Theater and went back and forth on the north-south axis, and at breeding and stopover peaks they occupied the sightlines of bridges and sluices and the air over the depot yard tracks. / When the wetland dried they moved temporarily to inland park fountains and rooftop gutters.

The waterfowl ate aquatic plants and organic floating matter, the waders ate the benthic life of shallow water, and the raptors ate rodents and weak birds. / The distance between safe perches, shallow water, and feeding grounds was the upkeep cost. / When HC06 the Noryangjin Delivery House drained the wetland water level one-sidedly, the waterfowl were driven to the depot ponds, the waders to the mud edges, and the raptors followed that concentration. / Fixing the water level raised stopover density and the risk of train-bird collision on the depot yard tracks together.

In spring and autumn the waterfowl and waders stopped first on the shallow water, and when food density rose the raptors followed. / The breeding grounds were in a separate protected area, and the depot ponds were used only as an intermediate stopover. / When the water level dropped sharply the waterfowl left first, and the food relationship of the waders and raptors also came apart in a chain.

Vision was the main sense, and they were sensitive to water-surface glare, vest color, and drone silhouettes. / By hearing they read engines, gunshots, and warning loudspeakers, and scent responded to fish meal and rot. / They did not decode electronic signals. / H06 Baksol's radar-based altitude classification confused balloons, drones, and birds, so it was corrected by eye.

There was no command system. / The waterfowl occupied the open water as a flock, the waders worked the shallow edges at intervals, and the raptors moved from the high wires and pylons following the density of the two functional groups. / When one functional group moved, the space use of the other functional groups changed because of food and alert responses. / When H06 summed them into one hostile score, the HC06 ecology watch recorded them again by altitude, water-surface zone, and head count for each functional group.

Individuals learned the repeating train times and the low-noise inspection windows, but the response differed by functional group. / A change in movement season across many generations was treated only as food and climate selection pressure, and a route change within one season was distinguished as learning. / The more they matched the city's timetable, the more there was a cost of growing dull to the irregular dangers of a natural wetland.

Vision was the main sense, so they took off at water-surface glare, the color of work vests, and drone silhouettes. Engine noise and loudspeakers told them only distance, and they did not know electronic signals or sluice numbers. When waterfowl covered the open surface, the waders were only pushed to the edges and the raptors to the wires, and one radar score from H06 Baksol had to be written again by altitude.

G06E01 · Grey Heron and Cormorant Open-Water Occupant 'Broadwing Perch'
Common species, variants and command scope
The open-water occupant 'Broadwing Perch' does not direct the flock with calls; it covers open water first through its size and wingspan. Despite its designation as a controller, it gives no orders.

A controller: an adult waterbird that covers open water first through its size and wingspan, rather than directing the flock with calls. Its eyes distinguish reflections on the water, the colors of work vests, and drone silhouettes; from engine noise and loudspeakers, it can judge only distance. It knows nothing of electronic signals or the water-level numbers inside the sluice gates, and its ankles sink at muddy edges, preventing it from standing there long.

When the fragmented Han River–Nanji wetlands dried up and only the water in front of Seoul Station’s central records deck remained, the first waterbird to arrive occupied the open surface, placing this body at the center. The overlapping shallows of G06-SC1 are its stage; the water left after HC06 turned on the pumps for visibility fixed its occupation in place.

By day it spreads its flock across the middle of Seoul Station’s central shallow water; when the level falls, it moves to the Gangnam Line drainage pond. It passes over the bridge walkway but does not stay there, and its talons are unsuited to wire perches.

Aquatic plants and suspended organic matter are its food; safe open water and a short takeoff distance are what it needs to stay. If HC06 lowers the water level, suspended matter gathers in one strip and strengthens its hold. Holding the water level steady increases its numbers and, with them, the risk of train collisions.

It grows larger only during spring and autumn stopovers; outside the migratory seasons, its wings become lighter and the birds disperse. When its feathers are soaked in turbid water, takeoff is delayed, exposing it to pursuit by raptors. If forcibly dispersed for a season, it occupies the same water earlier at the next stopover.

It gives no orders. When the water surface narrows, shorebirds are merely pushed toward the edges and raptors toward the wires. Even if H06 Baksol combines them into one score, the HC06 duty officer records altitude and water zones separately. If this bird leaves, the open water is vacated and shorebirds spread as far as the trackside.

In stage 1, it covers the middle of the narrowed water, blocking the view from the records deck. In stage 2, a single raptor pursuit sends the dense flock surging across the view of the sluice gates and the train arrival and departure tracks. In stage 3, after the same collision occurs three times, the response must set both zone-specific water levels and slowdown times rather than call for extermination.

Gunfire and nets scatter the flock to fountains and rooftop water catchments, making its next stopover unpredictable. Zone-specific water levels, fishmeal-waste collection, and drone altitude limits are the basics. Success is measured by the duration of clear sightlines, zero collisions, and turbidity—not carcasses.

Running the pumps longer to expand the open water increases labor and energy use; drying the water merely to gain visibility brings dust, stench, and rodents down on residents. Creating a new shorebird feeding ground outside the depot leaves this bird’s occupation intact while reducing crowding at the edges, but citizens bear the land and dredging costs.
The overlapping water of G06-SC1 is the stage for this occupation; the slowdown learning of G06-SC2 and the takeoffs during the migratory-bird week of G06-SC3 follow in a chain from the same body.
G06E02 · Grey Heron and Cormorant Roving Waterbird 'Driftwood'
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

The roving waterbird 'Driftwood' is a medium-sized waterbird that follows bands of floating organic matter instead of holding the middle of the water. Even when Broadwing Perch covers the surface, using only the band at the edge avoids conflict.

A common ecological type: a medium-sized waterbird that follows bands of floating organic matter rather than holding the middle of the water. Its bill sorts plant fragments from fishmeal scraps, and its eyes notice oil slicks before the color of rubbish. It cannot understand vibrations in wires or radar classifications, and gives up diving when turbidity prevents it from seeing the bottom.

During a season when rain washed fishmeal from market unloading into the edges of Seoul Station’s central water, individuals displaced from the open surface split off and pursued only floating matter. Standing water in the unsuccessfully restored wetland was a feeding ground; the longer collection was delayed, the farther their roaming route extended from the unloading area to the drainage pond.

Ordinarily it circles in the slow current outside the mudline of Seoul Station’s central water. When the wetland dries, it briefly moves to inland park fountains and rooftop water catchments. It visits the Gangnam Line pond only when floating matter gathers there, and does not fly over the train arrival and departure tracks.

It feeds more on floating organic matter and discarded fishmeal than on aquatic plants; a band of scent, not a clean water surface, sustains it. If HC06 collects the waste, it does not go to the pond. If the waste is left, it follows it low into the unloading alleys, overlapping with pedestrians.

If an oil slick mats its feathers during a stopover season, taking off becomes difficult and it retreats to fountains. After forced dispersal, it searches for the same smell from farther away. When the floating matter is cut off, its numbers fall the following season and it does not join the flock occupying the open water.

There is neither command nor a spacing rule. It follows floating matter when it moves; even when Broadwing Perch covers the surface, it avoids conflict by using only the band at the edge. If H06 turns its roaming tracks into a single hostility score, HC06 changes only the waste-collection time.

In stage 1, rain washes fishmeal from unloading into a band beneath the records deck. In stage 2, the band extends to the drainage pond and waterbirds skim the edge of the depot tracks. In stage 3, the smell reaches fountains and rooftops, turning urban water catchments into temporary stopovers.

Horns and drones drive it into alley puddles while leaving the band of scent in place. Fishmeal collection and covers at the unloading area break the route. Success is measured by the number of incursions onto depot tracks and by turbidity, not carcasses.

Leaving fishmeal at the market to keep the pond clear makes unloading workers and pedestrians bear the smell and low flights. Thorough collection reduces this bird’s numbers, but the flock occupying the open water then crowds more densely onto what remains. Providing both unloading-area covers and temporary water outside the pond reduces collisions, but leaves the cost of cleaning water catchments.

In G06-SC1, the lowered water level gathers floating matter into one band; during the migratory-bird week of G06-SC3, that band stretches beneath the bridge. The forced dispersal of G06-SC2 merely disrupts its learned scent route, making the next run more irregular.
G06E03 · Grey Heron and Cormorant Spaced Shorebird 'Mudfoot'
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope
The spaced shorebird 'Mudfoot' sweeps the shallow muddy edge at regular intervals. It has no leader; when a raptor looks down from above, the spacing collapses and the birds take off together.

A common ecological type: a shorebird that sweeps the shallow muddy edge at regular intervals. Its long bill probes for bottom-dwelling organisms, while its eyes first register the distance to neighboring birds and the colors of work vests. It cannot take off from open water; engine noise tells it only direction, and it cannot read electronic guidance.

When waterbirds covered the remaining water, shorebirds landed on the exposed mudline and this spaced gait became established. The unpartitioned edge of G06-SC1 is the basis of its form; as the mud extended to the trackside inspection passage, its range began to overlap with pedestrian traffic.

The exposed mudflat beneath Seoul Station’s central records deck and the receding-water edge of the Gangnam Line pond are its main habitats. When the water level is steady, the birds spread farther apart; when it drops sharply, they pack together as far as the inspection-passage ledge. They do not perch on wires or pylons.

It feeds on bottom-dwelling organisms in shallow water; if the mudflat dries or dredging turns over the bottom, its bill probes in vain. When HC06 holds the water level steady, it raises the density of bottom-dwelling life but also increases track incursions. Unilateral drainage expands the mudflat but exposes food all at once, drawing the birds into a crowd.

When bill tips wear down during the spring stopover, spacing narrows and disputes increase. A flock caught in nets for one season hides deeper in the inspection passage on its next migration at the mere sight of a human silhouette.

There is no leader; the birds simply maintain their spacing. When waterbirds cover the surface, they are pushed to the edge. When a raptor looks down from a wire, their spacing collapses and they take off together. If H06 combines shorebirds and waterbirds into one count, the HC06 duty officer records the number of birds at the edge separately.

In stage 1, they land only on the mudflat beneath the deck. In stage 2, their spacing extends into the trackside inspection passage, overlapping with workers’ feet. In stage 3, a raptor pursuit sends the flock surging up across the height of the train arrival and departure tracks.

Mass netting drives birds that have learned the spacing into alley drains, increasing mistaken captures. It is safer to use zone-specific water levels to keep the mudline outside the tracks and maintain a shallow feeding ground beyond the depot. Success indicators are the number of incursions and the density of bottom-dwelling life.

Creating a new shorebird feeding ground outside the depot reduces crowding at the edge, but shifts the land and dredging burden to another district. Drying the mud to drive the birds out kills bottom-dwelling life and moves the next season’s stopover to the bridge walkway. Giving up one strip of walking space to preserve the mudflat sacrifices a little visibility in exchange for clear tracks.

The zone-specific water levels and outside feeding ground of G06-SC1 are the negotiated solution for this spacing; in G06-SC3, movement along the edge sets off a chain of movements at other heights. Drone dispersal in G06-SC2 breaks the spacing, causing the birds to gather more tightly at the next inspection time.
G06E04 · Grey Heron and Cormorant Daytime Hider 'Shade Perch'
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

The daytime hider 'Shade Perch' is a small waterbird that stays in the shade of the records deck by day and comes out onto the water only at dusk. It does not lead a flock, competing only for shaded space.

An ordinary ecological type, this small waterbird stays in the shade beneath the records deck by day and comes out onto the water only at dusk. Its eyes startle first at fluorescent vests and drone silhouettes, while its nose distinguishes human sweat and disinfectant more readily than decay. Under electric lights at night, it loses its bearings and cannot connect itself to a radar blip.

When the sluice observation boat became busy during the day, individuals avoiding open water began using the shade beneath the deck as a place to nap. Repeated low-noise inspection windows taught them to take off at dusk, and as fluorescent vests became more common, they retreated deeper into the shade.

Its daytime resting places are the shaded pilings and the space beneath the railings of Seoul Station Central's waterfront records deck; only at dusk does it move to the edge of the Gangnam Line pond. It avoids the bridge walkway and the airspace above the depot tracks at midday, and hides in the shade of rooftop catch basins if the wetland dries out.

It feeds on insects at the water's surface and thin organic films at dusk; shade and low noise are necessary for it to remain. If the deck stays open all day, it moves into the shade along the depot tracks, increasing collision risk. Restricting daytime access, however, delays recordkeeping work.

If repeatedly startled by fluorescent colors over a season, it begins taking off earlier at dusk, bringing its flights into the peak train period. If its feathers rot in the damp shade, its night flights shorten; after exposure to forced lighting, it hides deeper inside structures at its next stopover.

It does not lead a flock, competing only for shaded spots. Even when the broad-winged roost covers the water, their daytime spaces do not overlap. If H06 reports heat spots in the shade as a bird flock, a person distinguishes by sight whether the birds are resting or taking off.

At stage 1, it stays only in the shade beneath the deck and does not obstruct sightlines. At stage 2, as fluorescent vests become more common, its dusk takeoff veers toward the arrival and departure tracks. At stage 3, its shaded refuge shifts beneath vehicles on the depot tracks, bringing it into the same space as the low-noise inspection window and maintenance workers.

Loudspeakers and flashes drive birds in the shade farther under dark vehicle bodies. Toning down vest colors, changing the lighting beneath the deck to indirect light, and keeping drones out of the shaded flight zone delay takeoff. Success means zero maintenance injuries and clear sightlines, not carcasses.

Closing the deck by day to give its shade to the birds delays sluice records; keeping fluorescent colors sends takeoffs toward the tracks. Announcing one hour at dusk as a low-noise window reduces time for recordkeeping work, but means maintenance workers and birds need not share the same shade.

The low-noise inspection window in G06-SC2 sets this bird's takeoff clock, and the crowd inspecting the sluice in G06-SC3 pushes it from the shade toward the depot tracks. The narrow water surface in G06-SC1 draws it to the edge of open water only at dusk.
G06E05 · Grey Heron and Cormorant Water-Level Learner 'Pump Time'
Common species, variants and command scope

Water-level learner 'Pump Time' is a specialist that reads the band of food on the sloping water surface when the pump runs. It does not direct the flock; it only signals the slope, and a schedule change breaks its learned pattern.

A specialist waterbird that reads the band of food gathered where the water surface slopes when the pump runs. Its ears distinguish the pump's low rumble from train engines, and its eyes track how fast the water level drops by a handspan. It cannot read the operating schedule itself or know how much water lies beyond a closed sluice.

When HC06 began turning on the pump at the same time to improve visibility, it learned within a season that floating matter and fry gathered on the sloping water surface. This is a mechanical clock learned in one season, not a change in migration timing across generations; changing the schedule breaks the learning.

It stays on the water within sight of the Seoul Station Central pump outlet and near the water-level gauge at the Gangnam Line pond. It disperses during the day when the pump is idle. On days when the XT01 wind corridor coincides with pump operation, the slope grows steeper and it follows the food as far as beneath the bridge.

It feeds on organic matter concentrated as the water level falls. Running the pump irregularly breaks its learned pattern and drives the birds toward the pond. Keeping the time fixed stabilizes stopover density but increases the risk of overlap with trains at that hour.

Once it stores the pump's low rumble as a safety signal for a season, it gathers at the same time on its next migration. If its feathers are damaged by the swift current, it cannot follow the slope and settles at the edge of the waders' area. A single forced drainage brings its arrival the following season forward by a day.

It does not direct the flock; it only signals the slope. Other waterbirds simply gather along that band. Even if H06 raises the density reading on radar, HC06 reassesses pump operation when the pump logs and visual observations disagree.

At stage 1, it gathers in front of the outlet only when the pump runs. At stage 2, that time overlaps with train arrivals and departures, and its takeoff brushes the depot tracks. At stage 3, even after a sudden schedule change, it gathers at the old time, leaving the birds facing empty water as trains pass at a different time.

Scattering the birds with a horn binds the pump's low rumble and danger into a single signal, causing chaos every time it runs thereafter. It is safer to use compartmentalized water levels to create a slope only on the side away from the tracks and announce pump times alongside the low-noise window.

Running the pump only by day for the sake of public visibility brings this learned behavior into the pedestrian peak. Tying pump operation to the migratory-bird slowdown period delays freight but keeps the food band and trains from competing for the same minute. Keeping the schedule secret makes recordkeeping easier, but startles birds and maintenance workers at the same time.

The compartmentalized water levels in G06-SC1 divide the slopes this specialist reads, and the timetable change in G06-SC2 brings pump learning into conflict with train learning. Sluice inspections in G06-SC3 run the pump more often, pushing the concentrated band beneath the bridge.
G06E06 · Grey Heron and Cormorant Benthic Forager 'Beak Spacing'
Common species, variants and command scope

Benthic forager 'Beak Spacing' is a wader that picks benthic organisms from the mud only as deep as its beak can reach. There is no leader setting the foraging order; when waterbirds cover the water, its beak becomes submerged and it stops working.

A specialist wader that picks benthic organisms from the mud only as deep as its beak can reach. It keeps enough distance from others that their beaks do not overlap, and its eyes look for breathing holes in the bottom rather than water turbidity. Unlike waterbirds sensitive to surface reflections, it relies chiefly on the texture of the mud; it does not understand the numbers on an electronic turbidity meter.

When aquatic plants dwindled and only mud remained in a wetland whose restoration had failed, some waders that had searched its edges began following benthic density so consistently that it became a specialization. Once Seoul Station Central began recording turbidity, the success or failure of these beaks appeared alongside the water-quality ledger.

It occupies the shallow mud at Seoul Station Central and the bottom exposed when the Gangnam Line pond recedes. If the water is too high, its beak cannot reach; if it dries completely, the benthic organisms die. It therefore does not go to inland fountains. It does not use pylon perches.

Benthic density is both its food supply and a measure of success. When the pump turns over the bottom, one meal is abundant and the following week is barren. If turbidity stabilizes but benthic organisms continue to decline, that indicates a failure in how the space has been arranged.

When the tip of its beak wears against stones, its spacing narrows and it drives away neighboring birds. After experiencing dredging for a season, it skips the same mud at its next stopover, leaving only a thin layer of mud along the lip of the inspection passage.

There is no leader setting the foraging order. Birds merely probe the richest benthic patches first; when waterbirds cover the water, their beaks become submerged and they stop working. Even if H06 increases its wader count, HC06 separately checks benthic density against beak marks.

At stage 1, it probes only the mud in front of the deck. At stage 2, benthic organisms shift to the drain toward the tracks, leaving beak marks on work platforms. At stage 3, after the bottom is overturned, the flock seeks moisture on the bridge walkway, bringing it into the path of passing pedestrians.

Removing the mud with an excavator kills the benthic organisms and makes the next season's stopover unpredictable. Leaving, through compartmentalized water levels, only enough depth for beaks to reach and postponing dredging until outside the migration period reduces collisions.

Dredging now for flood preparedness improves sluice safety but diminishes both this specialist's food supply and downstream purification. Removing or driving off a single functional group did not end the problem; it changed the other groups' use of space in unexpected directions.
This community depended heavily on sight.

Reflections on the water, the color of work vests, and the silhouettes of drones triggered takeoff and avoidance, and engine noise, gunfire, horns, and loudspeakers became cues for judging the distance and direction of danger.
They also responded to fishmeal and the smell of decay, but did not understand electronic signals.
The radar-based altitude classification of H06 Baksol could catch large movements early, but could confuse balloons, drones, and flocks of birds, so visual confirmation was needed.
The waterfowl occupied open water in flocks, the waders swept the edges keeping fixed distances apart, and the raptors watched the density of both groups from high power lines and pylons.
When H06 combined them into a single hostility score, the HC06 ecology watch recorded altitude, water zones, and numbers again by functional group.
The birds learned the repeating train times and the low-noise inspection hours.

Movement routes that changed within a season were the result of such learning, and changes in migration timing over several generations were distinguished as selection pressure applied by food and climate.
Birds grown used to the city timetable used the set slowdown sections as safety signals, but could become that much less sensitive to the irregular dangers of natural wetlands.
The situation began with a rearrangement of the water surfaces.
When the waterfowl were crowded onto narrow water and the waders spread onto the trackside inspection walkways, a single chase by a raptor sent the whole flock soaring.
This was a chain emergency cutting across the sluice sightlines and the depot's in-and-out tracks.

When the same collision repeated three times, it moved not to a purge but to the stage of a seasonal operating agreement, and train slowdowns, depot-track closures, and water zones had to be adjusted together.
Gunfire and mass netting looked fast but scattered the community unpredictably and lost its ecological legitimacy as well.
The basic response was water-level control by zone, collection of fishmeal and trash, alternative roosts outside the in-and-out tracks, securing low-noise work hours, and drone altitude limits.
HC06 provided open water for the waterfowl, shallow mud edges for the waders, and high roosts off the tracks for the raptors, each separately.
In the weeks of XT01 bird migration, train slowdown times and low-noise inspection times were announced together, and fishing and collection curfews were also adjusted by functional group.

Success was judged not by the number of birds driven off but by the time the sluice sightlines were secured, 0 collisions between trains and birds, the number of depot-track intrusions, and water turbidity.
Deciding which birds to protect and which to remove by appearance alone widened the room for smuggling and mistaken capture.
G06-SC1 ‘Three Functional Groups in Shallow Water’ began when the water level at central Seoul Station fell and waterfowl, waders, and raptors overlapped on a single narrow stretch of water.
Central Seoul Station and HC06 could run the pumps more to make the water level differ by zone.
Open water and mud edges were separated and clashes decreased, but labor and energy use rose.
Creating new wader feeding grounds outside the depot could reduce crowding at the edges, but meant accepting land and dredging costs.
Installing alternative raptor roosts on the edge of the wetland could lower depot-track collisions, but the places where rodents were hunted could shift toward residential areas.
H06's observation data had to show the positions and feeding relationships of all three functional groups together rather than point to one kind of bird as the cause.
In G06-SC2 ‘The Birds That Learned the Train Timetable,’ after the slowdown times at the Gangnam Line depot changed, the stopover flocks soared up in time with the track inspection hours.

The waterfowl had learned the old slowdown times as a safe takeoff signal, and the raptors had learned the flocks dropping low at those times as a hunting chance, so both kinds of learning collided with the new timetable.
Returning the slowdown times to the old ones made collisions easier to predict but delayed evacuation and logistics.
Installing alternative roosts for each functional group could separate their routes in the long run, but needed continuing maintenance and observation.

Dispersing them at once with horns and drones could clear the tracks for the moment, but it broke the learning by which the birds had linked operating signals to safe times, and made the next movement more irregular.
Whether the safety rules the wild animals had accumulated could be changed unilaterally for the sake of human operating efficiency became the central issue among S06, the Gangnam Line, HC06, and H06.

G06-SC3 ‘Tracks in Migration Week’ arose when large movements from the XT01 direction and sluice inspections coincided and the bridge walkways and depot in-and-out tracks were occupied again and again.
The waterfowl taking off from the water, the waders moving along the edges, and the raptors in pursuit made chain collisions at different heights.
Cutting service to fit the migration timetable reduced the chance of collision most directly but slowed evacuation and logistics.
Expanding the water and roost zones could separate the functional groups, but meant shrinking the citizens' walking spaces and the depot's work spaces.
Draining the water to drive the community out secured the sightlines at once, but made dust and stench and drew in rodents and other predators.
Removing the community entirely to hide the failure of restoration weakened even downstream purification and the international migration corridor.
In the end the coexistence agreement was neither a declaration that stopped the city for the birds nor an order that emptied the wetlands for the city.
It was a promise to decide openly how much movement right and space each side would yield to the other in which season, and not to push that cost onto the residents of particular zones alone.

Long-term management of the Grey Heron and Cormorant required going beyond forming temporary response teams each migration period to a system in which S06, the Gangnam Line, and HC06 handed over water and tracks as a single seasonal asset.

Central Seoul Station measured water-level gradients, turbidity, benthic density, and 15-minute occupancy rates by functional group, the Gangnam Line recorded takeoff altitudes, depot-track intrusions, emergency braking, and near-collision avoidances tied to operating hours, and H06 disclosed the visual-confirmation rate and misidentification rate for each radar classification.

When the waterfowl's mass takeoffs crossed the baseline as raptors' roosting time increased, or the waders' feeding alone decreased while turbidity was stable, it was judged a failure of spatial arrangement rather than simply of numbers.

When a timetable change or a failure of water-level control set off a chain emergency, forced dispersal was not repeated; the low-noise window was returned to the last agreed time, and then temporary water off the tracks and alternative roosts at different heights were opened to disperse the functional groups one after another.

Recovery was declared complete not after one safe passage but when 0 collisions, fewer intrusions, restored sluice sightlines, and benthic density within the permitted range were confirmed together over two consecutive migration periods.

The causes of failure were reflected in the next season's agreement, responsibility for slowdown sections and pump operation rotated, and compensation hours were allocated so that noise and passage restrictions did not fall on particular waterfront residents.

But keeping roosts off the tracks for long concentrated droppings on particular waters, building up nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen, and the insect emergence that followed could raise the next season's food density and draw even larger stopover flocks.
So measuring the nutrients and insect emergence beneath the roosts and resting their locations periodically became management as important as preventing collisions.
G06-SC1 · Three Functional Groups in the Shallow Water
Trigger: When the water level at Seoul Station Central fell, waterfowl, waders, and raptors overlapped on the same narrow water.
Ecological mechanism: As the feeding grounds of the functional groups overlapped, raptor pursuit changed the altitude of the whole assemblage.
Choices: Set the water level differently by section / Make a new wader feeding ground outside the depot / Install substitute raptor perches on the wetland outskirts
Outcomes: Sectioned water levels increased pump labor, and a new feeding ground cost land and dredging but reduced the edge concentration.
Substitute perches reduced track collisions, but the rodent-predation location could shift toward the dwellings.
Moral cost: Under the one name of protection, the needs of different functional groups could not be erased.
G06-SC2 · The Birds That Learned the Timetable
Trigger: When the slowdown hours at the Gangnam Line depot changed, the stopover flock surged up during the track inspection hours.
Ecological mechanism: The waterfowl and the raptors had learned the repeating train times as different safety signals, and their routes collided.
Choices: Restore the slowdown hours / Install substitute perches by functional group / Disperse them at once with horns and drones
Outcomes: Restoring the hours slowed logistics, and installing perches demanded long-term management. Forced dispersal broke the avoidance of the next running signal.
Moral cost: The dispute was whether the safety hours wild animals had learned could be changed one-sidedly for the sake of human running efficiency.
G06-SC3 · The Tracks of Migratory Week
Trigger: A large migratory movement from the XT01 direction overlapped a sluice inspection, and the bridge walkways and the depot entry and exit tracks were occupied repeatedly.
Actors: S06, S11, XT01, HC06, H06
Ecological mechanism: Waterfowl takeoff from the water, wader movement along the edges, and raptor pursuit made a chain of collisions at different heights.
Choices: Cut running to match the migratory timetable / Expand the water-surface and perch sections by functional group / Dry the water and send the assemblage out
Outcomes: Cutting the running slowed evacuation and logistics, and expanding the sections reduced other civic space. Draining the water made dust, stench, and an inflow of other predators.
Moral cost: Decide until which period the city's right of movement and the international movement ecology axis would yield to each other.

leaves.text: The Yongsan Raiders are people, and they stand at the lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding and at the leak pallets of the Itaewon passage alley. In the rainy season and the thaw they move on the ladders and car doors of the Yongsan–Itaewon transfer freight elevator shaft, and in the dry season they gather on that same lower level. Food sacks, sealed boxes, and water drums are in their hands. The Junction is written on the inventory board.

The Raider Chief, the Raider Elite Squad, and the Raider Scouts are three places in one alley. The Raider Chief sets the box count from the inner pallets, the Raider Elite Squad takes the door and the sacks, and the Raider Scouts watch the arrival of cars from the entrance. The three places are together in the same duty-watch view on a rainy-season night.

The place where the Junction's Itaewon freight duty watch first saw this group is the lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding on a rainy-season night. People stand along the rows of leak pallets, rods are at their waists, and box hooks are in their hands. A West Sea Granary Theater refrigeration slip is on the box in front of them and the lid is open. That box number is written in the same night's column on the duty watch's inventory board.

The place where the group gathers is the lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding and the rows of leak pallets in the Itaewon passage alley. In the rainy season and the thaw, people stand along the Yongsan–Itaewon transfer freight elevator shaft. When a West Sea Granary Theater refrigerated container reaches the alley, a West Sea Granary Theater signal is written on the duty board and the Yongsan Raiders are in front of the container door. In the dry season the footprints lie inside three pallet rows and the rows where people stand in the rainy season, the thaw, and the dry season are written on the inventory board.

The Yongsan Raiders move food sacks from West Sea Granary Theater refrigerated containers, Guro Alloy House sealed boxes, and transport slips from Sinnae Transport cars through the Itaewon passage alley. The Junction's Itaewon freight duty watch rewrites the remainder column on the inventory board by the count that enters the raiders' sacks. The duty watch counts the water drums beside the shaft door and writes that count on the board. A Jeonguram sequence slip lies on the sacks that remain.

In the rainy season people stand on every row of leak pallets in the Itaewon passage alley and a sack hangs at each car. In the thaw the Raider Elite Squad has gone up into the Yongsan–Itaewon transfer freight elevator shaft and an empty sack hangs on every step of the ladder. In the dry season the same people are gathered toward the wall of the lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding, and the Raider Scouts at the alley entrance stand in a single line.

From the place where the Junction's Itaewon freight duty watch stands, the Yongsan Raiders check the box count on the leak pallets and the door state of the Yongsan–Itaewon transfer freight elevator. The Raider Scouts face the entrance of the Itaewon passage alley, and the Raider Chief stands on the inner row of pallets. The door of a West Sea Granary Theater refrigerated container and a Guro Alloy House seal band lie in the same line of sight.

The Raider Chief is on the inner side of the leak pallets and sets the box count. The Raider Elite Squad takes the elevator door, the ladder, and the sacks. The Raider Scouts stand at the entrance of the Itaewon passage alley and watch the arrival of cars. The column on the inventory board where the Junction is written is in front of the Junction's Itaewon freight duty watch.

The range the Raider Chief sets is the box count on the leak pallets, the row where sacks are placed, and the places of the Raider Elite Squad and the Raider Scouts. The column on the Junction inventory board where the Junction is written, the Guro Alloy House seal slip, the Jeonguram sequence, and the Sinnae Transport slip are in front of the Itaewon freight duty watch.
From the inner side of the leak pallets, sets the box count and shows by place the row where sacks are put. The Raider Elite Squad and the Raider Scouts stand at that row and at the entrance.

The range is the entrance of the Itaewon passage alley and the front of the shaft where the container door is visible. The transport slip, the sequence slip, and the column where the Junction is written are in front of the Junction's Itaewon freight duty watch.
The Raider Scouts stand in a single line at the entrance of the Itaewon passage alley.
The faces of the Raider Scouts are turned toward the door of the Yongsan–Itaewon transfer freight elevator shaft.
Wheel marks of a Sinnae Transport car run on the entrance floor as far as the pallet rows.
The Raider Scouts' rods lie on the alley wall under the lamp.
When a West Sea Granary Theater signal is written on the duty board, the Raider Scouts extend their line to the front of the refrigerated container door.

The lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding on a rainy-season night is the place where the Junction's Itaewon freight duty watch first recorded the Yongsan Raiders. People stand along the rows of leak pallets, rods are at their waists, and box hooks are in their hands. A West Sea Granary Theater refrigeration slip is on the food box in front and the lid is open. The same number on the inventory board is written in that night's column.

In the duty watch's line of sight the Raider Scouts face the entrance of the Itaewon passage alley and the Raider Chief looks at the box count on the inner leak pallets. The hook of the Raider Elite Squad is caught on the corner of the Yongsan–Itaewon transfer freight elevator door. A Guro Alloy House seal band and a West Sea Granary Theater refrigeration slip lie side by side on one threshold. The duty watch writes the door state and the box count on the same line of the inventory board.

The Raider Chief's place is the inner row of pallets, and sacks lie on the side the hand indicates. The Raider Elite Squad's place is the ladder and the car door, and a sack hangs on the back. The Raider Scouts' place is a single line at the alley entrance, and the rods are on the wall under the lamp. The Junction is written on the inventory board outside those three places, and that column is in front of the Junction's Itaewon freight duty watch.

In the alley the Yongsan Raiders move food sacks from West Sea Granary Theater refrigerated containers, Guro Alloy House sealed boxes, transport slips from Sinnae Transport cars, and water drums. The count that enters the raiders' sacks is written in the remainder column of the inventory board. A Jeonguram sequence slip lies on the sacks left in the alley. Salt residue runs from the floor of the refrigerated car to the leak pallets.

In the rainy season and the thaw, people are on the ladders and thresholds along the Yongsan–Itaewon transfer freight elevator shaft. When a West Sea Granary Theater refrigerated container reaches the Itaewon passage alley, a West Sea Granary Theater signal is written on the duty board and the group is gathered in front of the container door. Dry-season footprints are inside three rows of leak pallets, and the rows where people stand in the rainy season, the thaw, and the dry season are written on the inventory board.

On a rainy-season night people stand along every pallet row and the lids of the food boxes are open. On a thaw morning the Raider Elite Squad is on the shaft ladder and the seal corner of a Sinnae Transport car is lifted. In the same alley on a dry-season day the group is gathered inside three rows and the water-drum caps are locked beside the shaft door. The three sights continue at one post of the Junction's Itaewon freight duty watch.

After the duty watch locks the shaft door, the elevator car is on the lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding and the sealed boxes with lifted corners stand toward the wall. The duty watch aligns the Junction inventory board, the Guro Alloy House seal check, the Jeonguram sequence slip, and the Sinnae Transport slip from the threshold into one box-count column and fixes them to the wall. The Raider Chief stands at the leak pallets outside the aligned board. The water-drum count is written in the side column of the board.

On the inventory board after the sequence is aligned, the remainder of the food sacks and water drums that left the alley is written. On the lower-level wall after the door is locked, the Jeonguram sequence slip is fixed and that slip's number is written in the duty watch's next column. On the board after the pallet place is left empty, the same number is written in the raiders' sack column, and the Raider Scouts stand at the entrance facing those sacks. In the first column of the inventory board on a dry-season day the rows where people stand in the rainy season, the thaw, and the dry season are written, and the Yongsan Raiders are gathered at the wall of the lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding.
G07-SC1 · Sealed Boxes at the Leak Pallets

Trigger: On a rainy-season night the Yongsan–Itaewon transfer freight elevator is stopped in the Itaewon passage alley and Guro Alloy House sealed boxes are in front of the leak pallets. The Raider Scouts stand along the pallet rows. A Jeonguram sequence slip is on the boxes.

Ecological mechanism: The Junction's Itaewon freight duty watch counts the boxes in front of the shaft door. The Raider Chief is on the inner side of the pallets and the Raider Elite Squad holds the box hooks. The corner of the Guro Alloy House seal band is wet.

Choices: Leave the elevator car on the lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding, lock the shaft door, and set the boxes against the lower-level wall. / After the duty watch checks the Guro Alloy House seal, pass the boxes out of the Itaewon passage alley according to the Jeonguram sequence slip. / Leave the duty-watch place on the leak-pallet rows empty and set the boxes where the raiders stand.

Outcomes: If the first is chosen, the boxes are on the lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding and the Yongsan Raiders stand in front of the locked shaft door. If the second is chosen, the boxes of the Jeonguram sequence are outside the alley and the Guro Alloy House mark remains on the seal band. If the third is chosen, the boxes are on the leak pallets and the mouths of the Raider Elite Squad's sacks are open.

Moral cost: After the door is locked, the Jeonguram sequence slip remains on the lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding and that number is written in the next column of the inventory board. After the boxes are passed by sequence, that day's water-drum count in the alley is written on the board as a figure lower by the box count. After the place is left empty, the same number is written in the raiders' sack column and the Raider Scouts face those sacks.
G07-SC2 · The Thaw of the Sinnae Transport Car

Trigger: On a thaw morning a Sinnae Transport freight car enters the Yongsan–Itaewon transfer freight elevator shaft and a Guro Alloy House seal band is on the car door. The Raider Elite Squad stands on the ladder.

Ecological mechanism: Moisture on the car floor runs to the leak pallets of the Itaewon passage alley. The Junction inventory board and the Sinnae Transport slip lie on the threshold, and the box counts on the two slips differ. The Raider Chief sets down sacks beside the car for that difference.

Choices: Align the Sinnae Transport slip with the Junction inventory board and lower the boxes of the difference onto the lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding. / Press the Guro Alloy House seal band down again and send the car to the upper stop line of the shaft. / Load the boxes of the difference into the raiders' sacks, and the duty watch writes the corrected count on the Sinnae Transport slip.

Outcomes: If the first is chosen, the boxes of the difference are at the wall of the lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding and the Sinnae Transport slip matches the inventory board. If the second is chosen, the seal band is on the car door and the car is at the upper stop line of the shaft. If the third is chosen, the mouths of the Raider Elite Squad's sacks are open and the corrected count is written on the transport slip at the threshold.

Moral cost: After the boxes are lowered to the lower level, that day's food sacks in the alley remain on the inventory board as a remainder of the difference. After the car is sent to the upper stop line, the Jeonguram sequence for the Itaewon passage alley remains on the empty threshold and continues as the number of the next column. After the load goes into the sacks, the same number is written in the raiders' column and the water-drum count is written beside that column.
G07-SC3 · The West Sea Granary Refrigerated Car

Trigger: On the night when the rainy season turns to the thaw, a West Sea Granary Theater refrigerated container has been pushed as far as the Itaewon passage alley. A West Sea Granary Theater signal is written on the Junction duty board. The Yongsan Raiders are gathered in front of the container door.
Actors: S07, S12, XT02, HC07, H07

Ecological mechanism: Salt residue runs from the container floor to the leak pallets. A Sinnae Transport car and Guro Alloy House sealed boxes are in the same row, and a Jeonguram sequence slip is on the food sacks. The Raider Chief counts the sacks, the Raider Elite Squad holds the door, and the Raider Scouts stand at the alley entrance.

Choices: Leave the refrigerated car on the lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding, and the Junction's Itaewon freight duty watch leaves only the figures of the West Sea Granary Theater signal on the inventory board. / Align the Jeonguram sequence with the Sinnae Transport slip, then pass the Guro Alloy House sealed boxes out of the Itaewon passage alley first. / Leave the refrigerated container door open and set the food sacks on the side where the raiders stand.

Outcomes: If the first is chosen, the refrigerated car is on the lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding and the West Sea Granary Theater signal figures are written in the side column of the duty board. If the second is chosen, the Guro Alloy House sealed boxes are outside the alley and the Jeonguram sequence matches the Sinnae Transport slip on one board. If the third is chosen, the food sacks are in front of the container door, the mouths of the Raider Elite Squad's sacks are open, and the Raider Scouts face that row.

Moral cost: After only the signal figures remain, the food sacks are on the lower level of the Yongsan stabling siding and that day's water-drum column in the alley is written on the inventory board together with that sack count. After the sealed boxes are passed first, the remaining sacks of the refrigerated car stay on the Jeonguram sequence and the Raider Scouts at the entrance stand in a single line. After the door is left open, the same sack number is written in the raiders' column and the West Sea Granary Theater signal remains as the figures beside that column.

Inside the sacks are filter crates with the Changdong Protection House mark and work lamps of the White Cross night-wage corridor. The filter count is written as the same figure on the White Cross night-wage duty officer's record board and on the raider chief's board. The work lamps lie across the mouths of the sacks.

At the start of the night the raider scouts stand at the end of the alley. After the sacks line up before the doors, the raider elite squad stands at each door. After the entrance curtains are layered, the raider chief stands before the differential-pressure board.

The hand of the White Cross night-wage duty officer is on the latch of the positive-pressure door, and the work lamp lights the inner alley. The Changdong Protection House supply duty officer is before the inner shelf of the sealed side chamber. The filter crates are set on that shelf.

The Central Technology Preservation Office patrol duty officer is writing the differential-pressure figures on both the raider chief's board and the duty record board. The White Cross night-wage duty officer and the Changdong Protection House supply duty officer stand on the inner side of the door where the board hangs. The raider chief stands on the outer side of the board.

By the count of filters that went into the sacks, the filters on the positive-pressure doors remain as a single layer. The White Cross night-wage duty officer writes the differential-pressure board again together with the curtain layers. The entrance curtains are layered one more time, and the Central Technology Preservation Office patrol duty officer stands inside the door with the record board left on the shelf beside the latch.

Trigger: On an early-winter night the filter crates of the Changdong Protection House are before the positive-pressure doors of the Dongdaemun night-wage corridor, and the Dongdaemun Raiders stand before the crates. The Central Technology Preservation Office patrol duty officer and Choidaon are beside the differential-pressure board of the same door.

Ecological mechanism: The raider chief reads the differential-pressure figures, and the raider elite squad takes the crate cords. While the filters are on the shelf, the positive-pressure doors stay shut toward the outside.

Choices: The Central Technology Preservation Office patrol duty officer moves the filter crates to the inner shelf of the sealed side chamber on the Jegi-dong side. / The Changdong Protection House supply duty officer writes the crate count half on the shelf and half on the raider sacks. / Choidaon advances the movement time on the differential-pressure board and shuts the positive-pressure doors.

Outcomes: After the crates are moved to the shelf, the raiders stand before the doors, the filter crates are on the side-chamber shelf, and the positive pressure holds. After the count is written by halves, the crates are divided between the shelf and the sacks, and the raider elite squad stands in the alley. After the doors are shut, the raiders stand at the ventilation-duct mouth and Choidaon is beside the shut door.

Moral cost: In the count divided by halves, the protection filters of the Changdong Protection House remain as a single layer, and after the doors are shut the passage on the Jegi-dong side lies on the side of the raiders' sacks.
G08-SC2 · Curtains of the night wage

Trigger: On a night when the White Cross night-wage duty officer is before the entrance curtains, the raider scouts stand at the end of the lower windbreak alley. The Central Technology Preservation Office patrol duty officer and the Changdong Protection House supply duty officer are beside the differential-pressure board of the same entrance.

Ecological mechanism: The raider scouts count the curtain layers and write them on a board, and the raider chief sets the place of the night-wage sacks before the doors. The Central Technology Preservation Office patrol duty officer leaves the differential-pressure figures on the record board.

Choices: The White Cross night-wage duty officer keeps the curtains at three layers and opens the night-wage passage toward the Changdong Protection House supply duty officer. / The Central Technology Preservation Office patrol duty officer writes the differential-pressure figures on both the raider chief's board and the duty record board. / The Changdong Protection House supply duty officer moves the night-wage sacks onto the shelf of the sealed side chamber.

Outcomes: After the passage is opened toward the Changdong Protection House, the raider elite squad stands outside the curtains and the night-wage goods are on the side-chamber side. After the figures are written on both boards, the raider chief and the White Cross night-wage duty officer stand before the same board, and the sacks remain at the doors. After the sacks are moved into the side chamber, the Changdong Protection House supply duty officer stands before the curtains and the raider scouts are at the duct mouth.
Moral cost: Where the passage is opened, the night-wage goods remain in the sack count, and where the figures are written together the duty officer spends the night beside the door.

Trigger: On a night when dust from the relay docks of the Korea Strait Theater is piled at the entrance of the Dongdaemun night-wage corridor, a higher figure is written on the entrance differential-pressure board. The White Cross, the Central Technology Preservation Office, the Changdong Protection House, and Choidaon are at the same entrance.
Actors: S08, S13, XT03, HC08, H08

Ecological mechanism: The raiders layer the curtains over the dust and set the sacks at the entrance between the layers. While the curtains are layered and the filter crates are at the entrance, the positive-pressure doors stay shut toward the outside.

Choices: The White Cross night-wage duty officer layers the curtains from the inner side of the raiders' hands and keeps the entrance on the duty side. / The Central Technology Preservation Office patrol duty officer moves the Korea Strait Theater relay crates that have no dust on them to the Changdong Protection House shelf. / Choidaon writes the figures on the differential-pressure board toward the shut door and leaves the raiders' sacks at the ventilation-duct mouth.

Outcomes: After the curtains are layered from the inside, the entrance is on the side of the White Cross night-wage duty officer and the raider elite squad stands at the outer layer. After the crates are moved to the shelf, the dust-marked sacks are at the entrance and the protection crates are on the Changdong Protection House shelf. After the figures on the differential-pressure board are written toward the shut door, the raiders are gathered at the duct mouth on the Jegi-dong side and Choidaon is beside the entrance board.

Moral cost: The sacks of the raider elite squad standing at the outer layer hold the night-wage work lamps, and after the group gathers toward the duct the passage of the sealed side chamber runs on into the raiders' foothold.
