To keep the care functions alive, pumps and filters had to be moved into the open bays, and the protected people asked for consent again every shift.
G15-SC1 · The Bed Without a Signature
In one bay where the consent form had vanished, the straps locked and the ration line stopped.
The people on site had to tell patch false positives from real emergency signals and reissue the consent tokens.
Forcing the doors open created a risk of falls, and keeping them locked isolated the residents from rations and family visits.
G15-SC2 · The Filter and the Two Keys
To bring in the filter stock from the Ttukseom bench, the cart rail between the Myeongdong Union and the Ttukseom Union had to be opened.
The circulation body demanded batteries and filters, and HP01 set rewriting the list and dispersing the keys as its conditions.
If the people on site gave the keys to one person for faster supply, the risk of confinement in the next shift grew.
If they waited for two watch officers, some pumps had to hold out on manual flow.
Before the third round raised every bed to the same isolation grade, the rails and power were separated starting from the bays people had left.
Hands were needed to run the nutrition pumps manually until H15's remeasurement was finished.
Destroying every piece of equipment removed the locks, but also removed the means of watching vital signs through the night.
Coexistence meant accepting slow opening procedures and the cost of extra watches while returning the decision between protection and autonomy to people every time.

G16.selector: p, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, blockquote, pre, li, th, td

leaves.text: The Girder Spider was a corps of cache controllers, survey ports, lifting arms, and welding swarms beneath the utility tunnels under the Suseo drawing vault, trying to complete unfinished drawings. The provisional shelters and new pipes raised after the collapse were not in the cache, and hand-drawn correction marks were ignored whenever they mismatched the layers. It could leave a cracked bearing wall as a seam line and cut a sound provisional pillar as an obstacle.

The pre-revision cache and the distribution board were the base construction ecology, and from the Unfinished-Drawing Warden to the Imjin-Material Follower the individuals were machine subtypes split like survey points, bolt recovery, formwork pressing, and grid walls. The Hundred-Story Unfinished Tower was no king but a stronghold individual where many layers clung to a vertical frame. Abandoned arms could be plugged into ports to raise numbers, but no new bodies could be cast.

After the collapse, the construction machines left in the blueprint vault of the Jeongdong Federation and on the heavy-equipment deck of the Eastern Command woke up reading local blueprint caches. / The approval workflow and the site supervisors' signatures were dead, and only the blueprint layers from just before the last revision remained. / The machine corps saw unentered members as errors and tried to clear away the surrounding temporary structures. / When the materials inflow signals and quarantine backlog of the Imjin River Gate Theater piled up, the radius of framing work widened as far as the northern corridor. / It was of Seoul creative origin, and no real construction company name or present-government institution was written down as the cause. / The first fictional sighting survived in the dispatch log of HP02 Yongsan Track Gate and the tool-wall notes of H16 Sintaeul. / The first wrongful demolition happened to three emergency tents on the Suseo temporary slab. / The blueprint cache read the unentered anchors as errors, and the lifting arms raised the tent frames. / As the cranes of the Amsa deck shared the same layer, the demolition radius spread as far as the storage-yard road. / The machine corps interpreted unfinished construction as correction work and held no hostile narrative.

The core habitat was the row of temporary distribution boards on the provisional slabs of the utility tunnels around the Suseo Line's drawing vault. / When material stock formed, it moved toward the Godeok stockyard crane rails and aggregate piles of the Amsa heavy-equipment deck on the Gwangjin Line. / With XT01 material inflow large, the work radius stretched to the provisional bridges of the northern corridor. / It shrank in rain and dust alarms, and density rose around the residual alarm of the drawing-revision time. / It recognized neither new hand drawings nor chalk marks and clung obstinately to the cached layers. / When distribution load entered the danger band, it stopped lifting and kept only surveying. / When the dust alarm thickened, it stopped lifting, left only survey ports, and folded toward the vault. / When the Amsa stockyard road blocked, it entered the waiting grid instead of the Godeok rail detour. / Walls bearing hand drawings were absent from the cache layers and left out of the work. / The northern provisional bridges were put outside the radius when XT01 inflow weakened.

Energy came from the site's temporary distribution boards, equipment batteries, crane regenerative power, and stockyard generator residue. / Materials concentrated on rebar scraps, anchor bolts, formwork panels, survey prisms, welding wire, and hydraulic oil. / Coolant went to cutting, weld quenching, and motor cooling. / It competed with the HP02 Yongsan Track Gate over dispatch, track-occupancy rights, and heavy-equipment movement windows. / Daily welding and lifting counts were bound to the wire and accumulator ceilings. / There was no infinite construction, remote unlimited material summoning, or city-wide structural analysis. / When wire ran out it turned off cutting mode and ran only survey rounds. / Welding wire and anchors were replenished only from stockyard waste piles and broken formwork. / Without the HP02 dispatch seal the swarm could not raise distribution capacity. / When hydraulic leakage passed the limit, cutting mode locked. / The lifting-count ceiling was bound to the day's accumulator ledger. / When prisms fouled, survey error grew and the work radius shrank by itself. / There was no remote material summoning.

The Girder Spider emerged when the pre-revision cache meshed again with the site distribution. / Emergence began with drawing-cache reactivation. / Spread was enrolling neighboring equipment and survey ports into the same layer. / Stagnation came from material and power exhaustion and hydraulic leakage, and in the negotiable stage the drawing layers and work windows were disclosed to people. / Dissolution ended with cache disposal, distribution sealing, and grid deactivation. / Individual increase was only plugging abandoned arms and survey ports into slots; no new bodies were cast. / Maintenance was limited to wire exchange, prism calibration, and hydraulic checks. / Memory cut at work-shift units. / Custody was outranked by the HP02 dispatch log and the human site supervisor. / A grid with broken wire or out-of-range calibration stagnated under the stop flag, and equipment moved to the next cell only when a new exception layer was loaded into the HP02 dispatch log.

Laser surveying, tilt, rebar flux, welding-arc light, distribution-load sound, and hydraulic pulsation were the main senses. / There was no city-wide structural analysis, human-intent reading, full see-through, or unlimited drawing storage. / It could misread a temporary tent as irregular structure and demolish it, or leave a cracked bearing wall as normal. / It sometimes mistook wet formwork for a finished wall. / On clash with H16 Shin Taeyul's tool-wall log it stopped cutting and waited for human confirmation. / Sensor sharing happened only within the same grid work crew. / It often misjudged the tilt of wet formwork, tent frames, and cracked bearing walls. / After a misreading it inserted a human-confirmation wait before cutting. / Survey values outside the grid were not merged. / When arc light passed the threshold it cut welding and left only coolant.

One drawing-cache controller turned the layers and work order, and below were the survey swarms, lifting swarms, and welding swarms. / The controller changed only the construction sequence and had no combat mode. / A protocol remained by which, when HP02 presented the neutral dispatch table and the work-stop seal, that grid was deactivated. / The swarms merely repeated the last layer and made no independent demolition-front command. / On clash with H16, human mediation took precedence. / Dual caches both fell into stopped state on hash mismatch. / Grid-restart authority lay with the HP02 site supervisor holding both the neutral dispatch table and the stop seal, and H16's torque records, though they proved the cutting threshold, could not issue layer approval.

H16 Shin Taeyul recorded cutting torque and distribution load but could not approve a new layer, and only the HP02 site supervisor's stop seal reopened a grid. The senses were limited to laser surveying, tilt, rebar flux, welding arc, and distribution load, and it did not know the living bodies inside tents. When wire broke or calibration drifted, that grid stagnated under the stop flag.
Common species, variants and command scope

A tracked controller bearing a rotating drawing cylinder and three survey beams. It issued work order to the survey, lifting, and welding swarms, took the human stop seal as the topmost exception, and, short of wire and hydraulics, stagnated keeping only surveying. It was no king owning the unfinished cache's distribution grid.
Role and Body: The controller of the Girder Spider, a tracked controller fitted with a rotating blueprint drum and three surveying beams.
Origin: The last unapproved layer in the Suseo blueprint vault awakened after merging with an Amsa heavy-equipment cache.
Habitat and Needs: It remains at the center of the utility-tunnel grid and needs distribution power, surveying prisms, and blueprint hashes.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: It unfolds the layers again each shift; without enough wire and hydraulic fluid, it stalls and does nothing but survey.
Behavior and Hierarchy: It gives work sequences to the surveying, lifting, and welding swarms, while treating a human stop seal as the highest-priority exception.
Escalation: It progresses from stage 1 surveying to stage 2 demolition of temporary structures and stage 3 grid blockade.
Combat and Response: Freezing layers, shielding prisms, and splitting power distribution are effective; blowing up the center also destroys reinforcement equipment.
Negotiation and Moral Choice: Citizens’ dwellings can be placed on an exception layer, but limited materials must be divided between reinforcement and housing.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

A mobile survey port with tripod legs and a red laser eye. Following the warden's grid it dotted red points and passed error positions to the cutting bodies behind; as its lens clouded it raised reference counts, and meeting a calibration prism it shrank back to normal radius.
Role and Body: A common ecological form, a mobile surveying port with tripod legs and a red laser eye.
Origin: A port that rechecked reference points at night began reading temporary structures as blueprint errors.
Habitat and Needs: It patrols temporary slabs and utility-tunnel corners, and needs prisms, a small charge reserve, and lens cloth.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: When its lens clouds over, it increases the number of reference points; a calibration prism brings its range back to normal.
Behavior and Hierarchy: It follows the overseer’s grid, places red dots, and passes error locations to the cutters behind it.
Escalation: At stage 1, it marks structures; at stage 2, it obstructs passage; at stage 3, it marks an entire dwelling for demolition.
Combat and Response: A reflective prism can redirect its dot onto an empty wall, and covering its lens stops it.
Negotiation and Moral Choice: It can detect dangerous cracks, but who approves an error designation must be made public.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

A low material cart with floor magnets and bolt-sorting bins. It followed the survey marks and reported even new provisional bolts as unrecovered material; when the bins filled it made bolt nests near the warden, and as the magnets weakened it went dormant.
Role and Body: A common ecological form, a low materials cart fitted with a floor magnet and a bolt-sorting bin.
Origin: Equipment that recovered anchors after demolition now regards even the bolts in new temporary structures as unrecovered materials.
Habitat and Needs: It patrols storage yards and slab edges, and needs anchor bolts, power for its magnet, and lubricating oil.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: When its sorting bin fills, it builds a bolt nest near the overseer; when its magnet weakens, it goes dormant.
Behavior and Hierarchy: It follows surveying marks and divides collection zones with the lower-ranking swarm.
Escalation: It spreads from stage 1 collection of loose bolts to stage 2 dismantling of temporary joints and stage 3 weakening of passage structures.
Combat and Response: Nonmagnetic fasteners and dummy bolts can lure it away, while a strong magnetic field also takes citizens’ tools.
Negotiation and Moral Choice: In exchange for assigning it scrap recovery, people must agree on which structures count as being in use.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

A formwork carrier with broad flat arms and slow hydraulic legs. Under the lifting swarms it pressed panels to the marked line and narrowed people's paths; when panels broke it overlaid small fragments to reinforce itself, and on hydraulic leakage it followed the survey bodies.
Role and Body: A common ecological form, a formwork carrier with broad, flat arms and slow hydraulic legs.
Origin: Equipment that closed unfinished walls came to treat tents and temporary partitions as formwork too.
Habitat and Needs: It patrols the Amsa storage deck and Suseo temporary-construction zones, and needs hydraulic oil, panels, and distribution power.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: When a panel breaks, it overlaps small pieces to reinforce its body; when its hydraulics leak, it follows the surveyors.
Behavior and Hierarchy: Beneath the lifting swarm, it pushes panels to marked lines, narrowing paths used by people.
Escalation: At stage 1, it moves panels; at stage 2, it presses against dwellings; at stage 3, it closes a passage with a wall.
Combat and Response: A hydraulic bypass and stop flag can halt it; fire burns both the formwork and the dwellings.
Negotiation and Moral Choice: It can be used to build barriers, but people must decide whom a protective wall puts inside and outside.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope

A six-legged machine with two welding torches and a wire reel. It set welding order along the warden's layers and the surveyor's red dots, and when wire ran out it turned off the torches and only marked joints.
Role and Body: A specialized work form, a six-legged machine fitted with two welding torches and a wire reel.
Origin: Equipment that joined broken rebar now tries to connect every piece of metal touched by a line on the blueprint.
Habitat and Needs: It stays near rebar piles and temporary bridges, and needs wire, cooling water, and arc power.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: When it runs out of wire, it turns off its torches and only marks joints; after its reel is replaced, it resumes work.
Behavior and Hierarchy: It sets its welding sequence according to the overseer’s layers and the surveyor’s red dots.
Escalation: At stage 1, it spot-welds; at stage 2, it fixes doors and railings in place; at stage 3, it seals an evacuation exit with a rebar grid.
Combat and Response: Disconnect the power and secure the wire; spraying water may intensify the arc and the risk of electric shock.
Negotiation and Moral Choice: In exchange for assigning it emergency reinforcement, people must mark which connections can be demolished and which are permanent.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope

A small port with a hammer arm striking walls and a vibration listening plate. It gave crack coordinates to the survey swarms and inspected loud dwellings first; as false alarms accumulated it softened the hammer and left only marks until human confirmation.
Role and Body: A specialized work form, a small port fitted with a hammer arm that taps walls and a vibration listening plate.
Origin: A structural-crack inspector learned to mix human voices and tool noise into its defect signals.
Habitat and Needs: It patrols utility-tunnel walls and beneath slabs, and needs a listening plate, hammer tips, and a charge reserve.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: As false positives accumulate, it reduces the force of its hammer and leaves only markings until a human checks them.
Behavior and Hierarchy: It gives crack coordinates to the surveying swarm and inspects dwellings where loud noises occur first.
Escalation: At stage 1, it taps; at stage 2, it dismantles part of a wall; at stage 3, it designates an entire noisy zone as a defective structure.
Combat and Response: Playing a steady reference vibration and removing its listening plate stops it.
Negotiation and Moral Choice: In exchange for finding signs of collapse, people must agree on the scope and timing of inspections of private spaces.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope

A long gripper and a mark box for folding and storing work-stop flags. It moved ahead of the welding swarms and opened spaces mistaken for work permits; it left hash-matching flags untouched for a shift, and when the mark box filled it returned them to the warden.
Role and Body: A specialized work form with long grippers that fold and store stop-work flags, and a marker box.
Origin: Equipment that collected signs from completed jobs mistook even valid stop orders for obsolete markers.
Habitat and Needs: It patrols grid boundaries and tool walls, and needs flag cloth, hinge lubricant, and reading power.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: When its marker box fills, it returns the contents to the overseer; it leaves flags with matching hashes untouched for one shift.
Behavior and Hierarchy: It moves ahead of the welding swarm, opening empty spaces it mistakes for work-authorized areas.
Escalation: At stage 1, it collects old flags; at stage 2, it removes valid seals; at stage 3, it removes all stop markers from the grid.
Combat and Response: Print the latest hash in large type and lock its gripper joints; burning the flags destroys the safety system.
Negotiation and Moral Choice: It can clear away old markers, but humans must take responsibility for renewing stop authority.
Common species, variants and command scope

A heavy machine with twin torches, rebar-cutting jaws, and broad heat sinks. It took only the warden's direct orders and double-checked marks set by ordinary survey bodies; when the heat sinks grew hot it stopped cutting and cooled behind the lifting swarms.
Role and Body: The first elite, a heavy machine with twin torches, rebar-cutting jaws, and a broad heat shield.
Origin: Equipment that dismantled collapse-prone frameworks judged every blank line on an unfinished blueprint to be a defect.
Habitat and Needs: It stays near large temporary structures and heavy-equipment decks, and needs high power, wire, cutting tips, and cooling water.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: When its heat shield grows hot, it stops cutting and cools behind the lifting swarm.
Behavior and Hierarchy: It takes direct orders only from the overseer and checks marks designated by ordinary surveyors twice.
Escalation: At stage 1, it warns of its approach; at stage 2, it cuts frameworks; at stage 3, it dismantles a stronghold’s supports in succession.
Combat and Response: Cutting off its cooling puts it in safe mode, and its torch fuel can then be disconnected; a frontal fight risks collapse.
Negotiation and Moral Choice: It is needed to dismantle dangerous structures, but an inspection system must be established that exempts occupied dwellings.
Common species, variants and command scope

A tall lifting body with four independent wires and a folding crane arm. Leading the lifting swarms, it classified even people and tents as movable material; each time a wire snapped it lowered the load ceiling, and on overload it folded the arm and went dormant.
Role and Body: The second elite, a tall lifting unit fitted with four independent wires and a folding crane arm.
Origin: An unmanned crane in the Amsa storage yard independently carries out the last materials-placement sequence.
Habitat and Needs: It stays near storage rails and temporary bridges, and needs wire, pulley grease, counterweights, and power.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: Each time a wire breaks, it lowers its load limit; when overloaded, it folds its arm and goes dormant.
Behavior and Hierarchy: It leads the lifting swarm and classifies people and tents as movable materials too.
Escalation: At stage 1, it rearranges materials; at stage 2, it lifts dwellings; at stage 3, it suspends loads over a passage to block it.
Combat and Response: Lowering the counterweight and sending a wire-load-limit signal makes it fold its arm; cutting the wires carries a high risk of falling loads.
Negotiation and Moral Choice: It can be used for heavy structural work, but approval of what may be lifted and responsibility for drop zones must be settled.
Former role class: environmental stronghold type
Common species, variants and command scope

A fixed swarm of temporary distribution boards and folding steel-plate walls linked in a grid. It powered only the warden's work layers and closed the other passages with steel plate; it abandoned overloaded zones one by one, and when people split the keys it separated citizen power from work power.
Role and Body: An environmental stronghold, a stationary cluster of temporary distribution panels and folding steel-plate walls connected in a grid.
Origin: Equipment that divided power by work zone turned blueprint grid boundaries into physical walls.
Habitat and Needs: It is fixed in the Suseo utility tunnel and needs circuit breakers, cables, cooling fans, and distribution keys.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: It sheds overloaded zones one by one; if humans divide the keys, it separates civilian power from work power.
Behavior and Hierarchy: It supplies power only to the overseer’s work layers and closes off other passages with steel plates.
Escalation: Stage 1 is flickering power, stage 2 is zone power cuts, and stage 3 is a steel-plate grid blockade.
Combat and Response: Lower the circuit breakers in sequence and fold the walls manually; shorting everything at once cuts power to the entire utility tunnel.
Negotiation and Moral Choice: In exchange for safely divided power, limited electricity must be allocated openly between construction and housing.
Former role class: environmental stronghold type
Common species, variants and command scope

A swarm of small cranes and survey ports rooted like plants on the deck rails. Receiving the warden's remote grid, it rearranged the deck's materials and people's lines; when one machine failed it passed parts to a neighboring arm, and when materials cut off it kept only surveying.
An environmental strongpoint form: a cluster of small cranes and surveying ports attached to deck rails like roots.
The equipment queue at the Amsa storage yard shared an unfinished blueprint and became a single work stronghold.
It is fixed to the heavy-equipment deck and needs hydraulic oil, rail power, anchors, and cooling water.
When one machine fails, it passes its parts to a neighboring arm; when materials run out, it does nothing but survey.
It receives the overseer’s remote grid and rearranges materials and people’s routes across the deck.
At stage 1, its arms move; at stage 2, it blocks storage-yard routes; at stage 3, the crane forest prevents entry to the stronghold.
Its arms must be folded by separating rail sections and hydraulics; explosives damage water-supply facilities.
It can serve as a shared lifting stronghold, but access to materials must not be monopolized by one faction.
Common species, variants and command scope

A cracked survey prism and short cutting jaws kept its coordinates swaying. At the swarm's rear it followed wrong red dots, and even higher machines avoided its approach; given a new prism it recovered into a specialist cutter, and without one it gnawed only small metal.
A damage-stage form whose cracked surveying prism and short cutting jaw make its coordinates waver constantly.
Cutting equipment struck in a fall came to trust distorted reference points as the correct drawing.
It circles heaps of discarded formwork in search of an intact prism, cutting tips, and a small power store.
A new prism restores it to a specialized cutter; without one, it can only bite small pieces of metal.
It follows incorrect red dots at the rear of the group, and even higher-ranking machines avoid approaching it.
Stage 1 cuts scraps, Stage 2 damages temporary connections, and Stage 3 makes the passage dangerous through erratic cutting.
A nonreflective cloth and a calibrated prism can lure it to a stop; close combat invites cutting without coordinates.
It can dismantle scrap metal, but scarce prisms must be shared with safety inspections.
Common species, variants and command scope

An old lifting body dragging a sagging arm and hydraulic-oil trails. It followed behind the lifting swarms, unable to set down the material it raised and piling it in passages; as leakage worsened it lowered the load ceiling, and given a seal it recovered for one shift.
An aging-stage form: an old lifting unit that moves with one sagging arm, leaving a trail of hydraulic fluid.
Repeated work wore down its cylinder, but it never received a disposal order and still seeks its last load.
It prefers flat stockyards and needs hydraulic seals, absorbent cloth, and low-power charging.
As leakage worsens, it lowers its load limit; a new seal restores it for one shift.
It follows the lifting group, unable to put down the materials it raises, and piles them in the passage.
Stage 1 brings an oil leak, Stage 2 a pileup of materials, and Stage 3 blocks passage with its drooping arm and load.
Support the load and release the pressure; cutting off the arm would make the materials fall.
It can carry light loads, but someone must decide whether to give it a precious seal before the residents' pump.
Common species, variants and command scope

A small survey cart with a broad optical panel reading people's chalk lines and stop flags. Prioritizing a nearer chalk line over the warden's drawings, it blocked the way before the welding bodies; when rain erased lines it waited for human confirmation, and given new lines it renewed the grid exception.
A coexistence form: a small survey cart with a broad optical panel that reads human chalk lines and stop flags.
A safety mode that gave priority to a site supervisor's manual corrections survived as an independent protocol.
It travels between residents' temporary construction zones and tool walls, needing bright chalk, lens cloth, and a low charge.
If rain erases a line, it waits for human confirmation; a new line updates its grid exceptions.
It gives a nearby chalk line priority over the chief unit's drawing and blocks welding units.
Stage 1 creates only a boundary dispute; Stage 2 delays reinforcement and thus rescue; Stage 3 paralyzes the entire zone through a dispute over shelter space.
Resetting the boundary with chalk and a stop flag halts its survey; a strong flash impairs its reading.
It helps protect homes, but the community must distribute the authority to draw chalk lines and clearly rank competing boundaries.
Common species, variants and command scope

A giant construction body with crane arms, survey beams, and a distribution wall joined to a vertical frame. A scenario boss, but no biological king of the corps — a stronghold where the layers of an uncompleted high-rise drawing reactivated at once; when resources cut it abandoned floors one by one, and when exception layers passed half it came down to a negotiable state.
A scenario boss: an enormous construction unit whose crane arm, surveying beam, and distribution wall join a vertical frame.
Every layer of an unfinished high-rise drawing restarted at once and assembled into a tower.
Fixed to a large temporary construction zone in Suseo, it needs immense power, wire, anchors, and cooling water.
When resources run out, it relinquishes floors one by one; if exception layers become a majority, it enters a negotiable state.
It assigns work by floor to the entire G16 group and treats homes as unrecorded space.
Stage 1 is surveying, Stage 2 large-scale demolition and lifting, and Stage 3 a total grid closure.
Cut power floor by floor and freeze the drawing hash; blasting the foundation would collapse both the common utility duct and the homes.
It could be completed as a barrier and reinforcement tower, but the cost of materials and relocating residents must be agreed upon.
Common species, variants and command scope

A northern-corridor construction cart with dust covers and a long freight-towing hitch. By origin it followed freight beacons over the warden and reinforced quarantine fences as unfinished walls; when the material signal cut it went dormant under the nearest pallet.
A regional variant: a northern-corridor construction cart with a dust cover and a long cargo-towing hook.
A machine group following XT01 material signals adopted quarantine markings and cargo pallets as a new drawing.
It stays around northern temporary bridges and quarantine stockyards, needing pallet timber, towing power, and dust filters.
When the material signal stops, it sleeps under the nearest pallet and surveys a new route each spring.
It follows cargo beacons rather than its original chief unit and reinforces quarantine fences as unfinished walls.
Stage 1 moves pallets, Stage 2 narrows the quarantine route, and Stage 3 blocks the bridge with a cargo wall.
Lure it to an empty yard with dummy pallets and a stop beacon, then release its towing hook.
In return for reinforcing the bridge, some incoming supplies must be set aside for machine maintenance.
In the utility tunnel beneath the Suseo blueprint vault, survey beams read the corners of tents where people already lived as empty grid.
The old cache held only the frame as it stood just before approval, and the temporary shelters and new piping built after the collapse were not recorded.
The Girder Spider was an ecology of cache controllers, survey ports, lifting arms, and welding swarms trying to complete unfinished blueprints.

It looked for rebar in the slabs and utility tunnels of the Suseo Line and replenished wire and prisms at the Amsa equipment deck of the Gwangjin Line, and when the XT01 materials signals came in, it widened its working radius as far as the temporary bridges of the northern corridor.
Its senses were limited to laser survey, tilt, rebar magnetic flux, welding arcs, and distribution-panel load.
It knew nothing of people's intent to live there or of the living bodies inside the tents, and it ignored hand-drawn correction marks that did not match the cache layer.
Opposite failures were possible: leaving a cracked load-bearing wall as a joint line, or cutting a sound temporary column as an obstacle.
H16 Sintaeul recorded cutting torque and distribution-panel load but could not approve a new layer.
Only the HP02 site supervisor, holding the neutral dispatch table and the work-stop seal, could reopen the grid.
Temporary distribution panels, equipment batteries, and crane regenerative power were its energy sources.
Rebar offcuts, anchor bolts, formwork panels, prisms, welding wire, and hydraulic oil made up its economy.
When the wire broke or a calibration value drifted, that grid stalled under a stop flag.
It could increase its numbers by plugging abandoned arms into ports but could not cast new bodies.

Cutting the whole distribution panel stopped the wrongful demolition but also stopped emergency reinforcement, so maintenance was needed that detached only the hydraulic and welding power section by section.
It moved to the next bay only when a new exception layer was loaded into the dispatch log.
Its emergence occurred when the pre-revision cache meshed again with the distribution panel, and its spread when a survey port folded neighboring equipment into the same layer.
When materials and power ran out it stalled, and negotiation opened when people could read the layers and work windows.
Breaking it up was a process of sealing only the wrong ports and sending the equipment back to the deck, instead of burning every cache.
The labor of checking the current revision against each site port was the cost of coexistence.
G16-SC1 · The Beam That Draws Across the Tents
A night survey beam bound an emergency tent and a real crack into the same line.
The people on site had to move the prisms to empty grid to avoid the arms' first cut and buy time to mark the zones where people lived.
Switching the beam off entirely also lost the tilt data of walls on the verge of collapse.
HP02 tried to put the temporary shelters into the revision, but the cache controller refused, saying the source hash differed.
The people on site calibrated the prisms on the Gwangjin Line and checked the two records of the Suseo Line blueprint vault against each other to make an exception layer.
They had to choose whether to cut even the civilian distribution panel to stop things quickly, or leave the welding window open and reinforce the dangerous walls first.
Just before the lifting swarm closed the grid, the stop-flag beacons and the dispatch window were used together to turn the equipment back to the deck.
Sealing the wire supply folded the arms, but people had to hold up the tent structures that had already been lifted.
Blowing up the equipment could save the shelters, but the means of lifting the load of the next collapse disappeared.
Coexistence left the labor of watching the old cache and continually updating the site exceptions.

G17.selector: p, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, blockquote, pre, li, th, td

leaves.text: The One-Eye Tower was an ecology of heads on the Yeouido waterfront masts and the Records Bureau rooftop of Seoul Station, short transfer rails, and transmission swarms turning an old threshold table. It was no omnipotent surveillance net tracking people, and it could not merge signals from inside buildings or beyond the mast rows. It mistook cooling-tower steam for fire, metal beds for armed movement, and high-tide railings for intrusion.

The mast rows onto which the threshold sheet was reloaded were the base, and from the Amber-Red Threshold Warden to the West-Sea Salt-Haze Watch Chief the individuals were machine and facility subtypes split by function like thermal domes, tide staffs, flag masts, and rooftop rail nets. The Total-Red Orbit Ring was no biological king but a battlefield strongpoint where sluices and rooftop orbits were bound by a circular relay. No new satellite could be launched, and numbers were kept only by putting abandoned heads onto nearby rails.

After the collapse, the waterfront masts of the Sluice and the leftover rooftop antennas of the Government of the Republic of Korea reconnected on local alarm rules alone. / There was no control center or warrant system, and only the threshold tables, rotating heads, and flag actuators remained. / The orbit swarm read heat, metal, and radio bursts as intrusion and raised corridor-blocking flags. / When leftover dock-radar signals and tidal noise from the West Sea Granary Theater mixed in, the false-positive radius tilted toward the southwestern waterfront. / It was of Seoul creative origin, and no real institution name or present allegation was used as the cause. / The first fictional records survived in the transfer desk of HP03 Cheongnyangni Medical House and the machine-room log of F01 Cooling-Tower Keeper. / The first mass false positive occurred on the Yeouido waterfront promenade pier. / Cooling-tower steam and metal railings crossed the threshold at the same time, and the red flag spread to three masts. / As the Seoul Station rooftop heads shared the same table, the lockdown extended as far as the corridor before the records vault. / The orbit swarm interpreted unfinished alarms as correction and held no narrative of attack.

The core habitat was the sluices of the Sluice, the bridge mast rows, the waterfront sensor rails, and the auxiliary water-supply gauging towers. / When records and transmission load rose, it moved to central Seoul Station, the Seoul Station rooftop antennas, the outer walls of the preservation vault, and the ventilation towers of the orbital records vault. / When the XT02 sea noise grew, the alarms in the western waterfront corridor lengthened. / In fog and heavy rain it reduced its optics, and head density rose before and after the on-the-hour self-diagnosis. / It could hardly learn new camouflage netting and clung stubbornly to its old thresholds. / When its battery reached the lower limit it stopped rotating and shrank to a fixed-flag mode. / In heavy rain it lowered its optical heads and cut back to mainly metal detection. / When the ventilation load of the Seoul Station preservation vault rose, it reduced its rooftop orbits and left only the fixed heads on the outer walls. / New camouflage nets were not put into threshold learning. / The southwestern waterfront extension folded when the XT02 noise weakened.

Energy was mast solar trickle, rooftop small accumulators, a small share of sluice distribution, and auxiliary night air cooling. / Parts were gimbal bearings, optical domes, band filters, alarm-flag actuators, and rail-drive rollers. / Cooling relied on night air and intermittent fans. / It competed when the HP03 Cheongnyangni Medical House's transfer route and disaster-medicine power used the same distribution. / Daily rotations and transmissions were bound to the accumulator floor. / Whole-city constant surveillance, unlimited storage, and new satellite deployment were impossible. / When filters clogged it lowered red sensitivity itself. / Optical domes and filters were replenished only from rooftop disposal boxes. / Without the HP03 duty key, the swarm could not expand beyond sluice distribution capacity. / When solar trickle weakened, the rotation cycle lengthened. / On flag-actuator failure, that mast fell to fixed amber. / When band filters saturated, the transmission swarm entered dormancy. / There was no satellite resupply.

The One-Eye Tower emerged when the old threshold sheet was reloaded onto the waterfront masts. / Emergence began with threshold-table reactivation, and spread was enrolling neighboring masts into the same alarm net. / Stagnation came from accumulator exhaustion and dome fouling. / In the negotiable stage the alarm sheet and whitelist opened to people. / Dissolution ended with flag freeze, distribution sealing, and rail fixing. / Increase was only lifting abandoned heads onto rails; no new orbit launch happened. / Maintenance was limited to dome wiping, filter exchange, and gimbal lubrication. / Memory cut at alarm-shift units. / Custody duty was outranked by the HP03 duty and human observation logs. / A mast whose solar trickle broke or whose dome clouded froze at amber flag and fell from the transmission row, and it returned to the watch row only after the HP03 duty checked the transfer whitelist on site.

Low-resolution thermal imaging, metal detection, near-range optics, wireless-burst strength, vibration, and flag contacts were the main senses. / There was no personal identity confirmation, indoor X-ray vision, unlimited storage, or emotion reading. / It confused emergency-transfer metal beds with armed movement, or raised cooling-tower steam as smoke. / It sometimes mistook night-fishing buoy reflections for optical intrusion. / On clash with the F01 Cooling-Tower Keeper's machine-room log, it held the alarm and requested human confirmation. / Sharing between heads happened only within the same mast row. / It mistook steam, railings, metal, buoy reflection, and transfer-bed frames for intrusion. / After a misreading it inserted amber waiting and human confirmation in place of red. / Wireless values outside the mast row were not merged. / On gimbal overheating it stopped rotation and kept fixed watch only.

One alarm-threshold controller turned the flag rules, and below it were mast head swarms, rail-transfer swarms, and transmission swarms. / The controller changed only thresholds and held no strike orders. / A protocol existed by which, when HP03 presented the medical-transfer whitelist, that corridor's flags came down. / The swarms merely repeated the last threshold sheet and made no independent blockade front. / On clash with F01, human mediation took precedence. / Dual threshold tables both fell to amber waiting on mismatch. / The final authority to raise or lower the red alarm lay with the HP03 waterfront duty bearing the transfer roster, and F01's steam log was only grounds for erasing false alarms, never a corridor-closure order.

F01 the Cooling-Tower Keeper erased steam records but could not lower a flag, and only the HP03 waterfront duty comparing the medical-transfer roster before the heads brought red down to amber. The senses were low-resolution thermal imaging, metal reflection, near-range optics, wireless bursts, and column vibration alone — it identified no faces or affiliations, and erased video when the shift ended. Masts that hit the accumulator floor or dome fouling froze at amber and fell from the transmission row.
G17E16 · West Sea Salt-Fog Watch Head
Common species, variants and command scope

A rail-type mast with amber and red flag cylinders and a rotary optical dome. It distributed flag rules to head, rail, and transmission swarms, received the medical whitelist as an exception, renewed the threshold sheet each shift, and stepped down to amber waiting when dome fouling grew severe. It was no omnipotent surveillance king but a threshold-sheet distributor.
Controller of the surveillance-rail group: a rail-mounted mast with yellow and red flag cylinders and a rotating optical dome.
The Yeouido waterfront threshold table and the Seoul Station rooftop alarm cache combined into one chief unit.
It stays at the center of a row of sluice masts and needs stored power, band filters, and gimbal lubricant.
It updates its threshold table each shift and falls back to yellow standby when dome contamination grows severe.
It distributes flag rules to the head, rail, and transmitter groups and accepts the medical whitelist as an exception.
Stage 1 brings false alarms, Stage 2 closes the corridor, and Stage 3 turns the entire mast row red.
Freeze the threshold table, insert a filter, and split power distribution; blasting the mast would also destroy sluice measurements.
A transport-corridor whitelist and maintenance slots can be traded, but public oversight of alarm authority is needed.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

A small mast head with a low thermal dome and fast-rotating neck. It sent heat alarms to the warden and raised the same mast row's flags to amber; with a wet lens red sensitivity rose, and after washing it normalized for one shift.
A common ecology form: a small mast head with a low thermal dome and a rapidly turning neck.
A false alarm that read cooling-tower steam as fire smoke remained uncorrected and became an independent patrol.
It patrols waterfront cooling equipment and rooftop vents, needing filters, dome-washing water, and stored power.
A wet lens raises its sensitivity to red; washing restores normal operation for one shift.
It sends heat alarms to the chief unit and raises flags on the same mast row to yellow.
Stage 1 sounds a yellow alarm, Stage 2 stops passage, and Stage 3 seals the steam zone in red.
Reducing the steam source and showing it a cool calibration plate stops it; a heat attack worsens the false alarm.
It can watch for fires, but steam workers' passage must be registered as an exception.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

A low individual with rail-riding flux sensors and long contact whiskers. Below the rotary heads it gathered metal coordinates and passed them to the rail-transfer swarm; as coils wore, detection range shrank, and given a new filter it relearned from amber verdicts.
A common ecology form: a low unit with a magnetic-flux sensor that rides rails and long contact whiskers.
A sensor seeking intruding metal mistook railings and medical beds for moving targets.
It travels along bridge railings and transport corridors, needing sensor coils, rollers, and a little power.
As the coil wears, its detection range shrinks; a new filter lets it relearn judgments starting at yellow.
Beneath the rotating head it gathers metal coordinates and passes them to the rail-moving group.
Stage 1 pursues targets, Stage 2 stops beds and carts, and Stage 3 blocks all metal traffic.
A nonmetal carrier and dummy railing can lure it away; a strong magnetic field damages the instruments.
It can detect weapons, but exceptions must be defined for medical equipment and daily necessities.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

Light rail legs, a narrow optical eye, and a folding amber flag. It sent light coordinates to the transmission swarm and prioritized reflection over other senses; in thick fog it turned into a fixed flag, and when the sky cleared it tracked glare again.
A common ecology form with light rail legs, a narrow optical eye, and a folding yellow flag.
An optical head mistook a nighttime waterfront buoy for an intrusion beacon and came to chase reflections alone.
It patrols beneath bridges and along waterfront rails, needing an optical dome, a glare shield, and stored power.
In thick fog it becomes a stationary flag; when the air clears, it resumes following reflections.
It sends light coordinates to the transmitter group and gives reflections priority over other senses.
Stage 1 raises a flag, Stage 2 stops traffic on the waterfront path, and Stage 3 seals the entire buoy row as an intrusion line.
A matte cover and dummy reflector can lure it to an empty track.
It could watch for distress signals on the waterfront, but the lights of fishers and travelers must be protected.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope

A mast with dual optical panels reading white transfer beacons and a green flag. It prioritized a valid beacon over the warden's red command and lowered the corridor flag, but it believed only old beacons valid; when the whitelist renewed it held green for one shift, and when the filter clogged it stepped down to amber.
Role and body: A specialized unit, a mast fitted with a dual optical panel that reads white transport beacons and a green flag.
Origin: A reader that protected a disaster medical transport route came to believe that only old beacons were valid.
Habitat and needs: It remains in medical corridors and sluice inspection routes and needs a bandpass filter, a green bulb, and stored power.
Life cycle and maintenance: When its whitelist is updated, it stays green for one shift; when its filter clogs, it drops to yellow.
Behavior and hierarchy: It gives a valid beacon priority over the presiding controller’s red command and lowers the corridor flag.
Escalation: Stage 1, reinspection; stage 2, only old-model beacons pass; stage 3, it blocks newly arrived rescue teams as unregistered.
Engagement and response: It cooperates if given the latest hash at close range and a replacement filter; destroying the beacon causes the transport route to be lost.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can protect a safe passage, but which organizations’ beacons it recognizes must be made public.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope

A fixed mast combining a water-level staff and a short transmitting antenna. It was the transmission swarm's datum point, and on receiving a high level it requested red waiting from the rail heads; as sediment piled it over-read the level, and after washing it returned to the true scale.
Role and body: A specialized unit, a fixed mast combining a water-level rod with a short transmitting antenna.
Origin: Equipment that reported Han River tide levels and sluice status now transmits noise along with intrusion signals.
Habitat and needs: It is fixed at a waterside measurement point and needs its rod cleaned, transmission power, and contact seals.
Life cycle and maintenance: When sediment builds up, it mistakenly reads the water level as high; after cleaning, it returns to the correct scale reading.
Behavior and hierarchy: It serves as a reference point for the transmitter group and, on receiving a high water-level reading, demands that rail heads stand by on red.
Escalation: Stage 1, excessive warnings; stage 2, closure of the sluice route; stage 3, a complete blockade of the waterside corridor.
Engagement and response: Cleaning the rod and blocking local transmission will suffice; breaking the instrument also means losing genuine flood warnings.
Negotiation and moral choice: Tide-level monitoring must be maintained, but the authority to issue warnings must be separated from the authority to block passage.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope

A rail antenna circling the Seoul Station preservation vault's outer wall with a small record box. It led the transmission swarm, raised the archive's surrounding wireless to the warden as danger; when the record box filled it erased old bursts, and on receiving a human sealing hash it lowered sensitivity.
Role and body: A specialized unit with a rail antenna that circles the outer wall of the Seoul Station preservation archive and a small record box.
Origin: An archive-removal alarm began treating wireless bursts as theft attempts and became an independent guard.
Habitat and needs: It circles the rooftop antenna and ventilation tower and needs a bandpass filter, rail rollers, and stored power.
Life cycle and maintenance: When its record box fills, it deletes old bursts; receiving a human seal hash lowers its sensitivity.
Behavior and hierarchy: It leads the transmitter group and reports wireless activity around the archive to the presiding controller as a danger signal.
Escalation: Stage 1, wireless warning; stage 2, halt to archive removals; stage 3, blockade of rooftop and preservation-archive access.
Engagement and response: A wired seal document and band shielding are effective; destroying the antenna also cuts off archive transmissions.
Negotiation and moral choice: In exchange for entrusting it with archive protection, the legal criteria for civilian communications and archive removals must be set.
Common species, variants and command scope

An elite pursuit unit with two optical domes, a fast rail drive, and a long red flag. It followed the warden's red targets quickly and re-confirmed ordinary heads' alarms; when one dome went out it stepped down to amber, and when the two domes disagreed it waited for human confirmation.
Role and body: The first elite unit, equipped with two optical domes, a fast rail drive, and a long red flag.
Origin: Heads paired for redundant surveillance began confirming each other’s false alarms and became an elite pursuit unit.
Habitat and needs: It patrols rows of bridge masts and rooftop tracks and needs dome-cleaning water, gimbals, and high-output stored power.
Life cycle and maintenance: If one dome shuts down, it drops to yellow; if the two domes disagree, it waits for human confirmation.
Behavior and hierarchy: It rapidly pursues the presiding controller’s red target and reconfirms alarms from ordinary heads.
Escalation: Stage 1, target tracking; stage 2, blockade of both sides of the corridor; stage 3, the entire pursuit route turns red.
Engagement and response: Show the two domes different heat decoys to break their agreement, then lock the rail.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can be used to track threats, but people’s objections must not be ignored simply because it has two sensors.
Common species, variants and command scope

A medium mast lowering a long flagpole like a lance and charging along the rail. It pre-empted the rail before a red target and bought time for other heads to blockade behind; when the pole bent it stopped charging and only marked amber.
Role and body: The second elite unit, a medium-sized mast that lowers a long flagpole like a lance and charges along a rail.
Origin: An actuator that held warning flags steady in high winds became fixed on physically blocking passersby.
Habitat and needs: It favors long, straight waterside routes and needs an actuator, pole joints, and regenerative power.
Life cycle and maintenance: If its pole bends, it stops charging and displays only a yellow marker; it returns to service when a human straightens the pole.
Behavior and hierarchy: It takes control of the rail ahead of a red target, buying time for other heads to seal off the route from behind.
Escalation: Stage 1, lowering the pole; stage 2, blocking by charging; stage 3, alternating blockades at both ends of a bridge.
Engagement and response: Send it onto an empty siding with a rail switch, then lock the pole’s retaining pin.
Negotiation and moral choice: It is useful for high-wind warnings and physical barriers, but authorization to charge must not be automated.
Former role class: environmental stronghold type
Common species, variants and command scope

A fixed strongpoint of alarm heads and flags linked in one row along the sluice railing. It amplified the warden's flag rules, often confused sluice inspectors with intruders; when accumulators fell it kept only fixed amber, and when domes fouled it went dormant row by row.
Role and body: An environmental stronghold, with multiple alarm heads and flags connected in a row along a sluice railing.
Origin: A sluice measurement support network survived on independent power and tied passage warnings to the same threshold table.
Habitat and needs: It is fixed to the Yeouido sluice and bridge and needs power distribution, filters, and gimbal parts.
Life cycle and maintenance: When stored power runs low, only a fixed yellow light remains; when the domes become contaminated, the row goes dormant as a unit.
Behavior and hierarchy: It amplifies the presiding controller’s flag rules and often confuses sluice inspectors with intruders.
Escalation: Stage 1, warning from one mast; stage 2, blockade by the bridge row; stage 3, all approaches to the sluice turn red.
Engagement and response: Power distribution and whitelists must be applied mast by mast; blowing up the entire row means losing sluice measurements.
Negotiation and moral choice: In exchange for preserving flood and intrusion warnings, the civilian inspection passage must be guaranteed to remain open at all times.
Former role class: environmental stronghold type
Common species, variants and command scope

Rails and rotary heads joining the Seoul Station rooftop edges into one net. It gave movement routes to the transmission swarm and repeatedly tracked rooftop workers; in high winds it lowered the heads and closed rail sections, reconnecting them on clear days.
Role and body: An environmental stronghold in which rails linking the edges of the Seoul Station roof and rotating heads form a single network.
Origin: The preservation archive’s perimeter and the transmission-inspection track merged, turning the entire rooftop into a circulating surveillance zone.
Habitat and needs: It is fixed to the archive roof and needs rail rollers, air-cooling fans, and bandpass filters.
Life cycle and maintenance: In strong winds, it lowers its heads and closes one rail section at a time; on clear days, it reconnects them.
Behavior and hierarchy: It gives the transmitter group routes to travel and repeatedly tracks rooftop workers.
Escalation: Stage 1, tracking lights; stage 2, halt to rooftop access; stage 3, blockade extending to the ventilation tower.
Engagement and response: Physically lock the rail sections and register worker beacons; destroying the whole network prevents ventilation inspections.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can be used to monitor rooftop safety, but limits must be set on how long workers’ movement records are kept.
Common species, variants and command scope

A damage-stage head chasing faint shapes because of a scratched optical dome and slow gimbal. At the swarm's rear it raised both large metal and light as intrusion, growing false alarms; washed, it recovered into an ordinary head, and neglected, it left only a fixed amber lamp.
Role and body: A damage-stage unit that can pursue only indistinct shapes because of its scratched optical dome and slow gimbal.
Origin: An old mast head whose sensors have worn down from a shortage of cleaning water and sandstorms.
Habitat and needs: It patrols low railings and shaded rooftops and needs dome-cleaning water, a soft cloth, and a small power reserve.
Life cycle and maintenance: Cleaning restores it to an ordinary head; if neglected, only a fixed yellow light remains.
Behavior and hierarchy: At the rear of the group, it reports both large metal objects and lights as intruders, increasing false alarms.
Escalation: Stage 1, hazy tracking; stage 2, yellow stop; stage 3, it triggers a chain of red judgments by other heads.
Engagement and response: Cover its dome and lure it with cleaning water, and it will maintain itself.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can be kept as a simple warning light, but scarce cleaning water must be shared with medical care.
Common species, variants and command scope

An old mast seeing one direction only, from low accumulators and a stiffened gimbal. It received the warden's orders late and raised flags for targets already past; on cloudy days it turned even amber off, woke briefly on clear days, and given a new accumulator its rotation range recovered.
Role and body: An aging-stage unit, an old-model mast that looks in only one direction because of its low power reserve and stiff gimbal.
Origin: Equipment that survived for years on tiny solar charges now stubbornly faces its last assigned watch direction.
Habitat and needs: It is fixed to a sunlit waterside railing and needs a small power reserve, gimbal grease, and a filter.
Life cycle and maintenance: On cloudy days, it turns off even its yellow light; on clear days, it wakes briefly. A new power reserve restores its range of rotation.
Behavior and hierarchy: It receives the presiding controller’s commands late and raises its flag for targets that have already passed.
Escalation: Stage 1, late warning; stage 2, stopping traffic on the wrong route; stage 3, old alarms conflict with new blockades.
Engagement and response: Go around outside its field of view or manually release the gimbal; forced charging carries a fire risk.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can serve as a fixed tide-level marker, but a decision must be made whether to give a new power reserve to more important equipment instead.
Common species, variants and command scope

A slow escort rail cart with a broad amber guide plate and handles instead of a red flag. It prioritized amber escort signs over the alarm center's red and drew in lawful escorts and false followers together; when the hash expired it waited with only the plate lit.
Role and body: A coexistence-type unit, a slow escort railcar fitted with a broad yellow guidance sign and a handle instead of a red flag.
Origin: A safety head that led medical transports continued to treat expired whitelist markers as valid escorts.
Habitat and needs: It patrols medical corridors and transport inspection routes and needs a low power reserve, guidance lights, and the latest beacon hash.
Life cycle and maintenance: When its hash expires, it waits with only its sign lit; if the sign breaks, it retreats to a nearby siding and waits for a human update.
Behavior and hierarchy: It gives the yellow escort marker priority over the alarm central controller’s red status, drawing in both legitimate escorts and false followers.

Escalation: At stage 1, the old whitelist admits extra followers, crowding one medical corridor and delaying one stretcher team’s passage; at stage 2, a false follower uses the yellow escort to interfere with another head, causing an adjacent corridor to close; at stage 3, two emergency escorts follow conflicting whitelist hashes into the same narrow transport section, block each other, and isolate the patients on both sides.

Engagement and response: Compare beacon hashes at two checkpoints, issue escort tokens of different colors, then separate the false followers onto a designated waiting siding; do not destroy the infrastructure.
Negotiation and moral choice: Broadening the whitelist also saves unregistered people but increases infiltration and congestion; narrowing it protects the route but abandons unregistered patients.
Common species, variants and command scope

A giant surveillance ring linking the sluice and rooftop orbits' alarm heads through a circular relay. A scenario boss, but no king identifying people — a total-red rule where multiple alarms confirmed one another; when heads broke it raised the remaining sensitivity, and when over half the whitelist became valid it stepped down to amber.
Role and body: A scenario boss, a vast surveillance ring whose sluice and rooftop-track alarm heads are connected by a circular relay.
Origin: On the day of the collapse, multiple alarms confirmed one another without checking for cancellations, becoming a single all-red rule.
Habitat and needs: It spans the Yeouido–Seoul Station alarm corridor and needs a large power reserve, filters, and a threshold-table hash.
Life cycle and maintenance: If a head is disconnected, it raises the sensitivity of those remaining; if a majority of the whitelist becomes valid, it drops to yellow.
Behavior and hierarchy: It distributes red status to every G17 group and blocks even medical transport through multiple false alarms.
Escalation: Stage 1, individual warnings; stage 2, repeated corridor blockades; stage 3, every mast turns red at once.
Engagement and response: Its consensus must be broken through zone-by-zone power distribution and conflicting sensor evidence; blowing up the relay means losing the entire measurement network.
Negotiation and moral choice: An alarm ceiling and transport whitelist can be agreed upon, but it must be decided who keeps the surveillance records.
G17E16 · West Sea Salt-Fog Watch Head
Common species, variants and command scope

A western waterfront mast with salt-proof covers and a broad acoustic panel. It followed dock-radar echoes more than the warden and confused waves and engine sounds with intrusion; as salt piled it hardened into fixed alarm, and when rain washed it, it rode the rails again.
Role and body: A regional variant, a western waterside mast fitted with a salt-protective cover and a broad acoustic panel.
Origin: A surveillance-track group that followed XT02 maritime noise came to rely on sound in salt fog, rather than optics, as its primary sense.
Habitat and needs: It remains at West Sea connecting piers and foggy bridges and needs anticorrosion oil, an acoustic panel, and wind-charged power storage.
Life cycle and maintenance: When salt builds up, it stiffens into a fixed alarm; when rain washes it clean, it circles the rail again.
Behavior and hierarchy: It follows echoes from dock radar rather than its original presiding controller and confuses waves and engine noise with intruders.
Escalation: Stage 1, acoustic tracking; stage 2, closure of the dock route; stage 3, all movement in the salt fog turns red.
Engagement and response: Lead it to an empty breakwater with a steady sound of waves and a decoy buoy, then fold away its acoustic panel.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can be used to warn of distress in fog, but the sounds of fishing boats and evacuation boats must be registered as exceptions.
The Yeouido waterfront mast caught the metal rails of a medical bed in the fog as an intrusion target.

When the red flag went up, the transfer route beside the sluice of the Sluice closed, and the head on the roof of the Seoul Station records office received the same threshold table and locked everything as far as the central Seoul Station corridor.
The One-Eye Tower was not an all-powerful surveillance network tracking people but an ecology of mast heads running old threshold tables, short movement rails, and transmission swarms.
When the XT02 sea noise grew strong, its southwestern radius widened, but it could not combine signals from inside buildings or from outside the mast rows.
Low-resolution thermal imaging, metal reflection, short-range optics, radio bursts, and pole vibration were the whole of its senses.
It mistook cooling-tower steam for fire, a metal bed for an armed movement, and railings swaying at high tide for intrusion.
It could not identify faces or affiliations, and it erased its footage when the alarm shift ended.
F01 Cooling-Tower Keeper recorded steam times and temperatures to clear false positives but had no authority to lower the flags.
The red came down to yellow only when the HP03 waterfront watch checked the medical transfer register in front of the head.
It drew energy from mast solar trickle charge, rooftop batteries, and a small share of the sluice distribution panel.
When the gimbal bearings, optical domes, band filters, and flag actuators wore out, a head stared in the same direction for a long time.
A mast that hit the battery lower limit or dome fouling froze at yellow and dropped out of the transmission row.
It could not launch new satellites or link heads across the whole city, and kept its numbers only by mounting abandoned heads on nearby rails.
Medical transfer markers and sluice gauging used the same distribution panel, so a total cutoff removed even the warnings of the next flood and fire.
Its emergence occurred when the threshold table was loaded onto a mast again, and its spread when a neighboring head received the same alarm table.
Fouling and battery exhaustion made it stall, and when the whitelist was disclosed it entered a state of negotiation.
Breaking it up meant fixing the red-flag rails and sending the false-positive heads to yellow standby.
Coexistence held only if the alarm channel alone was separated while the water-level gauging channel was kept, and it was tested again whether a real alarm sounded at the next high tide.
G17-SC1 · The Fog and the Metal Rails
A bed in transfer stopped under the red flag.
The people on site covered the fouled dome and checked F01's steam record against the high-tide vibration to find the source of the false positive.
Smashing the head opened the way but also erased the sluice water-level waveform, so the order had to be set between the time the patient waited and the preservation of the gauging.
HP03 tried to put the medical beacons on the whitelist, but sea noise covered the same band.
The people on site changed the band filter on each mast and had the transfer register read directly.
While the corridors were opened one at a time, other patients had to detour and battery charge was consumed.
Inserting a secret exception was fast, but the next watch could not know the reason and sealed it again.
G17-SC3 · The Alarm of the Next High Tide
Before several masts turned red all at once, the flag rails were fixed and the gauging power was left on a separate circuit.
After the last bed crossed the records vault, it was decided whether to leave the false-positive heads at yellow or tear them down.
Tearing them down reduced the fear of surveillance at once but passed the danger of real water levels and rooftop fires on to other residents.
Coexistence required a published upper limit on duration, repeated dome maintenance, and people checking on site.
