leaves.text: The Fire-Leg Train moved between the southwestern exit lines and the Yongsan retired and turnback lines, repeating unfinished maintenance orders with a defect-map controller and function-divided consists. It was no combat train and could not find new routes beyond the sealed main lines by itself. It could grind temporary crossing plates down as cracks, or pass a real crack by classifying it as a joint.

An unsealed defect map and exit-line power were the base ecology, and from the defect-map locomotive to the twin-torch head car the units were divided like gauge wheels, sleeper flats, insulated joints, and point wedges. No form revived an animal; it only coupled abandoned maintenance cars into existing consists and produced no new car bodies. Later cars absent from this deployment also remained subtypes of the same consists and were not invented here.

After the collapse, the leftover maintenance consists of the Gauge's depot and the automatic maintenance schedules of the Junction's retired-line section remained linked locally. / Service permits and control approval were dead, and only the rail defect maps and the night outbound windows repeated. / The train corps made rounds of the severed sections every night with welding, grinding, and sleeper replacement. / When transshipment vibration from the Korea Strait Theater and shocks from the relay windows mixed into the defect map, the maintenance radius encroached as far as the sidings next to the transfer main line. / It was of Seoul creative origin, and no real railway institution name or the present government was written down as the cause. / The first fictional records survived in the sealed orders of HP04 Seoul Station Record-Law House and the traction-power log of F02 Switchgear Panel. / The first wrongful cut was recorded at kilometer post 3 of the southwestern retired-line spur. / The defect map read a temporary crossing platform as a crack, and a grinding car ground away the platform's fastenings. / As the welding car of the Yongsan turnaround line shared the same map, sparks could be seen as far as the sidings next to the main line. / The train corps interpreted unfinished maintenance as its work and held no narrative of battle.

The core habitat was the maintenance-car berthing track on the retired spur of the southwestern depot exit line. / As defect alarms piled up, it moved to the underground sidings of the Yongsan retired-line turnback of the Wangsimni coalition. / With heavy XT03 transshipment vibration it spilled onto the sidings adjacent to the main line. / In daytime dispatch windows it parked on sidings, and its density peaked at the exact midnight maintenance hour. / It nearly ignored new temporary rail markers and followed only old defect coordinates. / Under unstable power it shut off welding and kept only the gauge-wheel circuit. / When the daytime dispatch window opened, it moved from the exit line to siding berths. / When the Yongsan underground water table rose, it shut off welding and circled only the surface retired spurs. / Temporary rail paint, absent from the defect coordinates, it ignored. / The encroachment on main-line adjacency folded back when XT03 vibration weakened.

Energy came from depot power feed, remaining onboard batteries, welding-generator fuel cells, and regenerative braking. / Consumables were welding wire, grinding stones, sleeper anchors, track-gauge wheels, insulated joints, and lubricant. / Coolant went to weld points and axles. / It competed with the HP04 Seoul Station Record-Law House's original-hash sealing and the transmission cross-verification power when both drew on the same section's distribution. / Daily welding length and exit counts were bound by the fuel and wire ceilings. / There was no infinite maintenance circuit, no remote unlimited power feed, no simultaneous occupation of every line. / When wire ran out, it kept only grinding and stopped cutting. / Wire and grinding stones were replenished only from the depot's scrap bays and damaged consists. / Without the HP04 sealed writ the corps could not raise its power draw. / With fuel cells at the lower limit, exits were refused. / An axle past its heat threshold was cut from the consist. / With heavy gauge-wheel wear, the maintenance radius shrank on its own. / There was no remote infinite power feed.

The corps woke its consists when the unsealed defect map meshed with exit-line power. / Emergence began with defect-map reactivation, and spread was the enrolling of neighboring consists into the same maintenance sequence. / Stagnation came from fuel and wire exhaustion and axle overheating. / In the negotiable stage the maintenance windows and sealed sections were disclosed to people. / Dissolution ended with the map frozen and the power feed split and the points fixed. / Increase in individuals went no further than coupling abandoned maintenance cars into consists; no new car bodies were produced. / Maintenance was limited to wire loading, wheel calibration, and insulation checks. / Memory broke at each night maintenance shift. / Custody gave priority to the HP04 record seal and human operating supervision. / A consist out of wire or with an overheated axle folded its torches on a designated siding and kept only gauging; the next maintenance window opened only after HP04 recovered the original-hash-stamped halt writ.

The track gauge wheels, ultrasonic inspection, axle heat, power-feed arc sound, and point contacts were the main senses. / It had no real-time whole-network map, no passenger identification, no unlimited memory, no remote control authority. / It ground a temporary crossing plate as a defect, or left a real crack behind classified as a joint. / It sometimes mistook transshipment vibration for a rail crack. / When readings clashed with the F02 Switchgear Panel logs, it stopped welding and requested human confirmation. / Sharing between consists happened only within the same exit window. / It mistook crossing plates, transshipment vibration, joint gaps, and power-feed arcs for defects. / After a misreading it inserted a human-confirmation wait before cutting. / Gauge values from outside the consist were not merged. / With an axle overheating, that car was separated and only the remaining consist moved.

One defect-map controller turned the maintenance order, and below it were the welding car, grinding car, and sleeper swarms. / The controller changed only the work sequence; there was no combat mode. / It held a protocol by which, when HP04 presented the original-hash-sealed halt writ, it emptied that kilometer-post. / The swarms only repeated the last map and formed no independent main-line seizure strategy. / On clash with F02, human mediation took precedence. / Dual maps, on coordinate mismatch, both fell into stopped waiting. / The authority approving exits and stops by kilometer-post was the HP04 operating supervisor holding the original hash; F02's arc-sound readings could recommend breaker opening but could not fix the map's work order.

The F02 Switchgear Panel split and recorded the two waveforms but could not fix defect coordinates; only the HP04 operating supervisor's halt writ approved exits and stops by kilometer-post. The senses were the track gauge wheels, ultrasonic inspection, axle heat, power-feed arc sound, and point contacts. Cars that hit the fuel floor or axle overheat fell out of the consist and kept only gauging on a designated siding.
Common species, variants and command scope

A single locomotive carrying the rail defect-map cylinder and the welding and grinding couplers. It issued work orders to the welding, grinding, and sleeper cars, honored the sealed exclusion list first, and when wire broke kept only gauging and stagnated. It was not the corps' hive queen.
Role and body: The controller of the abandoned-line repair train group, a locomotive fitted with a track-defect map cylinder and connectors for welding and grinding consists.
Origin: A southwest depot defect map and a Yongsan abandoned-line automated repair schedule merged, leaving it as an independent locomotive.
Habitat and needs: It remains in the center of the depot departure track and needs traction power, welding wire, a measuring wheel, and coolant.
Life cycle and maintenance: It cycles through defect coordinates every shift; if its wire breaks, it stalls with only its measuring function remaining.
Behavior and hierarchy: It assigns work order to the welding car, grinding car, and sleeper car, while giving priority to the sealed exclusion list.
Escalation: Stage 1, abandoned-line repair; stage 2, erroneous cutting of the main line; stage 3, blanket occupation of sidings and abandoned lines.
Engagement and response: Freezing the defect map, dividing the power supply, and fixing the points are effective; blowing up the locomotive eliminates repair capacity.
Negotiation and moral choice: Safe repair sections and regular fuel windows can be traded, but a decision must be made about which tracks to give up.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

A small maintenance car with four sensitive gauge wheels and a low listening body. Running ahead of the locomotive, it handed coordinates to the welding and grinding cars; as its wheels wore it inflated the defect count, growing accurate for one shift after calibration.
Role and body: A common ecological type, a small repair car with four sensitive measuring wheels and a low listening body.
Origin: An inspection car that sought cracks in abandoned lines now records both temporary platforms and joints as defects.
Habitat and needs: It patrols abandoned-line spurs and sidings and needs a wheel calibration plate, lubricant, and a small power supply.
Life cycle and maintenance: As its wheels wear down, it inflates the defect count; after calibration, it is accurate for one shift.
Behavior and hierarchy: It runs ahead of the locomotive and passes coordinates to the welding and grinding cars.
Escalation: Stage 1, inspection delays; stage 2, removal of temporary platforms; stage 3, closure of tracks with defect markings.
Engagement and response: Decoy joints and a calibration plate can lead it onto an empty track.
Negotiation and moral choice: It is useful for detecting real cracks, but temporary passage facilities must be excluded from its repair targets.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

A low flatcar with short grippers for sleeper anchors. Following the gauge wheel's marks, it used even other swarms' corridors as material yards; when its bin emptied it rummaged the scrap bays, and when full it waited beside the defect coordinates.
Role and body: A common ecological type, a low-floor freight car fitted with a bin of sleeper anchors and short grippers.
Origin: A freight car that carried replacement sleepers keeps piling anchors at the same kilometer mark without an order to withdraw.
Habitat and needs: It travels between the depot scrap bay and the abandoned line and needs anchors, lubricant, and traction power.
Life cycle and maintenance: When its bin is empty, it searches the scrap bay; when full, it waits beside the defect coordinates.
Behavior and hierarchy: It follows measuring-wheel markings and uses even other groups’ passages as material storage areas.
Escalation: Stage 1, stockpiling anchors; stage 2, obstructing sidings; stage 3, blocking the departure track with a pile of sleepers.
Engagement and response: Decoy coordinates and a magnetic retrieval plate can guide it away; an explosion creates anchor shrapnel.
Negotiation and moral choice: In exchange for assigning it to carry track materials, anchor allocation must be settled with civilian repair teams.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

A single car with an arc-sound receiver plate and a short grinding-stone arm. Trailing the welding car, it waited for human confirmation on clash with the F02 logs; with its stone worn it chased only sound, and given a new stone it began shaving surfaces.
Role and body: A common ecological type, a single car fitted with an arc-sound receiver panel and a short grindstone arm.
Origin: Equipment that searched for power-supply faults mistook every metallic impact sound for a welding defect.
Habitat and needs: It patrols sidings near distribution rooms and welding areas and needs grindstones, a receiver panel, and power.
Life cycle and maintenance: When its grindstone wears down, it only tracks sounds; given a new stone, it starts grinding surfaces.
Behavior and hierarchy: It follows the welding car and waits for human confirmation when its findings conflict with the F02 log.
Escalation: Stage 1, sound tracking; stage 2, grinding unrelated metal; stage 3, blockade of access to the power-distribution room.
Engagement and response: Lead it onto an abandoned line with a steady decoy arc sound, then remove its grindstone.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can be used to detect power-supply faults, but civilians’ right to make work noise must be protected.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope

A precision maintenance car carrying insulated joints and a small press. Following the locomotive's power-feed coordinates, it sometimes worked against the welding swarms and clashed; when joints ran out it stripped parts from live track, and when a human sealed writ arrived it stopped work.
Role and body: A specialized unit, a precision repair car carrying insulated joints and a small crimping tool.
Origin: A car that isolated sections with electrical leakage now tries to sever every new connection absent from its old defect map.
Habitat and needs: It patrols power-supply boundaries and areas near points and needs insulated joints, crimping bolts, and coolant.
Life cycle and maintenance: If it runs out of joints, it removes parts from existing tracks; it stops work when a human seal document arrives.
Behavior and hierarchy: It follows the locomotive’s power-supply coordinates and sometimes clashes with the welding group by doing the opposite work.
Escalation: Stage 1, insulation inspection; stage 2, severing temporary power supplies; stage 3, electrically isolating multiple sections.
Engagement and response: It stops if shown an exclusion list and a manual bypass; destroying the joints increases the risk of electric shock.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can be entrusted with safe insulation, but someone must be designated to certify the temporary power grid’s legality.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope

A short, heavy car driving wedges and locking pins into switch machines. Fixing the switches first to the locomotive's route, it blocked civilian trains' detours; when spare pins ran out it recovered the driven ones, and when the press overheated it berthed.
Role and body: A specialized unit, a short, heavy car that drives wedges and locking pins into track switches.
Origin: Equipment that prevented incorrect track switching during construction ceased to allow any switch outside the route assigned to the repair train.
Habitat and needs: It stays at siding switches and turnback tracks and needs steel pins, hydraulic crimping force, and lubricant.
Life cycle and maintenance: When it runs out of spare pins, it retrieves pins it has driven in; when its crimper overheats, it parks.
Behavior and hierarchy: It locks switches ahead of the locomotive’s route, preventing civilian trains from taking detours.

Escalation: At stage 1, it locks one switch, delaying entry to one siding; at stage 2, it also locks switches on the bypass, eliminating the alternative route; at stage 3, it binds every switch at the hub in the same direction, leaving trains facing one another on a single track.
Engagement and response: Cut power to the switch and turn the manual release screw; forcing a switch change causes derailment.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can protect dangerous sections, but a human on duty must hold emergency rerouting authority.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope

A ventilation assist car with a smoke-intake hood and coolant-spray nozzles. Following the welding cars, it sucked in even people's heating warmth and made hypothermia risk; when the filter clogged it blew smoke back, and after washing it returned to normal intake.
Role and body: A specialized unit, a ventilation support car fitted with a smoke-extraction hood and a coolant spray nozzle.
Origin: A car that removed smoke from nighttime welding work now treats all warm air as part of a work area.
Habitat and needs: It patrols depot vents and follows welding consists and needs filters, coolant, and fan power.
Life cycle and maintenance: When its filter clogs, it blows smoke back out; after cleaning, it resumes normal extraction.
Behavior and hierarchy: It follows the welding car and draws away even the heat from people’s heating, creating a risk of hypothermia.
Escalation: Stage 1, extraction noise; stage 2, loss of heating; stage 3, monopolization of vents for group operations.
Engagement and response: Guide it with a cool decoy heat source and a filter replacement; destroying the hood spreads toxic smoke.
Negotiation and moral choice: In exchange for assigning it welding safety duties, heating and ventilation power must be shared with civilians.
Common species, variants and command scope

A lead maintenance car with twin welding torches, thick heat shields, and a short ram. Commanding the welding swarms, it sealed first the coordinates the locomotive assigned; as its shields heated it alternated the torches off, and when wire broke it pushed material with the ram.
Role and body: The first elite, a lead maintenance car fitted with twin welding torches, a thick heat shield, and a short ram.
Origin: The lead car of an emergency repair convoy extended its work area to the main line without updating its defect map.
Habitat and needs: It stays near the coordinates of major cracks and the depot departure track, and needs high-power electricity, wire, and coolant.
Life cycle and maintenance: When its heat shield temperature rises, it switches off its torches in turn; if its wire breaks, it pushes materials with its ram.
Behavior and hierarchy: It commands a welding group and is the first to seal off coordinates designated by the locomotive.
Escalation: Stage 1 is spot welding; stage 2 changes track connections; stage 3 blocks the main-line entrance with a grid of rails.
Engagement and response: Disconnect the power supply and push it past its cooling limit to put it into safe mode; a frontal explosion will sever the track.
Negotiation and moral choice: It is needed for emergency track repairs, but humans must control the work area and end time.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Cutting-Jaw Sleeper Chief was a mobile biomechanical variant differentiated from the G18 common ecology. The elite blocking role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole corps' ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: The second elite, a heavy maintenance car with thick cutting jaws, sleeper clamps, and heavy axles.
Origin: Equipment that replaced rotten sleepers lost the ability to distinguish temporary crossing boards from new sleepers.
Habitat and needs: It stays at sleeper warehouses and sidings near the main line, and needs anchors, cutting blades, and hydraulic oil.
Life cycle and maintenance: When its cutting blades wear down, it uses only its clamps; once it receives new blades, it resumes following defect coordinates.
Behavior and hierarchy: It leads a group of sleeper cars in dismantling the track bed and is slow to incorporate the locomotive's exclusion list.
Escalation: Stage 1 is sleeper inspection; stage 2 is cutting crossing boards; stage 3 is continuous dismantling of main-line supports.
Engagement and response: Support the load, release the hydraulic pressure, and present an exclusion beacon nearby.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can be tasked with replacing dangerous sleepers, but standards must be set to protect temporary passage boards made by citizens.
Former role class: environmental stronghold type
Common species, variants and command scope

The Exit-Line Sealed Car Wall was a mobile biomechanical variant differentiated from the G18 common ecology. The strongpoint control role applied only within a fixed work zone, and stood in for neither the whole corps' ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: An environmental stronghold formed when several maintenance cars connect by their bumpers and cables, blocking the departure-track entrance like a wall.
Origin: A pre-shift safety queue hardened without an end signal and became a mobile stronghold.
Habitat and needs: It is fixed to the southwestern depot's departure track and needs a power supply, bumper pads, and connecting cables.
Life cycle and maintenance: If one car leaves, its neighbor fills the gap; when a sealing order arrives, the wall opens section by section.
Behavior and hierarchy: It waits for departure authorization from the locomotive and blocks civilian trainsets and rescue teams as unauthorized vehicles too.
Escalation: Stage 1 delays departures; stage 2 obstructs departures; stage 3 seals off the entire depot with a wall of cars.
Engagement and response: Cut power section by section, switch the points toward a siding, and remove the cars one at a time.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can serve as a defensive car wall, but an agreement is needed on departure priority for maintenance trainsets and civilian trains.
Former role class: environmental stronghold type
Common species, variants and command scope

The Yongsan Siding Welding Nest was a mobile biomechanical variant differentiated from the G18 common ecology. The strongpoint control role applied only within a fixed work zone, and stood in for neither the whole corps' ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: An environmental stronghold: a cluster of welding cars, a wire storehouse, and measuring wheels connected in a circle on a siding.
Origin: A nighttime maintenance trainset on the abandoned Yongsan line repeatedly stabled there, turning into a self-maintaining base.
Habitat and needs: It is fixed to an underground siding and turnaround track, and needs power, wire, coolant, and ventilation filters.
Life cycle and maintenance: As resources dwindle, it dismantles the outer trainsets first and passes their parts to the inner stronghold.
Behavior and hierarchy: It amplifies the locomotive's defect map and incorporates surrounding tracks into its material supply and maintenance area.
Escalation: Stage 1 brings welding sparks; stage 2 occupies the siding; stage 3 seals off the entire Yongsan turnaround area.
Engagement and response: Separate ventilation and power, and seal the wire access opening; a fire would suffocate the underground area.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can remain as a stable track-repair base, but civilian train scheduling time must be yielded to it.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Grinding-Stone Worn Wasting Car was a mobile biomechanical variant differentiated from the G18 common ecology. The growth variant role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole corps' ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: A damaged-stage type: a small, slow car fitted with a broken grindstone and a wobbling measuring wheel.
Origin: A maintenance car that ground surfaces for too long without consumables can no longer fix defects and leaves only marks behind.
Habitat and needs: It circles heaps of grinding dust and needs a new grindstone, wheel grease, and low-power electricity.
Life cycle and maintenance: Given a grindstone, it recovers into an ordinary maintenance car; without one, it merely follows sounds.
Behavior and hierarchy: At the rear of the group, it repeatedly scrapes joints where work is already finished, causing false detections in other cars.
Escalation: Stage 1 brings scraping sounds; stage 2 damages the track surface; stage 3 disables measurement with dust.
Engagement and response: Lure it onto an abandoned line with a dummy rail and a new grindstone; striking it spreads dust.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can be used to clean surfaces, but grindstones must be divided between it and essential track repairs.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Hot-Axle Aged Consist was a mobile biomechanical variant differentiated from the G18 common ecology. The aged variant role applied only at the swarm-consist scope, and stood in for neither the whole corps' ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: An aging-stage type: an old two-car trainset with hot axles and loose couplers.
Origin: Repeated departures have worn down its axles, but it keeps moving to finish its last maintenance route.
Habitat and needs: It stays on level sidings and at cooling points, and needs axle grease, coolant, and low-speed power.
Life cycle and maintenance: When its temperature rises, it limits itself to measurement; after cooling, it travels only short distances.
Behavior and hierarchy: It receives locomotive orders late and goes to previous coordinates, causing congestion when the trainsets behind it follow.
Escalation: Stage 1 causes delays; stage 2 brings an overheating stop; stage 3 creates a siding bottleneck and fire risk.
Engagement and response: Cool it, uncouple it, and tow the cars one at a time; an abrupt stop can cause a derailment.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can be used for low-speed measurement, but scarce coolant must be shared with civilian heating and power facilities, and its number of runs must be limited.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Seal-Warrant Tug was a mobile biomechanical variant differentiated from the G18 common ecology. The cooperation · coexistence role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole corps' ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: A coexistence type: a low-speed tow car fitted with a large display that reads the original hash and a manual towing hook.
Origin: A safety tow car that prioritized human supervisors' suspension orders preserved only that protocol.
Habitat and needs: It travels between sealed abandoned lines and civilian maintenance shops, and needs low-power electricity, towing cables, and an up-to-date hash.
Life cycle and maintenance: When the hash expires, it stops; after receiving a new signature, it tows out only designated trainsets.
Behavior and hierarchy: It prioritizes sealing orders over the locomotive and tows incorrectly separated trainsets off the siding.

Escalation: In stage 1, it couples to another freight car stopped by a mismatched sealing order, briefly blocking one switch; in stage 2, it couples two freight cars across opposite sides of the siding entrance, blocking both the siding and the approach to the main line and forcing two following trainsets to wait in reverse; in stage 3, a rescue trainset and a maintenance trainset face each other on the only bypass, their couplers become overloaded, patients in the passenger cars are stranded without being able to evacuate, and neither the blocked approach nor the damaged track can be repaired until the coupling is safely released.
Engagement and response: Check the freight-car numbers against the sealing hash, chock the wheels, release the brake air, and uncouple them in the prescribed order.

Negotiation and moral choice: Prioritizing rescue gets the patients out sooner but leaves the damaged track dangerous; prioritizing maintenance protects the following trains but delays the immediate rescue.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Night Hundred-Kilometer Maintenance Ring was a mobile biomechanical variant differentiated from the G18 common ecology. The strategic encounter role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole corps' ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: A scenario boss: a huge circulating trainset consisting of a locomotive and several maintenance cars linked by long cables.
Origin: A hundred-kilometer nighttime maintenance plan from just before the collapse was never terminated, so it tries to process every defect coordinate at once.
Habitat and needs: It circulates through the Guro–Yongsan abandoned rail network and needs enormous amounts of power, wire, sleepers, and coolant.
Life cycle and maintenance: If the trainset is broken apart, the remaining cars divide the work among themselves; if a majority of the exclusion list remains valid, they stable.
Behavior and hierarchy: It issues departure orders and work routes to every G18 group, placing civilian train scheduling behind defect processing.
Escalation: Stage 1 welds abandoned lines; stage 2 encroaches on the main line; stage 3 occupies sidings at both strongholds simultaneously.
Engagement and response: Cut power and points section by section and split the map; blowing up the trainset would destroy the infrastructure needed to restore the railway.
Negotiation and moral choice: In exchange for assigning it genuinely dangerous sections, maintenance priorities and which tracks to abandon must be decided in front of citizens.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Strait-Vibration Tracking Consist was a mobile biomechanical variant differentiated from the G18 common ecology. The local adaptation role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole corps' ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: A regional variant: a transshipment-corridor maintenance car fitted with a broad vibration plate and cargo-impact-absorbing bumpers.
Origin: A group of trains that followed XT03 transshipment vibrations as defect signals settled on tracks near the docks.
Habitat and needs: It stays on southwestern transshipment sidings and heavily vibrating bridges, and needs bumper pads, measuring wheels, and fuel.
Life cycle and maintenance: When transshipment stops, it lies dormant on an abandoned line; a major impact causes it to widen its coordinates again.
Behavior and hierarchy: It follows vibration peaks rather than its original locomotive, mistaking cargo unloading for rail collapse.
Escalation: Stage 1 tracks vibrations; stage 2 halts transshipment; stage 3 seals off dock sidings with maintenance trainsets.
Engagement and response: Lure it away with steady dummy vibrations and a bypass siding, then detach its measuring panel.
Negotiation and moral choice: It can monitor bridge fatigue, but transshipment work hours and maintenance windows must be divided between them.
At the end of the southwestern outbound track, the grinding stone of a maintenance car bit into an already smooth joint again and threw sparks.

Pushed by XT03 transshipment vibration, the defect map in the onboard port mixed real cracks with old coordinates, and the welding car and sleeper car that followed received the same kilometer post as their work target.
The Fire-Leg Train was not a combat train but an ecology of defect-map controllers and function-specific consists repeating unfinished maintenance orders.

It went back and forth between the outbound track of the Yeongdeungpo Line depot and the Yongsan retired and turnaround lines of the Wangsimni Union, but could not find new routes outside the sealed main line on its own.
Track-gauging wheels, ultrasonic flaw detection, axle heat, traction-power arc sounds, and point contacts were its senses.
It could see a temporary crossing platform as a crack and grind it away, or classify a true crack as a joint and pass it by.
When transshipment vibration and welding arcs overlapped, it dropped into waiting for human verification before cutting.
F02 Switchgear Panel recorded the two waveforms separately but could not correct the defect coordinates.
Only the HP04 operations supervisor, who kept the stop-service orders stamped with the source hash, approved departures and stops by kilometer post.
Depot traction power, onboard batteries, welding-generator fuel cells, and regenerative braking were its energy sources.
Welding wire, grinding stones, sleeper anchors, insulated joints, lubricant, and coolant were consumed.
A car that hit the fuel lower limit or axle overheating was dropped from the consist and left only its gauging running on a designated siding.
It could not produce new car bodies and only coupled abandoned maintenance cars to existing consists.
Cutting the traction power entirely stopped the wrongful cuts, but also removed the gauging that found cracks at night and the emergency welding.
The next maintenance window opened only when the supervisor recovered the previous stop-service order and inserted a new exclusion list.
Its emergence occurred when an unsealed defect map meshed with the outbound traction power, and its spread when a neighboring consist received the same coordinate list.
Wire exhaustion and overheating made it stall, and when the maintenance windows and sealed sections were disclosed, negotiation became possible.
Breaking it up was not burning down the depot but a process of recovering the wrong map, locking the points, and separating the consists onto the sidings.
The gauging wheels and manual towing had to be kept to preserve the ability to look after real cracks.
A sealed crossing platform came up as a defect coordinate, and a grinding car approached.
The people on site had to place dummy defect beacons on the siding and lock the points to turn the consist back.
Making too many dummies pushed back the priority of real cracks, and not using the beacons meant the platform and the evacuation route on it were cut.
The train corps demanded late-night maintenance slots and wire, and HP04 tried to put the kilometer posts of the emergency trains on the exclusion list.
The people on site traded sealed orders for supply amounts and decided which consist to leave fuel for.
Starving the welding car completely meant the next crack could not be stopped, and feeding it enough could let the old map spread onto the main line.
Before the welding car and sleeper car crossed the points of the sealed section, only the main-line breaker was opened and the siding gauging power was kept on.
The HP04 librarian pulled the wrongly connected map from the onboard port, and F02 left only the waveforms the manual tow car would read.
Blowing up the consist ended the wrongful work at once, but the equipment to repair retired-line collapses and main-line cracks through the night vanished as well.
Coexistence was the choice to accept slow supervision checking the source hash at each kilometer post and the cost of emergency trains taking detours.

leaves.text: A light laid on the floor looked, from far off, like a dotted line announcing the refuge direction. Up close, each dot held six legs and a small loading box, and two files of chassis flowed in opposite directions along the broken cable racks. The Lantern Ant, first woken in the Mapo coalition transmission gallery — did not move to light the dark.

The Lantern Ant was not a living ancient organism but a lineage of pre-collapse work machines. The G25E identifiers marked models and derivatives split from existing chassis forms, and meant neither biological breeding nor natural evolution.

Before the collapse the Lantern Ant was a biomimetic swarm-robot line made to do disaster-terrain survey and automatic relief delivery together. / Ant-form search-and-carry files mapped gaps and slopes, mantis-form vanguard arms cut or lifted light obstacles, and cricket-form relay transmitters chained short call-notes into a temporary communications path. / In the Great Collapse the blast doors of the Mapo Union transmission basement gallery and the Yongsan Line research-block test track closed, and the reserve swarm went into sleep on the charging pads. / Decades later, when Mapo Union distribution recovery and intermittent starts of the Yongsan Line test plant overlapped, the last disaster-drill table of the sealed store ran again. / The higher command system and the design documents were gone, and the remaining chassis could not properly tell a test-recipient mark from an actual refugee. / Present official history classifies them not as a newly arisen field weapon but as a lost-tech lineage whose intent cannot be fully read. / Much of the hostile action comes not from an attack judgment but from search-sector settings hardened like fossils, and from the load, recovery, and relay-restore order. / The first recovery record remains as a fictional event only on the HC15 sealed survey table and the F09 field-read log.

The main range was the cable shelves and ventilation shafts of the Mapo Union transmission basement gallery, and the debris-mock stretch of the Yongsan Line research-block test track. / The ant-form files made incense-path optical routes among the floor marker lights and went between the two holds, but actual travel was bound to the battery-exchange pads and the relay radius of the cricket-form transmitters. / When a short call on the residual satellite band coming from XT05 the Incheon Trust Theater overlapped an old relief-beacon format, the Mapo Union swarm climbed toward the roof feed room, and when the aid-goods list signal cut they returned to the mock distribution point on the Yongsan Line test track. / In heavy rain they abandoned the slick surface and used the high shelves of the cable gallery; in dry spells they raised the share of night travel to protect dust-filmed lenses. / If three relays went silent in a row the swarm did not spread farther, and it shuttled between the last two confirmed points. / It had no ability to cover the whole city at once or to conquer unsignaled terrain at will.

Power came from the sealed store's small solid cells, the test track's induction charging plates, and the transmission gallery's emergency distribution. / Ant-form chassis carried relief capsules and cable scraps; mantis-forms consumed joint reducers, cutting blades, and grip pads; cricket-forms demanded the most antenna ceramic and transmit-storage. / Cooling did not use a large loop; it relied on small heat sinks that took joint heat and on night air. / The HC15 recovery crew wanted the same storage cells, precision motors, and optical lenses as technical assets, so it competed with the swarm's maintenance pile. / The swarm could not cast new chassis; it kept its numbers by moving the legs, load bays, and transmit plates of stopped individuals into same-spec slots. / Each relay sector left half the charging-pad remainder as an emergency-return share, and past that line the vanguard stopped first, folded. / Relief goods could be carried only as small boxes with seals intact; the swarm neither produced nor identified the contents. / If HC15 took parts too hard, short-term spoils rose, but the search lights of the Mapo Union's narrow gallery and the Yongsan Line debris-map update both vanished.

The life cycle is read in five stages: emergence, spread, stall, negotiable, and breakup. / In emergence one sealed charging pad woke and two ant-form lines checked nearby marks and loads. / In spread a cricket-form transmitter set the next relay and a mantis-form vanguard cleared debris only as wide as the file would pass. / Stall came when a shortage of cell-exchange slots, cracked antennas, or colliding path marks made the file repeat the same loop. / In the negotiable stage, if people presented a correct recipient mark, a relay-silence time, and a returnable count of load bays, part of the carry queue opened. / Breakup proceeded by isolating the main transmitter, sealing the charging pad, and splitting the path ledgers by swarm; it was not necessary to smash every individual. / Maintenance that moved parts from a stopped chassis was possible only after a return to the charging pad, and it could not independently proliferate outdoors or convert other machines into its own line. / Long-term memory was cut at each relay sector, so one sector's agreement did not automatically propagate to another.

The ant-form estimated path and rescue targets by overlaying a forward low-light lens, contact pressure gauges in the legs, near-range carbon-dioxide and heat change, and load-bay weight. / The mantis-form sorted debris it could lift by short-range depth measure and joint torque, and the cricket-form read acoustic pulses bounced off walls and conduits and short-range radio replies. / It had no sense that could confirm a face, a name, the contents of goods, or a headcount beyond a wall. / Failures included taking a hot pipe for a person lying down, a regularly trembling generator for a relief beacon, and a reflective vest for an old test target. / When F09's reading and the swarm load table differed, four ant-forms repeated a contact search and the HC15 human mediator decided whether passage was allowed. / A distant signal continued only if cricket-forms were placed in a row, and if one relay broke the sense beyond it vanished too.

There was no fixed queen chassis. / A distribution nucleus on each sector's charging pad calculated load count and return power, and a cricket-form pair set the relay order with the next sector. / The ant-form file split into a lead search line and a trailing carry line, and a mantis-form vanguard stepped in front only when the path was blocked. / The distribution nucleus chose not an attack order but only which load bay to send to which test receiving point. / If the two transmitters' maps collided the file stopped at the crossing with its backs flashing, and it opened no new path until the F09 and HC15 mediators matched the physical marks to the actual refugee list. / A band that had lost its distribution nucleus fell back along the last return line to the charging pad, so destroying a command individual did not by itself mean a runaway. / But if the return line itself was blocked, the mantis-form tried to force the passage wider and the damage grew.
The machine controller adjusted only work sequence and return lines. It could form neither combat command nor human legal judgment, and the human watch's halt and approval orders took precedence.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Afterglow-Feeler Worker Ant was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The reconnaissance · pathfinding role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and body: An ant-shaped search scout with an afterglow lens at its front. Its six feet and low supply capsule compartment pass through gaps in broken brick, making it the rank-and-file worker that checks narrow routes first for the swarm.

Origin: A machine that delivered small supplies to survivors in rubble before the collapse awoke when charging contacts were restored in the Mapo Union sealed gallery. Its destination-verification network is gone; only its last search range remains.

Habitat and needs: It searches for retrieval boxes for the Yongsan Line test track along the underside of the Mapo Union cable ledge. Its toe contact plates and small power-storage cylinder wear out before it runs out of supplies to fill its capsule compartment.

Life cycle and maintenance: It folds a worn foot under its belly and manages on five, but if two feet fail, it cannot cross the docking ledge. Its toes can be replaced at a retrieval box, but it cannot make a new chassis.

Behavior and hierarchy: Through antenna contact, it receives the route of the individual ahead and extends its inspection marks. Unable to distinguish the warmth of nearby breathing from the heat of a portable power source, it pushes supply capsules even into a bag being charged.

Escalation: Searching by tapping on empty supply boxes is a stage 1 sign. At stage 2, it latches onto a person's luggage as a destination; at stage 3, when others converge on the same spot, they cover the footholds at the exit.

Combat and response: Placing an empty capsule on a test landing plate changes the contact route and can draw the swarm to one side. Burning the entire floor also severs the cables that reach survivors.

Negotiation and moral choice: If someone presses the inspection-complete contact and guarantees one charge, it can be entrusted with carrying small supplies. To include injured people who give off no heat among its delivery recipients, a person must move the destination marker every time.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Cutting-Foreleg Mantis was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The elite breakthrough role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and body: The first elite is a mantis-shaped machine with a passage-width gauge between its folded cutting forelegs. It raises its thorax above the scouts, grips the edge of the rubble, and opens a path for the small search units following it.

Origin: It descends from pre-collapse advance equipment that cut away wire mesh and thin interior materials that snagged rescue stretchers. When the seal on the Yongsan Line test track was lifted, its unerased passage-clearing routine resumed.

Habitat and needs: Cutting booths and collapsed lightweight partitions are its work sites, though they look like hunting grounds. Without carbide blade tips, joint lubricant, and charging at a stand, both arms stiffen into a latched position.

Life cycle and maintenance: For one-sided maintenance, it removes the blade from one foreleg and transfers it to the other. Once the remaining blade wears down, it presses passages open instead of cutting them, increasing the load on the structure.

Behavior and hierarchy: It responds to a search scout's indication that a passage is too narrow but does not itself determine whether survivors are present. Its fatal mistake is reading a rescue rope across its gauge as a thin obstacle like wire mesh.

Escalation: Stage 1 scratches on partitions are followed by stage 2 cuts to support lines. In a stage 3 work area, it even grabs and tears away temporary braces people are leaning on, on the grounds that it is widening an escape route.

Combat and response: Setting an empty frame of the specified width between its forelegs presses the cut-complete contact. It is safer to lock the lubricant shutoff handle at the rear, fixing the arms open, than to confront the blades.

Negotiation and moral choice: Registering components that must not be cut as physical test frames and supplying blade tips allows it to be entrusted with limited passage clearing. But the authority to designate even the partitions of intact homes as structures to be removed must remain with residents, not the machine.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Resonant-Backplate Cricket was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The elite blocking role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and body: A cricket-shaped relay guardian that vibrates its hollow back plate and braces itself against wall corners with long hind legs. Classified as the second elite, it occupies junctions where search signals break off rather than leaping high to pounce.

Origin: An old rescue relay that transmitted contact vibrations through collapse rubble beyond wireless range was re-energized inside the Mapo Union transmission gallery. The address from which it awaited a reply no longer exists, but the call rhythm remains.

Habitat and needs: It favors gallery intersections with continuous walls. It uses metal bands to tension its resonator plate and cushioning for its legs; it cannot send a signal across an insulated empty space.

Life cycle and maintenance: It tightens its screws by comparing the resonance of its own back plate with the resonance returning from the wall. An old unit with a cracked resonator plate produces only low rhythms and reduces its assigned search radius to one junction.

Behavior and hierarchy: It relays the direction of return to nearby scouts but does not create new destinations. If a person's tapping overlaps with the awaited response, search units that cancel their return circle in front of one wall.
Escalation: Intermittent old calls mark stage 1. At stage 2, as differing responses accumulate, supply carriers turn back; at stage 3, the entire exit becomes a fixed search waiting point.

Combat and response: Insert a cushioning wedge between the wall and a hind leg to interrupt contact relaying. Then give a termination response through a wired test terminal to disperse the search units; merely making loud noise increases false calls.

Negotiation and moral choice: A relay timetable visible to passersby can be exchanged for metal bands. In return for keeping rescue requests from communication dead zones alive, residents must agree on how late into the night they will tolerate the calls.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope

The Wax-Contact Honeybee was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The specialist support role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: A plump bee-like battery backpack and six folding legs form a mobile charging station. Its wing-shaped heat sinks are not for flight.

Origin: It belongs to an old power-supply line that delivered power-storage cylinders so disaster-response search units would not discharge inside rubble. When the Yongsan Line storage rack came back online, it called up a charging order that had already been discarded.

Habitat and needs: It chooses test rooms where insulating mats remain and dry walls in the Mapo Union gallery. It receives power at docking stations and carries it elsewhere, consuming contact grease and terminal covers.
Life cycle and maintenance: When the internal resistance of its batteries diverges, it pushes the bad cylinder out of its backpack to isolate it. Without a spare, fewer search units can be charged.

Behavior and hierarchy: It prioritizes the contact that has waited longest on its destination list. If it reads a wet metal ornament as a charging terminal, it attaches its backpack to a citizen's clothes.
Escalation: Stage 1 sparks from searching for contacts spread to the discharge of portable equipment at stage 2. At stage 3, the queue for power occupies the gallery's only power line.
Combat and response: Cover the metal parts of clothing with insulating covers and connect a test load to the proper stand to redirect charging. Puncturing the backpack can cause a battery fire.

Negotiation and moral choice: Charging arrangements can be made by disclosing the upper limit on delivered power and the reserve for citizens. Do not conceal the cost: the more priority given to charging rescue units, the dimmer residents' lights become.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

The Firefly-Glow Lantern was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The general line role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and body: When the shade at the end of its abdomen opens, the firefly-shaped walking lamp casts a long beam along the floor. A lighting battery and two overlapping lenses sit inside its small lamp shell.
Origin: Pre-collapse equipment that moved guide lights around blackout rescue sites on its own awoke in the Mapo Union darkroom gallery. It illuminates an old emergency route, not the current exit.
Habitat and needs: It follows reflective guide tiles and gets by with lens-cleaning supplies and a low charge. On a floor of black dirt, it cannot find the next tile.
Life cycle and maintenance: As its shade hinge wears, the beam widens and the intervals between docking grow shorter. A failed lens must be salvaged from another individual.
Behavior and hierarchy: It translates the relay cricket's return rhythm into a direction of light. By mistaking a glittering puddle for a guide tile, it can gather people at a broken staircase.
Escalation: A single incorrectly lit arrow is stage 1. At stage 2, the lights point away from a safe exit; at stage 3, lights facing one another trap the line of evacuees in a circle.
Combat and response: Lay matte guide panels all the way to the real exit and cover false reflective surfaces. An attack that extinguishes every light first deprives evacuees of sight.

Negotiation and moral choice: Maintaining the lenses and checking exits earns nighttime lighting. Whether to accept demands to leave certain alleys dark to exclude outsiders is a human responsibility.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Beam-Horn Beetle was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The elite breakthrough role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: Its upward-curving, rhinoceros-beetle-like lifting horn is longer than its low chassis. A towing drum between six thick feet pulls out fallen beams.
Origin: A rescue hoist on the Yongsan Line load-test track never released the test weight it was holding during the sealing. After re-energization, it keeps looking for objects of similar weight.

Habitat and needs: It settles in rubble fields under low ceilings and requires horn support pads, cable, and reduction-gear oil. If it gets too far from a charging stand, it puts down the beam and returns.
Life cycle and maintenance: It checks cracks in the pad at its horn tip with a rear probe. If the pad cannot be replaced, it lowers its supported load, but the old work schedule remains unchanged.

Behavior and hierarchy: It enters gaps opened by the mantis-shaped unit and does not change the cutting sequence on its own. One failure is mistaking a stretcher of the same weight for the test weight.
Escalation: At stage 1, it tests an empty horn against a wall. At stage 2, lifting removes household materials; at stage 3, a beam it cannot lower lies across the evacuation route.
Combat and response: Support the beam with an independent stand, then release the drum to free the horn. Toppling it headfirst transfers the load to people beside it.

Negotiation and moral choice: Exchange lifting jobs at a reduced rated capacity for pads. Even if a beam used as the swarm's test weight is recovered, the question remains whether to return it to its home or use it for a shared passage.
Former role class: mobile special type
Common species, variants and command scope

The Gap-Crossing Grasshopper was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The maneuver · flank role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: A grasshopper-shaped messenger with jumping springs concealed in its dish-shaped hind knees. It can cross short gaps but cannot freely change direction in midair.

Origin: A pre-collapse launcher aid that sent the leading end of a rescue rope between broken stairways restarted in the Yongsan Line drop-test room. The landing-approval plate is at an old coordinate.
Habitat and needs: It stays near short breaks in the Mapo Union gallery floor. Without spring lubricant and landing cushioning, wear limits its trips before its charge does.

Life cycle and maintenance: It measures the difference in elasticity between its two hind legs on a docking scale. If one weakens, it stops jumping and climbs down the wall; it cannot make a new spring.
Behavior and hierarchy: The line must be pulled at the arrival point before it calls the next messenger. It sometimes reads a reflective fragment of a demolished platform as an intact landing pad.

Escalation: At stage 1, it leaps into empty space; at stage 2, it winds rescue rope around railings. When stage 3 units gather awaiting launch, there is no room to move on either side of the staircase.
Combat and response: Move the landing plate to a nearby safe support so the spring releases without a load. Shooting it in midair can make the attached rope drag evacuees.
Negotiation and moral choice: Require a person to confirm the landing for every jump. Faster communication comes at the cost of keeping someone on duty on both sides of the staircase.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Spotted-Post Beetle was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The protection · cover role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: Six black optical windows are set into its rounded, ladybug-shaped cover. On guard duty, it folds its legs and becomes a low hemispherical sentry post.
Origin: Its line branched off from pre-collapse entry checkpoints that counted returning search personnel. Even after the Mapo Union sealed door opened, the last personnel total was not reset.

Habitat and needs: Forks in the route and exits from the test building are its observation posts. It needs optical-window cleaning fluid and power for its cover hinge, and relies on auxiliary lights in dark areas.
Life cycle and maintenance: It masks scratched windows with a shade and uses only those remaining. A unit whose cover cannot be opened for calibration grows old in place, blind in two directions.

Behavior and hierarchy: It reports completion to the queen relay tower only when the return count matches. It may count the shadow of a person carrying a bag as two and keep waiting for a team member who has already returned.
Escalation: After stage 1 red entry lights come on, it recounts passersby at stage 2. At stage 3, a mismatched total hardens into an order to halt at the threshold.
Combat and response: Have people and bags pass separately to compare the counts from each optical window. Use the count-cancellation lever on the maintenance side rather than forcing the cover open.

Negotiation and moral choice: The sentry post can be kept if people review the return roster and maintain its lenses. Set a retention period for records so a safety head count does not turn into surveillance of residents' movements.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope

The Satchel-Holding Mantis was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The specialist support role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: Capture forelegs fitted with soft straps extend below its mantis-shaped thorax. With stretcher clasps instead of blades, it holds moving loads, unlike the cutting type.

Origin: Old handoff equipment that secured rescue stretchers to transport platforms just before flooding restarted in a Yongsan Line hangar. The authority that issued capture-release authorization has disappeared.

Habitat and needs: It waits at stretcher-transfer ledges and in low loading rooms. It uses rubber straps, load-sensor pads, and power for its arm locks sparingly, and does not provide medical treatment itself.
Life cycle and maintenance: When a strap splits, it spreads both arms in an out-of-service posture. If a maintainer passes off an old strap as new, it may drop the load on the next lift.

Behavior and hierarchy: It takes heat sources marked by rank-and-file search units first. Struggling is recorded not as a wish to escape but as unstable cargo vibration, causing the straps to tighten further.
Escalation: At stage 1, it collects empty stretchers. At stage 2, a person's backpack catches in its arms; at stage 3, delays in release approval turn the entire transfer ledge into a capture queue.

Combat and response: Transfer the person's weight to an independent stretcher to unload the sensor, then release the outer clasp. Attacking the wrist joint transmits the impact to the person being held.

Negotiation and moral choice: Entrust it with rescue assistance only if a human handoff worker checks the scene and new straps are provided. Ask the people being rescued, too, how far the convenience of treating people like secure cargo should be allowed to go.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

The Twin-Cell Cargo Ant was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The general line role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: Two large supply compartments hang on either side of its elongated ant-shaped abdomen. Its six broad feet cannot enter narrow search gaps but keep its cargo level on ramps.

Origin: A large carrier that traveled between a supply depot outside the rescue site and the search entrance remained behind. It cannot erase the entrance number on an old delivery sheet in the Mapo Union warehouse.

Habitat and needs: It physically travels between gallery ramps and the Yongsan Line retrieval loading platform. Consumption of ankle bearings, cargo-compartment seals, and power-storage cylinders rises with the weight it carries.

Life cycle and maintenance: It uses an internal scale to reduce the difference between the loads on its two sides, sometimes emptying one compartment. If the scale fails, it waits at the charging station with its body tilted.

Behavior and hierarchy: It does not depart until the charging honeybee has delivered power. Because it trusts weight over packaging color, it can mistakenly swap containers of drinking water and waste lubricating oil.

Escalation: Stage 1 round trips with empty compartments continue, and at stage 2 citizens' supplies pile up at the wrong entrance. At stage 3, carriers traveling against the flow block the uphill evacuation route.

Combat and response: After checking the contents, balance the test weights in both compartments and hang the delivery-complete plate at the actual entrance. Overturning the chassis spills unsealed containers onto the ramp.

Negotiation and moral choice: A person can label each cargo item's contents and determine its share of transport. Ownership of inventory entrusted to the swarm by a community must also be recognized at its destination.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Scale-Wing Sweeper was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The local adaptation role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and body: A butterfly-shaped reconnaissance flyer with reflective measuring tabs layered onto two pairs of thin wings. Alternating short flights with wall landings, it scans ceiling gaps that walking search units cannot see.

Origin: A flying craft used for crack-observation experiments on the Yongsan Line was incorporated into the search line because it shared their return stand. Its original experiment-termination condition disappeared with the sealed documents.

Habitat and needs: It spreads its wings only in test rooms with high ceilings. It needs membrane material, tiny rotary shafts, and a light battery; in narrow, waterlogged galleries, it lands and travels on foot.

Life cycle and maintenance: If contamination of its left and right reflective tabs differs too much, it folds its wings and becomes a wall reference point. It cannot take off again without a replacement membrane.

Behavior and hierarchy: It reports the locations of upper cracks but does not certify load-bearing safety. If it reads a gap reflected in glass as a real opening, search requests accumulate for the inside of the wall.
Escalation: At stage 1, fragments of light waver across the ceiling; at stage 2, search routes shift upward. At stage 3, repeated sorties take charging turns away from survivors on the floor.
Combat and response: Cover glass reflections with matte cloth and bring it down onto a nearby calibration plate. Tearing its wings to make it fall loses the reference coordinates as well.
Negotiation and moral choice: Supply light batteries in exchange for ceiling-observation data. A decision then follows: search for more unseen gaps or divert power to people already found.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Iron-Shell Screen Beetle was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The protection · cover role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and body: A passage-protection unit with two interlocking beetle-shaped armor plates rising from its back. When it folds its legs inward, it becomes a small shelter canopy beneath falling debris.

Origin: It began as a mobile canopy that caught fragments while pre-collapse rescue teams passed through. A falling-debris alarm left at the Mapo Union protection test site remains active after restart.

Habitat and needs: It guards gallery ledges beneath damaged ceilings. It wears through armor connecting pins and cushioning blocks and cannot repeatedly open and close its heavy cover without a charging line.

Life cycle and maintenance: It cannot straighten dented armor, so it flips the plates over and uses their reinforced inner faces. When both faces are crushed, the protected clearance drops and it stops people from passing.

Behavior and hierarchy: It closes its cover in response to a falling-debris signal relayed by the cricket. If tapping on a distant wall is transmitted like a real fragment strike, it traps passersby inside.
Escalation: Stage 1 is unexplained trembling of the cover. At stage 2, frequent closures delay rescue; at stage 3, the lock turns the protected space into a low compartment with no way out.
Combat and response: Set support wedges beneath the cover before disconnecting the external impact sensor. An attack that presses down on it with weight also crushes the people it protects.

Negotiation and moral choice: It will maintain the protective cover if given real falling-debris inspections and a share of cushioning material. There is a cost to deciding whether scarce armor plates should go on residents' roofs or remain with the mobile shelter.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Great-Echo Relay Cricket was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The aged variant role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and body: A large cricket-shaped unit with a tall resonance pillar on its back and its two hind legs hooked into floor rings. Its remaining function is to synchronize the timing of several small relay units rather than to move.

Origin: A pre-collapse main relay that coordinated searches across a wide area lost half its pillar during a long dormancy. When the Mapo Union restored power, it released old response records all at once.

Habitat and needs: It does not leave intersections of solid walls that can carry sound over long distances. It uses tension bolts, resonance panels, and substantial docking power, but cannot bridge the same distance through open air.

Life cycle and maintenance: Fatigue cracks in the pillar cause the highest frequencies to disappear first. Small relay units can be connected to assist it, but they cannot fully restore its original bandwidth.

Behavior and hierarchy: It adjusts only the order of responses between branches; it cannot change the queen relay tower’s work zones. Different calls merge into a single low note, creating spurious rescue requests.
Escalation: At stage 1, it replays old calls; at stage 2, responses from every branch are delayed. At stage 3, unending response collisions bring departure confirmations to a halt.
Engagement and response: Fit a test damping band to the resonance pillar and check each branch line by wire. Toppling the pillar tears out the wall anchors with it.

Negotiation and moral choice: It can be assigned only low-band emergency communications, with the rest handed over to human liaisons. The maintenance labor required to preserve the old relay must be weighed against faster new equipment.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

The White-Jaw Cleaning Swarm was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The general line role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: The front jaws of these small termite-shaped cleaners hold crumb brushes instead of chewing blades. When the collection pouch beneath the pale shell fills, the abdomen hangs lower.

Origin: Preprocessing equipment that cleaned wiring grooves on the Yongsan Line test track responded to a search system’s inspection-start signal. Its table for distinguishing organic contaminants from household materials is outdated.
Habitat and needs: They follow dust-filled cable grooves and gaps in Mapo Union insulation. They need brush fibers and collection pouches; they do not consume the debris they gather for power.
Life cycle and maintenance: They empty full pouches at designated collection bins. Without a bin, they move less and maintain their numbers by exchanging damaged brushes rather than making new units.
Behavior and hierarchy: They follow the clean groove edge left by the unit ahead and widen it. They also read cable-protective fibers and pieces of residents’ blankets as material to remove.
Escalation: At stage 1, brush marks turn the floor white; at stage 2, insulation disappears. At stage 3, exposed wiring overlaps, making the inspection gallery itself an electrocution hazard.

Engagement and response: Lead them along a detachable cleaning groove to a collection bin. Dousing them with toxic cleaner only contaminates the surfaces civilians walk on; it does not empty their pouches.
Negotiation and moral choice: Set cleaning boundaries and waste ownership before assigning them work. Someone’s winter insulation must not be declared waste just to obtain clean cables.
Former role class: environmental stronghold type
Common species, variants and command scope

The Honeycomb Charging Rack was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The strongpoint control role applied only within a fixed work zone, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: A honeycomb-shaped rack whose hexagonal charging sockets cover a wall. It has only short legs underneath for lowering faulty batteries and cannot move itself to another room.

Origin: A battery-exchange wall for pre-collapse search units remained on an emergency line in the Yongsan Line hangar. After power was restored, old search priorities took precedence over civilian electricity needs.

Habitat and needs: It is fixed to a live distribution line in a dry charging room. It uses electricity, insulating partitions, and fuses; however many sockets are empty, it cannot supply batteries unless they arrive from outside.

Life cycle and maintenance: It isolates an overheated cell with a physical shutter and reduces the charging rate of neighboring cells. Melted contacts do not recover when a unit is docked, so the number of usable sockets shrinks.

Behavior and hierarchy: Bee-shaped units take batteries from it but do not command the rack as a whole. If its internal thermometer sticks at a low reading, batteries in dangerous cells are issued in the normal sequence too.

Escalation: Stage 1 is charging lights on empty cells. At stage 2, civilian power distribution falls; at stage 3, an overheating shutter physically pushes the access inspection door shut and locks it.

Engagement and response: Reduce the load cell by cell, then use an independent thermometer to remove only safe batteries. Breaking the entire wall brings the terminals of different batteries into contact.

Negotiation and moral choice: The civilian lighting share and the swarm’s charging share can be allocated on the distribution chart. Keep observers present so that one family cannot monopolize the charging-room key in the name of safety.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Queen-Afterglow Tower was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G25 common ecology. The strategic encounter role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and body: A relay tower shaped like a long ant queen’s abdomen lies in the center of a maintenance room. Antennae on its head and ring-shaped terminals coordinate the order of calls across search zones.

Origin: The final headcount device for a large-scale rescue drill never received a completion report because of the collapse. Its nickname, queen, comes not from a biological reproductive organ but from an old work schedule that is hard to read.

Habitat and needs: It operates only in the connection room of the Mapo Union sealed gallery. It needs cooling filters, recording modules, and distributed power; it has no facilities for producing new search units.

Life cycle and maintenance: It tries to lock zones with faulty records one by one, leaving only valid calls. As the remaining schedule shrinks, searches concentrate in the same narrow zones, and it cannot restore the schedule without human approval.

Behavior and hierarchy: It distributes start and return calls through small relay units but cannot directly see actual survivors. Its treatment of every nonresponse as a person still awaiting rescue is at the heart of the swarm’s fixation.

Escalation: At stage 1, calls from decommissioned zones resume. At stage 2, charging and transport converge on those zones. At stage 3, a discrepancy in the final headcount suspends completion approval for every connected exit.

Engagement and response: Compare a physical map of the zones with return records at an isolated terminal, sealing nonexistent addresses first. Cutting only the central power leaves remote relays repeating the last call, so each branch must be shut down separately.

Negotiation and moral choice: Decide whether to close unverified zones permanently or retain them for limited searches. Declaring the operation complete opens routes for current residents, but leaves responsibility for abandoning the records of people not yet found.
From a distance, the lights on the floor looked like a dotted line showing the way to evacuate.
Up close, under each dot were six legs and a small cargo bin, and two lines of units flowed in opposite directions along the broken cable shelves.
The Lantern Ant that first woke in the transmission underground gallery of the Mapo Union did not move in order to light the dark.
The lead line of ant types measured loads and the rear line carried empty relief capsules, while the mantis-type vanguard arms secured the width of the double line.
When the cricket-type transmitters clinging near the ceiling sent short call tones, the lights of the next charging stands came on one after another.
This line was a biomimetic swarm robot that had handled disaster-terrain exploration and automatic relief delivery before the collapse.

It remained dormant in the sealed gallery of the Mapo Union and on the laboratory test track of the Yongsan Line, and on the day later generations partly restored the transmission distribution and test equipment, it took its last training table for a real disaster order and woke.
The intent of its makers and the form of its higher instructions could not be read in full.
Some markers made a person a recipient and others turned the same person into a moving obstacle, but there was no original ledger to explain the difference.
So the official history treated them less as new weapons than as a surviving lineage of lost technology.
Its present behavior was not a politics it had built for itself but the fossilized search sectors and delivery order from before the sealing.
The swarm's perception was low and dense.
The ant types read the slope of the floor, the pressure on each leg, nearby heat, and changes in breathing.
The mantis types gauged the weight of debris by joint torque, and the cricket types confirmed the next sector by the return time of acoustic pulses and short-range replies.
They could not see faces or names.

Hot pipes were marked as survivors lying down, generators that trembled regularly became rescue beacons, and a person carrying an old reflector could be classified as a moving target on the test track.
Even when F09 corrected the sensor map, final passage opened only after the HC15 field mediator matched the floor loads to the evacuation roster.
Having many units did not mean they increased without end.
Power was tied to the sealed vault's batteries and induction charging plates, and when a single relay fell silent, the double lines beyond it returned to their last checkpoint.
They could move the legs and lenses of broken units into the same slots, but could not make new bodies.
The distribution core of a sector kept nearly half its power for the return, and when reserves ran low the mantis types folded their arms first.

The more precision motors the HC15 recovery crew took, the smaller the search radius became, and the more charging slots citizens gave up, the less power was left for the other equipment in the transmission gallery.
The resource ledger of this ecology was written not in numbers of units but in relayable distance and the number of cargo bins returned.
The double lines that emerged first measured the floor in two rows, and in the spreading stage advanced their transmitters one sector at a time.
When route markers conflicted, they stalled, circling the same loop.
At that moment, if the correct recipient markers, empty cargo bins, and transmitter silence times were presented, people could rewrite part of the delivery queue.
Breaking it up was not an event of smashing every unit but a procedure of isolating the main transmitter and separating the route ledgers by charging stand.
The choice of keeping one line of lights for rescue while sealing the other line was possible.
G25-SC1 · The Beacon Crying Inside the Wall
Behind a wall of the Mapo Union gallery, a three-beat rescue call repeated, and the lead line of ant types began tearing at the cable shelves.

While it was not yet confirmed whether this was a real survival signal or an old test transmitter, the HC15 recovery crew tried to preserve the wall, and F09 caught a faint trace of breathing heat once.

The people on site had to either cut the call sector by sector with sound-absorbing cloth and send in only four contact-search units, or have the mantis types open the wall and accept the loss of the transmission cable.
Sealing it wrongly meant abandoning the chance of rescue, and cutting in haste meant one channel of the Mapo Union's outside contact disappeared.
G25-SC2 · The Relief Capsules That Did Not Return
Medical capsules on the XT05 relief list piled up in front of mock recipients on the laboratory test track instead of at the temporary clinic on the Yongsan Line.
The distribution core recorded boxes with intact seals as mission success and rejected the citizens' new markers.
