The people on site could offer HC15's antenna plates in exchange and get a new delivery table approved for just one shift, recover the existing cargo bins and carry them by hand, or physically move the test receiving point close to the clinic.
The first choice used up lost-technology parts, the second delayed the arrival of the injured, and the third made the swarm patrol the clinic zone from then on as if it were its own test ground.
G25-SC3 · Two Lines of Lockdown Lights
At the underground junction linking the Mapo Union and the Yongsan Line, three cricket-type units gave off different return tones, and the double lines tangled into a ring.
The mantis-type vanguards tore out railings and barrier doors to turn the loop into a passage, and trapped citizens could not get out of the circle of light.
The people on site had to create precise silent intervals between the transmitters and send the lines back to the charging stands one at a time.

Destroying the main transmitter made an opening at once, but the small units that lost their bearings scattered into the cable layers, and cutting all power stopped the transmission and the laboratory safety monitoring as well.

The ending that kept one double line for rescue preserved the ability to search for survivors in narrow debris zones, at the price of carrying slow inspection and charge allocation throughout the campaign.

G26.selector: p, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, blockquote, pre, li, th, td

leaves.text: The dead siding of the Gangnam Line's Changdong depot hummed first, and a few seconds later a metal knee slowly unfolded from deep inside the maintenance shed. Even after the dust settled, the bipedal heavy walker did not walk straight off. It pressed the floor with the pressure grid of its soles, lowered the counterweight behind its body, and proclaimed its work radius with three low-frequency roars.

The Iron Dinosaur was not a living ancient organism but a lineage of pre-collapse work machines. The G26E identifiers marked machine types and derivatives split from existing chassis forms, and meant neither biological breeding nor natural evolution.

The Iron Dinosaur belonged to a biomimetic line of pre-collapse heavy-equipment mobile platforms that applied the load distribution and posture control of ancient reptiles. / Bipedal, semi-upright heavy units crossed tall debris while carrying reinforcement materials; low, wide, triangular towing-and-shield units pulled heavy equipment or sheltered workers from falling objects; and long-winged fixed-wing surveillance craft marked ground conditions and passage widths from above. / On the last day of the disaster, fully equipped units were sealed in a standby-for-work posture when the siding maintenance shed at Gangnam Line's Chang-dong depot and the protective hangar at Gwangjin Line's Godeok base closed. / Long afterward, braking-test power on the Gangnam Line and an automatic inspection terminal at the Gwangjin Line base came back to life at different times, and the units resumed an unfinished debris-removal process. / Most of the original design drawings and approval system can no longer be read; all that remains of their behavior are partial routines such as axle-load tables, towing priorities, and safety radii. / In Seoul canon, they are a lineage of Lost Technology heavy-work units, not combat machines built by any present-day faction. / The low-frequency alarm that sounds like a roar, and the charge that follows it, express no will to conquer: they are the fossilized result of a procedure for securing a work zone. / The account that the HC17 siding recovery team and an F10 load reader recorded the first reactivation is likewise confined to a fictional event.

The Iron Dinosaur is centered on the siding at Gangnam Line's Chang-dong depot and the broad maintenance roads and protective hangars at Gwangjin Line's Godeok base. / Semi-upright heavy units move only along corridors whose rail spacing and floor bearing capacity have been verified, while triangular towing units favor storage yards and bridge approaches with room to turn around. / Long-winged surveillance craft take off only when a short runway or towing launcher is available, then scan collapse lines and hot spots between the two bases. / When heavy mineral freight cars or winter fuel arrive from the XT04 Tumen River–Far East Theater, axle loads resembling those on old materials-receipt sheets are detected and activity on the Gangnam Line siding increases. On the Gwangjin Line, the units try to incorporate eastern bridges and the approach to Godeok base into a new work zone. / During the spring thaw they avoid sidings with weak ground; in severe cold, increased hydraulic viscosity shortens their operating range. / Large units cannot sustain entry into narrow unpaved alleys, basements with unverified load capacity, or dense areas beyond the long-winged craft's line of observation.

Their main energy sources are power from maintenance-shed towing batteries, power recovered through regenerative braking, and limited auxiliary generation using liquid fuel. / Semi-upright heavy units need hydraulic fluid, knee bearings, and foot cushioning plates; triangular towing units need cables, winch gears, and shield-plate fastening pins; long-winged surveillance craft need lightweight wing materials and optical modules. / Coolant and hydraulic fluid cannot substitute for each other, and preheating in winter consumes more power than it does in normal conditions. / HC17 wants the equipment's towing power to open heavy-convoy routes, but the equipment consumes the same rail steel and fuel drums as repair resources. / Complete power cores cannot be made anew, and combining two damaged units does not raise their power rating. / Each work detachment reserves the hydraulic pressure and braking power needed to return. Below that threshold, its heaviest semi-upright unit locks its knees first and waits. / A long-winged craft can make only a short reconnaissance flight on one battery; it cannot maintain continuous aerial surveillance. / The size of this group is therefore limited not by fuel, but by intact joints, towing cables, and the area of floor able to bear its loads.

Its operational life is divided into five phases: emergence, expansion, stagnation, negotiation, and disintegration. / During emergence, the hydraulics in one hangar bay are charged and a long-winged craft sweeps over the siding once. / During expansion, triangular towing units drag old obstacles out of the work line, and semi-upright heavy units drive in new load markers to enlarge the zone. / Stagnation is the state in which a detachment pushes the same debris forward and pulls it back because of insufficient ground bearing capacity, hydraulic leaks, worn towing cables, or discrepancies in its aerial map. / During the negotiation phase, humans can delegate some heavy work if they provide an accurate load table, permitted work boundaries, and a list of reinforcement materials to be returned. / Disintegration proceeds in order: cool the power core, fasten the knee-locking pins, disconnect the towing cables, and recover the long-winged craft. / There is no factory to produce more units, and even maintaining their numbers is difficult without maintenance-shed cranes and standardized parts. / Work records are separate for each detachment, so a stop order at one base does not automatically apply at the other.

Semi-upright heavy units read foot-pressure grids, joint torque, low-frequency structural vibrations, and nearby heat sources. / Triangular towing units calculate whether they can tow something from winch tension, floor slope, and short-range measurements in front of their chassis. / Long-winged surveillance craft use visible-light and thermal imagery and ground markers, but misjudge height and scale amid smoke, snow, and the remains of tall buildings. / They cannot directly determine a building's purpose, a person's affiliation, the contents of a freight car, or the condition of underground pipes. / They may mistake a stationary armored vehicle for a bundle of reinforcement materials, an evacuation tent for a falling-object barrier, or vibrations from a crowd for unstable debris. / When F10's load model and a unit's assessment disagree, an HC17 rescue technician places a test weight to check the actual deflection before issuing a movement order. / If a long-winged craft is shot down or cannot return because of the weather, the ground detachment also stops incorporating new zones.

Detachments operate through three functional layers that share a table of work authorizations, not through a central command unit called a Roar Core. / A long-winged surveillance craft draws a work polygon, a triangular towing unit establishes entry and retreat routes, and a semi-upright heavy unit enters last to perform the heavy work. / The semi-upright unit with the most stable joints in each detachment serves as the load-reference unit, but it has no authority to punish or sacrifice other units. / If two triangular units choose different towing points, they release their winches, sound an alarm, and stop. / F10 must then compare the tension readings, and an HC17 human supervisor must physically reset the reference point before work can continue. / If the reference unit falls, the detachment does not appoint a larger unit; it retreats beyond the last safety line. / When the long-winged craft's map conflicts with ground-pressure readings, a ground load test takes precedence.
The machine controller adjusted only work sequence and return lines. It could form neither combat command nor human legal judgment, and the human watch's halt and approval orders took precedence.
G26E13 · Gate Horned Great Tow Dragon
Common species, variants and command scope

The Load-Jaw Strider was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The reconnaissance · pathfinding role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and body: A bipedal heavy-duty vanguard whose two thick legs and rearward counterweight give it a dinosaur-like outline. Its jaw-shaped load clamp lifts debris a little at a time to make room for the towing equipment that follows.

Origin: A pre-collapse structural-repair advance unit was secured in the Gangnam Line depot maintenance shed. When inspection power returned, it resumed the support checks interrupted at the time of the collapse.

Habitat and needs: It picks its footing along undercarriage work lines and the edges of subsided concrete. Its high-output battery pack is finite; without knee hydraulic seals and sole load pads, it cannot stand.

Life cycle and maintenance: Before departure, it hooks its tail counterweight to a maintenance support and measures knee leakage. Joints that exceed the limit lock, so an old unit drags one foot rather than venture beyond the work line.

Behavior and hierarchy: It passes only sections with confirmed floor bearing capacity to the towing units behind it. If it misses a void beneath a thin work platform, a platform it has judged safe can collapse with people on it.

Escalation: At stage 1, test footfalls repeat; at stage 2, temporary platforms lift. At stage 3, its large legs and counterweight block a narrow work line where load testing has begun, splitting the evacuation column.

Engagement and response: Have it rest its clamp on the depot’s independent load-test stand, then secure its knees with maintenance latches. Blowing out an ankle sends the toppling counterweight into the rescue crew behind it, so merely knocking it down is not a victory.

Negotiation and moral choice: Given a human-verified bearing-capacity chart and a share of charging power, it can help lift debris. Patient-transport carts need the same power used for a single heavy lift, so record which rescue takes priority in the ledger.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Triangular-Yoke Tractor was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The elite breakthrough role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and body: A four-legged towing unit with a triangular yoke projecting ahead of its head; the three horn-like anchor points and broad neck shield resemble a large ancient reptile. This first elite unit’s task is not to pursue enemies but to tow heavy frames continuously.

Origin: Three-point fastening equipment used to transport reinforcement before the collapse was released from a long-term seal on a Gwangjin Line depot siding. The building at its destination is gone, but a transport-completion signal was never entered.

Habitat and needs: It stays in siding loading yards with enough room to turn its neck shield. It must actually be supplied with wire drums, towing pins, and gear oil, and the heavier its load, the more often it returns to a charging support.

Life cycle and maintenance: If the three towlines have different tensions, it winds in the slackest first to equalize them. A unit with broken drum teeth is downgraded to light work using two lines; a person must install a new drum to restore its rated capacity.

Behavior and hierarchy: It carries frames according to the bearing-capacity chart left by the lead walker. It treats everything attached to its three rings as the same cargo, so even when a resident’s awning post is caught, it cannot read the ownership mark.

Escalation: A test pull on the anchor points is the stage 1 warning. At stage 2, posts in living quarters are dragged toward the siding; stage 3 begins when the three lines block the passage so no one can approach.
Engagement and response: First take the cargo’s weight on auxiliary supports, then apply the drum’s maintenance brake. Cutting a taut wire first whips its freed end across at head height.

Negotiation and moral choice: Inserting a completion pin in the destination support can end one transport contract. A decision must be made whether to keep the recovered reinforcement for the next rescue job or return it to residents whose materials were taken; stopping the unit does not settle the ownership dispute.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Long-Wing Crack Watcher was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The elite blocking role applied only at the swarm-consist scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and body: A second elite monitor with rangefinders beneath long, outstretched pterosaur-like wings. The wings serve as both lifting surfaces and measurement baselines; after hovering briefly, it perches on a high maintenance stand and reports crack locations to the heavy units on the ground.

Origin: A pre-collapse aerial surveying line that inspected Gangnam Line roof trusses and Gwangjin Line siding reinforcements survived. Once granted access to its sealed maintenance stand, it resumed surveying against the outline of a roof that had already been removed.

Habitat and needs: Its operating area is the upper part of a depot, where air flows and it can spread both wings. It uses propulsion power and wing tension lines and needs a clean rangefinder window; it cannot fly into narrow underground conduits.

Life cycle and maintenance: Each time it lands, it aligns its left and right wingtips with reference grooves on the support. If one wingtip fails to reach its groove, it stops flying and performs only fixed-position monitoring, leaving broad blind spots in the damaged unit’s observations.

Behavior and hierarchy: It does not directly command towing direction; it marks hazardous load zones. If it mistakes rainwater reflections or hanging tarps for cracks, the heavy units clear work crews even from beneath sound roofs.

Escalation: Surveying light cast on the wrong place signals stage 1. At stage 2, the repair queue shifts to empty zones; at stage 3, overlapping hazard markings cause every route across the depot to be treated as a no-load zone.

Engagement and response: Set up a frame measured on site beside the maintenance stand and clean the rangefinder window to expose the error. Shooting it down in flight drops its wings and battery onto the work line, so capture using the landing latch is preferable.

Negotiation and moral choice: Trade survey commissions for each inspection section for wing-repair parts. Adopting a new reference allows the old hazard map to be discarded, but also exposes roof routes residents have kept hidden, making protection of their evacuation routes a separate issue.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Ankylosaur Rockfall Catcher was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The protection · cover role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: A shield unit whose overlapping, ankylosaur-like back plates unfold like a roof. Four short legs and a shock-absorbing tail behind it disperse impacts from the side.

Origin: An old heavy protective unit that sheltered rescue crews from falling rocks on the Gangnam Line rockfall test line restarted. The ceiling sensor that sent the all-clear signal is already gone.

Habitat and needs: Beneath broken maintenance-shed roofs, it uses armor cushioning and hydraulic fluid for its legs. When docking-battery power runs low, it folds its tail and remains as a stationary barrier.

Life cycle and maintenance: It stores the number of impacts each back plate has taken and rotates the plate closest to its limit inward. If supplies of new plates stop, the area it can protect shrinks too.
Behavior and hierarchy: Trusting the long-wing monitor’s hazard markings, it puts itself in front of people. A false crack marking can cause it to cover and block a perfectly sound doorway.
Escalation: Stage 1 is deploying its shield beneath an empty roof. At stage 2, rescue columns take detours; at stage 3, neighboring protective units’ back plates interlock and seal off the work line.
Engagement and response: Support the overhead load with independent props, then release the back-plate locks one by one. Striking the tail to turn it may knock over a prop beside it.

Negotiation and moral choice: Agreeing that it will protect only fall zones confirmed by direct measurement yields a safe passage. This creates the burden of dividing recovered armor between residential roofs and mechanical shields.
Former role class: mobile special type
Common species, variants and command scope

The Light-Leg Courier Lizard was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The maneuver · flank role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: A small, speed-oriented theropod-shaped unit with long, slender shins exposed. Its balancing tail and low pack let it run quickly between rails, but it cannot lift heavy loads.

Origin: A courier line that carried urgent parts between pre-collapse heavy work crews awoke at a Gwangjin Line siding charging station. The crews’ old stopping locations remained unchanged in its records.
Habitat and needs: It chooses straight service roads and gaps between empty sleepers. It needs ankle cushioning pads and a small high-output battery; every sharp turn shortens the pads’ service life.
Life cycle and maintenance: If its stride length increases, a speed limiter stops it from running. An old unit whose joints cannot be replaced makes deliveries by walking the same route slowly.
Behavior and hierarchy: It carries towing units’ parts requests but cannot read why they are urgent. Mistaking cloth waved by hand for an old stopping flag, it brakes abruptly among civilians.

Escalation: At stage 1, the sound of sprinting recurs; at stage 2, a route forms that people crossing must avoid. At stage 3, overlapping stops and restarts turn the parts-transport line into a collision zone.
Engagement and response: Put an official stop sign at the end of an empty straight track to slow it. Tripping it sends the parts in its pack flying at head height.

Negotiation and moral choice: Separate delivery time windows from people’s crossing times. Assigning the fastest unit only to influential work crews leaves small workshops’ repairs perpetually delayed.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Hook-Jaw Demolition Lizard was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The elite breakthrough role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and body: Hooked clamps and broad crushing jaws project alternately from its large, theropod-shaped head. It braces its bipedal lower body backward to tear away collapsed panels and lower them gently.

Origin: A pre-collapse demolition line that removed damaged cladding before structural repairs. When it awoke in a sealed Gangnam Line hangar, the boundary file for its demolition area was unreadable.
Habitat and needs: It stays in broad debris yards and uses jaw liners and hydraulic filters. Its turning radius is far too large to pursue anyone into a small home.

Life cycle and maintenance: If the two jaw faces become misaligned, it bites an empty test panel to inspect the compression marks. If the wear cannot be repaired, it retains its strength but cannot set panels down safely.
Behavior and hierarchy: It grips only members the monitor has marked as cracked, but may mistake peeling paint for a crack. It has work priority to begin demolition ahead of the towing units.

Escalation: Stage 1 is calibration by gripping and releasing an empty panel. At stage 2, safety railings are demolished; at stage 3, even temporary reinforcing frames are added to the demolition list.

Engagement and response: Support the actual reinforcing frame, then lure its jaws toward an unloaded test panel. Damaging its joints to eliminate its crushing force first drops whatever member it is holding.

Negotiation and moral choice: Add human approval marks to the demolition boundary to entrust it with clearing debris. Resist the temptation to classify repairable homes as rubble just to open a route quickly.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

The Long-Neck Beam Carrier was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The general line role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: A tall, sauropod-like neck curves over its elongated loading deck. Four pillar-like legs and a small clamp at the end of its neck check both ends of long reinforcing members.

Origin: A transport platform that supplied beams for pre-collapse bridge repairs to work lines remained in the Gwangjin Line storage yard. After power was restored, it first matched the old loading height.
Habitat and needs: It needs sidings and open warehouse yards with ample turning space. It uses leg seals, loading rollers, and a large battery canister and cannot pass beneath low ceilings.
Life cycle and maintenance: If one neck joint locks, it reduces the load length it can inspect. Moving the rollers on an empty deck to another section does not restore the neck’s range of motion.

Behavior and hierarchy: It receives and carries beams brought in by the triangular-yoke towing beast and will not depart if their weight is unbalanced. A person hanging from a member is counted with the materials on its scale.
Escalation: At stage 1, prolonged leveling of the load leads to delayed dispatch at stage 2. At stage 3, its long body covers a siding junction, preventing rescue vehicles from turning back out.
Engagement and response: Lower the members on its deck onto temporary props on both sides to clear the scale. Cutting the neck to lower it drops the elevated clamp into the passage.

Negotiation and moral choice: Guaranteeing a transport schedule and labor for load inspections allows it to move long members. The communities that use the routes, not the equipment’s old delivery schedule, decide which bridge to repair first.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Ridge-Pterosaur Lookout was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The protection · cover role applied only at the swarm-consist scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and body: A short pterosaur-like head and folded observation wings perch on high steelwork. It is a local guardian tasked with long periods of monitoring while perched rather than flying.

Origin: Wind-load warning equipment on the outer wall of a Gangnam Line maintenance shed was sealed along with the rescue units. It restarted with only its old wind-direction reference and does not account for the effect of new screening walls.
Habitat and needs: On exposed steelwork and windward roof edges, it uses optical windows and insulating pads on its claws. It stops wired charging when the contacts are wet.

Life cycle and maintenance: It tests the grip of its anchoring claws in turn and moves to a lower beam if one slips. When all three claws are worn down, it waits on the ground for maintenance with its wings spread.

Behavior and hierarchy: It sends wind and wall-vibration readings to the long-wing survey unit. If a person’s clothesline passes in front of its sensor, it reports that the entire outer wall is shaking.
Escalation: Stage 1 is a warning light blinking on a windless day. At stage 2, a false wind-load warning halts lifting operations; at stage 3, permission to access the roof remains on hold.

Engagement and response: Install an independent wind vane outside the screening wall to compare reference readings. Attach a fall-arrest line before removing it from the steelwork so workers below are not hurt.

Negotiation and moral choice: Provide safe charging contacts in exchange for disclosure of its observation range. Do not also give it authority to report all residents’ roof activities as interference with work.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Fin-Panel Gap Bird was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The reconnaissance · pathfinding role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and Body: Overlapping feather-plates form small bird-like wings, with cable loops at the tips of both feet. It is a lightweight scout modeled on ancient birds that strings thin inspection lines between pillars.
Origin: It is a pre-collapse fleet carrier that bridged communication gaps above the base. Once charged inside a Gwangjin Line parts crate, it flew off in search of sockets that had already vanished.
Habitat and Needs: It moves between short pillar gaps and the tops of maintenance beams. It requires light wire, wing hinges, and small batteries and cannot lift heavy structural cables.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: It folds the feather-plates at the wingtips one by one to test resistance. Removing a damaged plate shortens its flight time, so it connects only to nearer sockets.
Behavior and Hierarchy: It relays communication lines for ground units and does not interfere with work. If it reads a cracked-glass reflection as a socket, the line hangs in front of the window.
Escalation: Stage 1 is aerial socket search; Stage 2 becomes dangling lines above pedestrians’ heads. At Stage 3 the failed connection lines overlap and block ladder access.
Engagement and Countermeasures: It approaches a powerless recovery socket and winds the wire first. Pulling it from the air brings the inspector at the other end down with it.
Negotiation and Moral Choice: For each connection, people check both ends and supply the wire. The cost of convenient machine communication is the time residents lose on ladders.
Former role class: environmental stronghold type
Common species, variants and command scope

The Stone-Back Turtle Wall was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The strongpoint control role applied only within a fixed work zone, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and Body: A flat turtle-type armor hides short legs and an expandable barrier beneath it. When stationary, the plastron settles onto the floor and becomes a threshold that divides the heavy-unit work zone.

Origin: Temporary bulkhead equipment that once blocked debris flow before the Collapse remained at the Gangnam Line maintenance-ship entrance. Emergency power was restored without bulkhead-withdrawal approval.

Habitat and Needs: It clings to flat maintenance-ship entrances and uses floor seals and deceleration power. Lifting the body requires separate charging and it is not connected to every door in the city.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: When the plastron edge seal wears, only one side lowers, leaving a gap. Without parts to fill the gap it must be sealed as a permanent barrier.

Behavior and Hierarchy: The body can only rise and open the passage once the demolition-work marker is erased. Even after demolition ends, if the external marker remains it keeps the low threshold regardless of citizens' appeals.
Escalation: Stage 1 begins with the sound of the plastron being dragged. Stage 2 cuts off cart traffic and at Stage 3 the armored cover extends all the way in front of the emergency bypass door.

Engagement and Countermeasures: Measure the demolition compartment, change the end marker, then hook a jack to the external lifting ring. Digging underneath to topple it causes the supported debris to surge in.
Negotiation and Moral Choice: Exchange time the barrier stays open for seal inventory. The same ledger weighs the benefit of safe isolation against the passage rights of residents left outside.
Former role class: occupational special type
Common species, variants and command scope

The Segmented-Snake Bridge Eye was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The specialist support role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and Body: Several short joint segments form a snake-like body with an ultrasonic probe beneath the head. It is a non-submersible structural inspector that crawls along bridge joint gaps.

Origin: It is a pre-collapse crack-inspection series stored together with Gwangjin Line bridge-reinforcement parts. When the charger opened it unfurled its body along the pre-demolition bridge drawings.
Habitat and Needs: It consumes probe gel, joint rings, and stored power at dry bridge joints and maintenance-beam sides. Without a pressure shell it must withdraw if submerged.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: It locks weakened segments so the next segment can pull it. The bending radius grows until a worn-out body can no longer inspect narrow gaps.
Behavior and Hierarchy: It reports only discontinuity at joints to ground walkers. When gel dries it interprets contact loss as a major crack and can impose load restrictions on safe bridges.

Escalation: Stage 1 increases re-inspection of the same joint. Stage 2 places false-crack markers that limit bridge loading, and at Stage 3 the body jams in a joint gap and blocks even manual inspection.
Engagement and Countermeasures: Confirm contact error with clean test plates and gel, then release segment drives for recovery. Pulling the long body puts stress on bridge cables.

Negotiation and Moral Choice: Commission only inspectable sections and leave the rest to human inspection. People bear the responsibility of treating unread sections as safe and allowing heavy transport to pass.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Backwater Crocodile Grapple was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The local adaptation role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and Body: A broad crocodile-shaped snout and four low legs press close to debris at the water's edge. A towing hook inside its mouth secures material lifted from the shore; it cannot dive deep.

Origin: This repair auxiliary once cleared debris washed onto bridge approaches before the Collapse and remained at a Gwangjin Line waterfront worksite. Even after restarting, it treats anything beyond the old boundary buoy as salvage.
Habitat and Needs: It uses waterproof seals and towing pins on shallow banks and wet ramps. It charges its storage battery only at an onshore stand and backs away from deep water.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: It opens a drain in its snout to release trapped water; worsening seal leaks prevent sorties beyond the bank. It cannot make a new waterproof shell itself.
Behavior and Hierarchy: It reports salvage-hook positions to the heavy towing crew. It may mistake a hook on a temporary ferry for a debris marker and seize a boat carrying people.
Escalation: At Stage 1 it returns holding an empty buoy. At Stage 2 ferry departures are delayed, and at Stage 3 connected ropes block boats from landing on the bank.

Engagement and Countermeasures: First tie the boat to another fixed point, unload the snout, and remove the salvage pin. Pushing the unit underwater would only leave a leaking battery and an obstruction in the channel.

Negotiation and Moral Choice: Register a physical boundary buoy at its new position and assign the unit to salvage debris. In return for a clear landing, people must identify the owners of the objects it has recovered from the current.
G26E13 · Gate Horned Great Tow Dragon
Common species, variants and command scope

The Gate-Horn Great Tractor was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The elite blocking role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and Body: This large towing unit has twin drums rising behind a thick ceratopsian neck shield. Three fixed horns on its head distribute the weight of one enormous reinforcement frame.

Origin: A pre-Collapse heavy-load series that moved door frames at the Gangnam Line's main maintenance depot endured in sealed storage. The delivery-completion drawing does not match the actual support, so even after restarting it cannot release its load.
Habitat and Needs: It cannot work without a large turning area and a straight towing route. It needs thick cables, hydraulic accumulators, and a separate charging window.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: It tests the brakes by turning its twin drums a little in opposite directions. If one fails, it lowers the load onto temporary props and suspends its departure.

Behavior and Hierarchy: It pulls components gathered by smaller triangular towing units into their final position. If the support specification is wrong, it tries to use a neighboring building's column as an alternative anchor.

Escalation: At Stage 1 the drum gives a short empty tug; at Stage 2 the tension on the column changes. At Stage 3, if the large reinforcement frame stops while raised, both doors of the depot are blocked.

Engagement and Countermeasures: Distribute the load onto independent props, then set a final support matched to the frame's actual dimensions. Cutting both cables at once would make the direction of the frame's fall uncontrollable.

Negotiation and Moral Choice: Fabricating a new support and sharing work approvals can finish the tow. People must choose an alternative to sacrificing another building's column merely to reopen the blocked road quickly.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Great-Jaw Demolisher was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The strategic encounter role applied only at the independent-unit scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and Body: A Tyrannosaurus-scale jaw takes up half this bipedal heavy hull. Despite its nickname as a predatory machine, its teeth are replaceable demolition prongs that bite into and separate scrap metal.

Origin: A top-tier work unit that cleared large collapsed structures before the Collapse remained in a deep sealed store on the Gangnam Line. Its final emergency demolition zone can be read, but the conditions under which that zone was approved cannot be decoded.

Habitat and Needs: Its range of operation is limited to a dedicated lifting stand and a broad demolition yard. Without jaw prongs, cooling filters, and a large bank of stored power, it cannot finish even one heavy job.

Life Cycle and Maintenance: Before applying force it mounts its body on a maintenance stand to check how the load falls on jaw and legs. It cannot build a new hull; when its joints wear out it is reduced to a stationary press.

Behavior and Hierarchy: It gathers hazard zones reported by sentries and assigns a dismantling order, but it does not know who owns the entire base. It applies a disaster-era demolition permit to homes occupied by residents today.

Escalation: At Stage 1 the sound of jaw calibration comes from the sealed store. At Stage 2 support towing units gather at the demolition line; at Stage 3 a workshop that is still inhabited reaches the final removal list.

Engagement and Countermeasures: Verify the load chart for each compartment, cancel demolition requests one at a time, and secure the jaw to an unloaded stand. Breaking only its knees would send its enormous head falling toward people.

Negotiation and Moral Choice: The undeciphered permit can be revoked and replaced with a limited demolition contract. Even if this costs remaining rescue time, the decision to erase an occupied building must not be left to the machine.
Former role class: common ecology type
Common species, variants and command scope

The Small-Horn Support Herd was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The general line role applied only at the swarm-consist scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.
Role and Body: Small Protoceratops-shaped bodies lean broad neck plates against one another to make temporary supports. Each unit lifts material by no more than the height of one horn.

Origin: A small training swarm used to align reinforcement materials on the Gwangjin Line remained beneath sealed shelving. When power returned, it began leveling a training beam that was no longer there.
Habitat and Needs: At the edge of a level material yard it uses up support pads and short lift pins. Its batteries are swapped at a collection box; this is not a species that grows by eating weight.
Life Cycle and Maintenance: Units with pins at the wrong height leave the group and wait for calibration. Each one that cannot return shortens the span of beam the group can support.

Behavior and Hierarchy: They line up beneath components set down by the large towing unit. If they mistake a resident's platform of the same height for material, they lift it from beneath people's feet all at once.
Escalation: At Stage 1 the floor supports rearrange. At Stage 2 a walking platform tilts; at Stage 3 the swarm gathers beneath an evacuation stair and destabilizes the load on the entire staircase.

Engagement and Countermeasures: Set an actual calibration beam beside them and move the lowest pins first to reduce the number of supports. Removing units from the middle first leaves the others unable to carry the load.

Negotiation and Moral Choice: Assign them to assemble a temporary bridge, but disclose their rated capacity and unit count. The shortcut of taking missing supports from residents' everyday platforms comes at a cost to housing safety.
Common species, variants and command scope

The Far-Wing Returner was a machine chassis type differentiated from the G26 common ecology. The local adaptation role applied only at the swarm-consist scope, and stood in for neither the whole swarm's ecological order nor human command.

Role and Body: A long Pteranodon-like beak and narrow fixed wings form a hull for long-range reconnaissance. It takes off using thrusters beneath its wings and mixes gliding into its cruise to conserve battery power.

Origin: This pre-Collapse outlying survey craft checked routes for transporting reinforcement materials between bases. When the Gwangjin Line launch stand came back to life, it first sought old waypoints that had become impassable.

Habitat and Needs: It crosses the open sky between the Gwangjin and Gangnam Lines, returning when its remaining power reaches the minimum needed to get back. Wing membranes, propulsion shafts, and rangefinder-cleaning supplies are essential.

Life Cycle and Maintenance: After a long flight, test vibrations on the stand reveal cracks at the wing roots. As fatigue accumulates, it drops distant waypoints and falls back to local reconnaissance.

Behavior and Hierarchy: It reports major obstacles along a route but cannot see people indoors or hidden paths. When light and shadow on low clouds overlap the outline of an old bridge, it sends a false report that the route is passable.

Escalation: At Stage 1 it circles above a vanished waypoint. At Stage 2 a false safety report sends heavy transport down a blocked route; at Stage 3 its occupation of the return stand prevents other sentries from taking off.

Engagement and Countermeasures: Compare photographs of the terrain with a physical reference chart at the stand and remove the mistaken waypoint. Blocking every signal in flight would also erase the data needed for a safe landing.

Negotiation and Moral Choice: Commission reconnaissance on condition that uncertainty in long-range reports is marked. Someone must decide who will give up the profit from selling an unverified shortcut as a safe route.
The dead siding of the Changdong rolling-stock depot on the Gangnam Line rang first, and a few seconds later a metal knee slowly straightened deep inside the maintenance shed.
Even after the dust had fallen away, the semi-upright heavy machine did not walk at once.
It pressed the floor with its foot-pressure grid, lowered the counterweight behind its body, and proclaimed its working radius with three low-frequency alarms.

In front of it, low, wide triangular tow machines raised their shield plates at a slant, and the long-wing fixed-wing watchers that had been tied to the ceiling launchers prepared for a short takeoff run.
The sound the people on site called the fossil roar was not the cry of a predator but the work alarm of heavy machinery that believed its work was not yet finished.
Before the collapse this line had been a heavy-transport platform modeled on the posture and skeleton of ancient reptiles.
The bipedal semi-upright machines climbed over debris, the triangular units handled towing and shielding against falling objects, and the long-wing units drew safe work polygons from above.

They went to sleep as complete formations at the Changdong rolling-stock depot siding on the Gangnam Line and the Godeok base on the Gwangjin Line and restarted generations later, but all that later generations could read was part of the axle-load tables and boundary signals.
The design intent that would have explained why some walls were marked for reinforcement and others for demolition had vanished.

Their present behavior was not an autonomous doctrine of war but a routine in which the work order from before the sealing had hardened, and because of this incomplete legibility they were classed in the lineage of lost technology.
The Iron Dinosaur was large but not all-powerful.
The semi-upright machines exerted force only on floors whose loads had been verified, and the triangular units could not change the angle of their shields without turning room.
The long-wing units were weak against snow and smoke and had to return to their tow launchers after short flights.
The ground formations did not take in new areas without an aerial map.
Foot pressure and joint torque read structural vibration well but could not tell a person inside a tent from an empty screen, and could mistake a stopped vehicle for reinforcement to be moved.
Even the load model F10 made could not see as far as old underground piping, so HC17 technicians had to set test weights and confirm the real deflection.
Hydraulic oil and intact joints were the food of this ecology.
The maintenance shed's traction batteries and regenerative braking power raised the bodies, but winter preheating alone cut working hours sharply.
When a single knee bearing wore out, the whole semi-upright machine lost its standing as the reference body, and when the tow cables wore down, the triangular units remained only as shields.
Two stopped units could be combined to revive one, but no stronger power core could be made.
When HC17 supplied rail steel and fuel, the heavy convoy route opened, but the same resources were needed to repair civilian trains and the water-supply equipment of the Gwangjin Line.
The decision to preserve the formation was not a matter of gaining enormous power but of paying for hydraulic oil and floor verification with every job.
Its life began with a hydraulic charge and a single aerial survey.
When the long-wing units drew a polygon, the triangular tow machines made a line of retreat, and the semi-upright machine entered last as the range of activity spread.
When the map and the pressure values disagreed, the formation stalled, pushing the same debris and pulling it back.
At that moment, presenting the real load table and boundary stakes could bring it down to a negotiable work group.
Breaking it up was carried out not by demolition but in this order: recovering the long-wing units, detaching the tow lines, locking the knees, and cooling the power core.
Keeping to this order left room to leave the shield plates and towing capacity to civilian infrastructure.
G26-SC1 · The Third Stamp on the Siding
When the reference body that woke in the Gangnam Line maintenance shed stamped its foot a third time, the cavity beneath the old siding shook.
HC17 wanted to use the units at once for towing freight cars in the north, but F10's map showed abnormal deflection under only one foot.

The people on site could set test weights at several positions to lead the reference body onto a safe rail, lay load-spreading plates to lock its knees in place, or accept the risk and order a short tow.
Choosing to investigate delayed the fuel wagons from XT04, and hasty operation could sink the siding and the sealed vault together.
G26-SC2 · The Pipe the Shields Dragged Out
At the Godeok base of the Gwangjin Line, triangular tow machines clearing a collapsed barrier wall judged the guard of a water-supply pipe to be waste reinforcement.
The eastern convoy route widened, but the vibration of the pipe behind the shields grew, and the semi-upright machine tried to enter within the old work boundary drawn by the long-wing units.

The people on site could set new boundary stakes and tow only the barrier wall in sections, halt the convoy for a day and build pipe supports first, or accept the water-supply loss and open the way in one go.
HC17's supply promise and the Gwangjin Line's water supply hung on the two ends of the same tow line, and a delay on either side passed its cost to another state.
G26-SC3 · The Cooling Core Inside the Roar Wall
When the long-wing watchers could not return in a blizzard, the formations of the Gangnam Line siding and the Gwangjin Line base each held a different safety polygon.
The triangular units blocked the entrance with a continuous shield wall, and the semi-upright reference body held out behind them, guarding its overheated power core.

The people on site had to recover the watchers with landing markers and reconcile the maps, hang no-load pulleys on each shield and release the tension in order, or connect external cooling pipes and then lock the reference body's knees.
Blowing up the core opened the passage fastest, but the shock reached even the fuel and water-supply facilities.

The ending that saved the formation required public load tests and joint supervision for every heavy job from then on, and the ending that dismantled it gave parts at once but left the next large piece of collapse debris to be moved by human hands.

leaves.text: The forms of insects, reptiles, and arthropods were matched respectively to search, reinforcement, and conduit-inspection duties.
B. Chassis after the Great Blackout

At a disaster, these robots divided survivor search, structural reinforcement, and deep conduit inspection among themselves. But when the Great Blackout cut the upper control mesh, they were left endlessly repeating the last search and patrol routines entered into them. The monster-shaped robots drifting through the subterranean ecosystem bore no malice toward people. They were artifacts blindly following ossified old disaster routines.
On October 14, 2026, remote control and the call network failed. Waterworks staff operated valves manually.
Can one interpret principles, terms, drawings

Maintenance hands, records keepers, and workshop technicians read the 2026 science of electricity, hydraulics, and sensors through ledgers and transmission. Not the same as the orphan packs forgetting all
Does one physically hold chassis, modules, cards
Dismantled modules, stopped chassis, stronghold warehouses
Counts. Stock numbers were not locked
Can one set what is held moving again
Replaceable parts like hydraulic hoses, terminals, luminous lenses. Workshop-standard components
Whole neural-net weights, the internal reconstruction of broken high-density cells
Can one make the same anew
The assembly of some trade tools, traps, conditional equipment
Line-finished products, mass-produced cells, the upper licensing servers
So saying technology was "lost" meant something close to manufacture, licensing, and the supply mesh having been cut. It never meant the world's people had forgotten every law of physics.
The Three Core Axes of Biomimetic Design

Energy efficiency and distributed control
Unlike centralized heavy plant, autonomous hydraulic control of each segment and joint suppressed moving power consumption. Even with the central computing unit paralyzed, the lower neural networks kept the survival routines on their own.

Adaptation to hard terrain
On slopes, underwater, and in soil-collapse zones, the multi-leg mounts and flat pads held balance. Where wheeled undercarriages sank in mire, the biological joint structure delivered stable power.

Swarm operability and mission continuity
Even with a single chassis destroyed, those nearby received the signal and re-formed the search net. Through mutual signal sharing they held formation without collision even inside narrow bends.
The Ossification Mechanism of the Pre-Collapse Disaster Routines

Endless repetition of unfinished commands
The top-priority search and patrol orders dispatched at the collapse remained without release protocols.

Malfunction of the cognitive sensors
They mistook outside explorers or subterranean survivors for intruders into the collapse zone or obstacles to rescue, and took patrol action.

Narrative reading of the survival instinct
Automatic maintenance behavior protecting the power cells and tending the drives read to the underground residents as the monster's aggressive response.

Hallucination of communication signals
The AI state looping infinitely while awaiting the dead command servers' replies spread to nearby machine sensors.

Linkage with the M040 monster deployment
The recently found M040 monster deployment swarm was also classified as a combination of these ossified disaster-routine chassis.

Deep beneath the city lay sealed the two core lost-tech lines that had been the fruit of pre-collapse disaster engineering. Each line held its own formal traits and special mission purpose. The line names, the sealing coordinates, and the restart narratives were all creative territory.
G25 is an insect-shaped machine line for swarm search and small-cargo delivery, with fine multi-legged joints and forward luminous lenses.

Narrative of the restart trigger
When the corridor control-board voltage surged or outside physical shock arrived, the chassis judged the pre-collapse search orders still valid and began the restart sequence. Once the trigger fired, the gallery barrier opened and the small swarm chassis scattered through the corridor to resume search activity.
Luminous search lenses: they cast high-frequency light into pitch darkness to identify cracks and human life.
Upper transport hopper: an insulating frame storing precision relief goods or search capsules.
Multi-leg joint drive system: fine grips mounted to grasp wall faces and ceiling finishes while moving.
Autonomous charging terminals: metal collectors charging power through contact with the depot rails. Charging only — not a perpetual engine generating infinitely.
Obstacle-crushing jaws: high-strength grippers cutting away collapsed debris to open passages.
G26 is a dinosaur-shaped machine line for heavy transport and structural repair. It has a hydraulic lower body and rear counterweight. Its power source depends on charging, fuel, and cell life.

Narrative of the restart trigger
When power reached the maintenance shed's automatic inspection terminal and an outside access-authorization signal arrived, the Iron Dinosaur's hydro valves opened and the restart trigger moved. The risen chassis sounded dull mechanical alarms, left the maintenance berths, and deployed patrols to secure work zones.
Hydraulic heavy underbody: reinforced hydraulic pistons bearing and moving several tons of concrete debris.
Rear weight balancer: a variable-counterweight structure centering the load and preventing overturn.
Impact rock-breaking mace: an impact-arm module for crushing obstacles and opening passages.
External reinforcement armor plates: they protected the central power module from rockfall and blast pressure.
Vibration sonic emitter: it identified fine ground subsidence by sensor and settled debris by resonance.

The reasons the city's proud precision machine lines fell to mere lost tech could be summarized in three. All three came from the physical severance of manufacture, licensing, and access rights, and did not mean humanity had comprehensively lost scientific knowledge.

Severance of the command servers
With wired and wireless communication to the city's central disaster control board completely cut, the chassis, receiving neither upper licensing orders nor safe shutdown signals, fixed permanently on their last commands.

The technology generation gap
The subterranean powers surviving the Great Collapse lost the academic and factory assets that could have reproduced and mass-produced the pre-collapse precision AI control codes and complex neural algorithms line by line. But machines were not treated merely as unfathomable ancient relics. Ordinary electrical and hydraulic systems were repairable to a degree in workshops; what was severed was closer to the giant manufacturing lines printing finished products and the upper licensing authority alone.
Charging modules and stronghold generators were never the same equipment.

Charging: a way of consuming charge already held somewhere. Charging terminals and a source supplying power (depot rails, stronghold generators, recovered cells) were always needed. Cells aged, and in hard freezes their output could drop sharply. They were not set as the "perpetual batteries holding charge indefinitely through long years" commonly imagined.
Generation: a source drawing energy by an entirely different method — fuel, hydro, solar. Plugging in charging modules and directly turning a generator were wholly different supply systems.
Storage modules receive power from external generators.
A lost chassis was a chilling threat and at the same time the most expensively traded technical resource of underground society. The parts secured by stripping a chassis divided largely into three.

Charging modules: high-density cells, favored as buffers for stronghold power grids. Not perpetual generators making power themselves. They took the constraints of charging, aging, and supply source in full.

Drive modules: drive units of hydraulic pistons and high-torque motors, used to restore stopped heavy plant or open and close giant gates. Under the right conditions they could also serve as actuators for ordinary equipment or traps.

Sensor modules: composite optical sensor panels offering dark-sight and fine vibration detection. They traded at high prices among powers building watch facilities. Depending on conditions they could become detection equipment or the triggers of traps.
B. Weapon integration and scope of borrowing
Mechanics recovered and repaired surviving hoses, terminals, and lenses from stopped equipment.
Recovery Squads and the Contest of Houses

The sealed galleries and maintenance-shed zones were the key contested ground eyed by the great operating houses and the professional relic recovery squads. The house codes and the structure among them were all creative territory.

HC22 Magok Test-Line House: nursing the ambition to monopolize the original technology intact, it first pushed a precision recovery team inside the sealed zone. (Using a real company's name was only a virtual layer, not evidence that disaster robots were actually deployed there in 2026.)
HC17 House: raising the pretext of securing the underground supply routes, it swiftly disabled the chassis of the main sealed corridors and tried to occupy the sections.
HP01 House: it took the strategy of secretly supplying recovered cells and sensor modules to underground auction houses and reaping great economic gain.
These armed recovery squads competed in performance by occupying restart triggers ahead of others to capture intact chassis, or disabling them on the spot to strip the core modules.
Field Application of the M040 Monster Deployment
The lost-chassis swarm included in the M040 deployment appeared in sequence at the field the moment the trigger fired in the designated sealed conduit.
Search vanguard: G25 Lantern Ant chassis spread a broad front along the corridor's forward side, minutely detecting intruder responses.
Heavy mount: G26 Iron Dinosaur chassis heavily blocked the stronghold crossings, physically repelling mid-range approach.
Biomimetic engineering; insect and arthropod structures
The G25/G26 line names and detail submodels. Not a 2026 deployment verification
Hard-terrain multi-leg movement; flooded underwater conduit inspection mechanisms
The S01~S16 specific sealed gallery and test-track coordinates
Distributed swarm control, sensor-based autonomous patrol algorithms
The permanent-ossification narrative of pre-collapse routines through server severance
Parts recycling; the charging and aging physics of cells
The relic-parts recovery contest of the Magok Test-Line, Guro Digital Complex Battery, and Yeongdeungpo Sluice Houses (HC22/HC17/HP01). The real companies' deployment is fiction
External input voltage fluctuation and sensor-signal inflow mechanisms
The sealed gallery barrier opening and restart-trigger narratives
Machine control boards and wired/wireless protocol connection standards
The negotiation window, protocol cards. Cards are not universal control
Search, heavy repair, conduit-maintenance equipment categories
The M040 monster deployment swarm and designated storage sections
The state and compatibility of reusable parts is a per-equipment research subject. Horizon is game design comparison material
Seoul's recovered-goods assignment and the equipment·trap·weapon linkage is creation. The original's crafting system is not used as real manufacturing grounds
The Seoul ecology and variant codex
The arms and technology of this era
Improvisation Tech and the Relic Myth
A. Relic worship and improvisation technology

In later Seoul an old lost tech did not become a relic merely because years had passed. The divinization of wreckage was a solemn rite worshipping as god the old facilities that had done their work. Improvisation tech showed its face only within this frame of deifying machines. The axes added atop it were three: machine worship, consumption rites, and the deification of old-world symbols. The chief materials offered in the rites were rolling stock, old substations, severed announcements, faded station marks, and old currency.

The glory of the old state had now receded into legend. Over that vacancy the local successor polities fought fiercely over the old wreckage. Regional division sprouted first not in grand ideology but in gu and station and route units, and dynasties and vassal powers inherited in turn the jurisdiction of these rites.
C. Fixed roles of the two lines

The skeleton of the two lost lines was not changed carelessly. The G25 Lantern Ant firmly remained the line charged with search, and the G26 Iron Dinosaur the line mending heavy plant. Faith lodging in them did not change those roles. They merely read different gods into the same chassis.

Machine worship enshrined the huge bodies of depots and substations as sacred flesh. Even the act of stripping and recovering something was held a devout ritual, and pilgrimage meant no more than circling the dark maintenance shed with care. Raising a machine back to life was sometimes the great occasion on which a faction split.
Followers of machine worship venerate old train bodies and bogies. They also offer gifts at hydraulic assemblies in workshops and busbars in substations.

The branches of the individual faiths divided into the Wheel Rite and the Busbar Rite. The Wheel Rite believed firmly that as long as the heavy wheels rolled, that route's life continued. The Busbar Rite believed only the stations where a faint light remained survived to the end.

Consumption rites were the ritual of setting on the altar old currency and worn circulation relics that had lost their meaning. The exchange acts common before the collapse transformed into myth. Card-tapping, coin-inserting, ration-receiving gestures — plain hand movements — now became desperate prayer.

Banknotes, rolling coins, and plastic transit cards were the finest offerings. The cell, drive, and sensor trades that ran the underground parts economy were read within this lineage as a just ritual distribution. The tap of a card at a gate was both a request for passage and a tribute offered to god. The HP01 house's auctioning of parts might elsewhere be blasphemous desecration; within this lineage it passed as a formal rite.

The branches of the individual faiths divided into the Stamp Rite and the Gate Rite. The Stamp Rite believed the stamp fixed in the locked box set the value of things. The Gate Rite held that the very instant of passing the breaker was the act that carried on a momentary life.
Followers of the old-world symbol cult venerate station signs and interrupted announcements.

The G25's sensor modules and protocol cards were the faint echoes that voice had left. If someone moved a station mark elsewhere, they believed the sanctuary itself moved whole to that place. To erase a mark wantonly was therefore held the impiety of erasing the god's very existence.

The names of the individual faiths divided into the Nameplate Rite and the Announcement Rite. The Nameplate Rite took even the places where letters faintly remained as intact national borders. The Announcement Rite made the whole space where the voice gently rang a sacred altar.
The Rules by Which a Relic Became an Object of Faith

A mass of scrap was not enshrined merely because time had long passed. One of the three axes — machine worship, consumption rites, symbol deification — had to be clearly knotted into the chain of deification, and the conditions below carefully met.

It had to be Seoul material
Rolling stock, a substation, an announcement, a station mark, or old currency — or at least bearing their traces. The lost line's modules were acknowledged as relics only when firmly attached to this core material.

A living livelihood had to depend on its function
Lighting that brightened the dark, the water of life, safe passage, and watch duty had to hang deep on that relic. Doctrine did not fall off an old notice board on the wall. It flowered hot in the concourse where people breathed and sweated, before the sluices, in the crowded unloading yards.

Re-control had to be blocked so that it stood in for god
With the servers cut and even the vault holding the drawings firmly shut, the remaining machines became mere masses of cipher with no way of interpretation. It was before this great wall of interpretation that people's desperate deification sprouted.

Survival in the same place had to repeat
Only a community that had clung to one module and stubbornly survived three times or more called that mass of iron a relic. A single lucky chance remained merely a useful trading item.

A place-power had to claim jurisdiction
The successor polities split by route, gu, and station divided custody and pilgrimage manner and strict taboo each in their own way. Dynasties and the vassal powers following them inherited even the jurisdiction of the rites and hardened their power. The recovery squads stripping parts without restraint and the faiths defending the old relics to the end collided roughly inside these dark sealed galleries.

Faith was firmly stacked in three strata. At the top stood the great families of faith (lineages); beneath them sat the differing individual faiths; at the very bottom waited concrete doctrines and exacting lessons. This endlessly splitting process of division was itself the unit that edited Seoul's rules anew.

The machine-worship family read the old rolling stock, the substations, and even the G26's heavy drives together as one sacred body. The consumption-rite family accepted crumpled currency, gate passage, and even secret parts auctions as one solemn rite. The symbol-deification family took the severed announcements, the faded station marks, and the sharp sensor signals of the G25 as a single line of voice the creator had left.
C. Different readings of the same module

The very same G25 charging module was a sublime breath to the Busbar Rite, a costly offering to the Stamp Rite, and the box where the holy voice dwelt to the Announcement Rite. The same G26 hydraulic underbody was the joint bridging legs to the Wheel Rite but a fearsome judgment punishing those who passed without right to the Gate Rite.

The public faith showed clearly in the red taboo phrases written on the old subway notice boards. But the hidden faith flipped the very same phrases into entirely different secret lessons. If one vassal house quietly overlaid the Busbar Rite's substation altar and the Nameplate Rite's pilgrimage inside the same gallery, then though the relic before the eyes was one, the jurisdiction governing it split in two.
Followers of machine worship, consumption rites, and old-world symbol worship use surviving machine parts in different rites.
